# Interim statement on COVID-19 vaccine booster doses

*World Health Organization, 2021-08-10. Original: <https://www.who.int/news/item/10-08-2021-interim-statement-on-covid-19-vaccine-booster-doses>*

The World Health Organization's immunization advisory group said on 10 August 2021 that countries should focus on giving first vaccine courses widely, and that any booster doses should be based on evidence and aimed at those most in need. It said evidence on a broad need for boosters remained limited and inconclusive.

According to the statement, giving boosters while many populations had not received a first course would worsen inequities between countries.

# Huawei CFO Wanzhou Meng Admits to Misleading Global Financial Institution

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2021-09-24. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/huawei-cfo-wanzhou-meng-admits-misleading-global-financial-institution>*

Huawei's chief financial officer entered into a deferred prosecution agreement on bank and wire fraud charges, the Justice Department announced on 24 September 2021. Under the deal she admitted making false statements to a global bank in 2013 about Huawei's control of Skycom, a Hong Kong company operating in Iran.

According to the department, the charges will be pursued if she breaches the agreement, including by committing another crime. The United States withdrew its request for her extradition from Canada.

# UK government hands secret services cloud contract to AWS

*The Register, 2021-10-26. Original: <https://www.theregister.com/2021/10/26/uk_security_services_aws>*

The UK's intelligence agencies GCHQ, MI5 and MI6, and the Ministry of Defence, have signed a contract with Amazon Web Services to store classified data in UK-based data centres, The Register reports, citing the Financial Times. The deal was reportedly signed earlier in 2021.

According to The Register, sources said AWS will not have access to the data. Neither AWS nor the agencies commented.

# UK spy agencies to use AWS for top-secret material

*DatacenterDynamics, 2021-10-26. Original: <https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/uk-spy-agencies-to-use-amazon-web-services-to-host-top-secret-material-in-the-cloud>*

Britain's GCHQ, MI5 and MI6, along with the Ministry of Defence, will use Amazon Web Services to host top secret material, DatacenterDynamics reports, citing the Financial Times. The contract is estimated at £500 million to £1 billion over the next decade, with data held in Amazon data centres in the UK.

According to the report, the agencies say Amazon will have no access to the data. Privacy International criticised the deal as agreed in secret, and the report notes questions over whether the U.S. CLOUD Act could apply.

# Jury Convicts Chinese Intelligence Officer of Espionage Crimes, Attempting to Steal Trade Secrets

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2021-11-05. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/jury-convicts-chinese-intelligence-officer-espionage-crimes-attempting-steal-trade-secrets>*

A federal jury convicted a Chinese Ministry of State Security officer of conspiring and attempting to commit economic espionage and steal trade secrets, the Justice Department announced on 5 November 2021. The department says he was the first Chinese intelligence officer extradited to the United States for trial.

According to prosecutors, from 2013 he used aliases to target aviation companies, including trying to obtain GE Aviation's composite engine fan technology from an employee. He was arrested in Belgium in April 2018. Sentencing was to follow.

# AWS Announces Second Top Secret Cloud Region

*Nextgov/FCW, 2021-12-06. Original: <https://www.nextgov.com/emerging-tech/2021/12/amazon-web-services-announces-second-top-secret-cloud-region/187303>*

Amazon Web Services announced on 6 December 2021 a second cloud region for top secret U.S. government workloads, called AWS Top Secret-West, Nextgov reports. It serves defense, intelligence and national security agencies, and is meant to add geographic availability and resilience.

According to Nextgov, the first such region, in northern Virginia, has run since 2014, and both are cut off from the internet. AWS did not disclose where the new region is, beyond saying it is more than 1,000 miles from the first.

# Denver City Council approves ShotSpotter extension ($4.7M, 5yr)

*Denver7, 2022-01-01. Original: <https://www.denver7.com/news/local-news/denver-city-council-approves-long-contract-extension-with-gunshot-detection-company-shotspotter>*

Denver City Council voted 10-1 to extend its contract with gunshot detection company ShotSpotter for five years at $4.7 million, Denver7 reports. The service, used in Denver since 2015, uses audio sensors to locate gunfire.

According to Denver7, a police division chief said 85% of the company's alerts from 2018 to 2021 did not match a 911 call. Critics told the council the system is overpriced and unreliable and that the money would be better spent on mental health and crime prevention.

# Belarusian government officials charged with aircraft piracy for diverting Ryanair flight 4978

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2022-01-01. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/belarusian-government-officials-charged-aircraft-piracy-diverting-ryanair-flight-4978-arrest>*

Four Belarusian officials have been charged with conspiracy to commit aircraft piracy over the 23 May 2021 diversion of Ryanair Flight 4978 to Minsk, the Justice Department announced on 20 January 2022. They include the head and deputy head of Belarus's air navigation authority and two security service officers.

The indictment alleges they made up a bomb threat to force the Athens-to-Vilnius flight, which carried four U.S. nationals, to land so a dissident journalist on board could be arrested. All four remain at large. These are charges only: every defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# Individual pleads guilty to acting within the United States on behalf of Russian government

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2022-02-01. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/individual-pleads-guilty-acting-within-united-states-behalf-russian-government>*

A Mexican national living in Singapore pleaded guilty to acting in the United States on behalf of the Russian government without notifying the Attorney General, the Justice Department announced on 16 February 2022. According to the department, in February 2020 he followed directions from a person he believed was a Russian official, renting a home in Miami-Dade County, Florida, and arranging for a photo of a U.S. person's car and where it was parked.

Sentencing was set for 17 May 2022 in Miami. He faces up to 10 years in prison.

# COVID-19 pandemic triggers 25% increase in prevalence of anxiety and depression worldwide

*World Health Organization, 2022-03-02. Original: <https://www.who.int/news/item/02-03-2022-covid-19-pandemic-triggers-25-increase-in-prevalence-of-anxiety-and-depression-worldwide>*

Global prevalence of anxiety and depression rose by 25% in the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic, the World Health Organization said in a scientific brief released on 2 March 2022. The WHO says young people and women were hit hardest, along with people with existing physical health conditions.

According to the WHO, mental health services were severely disrupted and many people still could not get care by the end of 2021. It says 90% of surveyed countries had added mental health support to their COVID-19 response plans, while governments spent on average just over 2% of health budgets on mental health in 2020.

# Amazon, Microsoft and Google suspend cloud sales in Russia

*TechCrunch, 2022-03-10. Original: <https://techcrunch.com/2022/03/10/amazon-microsoft-and-google-have-suspended-cloud-sales-in-russia>*

Amazon Web Services, Microsoft and Google have stopped taking on new cloud customers in Russia, TechCrunch reports. AWS said on 8 March 2022 that it had stopped new sign-ups in Russia and Belarus, Microsoft said it was suspending all new sales in Russia, and Google Cloud said it was not accepting new Russian customers.

According to TechCrunch, IBM said it had suspended all business in Russia, while Cloudflare kept its services running there. IDC told the publication the global effect would be limited because Russia and Ukraine make up about 1% of worldwide ICT spending.

# Five individuals charged variously with stalking, harassing and spying on U.S. residents on behalf of the PRC

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2022-03-01. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/five-individuals-charged-variously-stalking-harassing-and-spying-us-residents-behalf-prc-0>*

Five people have been charged in cases over alleged efforts to stalk, harass and spy on U.S. residents on behalf of China, the Justice Department announced on 16 March 2022. The department says the targets included Chinese dissidents and pro-democracy activists, and one scheme sought to undermine a congressional candidate.

Charges vary by defendant and include acting or conspiring to act as an agent of China, interstate harassment, misusing identification and conspiring to bribe a federal official. Three defendants in New York were arrested on 15 and 16 March 2022 and two in China remain at large. These are charges only: every defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# Chinese National Charged With Acting As An Unregistered Agent Of The Chinese Government In The United States

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2022-03-30. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/usao-sdny/pr/chinese-national-charged-acting-unregistered-agent-chinese-government-united-states>*

A Chinese citizen has been charged in Manhattan federal court with acting as an unregistered agent of the Chinese government in the United States, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York announced on 30 March 2022. The complaint alleges that from February 2017 to February 2022 he took part in "Operation Fox Hunt", hiring private investigators to surveil people China sought to return and threatening them to go back or settle.

Prosecutors also allege he worked with a U.S. law enforcement officer as a co-conspirator. The office says he is at large in China. These are charges only: every defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# Man charged in transnational repression campaign while acting as illegal agent of the Chinese government

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2022-03-01. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/man-charged-transnational-repression-campaign-while-acting-illegal-agent-chinese-government>*

A Chinese national has been charged with acting as an illegal agent of the Chinese government in a campaign targeting people in the United States, the Justice Department announced on 30 March 2022. The complaint, unsealed in the Southern District of New York, alleges he hired private investigators to gather information on people China called fugitives, giving them 35 names including a U.S. citizen.

Prosecutors allege he threatened one target at a December 2019 meeting in New York City and worked with a U.S. law enforcement officer. He faces up to 10 years on one count and five on the other. These are charges only: every defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# Russia bans foreign software for critical infrastructure (Decree 166)

*DatacenterDynamics, 2022-04-01. Original: <https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/russia-bans-purchase-of-foreign-software-for-critical-infrastructure>*

Russia's president signed a decree, effective 31 March 2022, barring Russian entities from buying foreign software for use on significant critical information infrastructure without approval from an authorised federal body, DatacenterDynamics reports. The ban also covers services needed to use such software.

According to the publication, critical infrastructure includes systems in healthcare, manufacturing, communications, transport, energy, finance and telecommunications. The decree followed international sanctions over Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

# DTA renews gov-wide AWS deal for $174 million

*iTnews, 2022-05-01. Original: <https://www.itnews.com.au/news/dta-renews-gov-wide-aws-deal-for-174-million-578790>*

Australia's Digital Transformation Agency has renewed its whole-of-government agreement with Amazon Web Services for $174.1 million over three years, to May 2025, iTnews reports. It replaces a 2019 agreement first valued at $39 million that grew to $390.8 million.

According to iTnews, the deal applies to federal agencies and can be used by states, territories, universities and government-owned corporations case by case. It covers more than 200 AWS services and adds purchasing through AWS partners.

# NSA re-awards $10B WildandStormy cloud contract to AWS

*FedScoop, 2022-04-27. Original: <https://fedscoop.com/nsa-re-awards-10b-wildandstormy-cloud-computing-contract-to-aws>*

The National Security Agency has again awarded its WildandStormy cloud computing contract, worth up to $10 billion, to Amazon Web Services, FedScoop reports. The contract supports the agency's Hybrid Compute Initiative, which looks at keeping sensitive national security data in commercial cloud infrastructure.

Microsoft had protested the first award to AWS, and in December 2021 the Government Accountability Office upheld the protest, finding the NSA had improperly assessed technical proposals. The NSA says it re-evaluated the proposals and made a new best-value decision consistent with that ruling.

# U.S. Citizen and Four Chinese Intelligence Officers Charged with Spying on Prominent Dissidents, Human Rights Leaders and Pro-Democracy Activists

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2022-05-18. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/us-citizen-and-four-chinese-intelligence-officers-charged-spying-prominent-dissidents-human>*

A U.S. citizen living in Queens and four officers of China's Ministry of State Security have been charged over an alleged scheme to spy on pro-democracy activists and dissidents, the Justice Department announced on 18 May 2022. The indictment alleges that since at least 2011 the Queens resident gathered information on Hong Kong, Taiwanese, Uyghur and Tibetan activists and passed it to his handlers.

The department says the U.S. citizen was arrested on 16 March 2022 and the four officers remain at large. These are charges only: every defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# Five men indicted in transnational repression scheme to silence critics of the PRC

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2022-07-01. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/five-men-indicted-crimes-related-transnational-repression-scheme-silence-critics-people-s>*

Five men have been charged in a superseding indictment over an alleged scheme to stalk, harass and surveil critics of the Chinese government living in the United States, the Justice Department announced on 7 July 2022. The defendants include a Department of Homeland Security deportation officer and a retired DHS agent working as a private investigator, who are accused of obstruction of justice, including allegedly misusing federal law enforcement databases.

Other charges include conspiring to act as agents of China, interstate harassment and conspiring to bribe a federal official to obtain tax returns. The department says four defendants were arrested and one remains at large in China. These are charges only: every defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# Greek DPA imposes 20M euro fine on Clearview AI

*IAPP, 2022-07-13. Original: <https://iapp.org/news/a/greek-dpa-imposes-20m-euro-fine-on-clearview-ai-for-unlawful-processing-of-personal-data>*

Greece's data protection authority has fined Clearview AI €20 million, its largest fine to date, IAPP reports. The case began with a complaint from the nonprofit Homo Digitalis after the company did not answer a person's request to access her data.

According to IAPP, the authority found Clearview processed biometric data without a legal basis, failed to inform people or name an EU representative, and breached the right of access. It ordered the company to delete data on people in Greece and stop processing it.

# Google Cloud joins AWS, Azure in gov data sovereignty scheme

*iTnews, 2022-07-15. Original: <https://www.itnews.com.au/news/google-cloud-joins-aws-azure-in-gov-data-sovereignty-scheme-582705>*

Google Cloud has been certified at the highest "strategic" level of Australia's Hosting Certification Framework, joining Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure and six other providers, iTnews reports. The framework requires certified providers to let the government set ownership and control conditions.

According to iTnews, federal agencies must use certified providers for sensitive government data and whole-of-government systems in new contracts and extensions. Around 28 providers were still awaiting certification, and one unnamed agency received an exemption for at least a year.

# Denmark bans Chromebooks and Google Workspace in schools over data transfer risks

*TechCrunch, 2022-07-18. Original: <https://techcrunch.com/2022/07/18/denmark-bans-chromebooks-and-google-workspace-in-schools-over-gdpr>*

Denmark's data protection agency, Datatilsynet, has barred schools in Helsingør municipality from using Google Chromebooks and Google Workspace, TechCrunch reports. The regulator found that Google's data processing terms allow student data to be transferred outside the EU for support purposes without adequate protection under the GDPR.

The ban took effect immediately and the municipality was told to delete user data by 3 August 2022. TechCrunch reports the agency expects other Danish municipalities to take similar steps.

# Russian National Charged with Conspiring to Have U.S. Citizens Act as Illegal Agents of the Russian Government

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2022-07-29. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/russian-national-charged-conspiring-have-us-citizens-act-illegal-agents-russian-government>*

The Justice Department announced on 29 July 2022 that a Moscow resident who founded the Anti-Globalization Movement of Russia has been charged with conspiring to have U.S. citizens act as illegal agents of the Russian government. The indictment alleges that from December 2014 to March 2022, working with Russia's FSB, he recruited and directed three U.S. political groups in Florida, Georgia and California, funding protests, travel and local election campaigns.

The charge carries a maximum of five years in prison, the department says. These are charges only: every defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# Inside Fog Data Science, the secretive company selling mass surveillance to local police

*Electronic Frontier Foundation, 2022-08-01. Original: <https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2022/08/inside-fog-data-science-secretive-company-selling-mass-surveillance-local-police>*

The Electronic Frontier Foundation published an investigation in August 2022 into Fog Data Science, a data broker that sells local police a tool called Fog Reveal. According to the EFF, the tool lets police look up where people's phones have been, which it describes as mass surveillance, and PBS NewsHour reported on it as a low-cost cellphone tracking tool for police.

# Former Twitter employee found guilty of acting as agent of a foreign government

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2022-08-01. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/former-twitter-employee-found-guilty-acting-agent-foreign-government-and-unlawfully-sharing>*

A federal jury in the Northern District of California convicted a former Twitter media partnerships manager for the Middle East and North Africa of acting as an agent of Saudi Arabia without notifying the Attorney General, the Justice Department announced on 10 August 2022. He was also convicted of conspiracy, wire fraud, international money laundering and falsifying records, and acquitted on five other fraud counts.

According to the department, he accessed private information on Twitter accounts critical of the Saudi government and royal family on behalf of Saudi officials, in return for a $42,000 watch and $200,000 in payments to a Lebanese bank account. No sentencing date had been set.

# Member of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Charged with Plot to Murder the Former National Security Advisor

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2022-08-10. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/member-irans-islamic-revolutionary-guard-corps-irgc-charged-plot-murder-former-national>*

A member of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps was charged in Washington, D.C., with trying to arrange the murder of a former U.S. national security advisor, the Justice Department announced on 10 August 2022. Prosecutors allege he tried to hire people in the United States to carry out the killing for $300,000, allegedly in retaliation for a death in 2020.

The charges are use of interstate commerce in murder-for-hire and attempting to provide material support to a transnational murder plot. The department says he remains at large abroad. These are charges only: every defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# Failed COVIDSafe app deleted

*Australian Department of Health, 2022-08-01. Original: <https://www.health.gov.au/ministers/the-hon-mark-butler-mp/media/failed-covidsafe-app-deleted>*

Australia's health minister announced on 16 August 2022 that the COVIDSafe contact tracing app had been removed from app stores and its user data deleted. The government says the app cost more than $21 million, including $10 million to develop and $7 million in advertising.

According to the minister's office, the app had 7.9 million registrations but identified only 2 positive cases that manual contact tracers had not already found. The Office of the Australian Information Commissioner was to check that the data was handled correctly.

# Chinese Intelligence Officers Charged with Using Academic Cover to Target Individuals in United States

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2022-10-24. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/usao-nj/pr/chinese-intelligence-officers-charged-using-academic-cover-target-individuals-united>*

Four Chinese nationals, three of them officers of China's Ministry of State Security, were charged in New Jersey with conspiring to act as agents of China in the United States, the Justice Department announced on 24 October 2022. Prosecutors allege that from 2008 to 2018 they used an academic institute at Ocean University of China as cover to recruit U.S. professors, a former federal law enforcement officer and a state homeland security official, including through paid trips to China.

These are charges only: every defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# Two arrested and 13 charged in three separate cases alleging malign schemes in the United States

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2024-05-01. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/two-arrested-and-13-charged-three-separate-cases-alleged-participation-malign-schemes-united>*

The Justice Department announced on 24 October 2022 charges against 13 people in three cases alleging schemes by the Chinese government in the United States; two were arrested in New York. Prosecutors allege that seven defendants, including Chinese officials, sought to force U.S. residents to return to China; that two alleged Chinese intelligence officers tried to bribe a government employee for files from a federal prosecution; and that four people recruited U.S. academics and former officials as intelligence sources.

The other 11 defendants remain at large. These are charges only: every defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# Extended reality headsets work by streaming sensor, eye and body data to manufacturers, developers and servers

*Daniel Berrick and Jameson Spivack, Future of Privacy Forum, 2022-10-31. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/understanding-extended-reality-technology-data-flows-xr-functions/>*

Daniel Berrick and Jameson Spivack, in the first of a two-part Future of Privacy Forum series on virtual, augmented and mixed reality, explain how these devices work and what personal data they collect and pass on. They argue that immersive features depend on many sensors, large and varied data and machine learning, and that this exposes both users and bystanders to privacy risks.

The authors walk through five functions: mapping the room with cameras, depth sensors and motion units; tracking controllers and hands, sometimes by building 3D models of the user's joints; eye tracking for iris or retina log-in and for sharpening the image where the user looks; animating avatars from gaze, facial expression and body movement; and, in future, inferring a user's interests and physical, mental or emotional state. They note that many of these functions send data to manufacturers, developers or multiplayer servers.

Berrick and Spivack warn that behavioural inferences drawn from gaze, pupil dilation and motion, especially if combined with brain-computer interfaces, could build detailed profiles and reveal highly sensitive traits.

# Enforcement of Europe's data protection law on automated decisions holds lessons for the EU AI Act

*Sebastião Barros Vale, Future of Privacy Forum, 2022-11-03. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/gdpr-and-the-ai-act-interplay-lessons-from-fpfs-adm-case-law-report/>*

Sebastião Barros Vale, writing for the Future of Privacy Forum, draws on the Forum's May 2022 review of court and regulator decisions on automated decision-making under the GDPR to ask what they mean for the EU AI Act, then still a proposal. He argues that the GDPR already protects people well beyond its Article 22 rule on solely automated decisions, through its transparency, fairness and consent requirements, and that the two laws can complement each other.

He notes that the AI Act's roles of provider and user do not map neatly onto the GDPR's controllers and processors, and suggests that providers have a general duty to help users comply with the GDPR, that rules on using sensitive data for bias testing and on collecting publicly available data be made clearer, and that human reviewers be trained against automation bias. He also points out that many of the Act's high-risk uses are already being examined under the GDPR, and that AI systems which affect people without using personal data may leave a gap in redress that the Act could fill.

# Extended reality headsets depend on body-based data that current privacy laws may not clearly cover

*Daniel Berrick and Jameson Spivack, Future of Privacy Forum, 2022-11-17. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/understanding-extended-reality-technology-data-flows-privacy-and-data-protection-risks-and-mitigation-strategies/>*

Daniel Berrick and Jameson Spivack of the Future of Privacy Forum argue that virtual, augmented and mixed reality devices rely on many sensors, large volumes of data and machine learning, and that the body-based data they collect, such as eye movements, gaze, pupil dilation and gait, can be used to draw sensitive inferences about health, identity and, allegedly, emotions or cognitive states, whether those inferences are accurate or not. They also flag the identification of users through their movements, the collection of data about bystanders, and the limited control users have over data they produce unconsciously.

They say it is unclear whether laws such as the GDPR and the Illinois biometric privacy law cover this kind of data, and that some limits on collection may be hard to apply because core functions of the devices need it. They recommend processing and storing data on the device, purpose limitation and data minimisation, privacy-enhancing technologies, protections for bystanders, user controls over eye-tracking and facial-expression data, and internal governance such as review boards.

# Microsoft 365 faces more GDPR headwinds in Germany (DSK assessment)

*The Register, 2022-11-30. Original: <https://www.theregister.com/2022/11/30/office_365_faces_more_gdpr/>*

Germany's conference of federal and state data protection authorities, the DSK, concluded that Microsoft 365 still does not meet GDPR requirements and cannot be used lawfully by schools or public authorities in Germany, The Register reports. The finding followed two years of talks between a working group and Microsoft, and cited Microsoft's access to unencrypted data and U.S. surveillance laws.

According to The Register, the assessment does not apply to businesses or consumers. Microsoft disputed it, saying its products meet or exceed EU data protection law.

# Pentagon awards AWS, Google, Microsoft, Oracle spots on $9B JWCC

The Pentagon picked Amazon Web Services, Google, Microsoft and Oracle on 7 December 2022 for its Joint Warfighting Cloud Capability contract, which has a ceiling of $9 billion, DefenseScoop reports. # Public comments on the FTC's proposed privacy rulemaking agree on data minimisation and split on the agency's authority

*Tatiana Rice, Felicity Slater and Chloe Suzman, Future of Privacy Forum, 2022-12-12. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/record-set-assessing-points-of-emphasis-from-the-public-input-on-the-ftcs-privacy-rulemaking/>*

Tatiana Rice, Felicity Slater and Chloe Suzman of the Future of Privacy Forum review a sample of 70 of the more than 1,200 public comments on the Federal Trade Commission's advance notice of rulemaking on commercial surveillance and data security. They find broad agreement on a rule requiring data minimisation, which some commenters tied to better data quality for AI and machine learning, and on requiring reasonable data security programmes.

They report that the main disagreement was over whether the Commission has the authority to make a rule of this scale, with opponents relying on the Supreme Court's major questions doctrine, and over the term "commercial surveillance" itself. They also describe comments on algorithmic discrimination in housing, credit, employment and health care, on health data after the Dobbs decision and on children's data, and note that the notice was only an early step before any proposed rule, hearings and court review.

# Cloud-based fingerprint system for UK police nears completion

*Computer Weekly, 2023-01-01. Original: <https://www.computerweekly.com/news/252528242/Cloud-based-fingerprint-system-for-UK-police-nears-completion>*

A cloud-based system for sharing fingerprints and crime scene images among the 43 police forces in England and Wales was close to completion, Computer Weekly reported on 12 December 2022. Built by the Police Digital Service on Amazon Web Services under the Transforming Forensics programme, it links to the Home Office's national fingerprint database of 8.4 million records, with the first full deployment planned for March 2023.

According to the report, the system is meant to identify suspects within hours rather than days. An independent privacy consultant told Computer Weekly that AWS's terms fall short of UK data protection law for sensitive policing data.

# Medical software in Russia (EGISZ / EMIAS)

*TAdviser, 2025-01-01. Original: <https://tadviser.com/index.php/Article:Medical_software_in_Russia>*

TAdviser's reference article on medical software in Russia tracks how the country regulates software as a medical device. It reports that the health regulator Roszdravnadzor set new classification criteria in February 2020, that a government decree in November 2020 allowed one-stage registration for certain software, and that in 2021 the regulator registered its first AI medical software in the highest risk class, a tool for analysing X-rays.

TAdviser also says the regulator simplified software updates in December 2022, and that in 2023 the Ministry of Digital Development set up an industrial competence center for import substitution of pharmaceutical software.

# Veterans minister on assisted-dying discussions

*Global News, 2022-12-21. Original: <https://globalnews.ca/news/9352616/veterans-affairs-minister-year-end-maid>*

Canada's veterans affairs minister said an internal investigation found four cases in which the same Veterans Affairs Canada service agent discussed medical assistance in dying with veterans, Global News reports from a year-end interview. The minister said his earlier description of an isolated incident was not correct.

According to Global News, the employee was suspended pending the investigation and the matter was referred to the RCMP. The minister said he believed these might be all the cases but did not know for certain.

# Chinese National Sentenced to Eight Years in Prison for Acting Within the U.S. as an Unregistered Agent of the People's Republic of China

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2023-01-25. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/usao-ndil/pr/chinese-national-sentenced-eight-years-prison-acting-within-us-unregistered-agent>*

A Chinese citizen who had joined the U.S. Army Reserves was sentenced in Chicago to eight years in prison for acting as an unregistered agent of the People's Republic of China, the Justice Department announced on 25 January 2023. A jury had convicted him in 2022 on three counts, including making a false statement to the Army.

According to the department, he gave a provincial Chinese intelligence office background information on engineers and scientists, some working for U.S. defense contractors, as possible recruits.

# Justice Department Announces Charges and New Arrest in Connection with Assassination Plot Directed from Iran

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2023-01-27. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-charges-and-new-arrest-connection-assassination-plot-directed>*

The Justice Department announced on 27 January 2023 charges against three members of an Eastern European criminal group in a plot, which it says was directed from Iran, to kill a Brooklyn-based journalist and human rights activist who criticises the Iranian government. The charges include murder-for-hire and money laundering conspiracy.

According to prosecutors, one defendant was paid $30,000, bought an AK-47 rifle and surveilled the target's home in July 2022 before being arrested. The group's alleged leader was brought to New York and another leader was arrested in the Czech Republic. These are charges only: every defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# FTC enforcement action to bar GoodRx from sharing consumers' health information

*Federal Trade Commission, 2023-02-01. Original: <https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2023/02/ftc-enforcement-action-bar-goodrx-sharing-consumers-sensitive-health-info-advertising>*

The Federal Trade Commission announced in February 2023 an enforcement action against GoodRx, which it says shared users' sensitive health information with Facebook and Google for advertising and failed to report those disclosures. The action would bar GoodRx from sharing health information for advertising and includes a $1.5 million civil penalty, according to reports.

It was the first enforcement action under the FTC's Health Breach Notification Rule, according to legal commentary on the case.

# MoD issues revised cloud strategy

*Computer Weekly, 2022-11-01. Original: <https://www.computerweekly.com/news/365530572/MoD-issues-revised-cloud-strategy-as-it-prepares-to-move-top-secret-data-off-premise-by-2025>*

The UK Ministry of Defence published a revised cloud strategy that aims to move secret and top secret data to the cloud by 2025, Computer Weekly reported on 8 February 2023. The 39-page strategy describes the ministry's current technology as too fragmented, insecure and outdated, and calls for a multi-cloud approach.

According to Computer Weekly, about 400 workloads at the official classification had already moved, the ministry planned a separate procurement framework for secret workloads in late 2023, and it had awarded 162 cloud-related contracts worth about £211 million since 2020.

# Future of Privacy Forum asks the US commerce department to back a federal privacy law covering automated decisions

*Adonne Washington, Future of Privacy Forum, 2023-03-07. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/fpf-files-comments-with-the-national-telecommunications-and-information-administration-ntia-on-privacy-equity-and-civil-rights/>*

Adonne Washington, writing for the Future of Privacy Forum, summarises the Forum's comments to the US National Telecommunications and Information Administration on privacy, equity and civil rights. She argues that digital tools now shape access to education, jobs, housing, credit, insurance and government benefits, and that when they reinforce human bias people lose opportunities and trust.

According to Washington, the Forum asked the agency to support a comprehensive federal privacy law that limits data collection, protects sensitive data and civil rights, and covers automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects; to push for a common approach to privacy, AI and civil rights across federal agencies, including in procurement; and to keep consulting marginalised communities on privacy and automated decision-making. The blog post summarises the filing; the full comments are a separate document.

# GDS goes serverless with One Login

*Computer Weekly, 2023-01-01. Original: <https://www.computerweekly.com/news/365533652/GDS-goes-serverless-to-bring-personalisation-to-online-government-services-with-One-Login>*

The UK Government Digital Service is building One Login, its £400 million digital identity and sign-in system for government services, on a fully serverless architecture hosted by Amazon Web Services, Computer Weekly reported on 23 March 2023. The system replaces the earlier Verify system and is meant to give users a more personalised and consistent experience across services.

According to Computer Weekly, departments were testing it in beta, HM Revenue & Customs was due to start moving to it in summer 2023, and the team was deploying more than 200 production changes a week.

# Russian National "Illegal" Charged with Acting as Agent of a Russian Intelligence Service in the United States

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2023-03-24. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/usao-dc/pr/russian-national-illegal-charged-acting-agent-russian-intelligence-service-united-states>*

A Russian national who allegedly worked as an "illegal" agent of a Russian intelligence service under a false Brazilian identity was charged in Washington, D.C., the Justice Department announced on 24 March 2023. Prosecutors allege he used the identity to obtain a U.S. student visa, attend a university in the District of Columbia, and collect information on U.S. persons and foreign policy for his handlers.

The charges include acting as an agent of a foreign power, visa fraud, bank fraud and wire fraud. According to the department, he is in custody in Brazil on fraud charges over the false identity. These are charges only: every defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# Workplaces adopting large language models need policies on data, ownership and bias

*Stephanie Wong, Future of Privacy Forum, 2023-03-30. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/lets-look-at-llms-understanding-data-flows-and-risks-in-the-workplace/>*

Stephanie Wong, writing for the Future of Privacy Forum, argues that employees are adopting generative AI tools such as large language models faster than organisations can govern them, and sets out three areas to consider: legal and privacy obligations, ownership and originality, and ethics, bias and misinformation. She notes that data typed into these tools may be used for training or exposed, that use is not truly anonymous, that the GDPR raises questions about controllers, lawful grounds and erasure, and that the EU AI Act's treatment of the models was still uncertain.

She recommends that staff avoid entering personal, sensitive or confidential information, that organisations set clear rules on when use is encouraged, permitted, discouraged or prohibited, check outputs for bias and accuracy, take particular care where the tools influence decisions such as hiring or health care, and consult affected people and several disciplines in drafting their policies.

# Future of Privacy Forum urges California's privacy regulator to focus automated-decision rules on significant effects

*Keir Lamont, Future of Privacy Forum, 2023-03-31. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/fpf-files-comments-to-inform-new-california-privacy-rulemaking-process/>*

Keir Lamont, writing for the Future of Privacy Forum, describes the Forum's comments to the California Privacy Protection Agency ahead of its rulemaking on cybersecurity audits, risk assessments and automated decision-making under the state's amended consumer privacy law. He says the aim was to help people use their new rights, keep the rules clear, and align them with other US and global privacy frameworks.

On automated decision-making, Lamont reports that the Forum recommended covering systems that produce legal or similarly significant effects, clarifying how the law applies to decisions and profiling with different degrees of human involvement, and giving people meaningful access rights about such systems. On risk assessments, it asked for guidance that allows flexibility by context and builds on existing best practice. The post does not set out specific recommendations on cybersecurity audits.

# Online harassment persists because the law gives platforms little reason to act, so their legal shield should depend on reasonable care

*Danielle Citron, Democracy: A Journal of Ideas, Spring 2023. Original: <https://democracyjournal.org/magazine/68/combating-online-harassment/>*

Danielle Citron, a law professor at the University of Virginia, argues in Democracy's spring 2023 symposium on democracy and technology that cyber harassment falls hardest on women and minorities, silences them, pushes them out of public life and is getting easier with tools such as deepfakes. She acknowledges progress in platform rules and state criminal laws, but argues the problem persists because Section 230 shields platforms from liability and engagement-driven business models reward provocative content.

She proposes treating companies as guardians of data who owe users duties of care, loyalty and non-discrimination; letting platforms keep their legal shield in harassment and intimate-privacy cases only where they take reasonable steps against abuse; more pro bono help for victims; fuller use of the existing federal cyberstalking law; and product design and user education aimed at prevention.

# 40 officers of China's national police charged in transnational repression schemes targeting U.S. residents

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2023-04-01. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/40-officers-china-s-national-police-charged-transnational-repression-schemes-targeting-us>*

Forty officers of China's Ministry of Public Security and others were charged in Brooklyn in two cases of harassing Chinese dissidents in the United States, the Justice Department announced on 17 April 2023. In one case, 34 officers of a group called the 912 Special Project Working Group are accused of running thousands of fake social media accounts to harass dissidents and disrupt online meetings.

In the other, 10 people, including officials of the Cyberspace Administration of China and a former employee of a U.S. telecommunications company, are accused of working to block accounts and shut down meetings on that company's platform. The department says all defendants are believed to be in China or elsewhere in Asia. These are charges only: every defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# Two arrested for operating illegal overseas police station of the Chinese government

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2023-04-01. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/two-arrested-operating-illegal-overseas-police-station-chinese-government>*

Two New York City residents were arrested on 17 April 2023 on charges of helping run an undeclared police station in Manhattan's Chinatown for a provincial branch of China's Ministry of Public Security, the Justice Department says. Prosecutors describe it as the first such overseas police station in the United States.

According to the department, the two are charged with conspiring to act as agents of the People's Republic of China and with obstruction of justice for deleting messages with a Chinese official after learning of an FBI investigation. These are charges only: every defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# U.S. Citizens and Russian Intelligence Officers Charged with Conspiring to Use U.S. Citizens as Illegal Agents of the Russian Government

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2023-04-18. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/us-citizens-and-russian-intelligence-officers-charged-conspiring-use-us-citizens-illegal>*

Three Russian nationals the Justice Department says are tied to Russia's FSB intelligence service and four U.S. citizens were charged with conspiring to use Americans as illegal agents of the Russian government, the department announced on 18 April 2023. According to the superseding indictment in Florida, from 2014 to 2022 the Russians directed U.S. political groups, including the African People's Socialist Party, Uhuru Movement and Black Hammer, to spread pro-Russian propaganda and funded a 2019 local election campaign.

In a separate case in Washington, D.C., a Russian national was charged with conspiring with an FSB officer to recruit U.S. academics. These are charges only: every defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# Laws on AI are converging on risk regulation, which brings known weaknesses and a built-in choice to deploy

*Margot E. Kaminski, Lawfare, 2023-04-21. Original: <https://www.lawfaremedia.org/article/the-developing-law-of-ai-regulation-a-turn-to-risk-regulation>*

Margot E. Kaminski, a law professor at the University of Colorado, argues that the emerging law of AI is converging on risk regulation, which she says suits AI's systemic, large-scale and often future harms better than lawsuits after the fact. She adds that the approach carries known problems from other fields, and that choosing it is itself a decision to build and deploy AI rather than take a more precautionary path.

Drawing on the critique that much scholarship tries to fix technology rather than ask whether it should be used at all, she urges regulators to look beyond AI impact assessments and says light-touch risk regulation will not be enough if they mean to address AI harms in earnest.

# Statement on the fifteenth meeting of the IHR Emergency Committee: end of the COVID-19 emergency

*World Health Organization, 2023-05-05. Original: <https://www.who.int/news/item/05-05-2023-statement-on-the-fifteenth-meeting-of-the-international-health-regulations-(2005)-emergency-committee-regarding-the-coronavirus-disease-(covid-19)-pandemic>*

The World Health Organization's Director-General determined that COVID-19 no longer constitutes a public health emergency of international concern, following the fifteenth meeting of the International Health Regulations Emergency Committee on 4 May 2023, WHO said on 5 May 2023. The committee cited falling deaths and hospitalisations and high levels of population immunity, and advised moving to long-term management of the disease.

WHO issued seven temporary recommendations, including keeping surveillance, adding COVID-19 vaccination to routine programmes and lifting travel-related health requirements. It noted the virus continues to evolve.

# Massachusetts man indicted for acting as illegal agent of the PRC

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2023-05-01. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/massachusetts-man-indicted-acting-illegal-agent-people-s-republic-china>*

A 63-year-old resident of Brighton, Massachusetts, was arrested and indicted on charges of acting as an illegal agent of the People's Republic of China, the Justice Department announced on 15 May 2023. Prosecutors allege that from 2018 to 2022 he gave Chinese officials information on Boston-area dissidents and community groups, including photographs of pro-democracy protesters, and organised a counter-protest, without notifying the U.S. Attorney General.

The department says he faces up to 10 years in prison on the main charge. Until convicted, the defendant is presumed innocent.

# European regulators enforce the GDPR's privacy-by-design duty unevenly, though it underpins some of the largest fines

*Christina Michelakaki and Isabella Perera, Future of Privacy Forum, 2023-05-17. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/new-fpf-report-unlocking-data-protection-by-design-and-by-default-lessons-from-the-enforcement-of-article-25-gdpr/>*

Christina Michelakaki and Isabella Perera present a Future of Privacy Forum report on how European regulators and courts enforce Article 25 of the GDPR, the duty to build data protection into systems by design and by default. They draw on more than 92 regulator decisions, court rulings and guidelines from 16 EEA countries, the UK and the European Data Protection Board, including a case about emotion-recognition AI used in customer support.

The authors find that regulators disagree on whether the duty is preventive: some act before any other breach occurs, while others will not find a violation for an isolated incident. They report that most regulators avoid saying which protective measures are adequate and say little about privacy-enhancing technologies, that Article 25 is usually applied alongside the general principles and the security article, and that despite its abstract wording it has been the basis for some of the largest GDPR fines.

Michelakaki and Perera argue that understanding how the duty works in practice will matter for managing generative AI and other technologies that process personal data in complex ways.

# Illegal Agents of the PRC Government Charged for PRC-Directed Bribery Scheme

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2023-05-26. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/illegal-agents-prc-government-charged-prc-directed-bribery-scheme>*

Two people were arrested in California and charged in New York with acting as illegal agents of the People's Republic of China in a bribery scheme, the Justice Department announced on 26 May 2023. # Singapore's AI Verify lets companies test their own AI systems against governance principles, with clear limits

*Josh Lee Kok Thong, Future of Privacy Forum, 2023-06-06. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/ai-verify-singapores-ai-governance-testing-initiative-explained/>*

Josh Lee Kok Thong, writing for the Future of Privacy Forum, explains AI Verify, the testing framework and toolkit Singapore's media and privacy regulators launched in 2022 as part of the country's voluntary, light-touch approach to AI governance. He describes a framework built on eleven internationally recognised principles, from transparency and explainability to safety, fairness and human oversight, and a toolkit that bundles open-source tests and produces a report, run by companies inside their own systems so models and data stay private.

Lee stresses that AI Verify does not set ethical standards or sort systems into risk tiers, and that passing its tests does not mean a system is safe, unbiased or ethical; it only lets developers back up claims about their systems. He sees its strengths in its grounding in international principles, its fit with the EU AI Act and the US NIST risk framework, and its mix of technical and process checks.

He notes its limits at the time: it was still a minimum viable product, handled only some model types and sizes, offered no thresholds, and did not yet cover security, data governance or societal well-being. Its success, in his view, depended on staying cheap and accessible, proving itself technically sound and keeping pace with international regulation.

# Federal jury convicts three defendants of interstate stalking for Chinese nationals

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2023-06-01. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/federal-jury-convicts-three-defendants-interstate-stalking-chinese-nationals-united-states>*

A federal jury in Brooklyn convicted three people of interstate stalking-related crimes in a campaign carried out on behalf of the People's Republic of China, the Justice Department announced on 20 June 2023. According to the department, between 2016 and 2019 they surveilled and harassed U.S. residents to pressure them to return to China, as part of the Chinese effort known as Operation Fox Hunt.

One defendant, a retired U.S. police officer working as a private investigator, and one other were also convicted of acting as illegal agents of China. The department says the defendants face maximum sentences of 10 to 25 years.

# China's draft generative AI rules put heavy duties on providers and leave key terms and open-source models unclear

*Yirong Sun and Jingxian Zeng, Future of Privacy Forum, 2023-06-23. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/unveiling-chinas-generative-ai-regulation/>*

Yirong Sun and Jingxian Zeng, in a guest post for the Future of Privacy Forum that they say does not necessarily reflect the Forum's views, analyse China's April 2023 draft measures on generative AI services. They see the regulator's main concern as AI being used to sway public opinion or spread false or sensitive information, alongside data leaks, fraud and infringement.

The authors note that the rules cover services offered to 'the public' in mainland China without defining the term, leaving in-house, institutional and open-source uses uncertain, and appear to reach services offered from abroad. They describe duties across the whole lifecycle: lawful training data and labelling checks, a security assessment and algorithm filing before launch, labelling of generated content and real-name users during service, and removal of non-compliant content afterwards, with providers treated as the producers of what their products generate.

Sun and Zeng question whether the requirement that outputs be true and accurate is technically achievable, warn that providers may push risk up to model developers by contract, and argue that open-source models modified by chains of contributors can hardly meet the disclosure and assessment duties. They add that the measures must be read with China's other algorithm and data laws and its wider industrial policy.

# US biometric privacy laws may reach headset eye tracking, face analysis and voice data even when no one is identified

*Jameson Spivack, Tatiana Rice and Daniel Berrick, Future of Privacy Forum, 2023-07-27. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/old-laws-new-tech-as-courts-wrestle-with-tough-questions-under-us-biometric-laws-immersive-tech-raises-new-challenges/>*

Jameson Spivack, Tatiana Rice and Daniel Berrick of the Future of Privacy Forum examine how US biometric privacy laws apply to extended reality devices, which collect eye, hand and body data. They argue that with heavy litigation under Illinois's biometric privacy law and a new FTC policy statement, and no agreed meaning of 'biometric', both users and companies face uncertainty.

The authors find that face, iris and hand scans used to log users in are clearly covered, but that some broad definitions, especially Illinois's, may also reach face analysis that identifies no one: courts have let claims proceed against augmented-reality try-on apps that only map the face. They point to two ways companies have reduced liability, keeping scans unlinkable to identity and processing data only on the device.

On voice and eye tracking the authors see the law as unsettled: ordinary recordings are generally outside the laws, but some courts have asked whether data could identify people rather than how it is used, and no court has yet decided whether gaze data counts as face geometry, an iris scan or neither.

# A checklist for workplace rules on employees' use of generative AI tools

*Amber Ezzell, Future of Privacy Forum, 2023-08-01. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/fpf-releases-generative-ai-internal-policy-checklist-to-guide-development-of-policies-to-promote-responsible-employee-use-of-generative-ai-tools/>*

Amber Ezzell, writing for the Future of Privacy Forum, presents a checklist to help organisations write or review internal policies on employees' use of generative AI. She says it was shaped by talks with practitioners at more than 30 organisations, whose approaches ranged from outright bans without approval to no policy at all.

Ezzell groups the guidance under four headings: making sure existing data protection and security rules are updated for approved uses and that staff know they still apply; training on responsible use, risk, ethics and bias, with regular reminders; setting out when company accounts must be used, which uses are allowed, and how use should be documented and disclosed; and requiring staff to check outputs for accuracy, currency, bias and possible copyright problems, with qualified review of any generated code for security flaws.

# Two U.S. Navy Servicemembers Arrested for Transmitting Military Information to the People's Republic of China

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2023-08-03. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/two-us-navy-servicemembers-arrested-transmitting-military-information-peoples-republic-china>*

Two U.S. Navy servicemembers in California were arrested on charges of sending military information to the People's Republic of China, the Justice Department announced on 3 August 2023. A machinist's mate at Naval Base San Diego is charged with conspiring to send national defense information to a Chinese intelligence officer, including technical manuals on ship weapons and propulsion; prosecutors say he was paid thousands of dollars.

A petty officer at Naval Base Ventura County is charged with receiving about $14,866 in bribes for sending operational plans for a military exercise and radar blueprints, according to the department. These are charges only: every defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# Freedom of thought is the overlooked right in the misinformation debate, and a nudge offering other sources could protect it

*Richard Mackenzie-Gray Scott, Tech Policy Press, 2023-08-23. Original: <https://www.techpolicy.press/the-algorithmic-management-of-misinformation-that-protects-liberty/>*

Richard Mackenzie-Gray Scott, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Oxford, argues that many responses to misinformation, such as wider platform liability, removing or downranking content and deplatforming, risk harming free speech, and that freedom of thought, which comes before speech, has been overlooked. He says platform design and algorithmic curation work against reflection by rewarding quick reactions and narrowing what people see.

He proposes an "alternative source" nudge: when a user goes to share content containing misinformation, a pop-up offers links to other, third-party sources without labelling the content true or false, leaving the judgment to the user. He argues it should be used mainly during spikes such as elections or crises, warns that the choice of sources, feedback loops and too much friction are real risks, and calls for public scrutiny and published effectiveness data before it is widely adopted.

# How artificial intelligence gave a paralyzed woman her voice back

*UC San Francisco, 2023-08-23. Original: <https://www.ucsf.edu/news/2023/08/425986/how-artificial-intelligence-gave-paralyzed-woman-her-voice-back>*

Researchers at UC San Francisco and UC Berkeley developed a brain-computer interface that let a woman paralysed by a stroke speak through a digital avatar, with synthesised speech and facial expressions, for the first time in 18 years, UCSF reports. The system decodes brain signals into text at nearly 80 words per minute, against 14 words per minute with her previous device, by recognising the sounds that make up words rather than whole words.

The study was published in Nature on 23 August 2023.

# Data protection authorities became the first regulators of generative AI by applying existing privacy law

*Gabriela Zanfir-Fortuna, Future of Privacy Forum, 2023-09-12. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/how-data-protection-authorities-are-de-facto-regulating-generative-ai/>*

Gabriela Zanfir-Fortuna, writing for the Future of Privacy Forum, argues that data protection authorities became the first regulators to act on generative AI because the services depend on personal data for training and operation. She lists their recurring concerns: no lawful basis for training on personal data, too little transparency, weak ways to exercise access, erasure and objection rights, inaccurate personal data in outputs, and gaps in security and in protecting sensitive and children's data.

She surveys action as of September 2023: an emergency order in Italy later lifted after changes, an EU-level task force, a joint Canadian investigation, a coordinated Ibero-American action, a warning in Japan, inquiries in Brazil and by the US FTC, and a fine in South Korea, noting that only Italy and South Korea had reached enforcement. She also summarises the G7 data protection authorities' June 2023 statement, which called for privacy by design and impact assessments across the AI lifecycle.

Zanfir-Fortuna concludes that the similarity of these concerns across countries shows regulators are already governing generative AI through data protection law, without waiting for AI-specific statutes, and that this common ground favours cooperation among them.

# Transparency, bias checks, ethics codes and user choice are only half-measures on AI; lawmakers need duties, design accountability and bright-line bans

*Woodrow Hartzog, U.S. Senate Committee on the Judiciary, Subcommittee on Privacy, Technology, and the Law (written testimony), 2023-09-12. Original: <https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/2023-09-12_pm_-_testimony_-_hartzog.pdf>*

Woodrow Hartzog, a law professor at Boston University, told a Senate Judiciary subcommittee hearing on legislating AI, drawing on research with colleagues at the Cordell Institute at Washington University in St. Louis, that the approaches industry has favoured, such as transparency, bias mitigation, ethical principles and individual choice, are worthwhile but amount to "half-measures" that risk giving the impression lawmakers have done enough.

He urges Congress to accept that AI systems are not neutral and to hold developers accountable for their design choices; to impose substantive duties of loyalty, care and confidentiality and require a sound basis before data is processed or systems are deployed; and to resist the idea that AI is inevitable by setting bright-line rules, including outright prohibitions for the most dangerous designs and uses. He argues that the procedural approach has failed in privacy law over the past 25 years.

# Future of Privacy Forum and four hiring-software companies set out best practices for AI in hiring and employment

*Future of Privacy Forum, Future of Privacy Forum, 2023-09-19. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/future-of-privacy-forum-and-leading-companies-release-best-practices-for-ai-in-employment-relationships/>*

The Future of Privacy Forum announces best practices for AI tools used in hiring and employment, written with four hiring and employment software developers through an expert working group. It argues that AI hiring tools can help match candidates with jobs but carry risks for candidates, employers and regulators if left unaddressed.

The group recommends clearly assigned responsibilities between developers and deployers; no secret use of AI for hiring, firing or other consequential actions; testing for fitness and bias; anti-discrimination protections that go beyond the law where needed; no use of facial characterisation or emotion inference in hiring without public evidence of efficacy and fairness; governance based on the US NIST AI Risk Management Framework; no claims that tools are 'bias-free'; and informed human oversight. The Forum says the guide may be updated as AI rules and standards develop.

# Future of Privacy Forum tells New York City lawmakers how schools should govern AI tools

*Jamie Gorosh, Future of Privacy Forum, 2023-09-27. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/fpf-weighs-in-on-the-responsible-use-and-adoption-of-artificial-intelligence-technologies-in-new-york-city-classrooms/>*

Jamie Gorosh, writing for the Future of Privacy Forum, summarises the Forum's testimony to New York City Council committees on AI in public schools. She reports five recommendations: shared definitions and principles for AI in education, special attention to high-risk tools that make decisions about students or teachers, risk-based rules that target harm without blocking useful tools, more transparency in procurement, and adopting AI only where it genuinely improves students' education.

Gorosh notes that AI is already built into many of the thousands of tools districts use, from autocomplete to dropout-risk flags, and cites an audit that found the city's education department lacked an AI governance framework. She points to the state's 2020 moratorium on biometric identification in schools as an example of a rule so broad it had unintended effects.

The testimony, as she describes it, also warns that self-harm monitoring tools that scan student writing for keywords can wrongly flag students and lead to police or social-service involvement or discipline, that AI accuracy varies across groups, and that new tools usually expand the collection and sharing of student data that schools must protect.

# U.S. Navy Service Member Pleads Guilty to Transmitting Sensitive U.S. Military Information to Chinese Intelligence Officer

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2023-10-10. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/us-navy-service-member-pleads-guilty-transmitting-sensitive-us-military-information-chinese>*

A U.S. Navy petty officer who held a security clearance at Naval Base Ventura County pleaded guilty to conspiracy and receiving bribes for sending sensitive military information to a Chinese intelligence officer, the Justice Department announced on 10 October 2023. According to the department, from August 2021 to at least May 2023 he sent plans for a large Indo-Pacific military exercise, operational orders and blueprints for a radar system in Okinawa, Japan, in exchange for at least $14,866.

The department says he used encrypted communications and destroyed evidence. Sentencing was set for 8 January 2024, and he faces up to 20 years in prison.

# Future of Privacy Forum backs a US election rule against deliberately deceptive AI-generated campaign ads

*Amber Ezzell, Future of Privacy Forum, 2023-10-19. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/fpf-submits-comments-to-the-fec-on-the-use-of-artificial-intelligence-in-campaign-ads/>*

Amber Ezzell, for the Future of Privacy Forum, reports the Forum's comments to the US Federal Election Commission, which supported a petition asking the Commission to make clear that its rule on 'fraudulent misrepresentation' covers deliberately deceptive AI-generated campaign ads. The letter argues that rules on the use of generative AI in election content should be put in place before the technology advances further.

The comments say generative AI can erode public trust and campaign integrity, and that deceptive design in elections risks misinformation, voter suppression and harassment of candidates, especially people from marginalised groups. Used responsibly, the letter adds, the same tools can help campaigns reach different communities, and it urges the Commission to look at risk mitigation, education and outreach for the populations most at risk. An op-ed the author co-wrote earlier that year is attached.

# Handing decisions about people to algorithms, alone or alongside humans, is harder than its advocates claim

*Daniel J. Solove, TeachPrivacy (blog), 2023-10-19. Original: <https://teachprivacy.com/ai-algorithms-and-awful-humans/>*

Daniel J. Solove, writing with Hideyuki Matsumi of Vrije Universiteit Brussel, introduces a short essay (then forthcoming in the Fordham Law Review) on two common cases for automation: that human decisions are so flawed that machines should take over, and that machines and people decide better together. The authors argue that both are too optimistic when the decision is about a person.

They argue that algorithms do not reason like unbiased humans but reach conclusions by different routes, that prejudice can survive automation, and that machines lack the moral and emotional sensitivity that judgments about people's lives require. They add that automated systems favour what can be counted over qualitative information, which can change what a decision is, and that people are poor at checking machine outputs. In their view, society is adopting algorithmic decision-making too eagerly and should first understand these mismatches.

# Future of Privacy Forum says the 2023 US AI executive order will reach far into the private sector

*Future of Privacy Forum, Future of Privacy Forum, 2023-10-30. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/fpf-statement-on-biden-harris-ai-executive-order/>*

In a short statement, the Future of Privacy Forum calls the October 2023 White House plan on AI very comprehensive and says that, although the executive order is aimed at the government's own use of AI, its effect on the private sector will be profound.

The Forum points to requirements for government vendors, priorities on worker surveillance, education and housing, standards for risk assessments and bias mitigation, and investment in privacy-enhancing technologies. It singles out the order's call for bipartisan privacy legislation, which it describes as the most important precursor to protections for AI that affects vulnerable people.

# Microsoft quietly launches Israeli Azure cloud region

*DatacenterDynamics, 2023-10-31. Original: <https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/microsoft-quietly-launches-israeli-azure-cloud-region>*

Microsoft has opened its Israel Central Azure cloud region near Modiin, between Tel Aviv and Jerusalem, DatacenterDynamics reports. The region was first announced in 2020 and had been expected in 2021, then early 2022; it was initially listed with three availability zones, later marked as coming soon.

According to DatacenterDynamics, Microsoft was the last of the major U.S. cloud providers to open an Israeli region, after Oracle, Google and AWS, and did not respond to questions about the launch. AWS and Google won Israel's $1.2 billion Project Nimbus government cloud tender in 2021.

# A step-by-step guide to the conformity assessments the EU AI Act requires for high-risk systems

*Katerina Demetzou and Vasileios Rovilos, Future of Privacy Forum, 2023-11-17. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/fpf-and-onetrust-release-collaboration-on-conformity-assessments-under-the-proposed-eu-ai-act-a-step-by-step-guide-infographic/>*

Katerina Demetzou and Vasileios Rovilos present a Future of Privacy Forum guide and infographic, made with a compliance software company, on conformity assessments under the EU AI Act, then still being negotiated. They describe these assessments as the main accountability tool for high-risk AI systems and note that they borrow from existing EU product-safety law.

The authors set out a decision flow for working out whether a system must be assessed, then walk through each requirement and when it applies across the system's life: risk management, data governance, technical documentation, record keeping, transparency, human oversight, and accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity. They stress that technical standards being drafted at the Commission's request will be central to how compliance works in practice, while cautioning that those plans could change once the Act was final.

# Palantir wins GBP330m NHS contract

*The Register, 2023-11-22. Original: <https://www.theregister.com/2023/11/22/palantir_wins_nhs_contract>*

Palantir won a seven-year, £330 million contract from NHS England to build the Federated Data Platform, The Register reports, announced on 22 November 2023. The platform is meant to connect data held in separate NHS systems to support care and planning, and Palantir's partners include Accenture, PwC, NECS and Carnall Farrar.

According to The Register, Palantir had earlier received about £60 million in NHS contracts awarded without competition. Critics raised concerns about lock-in, and the National Data Guardian said the public wants assurance the NHS keeps control.

# White House and eight US states issue executive orders on government use of AI and generative AI

*Beth Do, Future of Privacy Forum, 2023-12-06. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/a-blueprint-for-the-future-white-house-and-states-issue-guidelines-on-ai-and-generative-ai/>*

Beth Do, writing for the Future of Privacy Forum, compares executive orders on AI issued since July 2023 by the White House and eight states: California, Kansas, New Jersey, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Virginia and Wisconsin. She notes that some cities issued their own generative AI guidelines while Maine paused state use of generative AI pending a risk review.

Do finds the federal order the most prescriptive, with many reports and standards on auditing, content authentication and privacy-enhancing technologies, and California's the most detailed among the states. She observes that several states address only generative AI while others cover AI broadly, that only two define generative AI, and that some orders give agencies power to set binding standards while others create advisory task forces.

Although the orders govern government use, Do argues they will reach companies through procurement standards, through how regulators judge AI compliance with existing law, and through legislation the agencies may later seek.

# UK government renews preferential pricing agreement with AWS

*Computer Weekly, 2024-01-01. Original: <https://www.computerweekly.com/news/366562418/UK-government-quietly-renews-public-sector-preferential-pricing-agreement-with-AWS>*

The UK's Crown Commercial Service renewed its preferential pricing agreement with Amazon Web Services for the public sector, Computer Weekly reports, with the new deal announced on 7 December 2023. The One Government Value Agreement 2.0 runs for three years under a memorandum of understanding; the first version, from October 2020, offered baseline discounts of up to 18%.

The service did not publish the new discount levels but said the benefits were well above the earlier deal. Computer Weekly notes the renewal comes while the Competition and Markets Authority is examining the cloud market, including such pricing schemes.

# Five open questions for US state privacy law in 2024, including how California will regulate AI

*Keir Lamont, Future of Privacy Forum, 2023-12-11. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/five-big-questions-and-zero-predictions-for-the-u-s-state-privacy-landscape-in-2024/>*

Keir Lamont, for the Future of Privacy Forum, notes that the US entered 2024 as the only G20 country without a national privacy framework, while state lawmaking accelerated in 2023. Rather than predict, he poses five questions: whether any state will break from the prevailing model for comprehensive privacy laws; what California will do on AI; whether 2024 will finally bring enforcement actions; which states will amend their existing laws; and whether these laws are constitutional.

On AI, Lamont describes two overlapping and partly conflicting California efforts: the privacy agency's draft rules on automated decision-making, which would reach systems that merely 'facilitate' human decisions, and a bill on automated decision tools aimed at systems that are the 'controlling factor' in consequential decisions. He also notes that cure periods may explain the scarcity of enforcement so far, and that a court's injunction against California's Age-Appropriate Design Code revived constitutional challenges to state privacy laws.

# Rite Aid banned from using AI facial recognition

*Federal Trade Commission, 2023-12-19. Original: <https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2023/12/rite-aid-banned-using-ai-facial-recognition-after-ftc-says-retailer-deployed-technology-without>*

The Federal Trade Commission announced in December 2023 that Rite Aid will be banned from using AI facial recognition technology for five years. The FTC says the retailer deployed the technology in its stores without reasonable safeguards, and that it falsely tagged consumers as shoplifters.

# Transparent brain-computer interface uses AI and nanotech

*Psychology Today, 2024-01-01. Original: <https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/the-future-brain/202401/transparent-brain-computer-interface-uses-ai-and-nanotech>*

Researchers at UC San Diego built a transparent brain implant made of graphene that records electrical signals from the surface of the brain while allowing deeper brain activity to be imaged at the same time, Psychology Today reports. Machine learning was then used to predict activity in deeper layers from the surface recordings alone.

The work was demonstrated in laboratory mice and published in Nature Nanotechnology in January 2024.

# Kafka's fiction and why giving people control over their data is a dead end for privacy law

*Daniel J. Solove, TeachPrivacy (blog), 2024-01-06. Original: <https://teachprivacy.com/kafka-in-the-age-of-ai-and-the-futility-of-privacy-as-control/>*

Daniel J. Solove and Woodrow Hartzog of Boston University School of Law introduce an essay (then forthcoming in the Boston University Law Review) that reads Franz Kafka's fiction against modern privacy law. They argue that most privacy statutes follow what they call an individual control model, giving people rights to manage their own data, and that Kafka's characters, who submit to the systems that harm them and blame themselves, show why this fails.

In their account, people handed control over their data tend to give it back to large organisations even at their own expense, and this would remain true if manipulative design were removed. They argue that AI deepens the problem. Their proposal is that privacy law should stop aiming chiefly at individual control and instead build a societal structure that keeps the collection, use and disclosure of personal data in check.

# AWS wins GBP94m contract with UK DWP

*DatacenterDynamics, 2023-01-01. Original: <https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/aws-wins-94m-contract-with-uk-govs-dwp>*

Amazon Web Services won a three-year, £94 million public cloud hosting contract with the UK Department for Work and Pensions, DatacenterDynamics reports. The contract was signed on 1 December 2023, runs to November 2026 and was awarded under the second One Government Value Agreement between AWS and the Crown Commercial Service.

According to the report, the department has used AWS since 2016 and its previous three-year deal was worth £57 million.
