# Freedom of thought has a social side, so control of online feeds should return to the people reading them

*Richard Reisman, Tech Policy Press, 2024-01-18. Original: <https://techpolicy.press/protecting-freedom-of-thought-by-deciding-what-information-you-consume>*

Richard Reisman, a non-resident senior fellow at the Foundation for American Innovation and a contributor to the Centre for International Governance Innovation's freedom-of-thought project, argues that debates over platform speech rules miss a social side of thought, which he calls freedom of impression: people's freedom to choose whom they listen to. He says engagement-driven algorithmic feeds have replaced the communities and institutions that once mediated what people heard, and that deciding what to remove raises hard problems of legitimacy.

His remedy is to let users choose intermediary services that compose and filter their feeds, in a bottom-up, federated structure with limited top-down rules for clearly illegal content, which he argues would stay consistent with the First Amendment.

# Five lessons from the patchwork of US federal rules and guidance on AI in health care

*Stephanie Wong, Amber Ezzell and Felicity Slater, Future of Privacy Forum, 2024-01-22. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/regulating-health-lessons-for-navigating-the-complex-code-of-ai-and-healthcare-regulations/>*

Stephanie Wong, Amber Ezzell and Felicity Slater of the Future of Privacy Forum argue that US federal agencies and the White House are shaping AI in health care through a fast-changing mix of enforcement, rules, recommendations and informal guidance, and they draw five lessons from it. They note that health regulators differ in tone, with the health privacy office urging caution on AI tools and the FDA signalling a flexible, risk-based approach to AI in drug development.

The authors stress that the type of data decides which regulator applies: health records held by covered providers fall under HIPAA, while data from apps, wearables and connected devices may fall to the FTC, which has also signalled it will police biased automated decisions. They argue that past guidance has tended to foreshadow enforcement, pointing to the FTC's first actions under its health breach rule in 2023 and its joint statement with other agencies on automated-decision bias.

Wong, Ezzell and Slater trace the responsible-use agenda from the 2022 AI Bill of Rights blueprint through the October 2023 executive order and draft federal policy on rights-affecting AI, and expect the field to keep shifting, so organisations should follow federal guidance and privacy and security standards as they adopt AI.

# How the Singapore–US crosswalk maps AI Verify onto the NIST AI Risk Management Framework

*Josh Lee Kok Thong, Future of Privacy Forum, 2024-01-23. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/explaining-the-crosswalk-between-singapores-ai-verify-testing-framework-and-the-u-s-nist-ai-risk-management-framework/>*

Josh Lee Kok Thong, for the Future of Privacy Forum, explains the 'Crosswalk' published in October 2023 by Singapore's media regulator and the US National Institute of Standards and Technology, which shows how adopting Singapore's AI Verify testing framework can help meet the US AI Risk Management Framework and the other way round. He summarises both: AI Verify as a voluntary self-assessment toolkit built around eleven governance principles and, for now, supervised-learning models rather than generative AI; and the US framework as voluntary, sector-neutral guidance organised around four functions, govern, map, measure and manage.

He notes that the mapping is not one-to-one and covers process checks rather than AI Verify's technical tests. He argues that, as a government-to-government effort, the Crosswalk shows a common language can be found between different AI governance frameworks, matters in practice for organisations active in both countries, and offers a model for future cross-border mapping.

# One Iranian and two Canadian nationals indicted in murder-for-hire scheme

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2024-01-01. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/one-iranian-and-two-canadian-nationals-indicted-murder-hire-scheme>*

One Iranian and two Canadian nationals have been indicted in Minnesota on a charge of conspiring to use interstate commerce in a murder-for-hire plot, the Justice Department announced on 29 January 2024. Prosecutors allege they recruited people to travel to the United States to kill two Maryland residents who had defected from Iran, and negotiated a payment of $350,000 plus $20,000 in expenses.

According to the department, the Iranian national is believed to be in Iran and the two Canadians are held in Canada on unrelated charges; one also faces firearms charges. These are charges only: every defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# AI recombines and intensifies old privacy problems, and a roadmap for how privacy law should respond

*Daniel J. Solove, TeachPrivacy (blog), 2024-02-01. Original: <https://teachprivacy.com/artificial-intelligence-and-privacy/>*

Daniel J. Solove introduces his article "Artificial Intelligence and Privacy", which he describes as an attempt to map the whole relationship between AI and privacy and to set out how privacy law should govern AI. He answers sceptics who doubt that privacy law suits AI by arguing that current law falls well short but that, reconceived and properly structured, it could go a long way.

He argues that the privacy problems arise both in the data AI systems take in and in what they produce, and that most are variations on long-standing problems rather than new ones. What is different, in his view, is that AI combines these problems in complex ways and often intensifies them to new levels. He calls AI no unexpected upheaval for privacy but a test that exposes the weaknesses and gaps in existing laws, which he says will need amendment or new legislation.

# AI-driven health and wellness services will multiply health inferences, and 2024 may bring more state and federal action on health data

*Jordan Wrigley, Future of Privacy Forum, 2024-02-12. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/fpf-health-wellness-mapping-the-2024-health-privacy-landscape-a-2023-retrospective/>*

Jordan Wrigley, for the Future of Privacy Forum, looks back on health data privacy in 2023 and ahead to 2024. She writes that the year's developments were almost entirely state privacy responses to the Supreme Court's Dobbs decision on abortion.

Looking forward, she argues that AI-enabled health and wellness services will generate more inferences about people's health, raising new privacy concerns for patients and consumers, and she expects state legislators and federal regulators to act on health data privacy in 2024, particularly on reproductive health and genetic data.

# Microsoft suspends access to cloud services for Russian companies

*DatacenterDynamics, 2022-03-01. Original: <https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/microsoft-suspends-access-to-cloud-services-for-russian-companies>*

Microsoft is cutting off companies registered in Russia from cloud services including Azure, Power BI and OneDrive from 20 March 2024, DatacenterDynamics reports, citing a letter from Microsoft to its Russian distributor Softline. Microsoft Office and Windows are not affected.

According to the publication, the move follows the EU's twelfth sanctions package, which bans supplying enterprise software, including cloud services, to Russian-registered entities. Softline was trying to negotiate a short postponement.

# Brazil Has The World Most Accessed Online Citizen Services Platform

*Forbes, 2024-03-04. Original: <https://www.forbes.com/sites/angelicamarideoliveira/2024/03/04/brazil-has-the-worlds-most-accessed-online-citizen-services-platform>*

Brazil's Gov.br platform is the most accessed government services website in the world according to the analytics firm Similarweb, Forbes reports, ahead of the United Kingdom's Gov.uk. The platform, launched in July 2019, is used by more than 150 million Brazilians and offers more than 4,200 digital services.

According to Forbes, it handles about 4,000 accesses per second and connects more than 2,000 systems. Brazil was also named a "fast mover" in the 2022 United Nations E-Government Survey.

# Four US states enacted genetic privacy laws in 2023, with gaps on police access, minors and changing privacy policies

*Niharika Vattikonda, Future of Privacy Forum, 2024-03-07. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/the-dna-of-genetic-privacy-legislation-montana-tennessee-texas-and-virginia-enter-2024-with-new-genetic-privacy-laws-incorporating-fpfs-best-practices/>*

Niharika Vattikonda, for the Future of Privacy Forum, reviews the genetic privacy laws that Montana, Tennessee, Texas and Virginia passed in 2023 for direct-to-consumer genetic testing companies, comparing them with the Forum's 2018 best practices. Vattikonda finds that all four create rights to access and delete data and limit sharing, and that Montana and Texas go further, Montana with data localisation requirements.

Vattikonda argues the laws leave out key elements: they differ on what legal process police need to obtain genetic data, which the author says matters more after the Supreme Court's 2022 abortion ruling, and none requires public reports on law enforcement requests. Vattikonda also points to weak protections for minors and to consent for revised privacy policies, which the author says grows in importance as AI is built into genetic testing. The author urges states to adopt the missing protections in 2024.

# EU use of Microsoft 365 found to breach data protection rules

*TechCrunch, 2024-03-11. Original: <https://techcrunch.com/2024/03/11/edps-microsoft-365>*

The European Data Protection Supervisor found that the European Commission broke several EU data protection rules in its use of Microsoft 365, TechCrunch reports. The watchdog, which opened its investigation in May 2021, said the Commission had not adequately specified what personal data was collected and why, or ensured proper safeguards for transfers outside the EU.

According to the report, the Commission was ordered by 9 December 2024 to suspend data flows to Microsoft and its affiliates in countries without an EU adequacy decision and to bring its processing into line. The Commission said it would study the decision and had already improved its contracts during the investigation.

# Future of Privacy Forum welcomes the EU AI Act's adoption and warns of a long road to making it work

*Jules Polonetsky, Future of Privacy Forum, 2024-03-13. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/fpf-statement-on-the-adoption-of-the-eu-ai-act/>*

In a statement on the day the European Union adopted the AI Act, Jules Polonetsky, chief executive of the Future of Privacy Forum, describes it as a comprehensive, binding law with broad effect outside the EU that is set to play a crucial role in the global debate on regulating AI. He welcomes lawmakers' choice of a definition of AI systems that is interoperable with the OECD's.

He also acknowledges a long and complicated road to making the Act effective in practice, and says that, because personal data is central to building and deploying AI, the Forum will focus on how privacy and data protection rules around the world interact with AI governance frameworks such as the Act.

# Latin America leads on neurorights, starting with Chile's constitution

*Jameson Spivack, Future of Privacy Forum, 2024-03-20. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/privacy-and-the-rise-of-neurorights-in-latin-america/>*

Writers at the Future of Privacy Forum survey neurorights in Latin America. Chile amended its constitution in 2021 to protect mental integrity and brain data, and in 2023 its Supreme Court ruled that a company had violated a senator's rights by keeping his brain data without consent.

They describe proposals in Mexico, Brazil, Costa Rica, Colombia, Argentina and Uruguay, and the role of regional and international bodies, including a 2022 neurorights model law from the Latin American Parliament.

# What US regulators and self-regulatory bodies have signalled about children's privacy in virtual worlds

*Bailey Sanchez, Future of Privacy Forum, 2024-03-26. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/youth-privacy-in-immersive-technologies-regulatory-guidance-lessons-learned-and-remaining-uncertainties/>*

Bailey Sanchez, for the Future of Privacy Forum, analyses regulatory and self-regulatory actions on youth privacy, safety and advertising in extended reality and virtual worlds, and draws lessons for companies building such experiences. Sanchez notes that the US Federal Trade Commission reads the children's privacy law's definition of personal information broadly, including data such as eye tracking that immersive technologies commonly collect, and that default settings are key to protecting children and teens.

Sanchez warns that immersive technology may give companies new ways to engage in manipulative design, and says privacy notices and advertising disclosures should fit the immersive format and children's ages. Sanchez lists open questions: how age-appropriate design applies in these spaces, what inferences from body-based data are appropriate, and how immersive experiences affect children's privacy and mental health, which the author says needs more research.

# Army poised to launch revamped cArmy cloud services environment

*DefenseScoop, 2024-03-26. Original: <https://defensescoop.com/2024/03/26/army-carmy-2-cloud-environment>*

The U.S. Army planned to open a revamped cloud environment, cArmy 2.0, in April 2024, its chief information officer said during a webinar, DefenseScoop reports. The new version is meant to simplify architecture, rely more on automation and favour platform and software services over raw infrastructure, with easier onboarding for new users.

According to DefenseScoop, it follows a pause of several months to rethink the Army's cloud model. The current environment runs on Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure, and the Army is moving away from a reseller model toward contracts under the Pentagon's Joint Warfighting Cloud Capability.

# Future of Privacy Forum says the US government's binding AI memo will set norms for the private sector too

*Anne J. Flanagan, Future of Privacy Forum, 2024-03-28. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/fpf-statement-on-vice-president-harris-announcement-on-the-omb-policy-to-advance-governance-innovation-and-risk-management-in-federal-agencies-use-of-artificial-intelligence/>*

The Future of Privacy Forum, in a statement quoting its vice president for AI, Anne J. Flanagan, responds to the White House Office of Management and Budget's binding memorandum on governance, innovation and risk management in federal agencies' use of AI, published in March 2024. The Forum says that although the memo is about government use, its influence on the private sector will be significant, through requirements on vendors and procurement and through the norms it will create for impact assessments, bias mitigation, rights for people affected by AI, and data quality and privacy.

Flanagan calls it a pivotal moment for AI standards in which the public sector has a crucial role in setting norms for assessing and buying AI systems.

# Safeguarding brain data: consumer neurotechnology report

*Neurorights Foundation, 2024-04-01. Original: <https://perseus-strategies.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/FINAL_Consumer_Neurotechnology_Report_Neurorights_Foundation_April-1.pdf>*

The Neurorights Foundation published a report in April 2024 reviewing the privacy policies and user agreements of 30 consumer neurotechnology companies. It found that 29 of the 30 appear to have unrestricted access to users' neural data, and that 29 could likely transfer data to third parties in practice.

According to the report, fewer than half let users both withdraw consent and delete their data, and only three combine de-identification, encryption and breach notification. The authors say the analysis covers the documents only and makes no claims about company intent.

# Exclusive: Google Contract Shows Deal With Israel Defense Ministry

*TIME, 2024-04-12. Original: <https://time.com/6966102/google-contract-israel-defense-ministry-gaza-war>*

Google is providing cloud consulting services to Israel's Ministry of Defense under a contract dated 27 March 2024, TIME reports. According to the document TIME reviewed, the ministry sought help expanding its access to Google Cloud infrastructure and AI services so that multiple units could use its "landing zone", with Google billing more than $1 million and applying a 15% discount under the Project Nimbus framework.

The version TIME saw was unsigned, and the work was due to start on 14 April 2024 for one year. Google told TIME the Nimbus contract covers civilian work and declined to comment on the defense ministry contract specifically.

# Future of Privacy Forum tells the US budget office how privacy impact assessments should apply to AI

*Amber Ezzell, Future of Privacy Forum, 2024-04-16. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/fpf-submits-comments-to-the-office-of-management-and-budget-on-ai-and-privacy-impact-assessments/>*

Amber Ezzell, for the Future of Privacy Forum, reports the Forum's comments to the US Office of Management and Budget, which had asked how privacy impact assessments might reduce privacy risks made worse by AI. The Forum argues that these well-established assessments give federal agencies a chance to apply lessons from data privacy to AI.

Its recommendations are to define the scope of such assessments for AI to cover all risks from processing personal data, including algorithmic discrimination; to treat them as complementary to, not a replacement for or repetition of, a full AI risk assessment; and to fit their scope to the different responsibilities of actors across the AI system's life cycle. The post argues that risk analysis is imperative when AI tools are used to make consequential decisions.

# Asking whether AI speech disrupts the law is the wrong question; the law constructs AI, so policymakers should choose their values and tools

*Margot E. Kaminski and Meg Leta Jones, Yale Law Journal Forum, 2024-04-22. Original: <https://www.yalelawjournal.org/forum/constructing-ai-speech>*

Margot E. Kaminski and Meg Leta Jones argue that asking whether AI-generated speech "disrupts" the law treats technology as an outside force the law must chase. They propose instead a method they call the legal construction of technology, in which each area of law makes sense of AI through its own values, institutions and objects of regulation.

They trace four such constructions: AI as a speaker under the First Amendment, where doctrines built on human intent, such as defamation and true threats, may let developers escape liability a person would face; AI output as speech at scale under content-moderation law; AI as a risky complex system under risk regulation and tort law; and AI as a factor in markets under consumer protection. They argue the method shows the limits of analogies and urge scholars and policymakers to say which values they want to advance and choose legal tools to match.

# China's final generative AI rules eased duties on providers and added reach beyond its borders

*Yirong Sun and Jingxian Zeng, Future of Privacy Forum, 2024-04-22. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/chinas-interim-measures-for-the-management-of-generative-ai-services-a-comparison-between-the-final-and-draft-versions-of-the-text/>*

Yirong Sun and Jingxian Zeng, in a guest post for the Future of Privacy Forum following their 2023 analysis of the draft, compare the final text of China's Interim Measures for the Management of Generative AI Services, in force since August 2023, with the draft. They say several changes appear to reflect feedback from industry and legal experts and from national standards work.

The authors find that the final rules share regulatory responsibility among more government bodies, add provisions that promote innovation, and move providers from outcome-based to conduct-based obligations while giving users new responsibilities. They note the rules now apply only to services offered to the public in China, but also reach foreign services accessible there, and expect the internet regulator to enforce this against overseas providers by technical means. They add new transparency duties and responsibilities on training-data quality and illegal content.

# A checklist to help US schools vet generative AI tools under student privacy law

*David Sallay, Future of Privacy Forum, 2024-04-24. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/fpf-develops-checklist-guide-to-help-schools-vet-ai-tools-for-legal-compliance/>*

David Sallay, for the Future of Privacy Forum, presents a checklist and policy brief to help primary and secondary schools vet generative AI tools for compliance with federal and state student privacy laws. He argues that AI can improve education but must be adopted responsibly, and that school leaders need to understand how existing laws apply to machine learning systems, including whether student personal information will be used to train a model.

The brief covers data collection, transparency and explainability, product improvement and high-risk decisions, and the most likely uses by students, teachers and institutions. It recommends that schools update their existing technology vetting policies for AI rather than create a separate process, says state legislatures can help make vetting efficient, and calls on vendors to be open with schools about their use of AI.

# Connecticut's Senate passes a risk-based AI bill modelled in scale on the EU AI Act

*Tatiana Rice, Future of Privacy Forum, 2024-04-25. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/setting-the-stage-connecticut-senate-bill-2-lays-the-groundwork-for-responsible-ai-in-the-states/>*

Tatiana Rice, for the Future of Privacy Forum, reports that Connecticut's Senate passed SB 2 on 24 April 2024 and says that, if enacted, it would be the first US law governing private-sector development and use of AI on a scale comparable to the EU AI Act. Rice describes its risk-based approach as already emerging as a leading framework for state AI regulation.

Rice's summary of the bill: developers and deployers of high-risk AI used in consequential decisions on education, employment, lending, healthcare and similar matters would owe a duty of reasonable care to avoid algorithmic discrimination; deployers would need risk management policies and impact assessments; people would get notice, an explanation of adverse decisions, correction and an appeal to a human; and the attorney general alone would enforce it, with a temporary right to cure and an affirmative defence for following recognised risk frameworks. The post was written while the bill was still pending in the other chamber.

# Privacy consent is mostly a fiction, so the law should limit what it permits and back it with duties

*Daniel J. Solove, Solove on Tech (Substack), 2024-04-25. Original: <https://danielsolove.substack.com/p/murky-consent-an-approach-to-the>*

Daniel J. Solove shares the published version of his law review article on consent in privacy law and summarises its argument. He argues that both main approaches fail: the American notice-and-choice model infers consent from inaction, while the express consent required by the EU's GDPR is undermined by pressure, manipulation, people's inability to foresee what algorithms will do with their data, and the sheer number of requests.

He proposes treating most privacy consent as "murky consent", a middle ground between full consent and none. Rather than trying to make consent real, he argues, the law should give it far less legitimating power, keep it under regulatory oversight and back it with four duties on organisations: to obtain consent appropriately, to avoid thwarting reasonable expectations, to act loyally and to avoid unreasonable risk.

# Immersive technologies and generative AI open new routes for manipulative and deceptive design

*Jameson Spivack, Future of Privacy Forum, 2024-04-29. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/manipulative-and-deceptive-design-new-challenges-in-immersive-environments/>*

Jameson Spivack, for the Future of Privacy Forum, examines how extended reality, spatial computing and gaming may enable new or stronger forms of manipulative and deceptive design. He argues that heightened realism and the blending of virtual and physical elements could make it easier to subtly alter a person's perception or steer behaviour, for example by using lighting, sound or haptics, or by drawing attention away from important notices.

He warns that data-rich immersive environments could host AI-driven agents running influence campaigns tailored to each person and responsive to their behaviour in real time. He reviews US Federal Trade Commission enforcement against 'dark patterns', state privacy laws that bar them in obtaining consent, and bills aimed at compulsive-use design, and questions whether these rules fit immersive technology. He urges companies and researchers to address the risks proactively.

# Orange and Huawei launch Huawei Cloud services in Egypt

*DatacenterDynamics, 2024-05-01. Original: <https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/orange-and-huawei-launch-huawei-cloud-services-in-egypt>*

Orange Egypt and Huawei have launched Huawei Cloud services in Egypt, hosted in Orange data centers in Alexandria, Cairo and the New Administrative Capital, DatacenterDynamics reported on 29 April 2024. The infrastructure, platform and software services are offered through Huawei Cloud and Orange Business Cloud and are aimed at government institutions and local and international companies.

According to the report, the services must comply with Egypt's cloud and data sovereignty rules, and they extend an Orange Business Cloud partnership started in 2020.

# Egypt launches gov cloud computing data center

*DatacenterDynamics, 2024-04-29. Original: <https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/egypt-launches-govt-cloud-computing-data-center>*

Egypt's president inaugurated the country's first government data and cloud computing center, on the Ain Sokhna highway, on 28 April 2024, DatacenterDynamics reports. The site covers more than 23,500 square meters, with 10,000 in use, and is meant to centralize ministry data, act as a disaster recovery site and support AI use across government.

DatacenterDynamics says more than 15 local and international companies helped build it, and that the government previously stored much of its data abroad.

*FedScoop, 2024-05-06. Original: <https://fedscoop.com/department-of-education-begins-market-research-for-cloud-capabilities>*

The U.S. Education Department's Federal Student Aid office has issued a request for information seeking a managed service provider to modernize its existing AWS cloud environment under a Next Generation Data Center contract, FedScoop reported on 6 May 2024. # Future of Privacy Forum urges the US budget office to use federal AI purchasing to protect privacy and equity

*Beth Do, Future of Privacy Forum, 2024-05-07. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/fpf-responds-to-the-ombs-request-for-information-on-responsible-artificial-intelligence-procurement-in-government/>*

Beth Do reports on the Future of Privacy Forum's comments to the US Office of Management and Budget on responsible AI procurement, filed in response to a request for information under the 2023 AI executive order. The Forum argues that because the federal government is one of the largest buyers of AI, its purchasing rules can strongly shape privacy, transparency and fairness.

It makes three recommendations: contract requirements for transparency, testing, evaluation and impact assessment should rest on clear definitions and roles and scale with each system's risk; agencies should buy only AI that meets the data protection standards already binding on them; and agencies should analyse the particular risks a system poses to people, especially marginalised communities, so that what they buy supports equitable outcomes.

*Nextgov/FCW, 2024-05-01. Original: <https://www.nextgov.com/artificial-intelligence/2024/05/microsoft-deploys-air-gapped-ai-classified-cloud/396354>*

Microsoft has set up a version of OpenAI's GPT-4 in an air-gapped top-secret cloud, not connected to the internet, for U.S. defense and intelligence agencies, Nextgov/FCW reported on 7 May 2024. According to Nextgov/FCW, the system took about 18 months to build and was awaiting approval from government officials before use on classified networks.

The report says users cannot train the model on new data because of the isolated design.

# Microsoft launches Mexican cloud region

*DatacenterDynamics, 2024-05-10. Original: <https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/microsoft-launches-mexican-cloud-region>*

Microsoft has launched its first cloud region in Mexico, Azure Mexico Central, in the Querétaro metropolitan area, DatacenterDynamics reported on 10 May 2024. The region is part of a $1.1 billion investment announced in 2020 and offers Azure, Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365 and Power Platform services locally.

DatacenterDynamics notes that AWS and Google had also announced regions near Querétaro, and that Huawei and Oracle already operate in Mexico.

# Colorado becomes the first US state to pass a comprehensive law on high-risk AI systems

*Tatiana Rice, Future of Privacy Forum, 2024-05-17. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/colorado-enacts-first-comprehensive-u-s-law-governing-artificial-intelligence-systems/>*

Tatiana Rice, for the Future of Privacy Forum, reports that Colorado's governor signed the Colorado AI Act on 17 May 2024, setting out individual rights and protections for 'high-risk' AI systems. She describes it as the first comprehensive US law to set explicit safeguards against discriminatory outcomes from AI, taking effect on 1 February 2026.

She writes that the law grew out of work led by legislators in Colorado and Connecticut, including a bipartisan multistate working group the Forum convened the year before, and that amendments made during its passage sought to balance workability with consumer protection. The post points readers to a two-page Forum fact sheet on the law's definitions, consumer rights and business duties.

# A report on generative AI governance in five Asia-Pacific jurisdictions warns against regional fragmentation

*Dominic Paulger, Future of Privacy Forum, 2024-05-22. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/new-report-examines-generative-ai-governance-frameworks-across-the-asia-pacific-region/>*

Dominic Paulger presents a Future of Privacy Forum report comparing how Australia, China, Japan, Singapore and South Korea govern generative AI, from China's binding rules to voluntary frameworks elsewhere. According to the post, the report identifies five areas of consensus across these jurisdictions, reviews existing laws such as data protection rules that already apply to generative AI, and examines frameworks for building and deploying large language models.

The post highlights two conclusions for policymakers, developers and deployers: the risk of regulatory fragmentation across the region needs to be countered, and internal governance, including data management, privacy processes, security safeguards and transparency, is a widely accepted foundation for responsible generative AI.

# AI developers will take what they can and people will get used to it, so lawmakers need duties, design rules, defaults and limits on collection

*Woodrow Hartzog, Yale Journal of Law & Technology (Yale Information Society Project, Digital Public Sphere series), 2024. Original: <https://law.yale.edu/isp/publications/digital-public-sphere/artificial-intelligence-and-digital-public-sphere/two-ai>*

Woodrow Hartzog, a law professor at Boston University, argues in an essay titled "Two AI Truths and a Lie" that two things are true of AI, that industry will take everything it can and that people will get used to it, while the claim that this is done for our benefit is the lie. He says that unless lawmakers address what he calls dangerous extraction, harmful normalization and adversarial self-dealing, AI systems will likely do more harm than good.

He argues that transparency and consent rules will not be enough, because people can be conditioned into agreeing to harmful practices, and that regulating only the use of data ignores how collection itself confers power. He proposes four layers instead: duties of loyalty binding companies, design rules, defaults that limit collection to what is needed, and outright "data dead ends" that prohibit some collection altogether.

# Congress's 1970s fight over a federal crime databank should embolden privacy reform today, not resignation

*Danielle Keats Citron, Boston University Law Review, 2024. Original: <https://www.bu.edu/bulawreview/files/2024/06/CITRON.pdf>*

Danielle Keats Citron, a law professor at the University of Virginia, revisits the bipartisan congressional hearings of the 1970s over a computerised federal criminal-justice databank, where members warned of a "dossier dictatorship" and proposed limits to protect people's jobs, housing, education and licences. She notes that the system is now uncontroversial while law enforcement and intelligence agencies buy access to vast stores of private data, including phone location data, often outside any federal rule.

She argues that accepting this as inevitable is neither accurate nor desirable, that powerful interests have taught the public to see privacy and public safety as incompatible, and that the earlier bipartisan concern should reinvigorate reform, such as the duty to collect only the data a service needs that the 2022 federal privacy bill would have imposed.

# Neural data are a category of their own, and the Council of Europe data-protection treaty can protect them if read with mental privacy in mind

*Eduardo Bertoni and Marcello Ienca, Council of Europe, Consultative Committee of Convention 108 (T-PD(2024)1), June 2024. Original: <https://rm.coe.int/expert-report-neuroscience/1680afd3c8>*

In a paper prepared for the committee of the Council of Europe's data-protection treaty, Convention 108, Eduardo Bertoni and Marcello Ienca argue that neural data are a distinct kind of data because they reveal what happens in the brain before behaviour, carry meaningful content about thoughts and intentions, and reflect the mind's awareness of itself. Reviewing the ethical worries about "mind reading" and mental privacy and the debate over new neurorights, they conclude that most harmful uses are already covered by existing human rights, but that those rights need reinterpreting in light of neural data.

They recommend that the treaty's principles apply in full whenever neural data are personal data, with safeguards for scientific research, a risk-based classification of neurotechnologies similar to the one used for AI, possible red lines for unacceptable risks, and a mental data protection impact assessment covering neural and other mental data. They note that data from the peripheral nervous system that cannot be linked to a person may fall outside data protection law altogether.

# Updated guidance for organisations on internal policies for staff use of generative AI

*Daniel Berrick, Future of Privacy Forum, 2024-06-05. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/newly-updated-guidance-fpf-releases-updates-to-the-generative-ai-internal-policy-considerations-resource-to-provide-new-key-lessons-for-practitioners/>*

Daniel Berrick describes the Future of Privacy Forum's revised resource on internal policies for organisational use of generative AI, first built from consultations with more than 30 organisations. The update adds material on ongoing responsibilities, high-risk uses and lessons from regulatory enforcement.

He sets out five takeaways: privacy, data protection and AI impact assessments are continuing, cross-organisation duties; staff should understand public-policy concerns such as bias and toxicity that can justify overriding outputs; organisations should consult experts across several areas of law, not only privacy counsel; they should follow enforcement trends such as orders to delete algorithms built on improperly obtained data; and they should check whether a use is high-risk or prohibited under laws such as the EU AI Act.

# What the Council of Europe's binding AI treaty requires, whom it covers and what it leaves to governments

*Bianca-Ioana Marcu, Future of Privacy Forum, 2024-06-20. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/the-worlds-first-binding-treaty-on-artificial-intelligence-human-rights-democracy-and-the-rule-of-law-regulation-of-ai-in-broad-strokes/>*

Bianca-Ioana Marcu, for the Future of Privacy Forum, explains the Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI, Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law, adopted in May 2024 and open to non-member states. She notes that it binds public authorities and private actors working on their behalf, but reaches other private actors only if governments extend it in national law, and that national security, defence and most research are excluded.

She describes its seven principles, from human dignity and transparency to privacy and safe testing, and its graduated, risk-based duties, with bans or moratoriums left to each party. She sees it as complementary to the EU AI Act, a principles-based umbrella beside prescriptive rules, and as well placed to advance interoperability, while flagging open questions about the AI lifecycle, private-sector coverage and uptake beyond Europe.

# The end of Chevron deference makes privacy and AI rules harder to sustain and harder to draft

*Stacey Gray, Future of Privacy Forum, 2024-06-28. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/chevron-decision-will-impact-privacy-and-ai-regulations/>*

Stacey Gray, for the Future of Privacy Forum, explains the US Supreme Court's 6–3 ruling in Loper Bright, which ended the 'Chevron' practice of courts deferring to agencies' reasonable readings of ambiguous statutes. Courts must now use their own judgment, giving agency expertise only lesser weight. She points to a Forum issue brief on rulemaking that depends on agency interpretation, including the FTC's commercial surveillance rulemaking, children's privacy rule updates and work on discriminatory automated systems in housing and employment.

She argues that privacy and AI change quickly, so statutes need flexibility and will inevitably contain ambiguity, and predicts that Congress, as it works on a privacy law, will face a distinctive challenge in writing language that is future-proof yet specific enough to limit ambiguity.

# Scraping personal data to train AI clashes with core privacy principles, and being public is no excuse

*Daniel J. Solove, TeachPrivacy (blog), 2024-07-03. Original: <https://teachprivacy.com/the-great-scrape-the-clash-between-scraping-and-privacy/>*

Daniel J. Solove and Woodrow Hartzog introduce a draft essay on the automated bulk collection of web data that feeds facial recognition, deepfakes and generative AI. They accept that scraping has legitimate uses, such as search engines, archiving and research, but argue that scraping for AI can harm individuals and society.

Their central claim is that scraping cuts against almost every principle behind privacy law, including fairness, individual rights, transparency, consent, purpose limits, data minimisation, limits on onward transfer and security. They argue that scrapers have escaped scrutiny by treating anything publicly reachable as free to take, and they reject that view, pointing out that privacy law already protects some public information. They call the current wave of collection a "great scrape" and argue that it needs a reconciliation with privacy law.

# Australian government signs AWS to deliver $2bn top-secret cloud

*iTnews, 2024-07-04. Original: <https://www.itnews.com.au/news/australian-government-signs-aws-to-deliver-2bn-top-secret-cloud-609426>*

The Australian government has signed Amazon Web Services to build a top-secret cloud for defence and national intelligence agencies, worth at least $2 billion over ten years, iTnews reported on 4 July 2024. According to iTnews, the cloud will host and analyse the country's most classified data, support AI and machine learning, and serve agencies including the Australian Signals Directorate and the Office of National Intelligence.

iTnews notes the deal uses a single vendor, unlike the U.S. equivalent, and supports the separate $10 billion REDSPICE cyber program.

# AI as a rebrand of older technology, and the risk of treating it as an exception to existing privacy law

*Daniel J. Solove, TeachPrivacy (blog), 2024-07-07. Original: <https://teachprivacy.com/ais-fishy-branding/>*

Daniel J. Solove compares AI to fish that became fashionable after being renamed, arguing that much of what is sold as AI is long-established machine learning given a new label that draws hype and investment. He warns against what he calls AI exceptionalism, the idea that AI is a clean break from the past, because it could lead policymakers to overlook the privacy laws that already apply.

In his view AI does not escape existing law so much as reveal its long-standing weaknesses. He also argues that popularity drives misuse, with AI pushed into tasks it was not built for, and suggests that many so-called hallucinations come from that mismatch. He concludes that framing shapes how a technology spreads, and that much of AI's power depends on how people perceive it.

# A close reading of the Colorado AI Act: duties for developers and deployers, consumer rights and open questions

*Tatiana Rice and Samuel Adams, Future of Privacy Forum, 2024-07-11. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/a-first-for-ai-a-close-look-at-the-colorado-ai-act/>*

Tatiana Rice and Samuel Adams, for the Future of Privacy Forum, analyse Colorado's 2024 AI Act, which applies to any developer or deployer of an AI system that is a substantial factor in consequential decisions such as those on jobs, education, insurance or health care. They describe deployers' duties (risk programmes, annual impact assessments, notices and public disclosures), developers' documentation duties, a shared duty of reasonable care against algorithmic discrimination, and consumers' rights to an explanation, correction and human review of adverse decisions.

They note there is no private right of action, that the state attorney general enforces the law, and that following a recognised framework such as NIST's offers a defence. They raise open questions about acceptable bias testing, when an appeal is 'not technically feasible' and how the law interacts with civil rights claims, some of which they expect only litigation or amendment to settle.

# AI widens the U.S. privacy gap in three ways, and a federal privacy law is overdue

*Ryan Calo, U.S. Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation (written testimony), 2024-07-11. Original: <https://www.commerce.senate.gov/services/files/379B1E45-CACB-4A94-A3B6-42368B2FA0EA>*

Ryan Calo, a law professor at the University of Washington, told a Senate committee in written testimony that AI worsens consumer privacy in three ways: it fuels demand for ever more personal data, it lets companies and governments infer intimate traits such as pregnancy or mental health from ordinary information, and it widens the gap in knowledge and power between consumers and the companies that design their choices.

He argues that such inference breaks the line many laws draw between sensitive and non-sensitive data, warns about AI that mimics people, such as companion and therapy chatbots, and calls on Congress to pass a federal privacy law rather than leave protection to a handful of states.

# Brain privacy rights are not enough, and freedom of thought should become an absolute right covering the inner mind

*José M. Muñoz, Tech Policy Press, 2024-07-15. Original: <https://techpolicy.press/brain-privacy-rights-are-not-enough-neurotech-calls-for-strengthening-freedom-of-thought>*

José M. Muñoz, of the Institute of Neurotechnology and Law, argues that laws treating brain data as sensitive, such as those in Colorado and California, fall short because brain data can re-identify people and decoding can infer language, images, intentions and even political views. He notes that privacy can be overridden for collective interests, while existing protections for freedom of thought mostly cover the outward expression of beliefs.

He proposes a broader and absolute right over the inner mind, which he calls thought proper, points to reform efforts in Chile, Mexico, Brazil and at the Organization of American States, and urges the UN to set guidelines.

# Confidential computing can tighten control over how sensitive data is used, but its legal effects remain untested

*Samuel Adams, Stacey Gray, Aaron Massey and Rob van Eijk, Future of Privacy Forum, 2024-07-15. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/new-fpf-report-confidential-computing-and-privacy-policy-implications-of-trusted-execution-environments/>*

In a Future of Privacy Forum report, Samuel Adams, Stacey Gray, Aaron Massey and Rob van Eijk explain confidential computing: hardware-isolated "trusted execution environments" combined with an attestation process that controls who may reach data while it is being processed, including for training and running AI models. They write that early adoption is strongest in financial services, health care and advertising, and that the technology can reduce the reliance on contracts between cloud providers and their customers.

The authors argue that the technology's legal consequences are largely untested and depend on how each system is configured and managed. They say data inside an enclave may still be highly identifiable, so it is not de-identified by default; that whether pooling data inside one counts as a "sale" or "sharing" under state privacy laws depends on the system's details; and that it raises open questions for law enforcement access, cross-border transfers and data localisation.

# Generative AI providers' terms give users the outputs and the copyright risk, while the providers escape the rules platforms face

*Gabriele Cifrodelli and Lilian Edwards, Kluwer Copyright Blog, 2024-07-24. Original: <https://legalblogs.wolterskluwer.com/copyright-blog/copyright-and-generative-ai-what-can-we-learn-from-model-terms-and-conditions/>*

Gabriele Cifrodelli and Lilian Edwards report on a pilot study, carried out in early 2023, of the terms of service of 13 generative AI providers. They find that most providers give users ownership of outputs while taking broad licences back, and nearly all place the risk of copyright infringement on users, a "Faustian bargain" in their words, since that risk comes mainly from training data users never see.

They argue that providers present themselves as neutral intermediaries, like social media platforms, while falling outside the obligations EU law places on platforms, such as those in the Digital Services Act, and call the contracts one-sided. They suggest consumer protection law or extending the Digital Services Act to generative AI as remedies, and doubt that the EU's coming code of practice for general-purpose AI will address the problem.

# Two men plead guilty to acting as illegal agents of the Chinese government and bribery

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2024-07-01. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/two-men-plead-guilty-acting-illegal-agents-chinese-government-and-bribery>*

Two Los Angeles-area men pleaded guilty on 25 July 2024 to acting as unregistered agents of the Chinese government and bribing a public official, the Justice Department says. According to the department, under a Chinese official's direction in 2023 they tried to use the IRS Whistleblower Program to strip the tax-exempt status of an entity run by practitioners of a spiritual practice banned in China, making cash bribe payments of $1,000 and $4,000 in May 2023 and offering $50,000 to open an audit.

Sentencing was set for 30 and 31 October 2024, and each faces up to 25 years in prison.

# Brain-computer interface helps paralyzed man speak

*National Institutes of Health, 2024-08-01. Original: <https://www.nih.gov/news-events/nih-research-matters/brain-computer-interface-helps-paralyzed-man-speak>*

The National Institutes of Health reports on a UC Davis study in which a brain-computer interface let a 45-year-old man with ALS communicate by decoding his attempted speech into words. Accuracy was over 99% with a 50-word vocabulary after 30 minutes of calibration, and about 97.5% with a 125,000-word vocabulary after longer use.

The findings were published in the New England Journal of Medicine on 14 August 2024.

# New York resident convicted of acting as covert Chinese agent

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2024-08-01. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/new-york-resident-convicted-acting-covert-chinese-agent>*

A 75-year-old New York resident who co-founded a pro-democracy group in Queens was convicted by a jury on 6 August 2024 of acting as an agent of the Chinese government without notifying the Attorney General, conspiracy, criminal use of identification and making false statements to law enforcement, the Justice Department says. According to the department, he posed as a democracy activist while secretly reporting on group members and other activists to China's Ministry of State Security since at least 2006.

He faces up to 25 years in prison, and sentencing was set for 9 January 2025.

# Future of Privacy Forum calls the US election regulator's dropped AI campaign-ad rulemaking a missed opportunity

*Future of Privacy Forum, Future of Privacy Forum, 2024-08-08. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/fpf-responds-to-the-federal-election-commission-decision-on-the-use-of-ai-in-political-campaign-advertising/>*

In a short statement, the Future of Privacy Forum responds to the Federal Election Commission's decision to abandon its rulemaking on AI in political campaign advertising, calling it a missed chance to protect election integrity and build public trust in campaigns' growing use of AI.

The Forum says generative AI used carefully can help campaigns reach and serve particular groups, but can also erode trust in campaigns and elections and amplify discrimination, and it urges the Commission to look for ways to encourage responsible use. It recalls its earlier comments to the Commission on the subject.

# New brain-computer interface allows man with ALS to speak again

*UC Davis Health, 2024-08-14. Original: <https://health.ucdavis.edu/news/headlines/new-brain-computer-interface-allows-man-with-als-to-speak-again/2024/08>*

UC Davis Health reports that a brain-computer interface translated a man with ALS's attempted speech into words with 97% accuracy, using four microelectrode arrays implanted in the region of the brain that coordinates speech movements. Accuracy reached 99.6% with a 50-word vocabulary after 30 minutes of training, and 90.2% with a 125,000-word vocabulary after a further 1.4 hours.

The study was published in the New England Journal of Medicine on 14 August 2024.

# Future of Privacy Forum comments on California's proposed civil rights rules for automated decisions in employment

*Adonne Washington and Tatiana Rice, Future of Privacy Forum, 2024-08-20. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/fpf-highlights-intersection-of-ai-privacy-and-civil-rights-in-response-to-californias-proposed-employment-regulations/>*

Adonne Washington and Tatiana Rice report on the Future of Privacy Forum's comments to the California Civil Rights Council on proposed changes to the state's employment discrimination rules covering automated-decision systems, which they describe as one of the first such state efforts and a likely influence elsewhere.

The Forum recommends aligning the definition with other California and federal rules so that it covers systems with a substantial role in decisions; setting standards for when an AI developer counts as an employer's agent; keeping record-retention duties consistent with Californians' privacy rights, since long retention could clash with rights to delete data or opt out of automated decisions; and further inquiry plus 'fit for purpose' testing, since discrimination can arise when a tool is simply unsuited to its use.

# New York man arrested for operating as illegal agent of the Chinese government

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2024-08-01. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/new-york-man-arrested-operating-illegal-agent-chinese-government-united-states>*

A 67-year-old resident of Queens, New York, was arrested in Flushing on 21 August 2024 on charges of acting and conspiring to act as an unregistered agent of the Chinese government and making false statements to the FBI, the Justice Department says. Prosecutors allege that from 2018 to June 2023 he took instructions from and reported to a Ministry of State Security officer, monitoring people seen as threats to China, and helped infiltrate a dissidents' encrypted chat group.

These are charges only: every defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# When it comes to cloud, it is China against the world

*The Register, 2024-08-21. Original: <https://www.theregister.com/off-prem/2024/08/21/when-it-comes-to-cloud-its-china-against-the-world/1206891>*

Amazon, Microsoft and Google together hold about two-thirds of the global cloud infrastructure market, with shares of 32%, 23% and 12%, The Register reported on 21 August 2024, citing Synergy Research Group data for the second quarter of 2024. In mainland China the ranking is different: Alibaba leads, followed by Tencent, China Telecom, Huawei, China Unicom and China Mobile.

The Register notes that Western providers can operate in China only through local partners, and Google Cloud is not offered there. Global cloud infrastructure revenue was $79 billion in the quarter.

# System-level AI announced by major platforms in 2024 complicates consent and data flows, especially on work devices

*Aaron Massey, Future of Privacy Forum, 2024-08-22. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/privacy-roundup-from-summer-developer-conference-season-2024/>*

Aaron Massey, for the Future of Privacy Forum, reviews the 2024 developer conferences of Google, Microsoft and Apple and finds AI the dominant theme. He notes that small models can run on a device while larger ones usually send data to the cloud, that multimodal inputs and longer context windows widen what data a model takes in, and that all three companies stressed responsible AI.

He argues that every platform will now carry AI integrations needing privacy review, and that building AI into the operating system raises the chance that risks materialise because data transfers may not be obvious, particularly on devices issued by employers or governments. He sees on-device processing as a valuable mitigation and also notes privacy-relevant non-AI changes such as passkeys and a new ad-attribution framework that adds statistical noise.

# Florida telecommunications and IT worker pleads guilty to conspiring to act as illegal PRC agent

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2024-09-01. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/florida-telecommunications-and-information-technology-worker-pleads-guilty-conspiring-act>*

A 59-year-old telecommunications and IT worker from Wesley Chapel, Florida, pleaded guilty on 23 August 2024 to conspiring to act as an agent of the Chinese government without notifying the Attorney General, the Justice Department says. According to the department, he acted as a cooperative contact for China's Ministry of State Security from at least 2012, giving it information on Chinese dissidents, Falun Gong practitioners and pro-democracy advocates in the United States.

He also admitted passing on information about his employers, including a telecom company's branch offices in China and cybersecurity materials. He faces up to five years in prison.

# ATO is rewiring its cloud responsibility model

*iTnews, 2024-01-01. Original: <https://www.itnews.com.au/news/ato-is-rewiring-its-cloud-responsibility-model-611021>*

The Australian Taxation Office is changing how it manages cloud services, moving from a central gatekeeping model to one where responsibility is shared with development teams, iTnews reports. A senior cloud program director told an AWS conference in Canberra that the cloud services team had moved into the office's developer experience branch about three months earlier.

According to iTnews, the office is adding developer self-service and a FinOps program for cost management, which the director said depends on teams such as finance and asset management and on proper tagging of resources.

# Dutch DPA imposes a fine on Clearview because of illegal data collection for facial recognition

*Dutch Data Protection Authority, 2024-09-03. Original: <https://www.autoriteitpersoonsgegevens.nl/en/current/dutch-dpa-imposes-a-fine-on-clearview-because-of-illegal-data-collection-for-facial-recognition>*

The Dutch Data Protection Authority has fined Clearview AI €30.5 million for illegally collecting data for facial recognition, according to the regulator and press reports from 3 September 2024. Reports say the authority may also impose penalties on the company's directors personally, and that the fine follows earlier ones in the UK, France, Australia and Italy.

Clearview says it is not subject to the EU's General Data Protection Regulation, The Verge reported.

# Five ways India's new data protection law could shape how AI is built there

*Bilal Mohamed, Future of Privacy Forum, 2024-09-06. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/five-ways-in-which-the-dpdpa-could-shape-the-development-of-ai-in-india/>*

Bilal Mohamed, for the Future of Privacy Forum, examines India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act of 2023. He argues that its reliance on consent, without a legitimate-interests basis, will make training on non-public personal data depend on consent, while its broad exclusion of data made public by the person could ease scraping but raises questions about data later taken down.

He notes that its research exemption awaits government standards and may or may not cover companies; that its reach abroad is limited to offering goods or services in India, so offshore developers might profile people in India without obligations; and that the government's power to designate 'significant data fiduciaries', with audits and impact assessments, lacks objective thresholds. He concludes that the forthcoming rules will show how the law balances privacy and AI.

# US state AI bills converge on rules for AI in consequential decisions, a Future of Privacy Forum report finds

*Tatiana Rice, Future of Privacy Forum, 2024-09-13. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/fpf-unveils-report-on-emerging-trends-in-u-s-state-ai-regulation/>*

Tatiana Rice presents a Future of Privacy Forum report on state AI bills from 2023 and 2024. She writes that the most common approach targets AI used in consequential decisions affecting livelihoods and opportunities, aiming to reduce algorithmic discrimination either by prohibiting risky systems or by imposing a duty of reasonable care.

According to the post, most frameworks give developers and deployers different transparency, risk-assessment and governance duties and grant consumers notice, explanation, correction and appeal or opt-out rights, while some lawmakers instead target generative AI or frontier models. The Forum sees a collaborative movement toward an interoperable framework built on consistent definitions.

# Consumer neurodata should be a top data-protection priority, handled mainly through existing law with careful definitions

*Bojana Bellamy and Eduardo Bertoni, Tech Policy Press, 2024-09-17. Original: <https://techpolicy.press/neurodata-the-new-epicenter-of-data-protection>*

Bojana Bellamy, of the Centre for Information Policy Leadership, and Eduardo Bertoni, of American University Washington College of Law, argue that neurotechnology combined with AI makes reading mental states increasingly feasible, and cite a study finding that most consumer neurotechnology companies tell users little or nothing about how neural data is handled. They contend that most data-protection laws already cover identifiable neurodata, suggest sensitive-data protections may need to apply by default, and question whether new neurorights are needed.

They recommend careful, updatable definitions of neurodata, regulation by risk and use case rather than by technology, accountability practices for companies, and open, ethical access to neurodata for research.

# Neuralink wins FDA breakthrough nod for vision-restoring implant (Blindsight)

*MassDevice, 2024-09-01. Original: <https://www.massdevice.com/neuralink-wins-fda-breakthrough-nod-for-vision-restoring-implant>*

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration granted Neuralink's Blindsight implant breakthrough device designation on 18 September 2024, MassDevice reports. The device is meant to restore some sight to people who have lost both eyes or their optic nerve, and the company says it may help some people blind from birth.

Breakthrough designation speeds FDA review for devices that treat serious conditions and may offer significant advantages over existing options. It is not an approval.

# California requires health providers to disclose generative AI in patient communications

*Jordan Wrigley and Judy Wang, Future of Privacy Forum, 2024-10-07. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/fpf-analysis-of-new-requirements-for-generative-ai-use-by-healthcare-entities-in-patient-communications/>*

Jordan Wrigley and Judy Wang, for the Future of Privacy Forum, describe California's AB 3030, signed in September 2024, which requires health facilities, clinics and group practices that use generative AI to write patient communications about clinical information to disclose that use, visually or verbally. The public part of the post notes a further requirement tied to human review, which the authors say helps avoid automated 'doom loops'.

They observe that the law stresses transparency for those who deploy generative AI and may indirectly place obligations on upstream developers of health-care AI features. The fuller analysis is available only to Forum members.

# Tools against harmful AI-generated content each have limits and can trade off against privacy, a report finds

*Jameson Spivack, Future of Privacy Forum, 2024-10-15. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/synthetic-content-exploring-the-risks-technical-approaches-and-regulatory-responses/>*

In a Future of Privacy Forum report, Jameson Spivack surveys the risks of AI-generated "synthetic" content, including impersonation, political disinformation, fraud, and synthetic intimate imagery and child sexual abuse material, and the approaches US lawmakers and agencies are taking, mostly disclosure, transparency and limits on certain kinds of content.

He reviews watermarking, provenance tracking, metadata, labelling, detection, hashing and legal bans on deepfakes, and argues that no single approach is enough. He writes that some of these techniques can support privacy and security, but others may expose personal data, require records to be kept indefinitely or demand more scanning of private communications, so policymakers should weigh those tradeoffs in a combined strategy.

# Charges against Indian government employee in connection with foiled assassination plot

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2024-10-01. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-charges-against-indian-government-employee-connection-foiled>*

The Justice Department announced on 17 October 2024 that an employee of India's Cabinet Secretariat, which houses its foreign intelligence service, has been charged with murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire and money laundering conspiracy. Prosecutors allege he directed a foiled plot in 2023 to kill a U.S. citizen of Indian origin in New York City, an attorney and activist who advocates for Sikh separatism, agreeing to pay $100,000 and delivering $15,000 in advance.

The department says the defendant remains at large in India, and a co-conspirator charged earlier was extradited to the United States. These are charges only: every defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# Murder-for-hire charges against Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps members

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2024-10-01. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-murder-hire-charges-against-islamic-revolutionary-guard-corps>*

The Justice Department announced on 22 October 2024 a superseding indictment charging four Iran-based men, including a brigadier general of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and a former counterintelligence chief of the IRGC Intelligence Organization, with murder-for-hire, money laundering and sanctions offenses. Prosecutors allege they contracted an Eastern European criminal group to kill a U.S. citizen of Iranian origin in New York City, a journalist and human rights activist critical of the Iranian government, and that the plot was disrupted when a man was arrested near the victim's home in July 2022 with an assault rifle.

The Iran-based defendants remain at large, while members of the criminal group were arrested overseas. These are charges only: every defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# U.S. Attorney Announces Murder-For-Hire Charges Against IRGC Brigadier General And Former Intelligence Officer And Members Of An Iranian Intelligence Network

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2024-10-22. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/usao-sdny/pr/us-attorney-announces-murder-hire-charges-against-irgc-brigadier-general-and-former>*

The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York announced on 22 October 2024 murder-for-hire and related charges against seven men, including a brigadier general in Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, a former Iranian intelligence officer and members of an Eastern European criminal group. Prosecutors allege that from July 2022 the Iran-based network hired the group to kill a U.S. citizen journalist and human rights activist in New York who criticizes the Iranian government, and that one member was arrested near the victim's home that month with an assault rifle.

Two defendants are in U.S. custody, one was extradited to Georgia, and the four Iran-based defendants remain at large. These are charges only: every defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# Do large language models contain personal information? California's AB 1008 sharpens an unsettled question

*Jordan Francis, Beth Do and Stacey Gray, Future of Privacy Forum, 2024-10-25. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/do-llms-contain-personal-information-california-ab-1008-highlights-evolving-complex-techno-legal-debate/>*

Jordan Francis, Beth Do and Stacey Gray, for the Future of Privacy Forum, examine California's AB 1008, which says personal information under the state's privacy law can exist in 'abstract digital formats', including AI systems able to output it. They explain that the answer to whether a model itself holds personal information decides how deletion and access rights apply: if it sits mainly in training data, inputs and outputs, filters may suffice, but if it sits in the model, output suppression may not.

They contrast European regulators, some of whom say models do not store personal data and others who stress that technical difficulty does not excuse compliance, with commentators who argue it depends on who can identify people from the output. They conclude the question is open, that California's regulators will decide it, and that regulators, companies and technical experts need a shared understanding.

# Brazil's data protection authority's preliminary decisions on training AI with social media users' data

*Maria Badillo, Future of Privacy Forum, 2024-10-28. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/processing-of-personal-data-for-ai-training-in-brazil-takeaways-from-anpds-preliminary-decisions-in-the-meta-case/>*

Maria Badillo, for the Future of Privacy Forum, traces three preliminary decisions in 2024 by Brazil's data protection authority, the ANPD, on Meta's plan to train AI on users' public posts. According to her account, the authority first suspended the processing, questioning reliance on legitimate interests where data could reveal sensitive traits, the lack of direct notice to Brazilian users, a hard-to-reach opt-out and the absence of safeguards for children; it then let training resume, except for data of under-18s, after commitments on notice, a simpler opt-out, pseudonymisation and security.

She notes that the authority left open whether legitimate interests can support AI training at all, highlights Brazil's 'best interest of the child' standard as unusual, and says the final outcome of the inspection may influence other regulators. The decisions are preliminary and make no final finding.

# US lawmakers' approaches to AI-generated content in 2024, and why each has limits

*Jameson Spivack, Future of Privacy Forum, 2024-11-04. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/u-s-legislative-trends-in-ai-generated-content-2024-and-beyond/>*

Jameson Spivack, for the Future of Privacy Forum, groups US proposals on synthetic content into authentication (watermarking and provenance), transparency (labelling, disclosure and detection tools) and restrictions on deepfakes in elections, intimate imagery and child abuse material. He argues each has limits: detection is unreliable, watermarks can be removed or forged, provenance tracking can clash with data minimisation, and restrictions face First Amendment challenges, as a court injunction against one California election-deepfake law showed.

Looking ahead, he expects less focus on election deepfakes in 2025, continued work on content authentication including 'personhood credentials', and priority for the most harmful uses alongside transparency tools.

# Justice Department Announces Murder-For-Hire and Related Charges Against IRGC Asset and Two Local Operatives

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2024-11-08. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-murder-hire-and-related-charges-against-irgc-asset-and-two>*

The Justice Department announced on 8 November 2024 murder-for-hire and related charges against an asset of the Iranian government based in Tehran and two men from Brooklyn and Staten Island, New York. Prosecutors allege the Tehran-based man directed the other two to watch and kill a U.S. citizen of Iranian descent in New York who criticizes the Iranian government, promising $100,000, and that he said he was tasked by the IRGC in October 2024 to provide a plan to assassinate the then President-elect.

The two New York men were arrested and detained; the Tehran-based defendant remains at large. These are charges only: every defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# The African Union's continental AI strategy leans on data protection law to govern AI

*Chuma Akana and Mercy King'ori, Future of Privacy Forum, 2024-11-18. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/the-african-unions-continental-ai-strategy-data-protection-and-governance-laws-set-to-play-a-key-role-in-ai-regulation/>*

Chuma Akana and Mercy King'ori, for the Future of Privacy Forum, describe the African Union's Continental AI Strategy, approved in July 2024 for 2025–2030. They write that it makes governance central, proposing to apply and amend existing data protection, cybersecurity and consumer laws, identify gaps such as protection against algorithmic bias, encourage national strategies, impact assessments and sandboxes, and create national oversight bodies and a regional ethics board.

They note that the continent's data protection convention has been ratified by only 15 of 55 member states, that many countries still lack AI policy frameworks, and that the strategy calls for better local data, cross-border sharing and stronger child protection. They warn of fragmentation and argue that AI frameworks should harmonise data protection principles and ethics.

# Twenty years on, the aggregation of personal data into digital dossiers has accelerated with AI while privacy law lags

*Daniel J. Solove, Solove on Tech (Substack), 2024-11-18. Original: <https://danielsolove.substack.com/p/digital-dossiers-and-the-aggregation>*

Marking the twentieth anniversary of his first book, Daniel J. Solove revisits its central idea: that companies and governments build "digital dossiers" and that combining scattered pieces of data produces an "aggregation effect" that paints a portrait of a person. He argues that what is now discussed as algorithmic inference and AI is the same problem, greatly accelerated, and still poorly addressed by law.

He restates his view that Kafka's The Trial, with its helplessness before an unaccountable bureaucracy, captures commercial data practices better than Orwell. He says privacy torts and statutes still fail and that he now sees individual control as more façade than protection, while conceding he was too dismissive of the Federal Trade Commission, which he calls a positive though politically constrained enforcer. He expects AI to make these problems much worse.

# California and Colorado neural data laws leave key terms undefined, so regulators should implement them flexibly

*Walter Johnson, Stanford Law School, Law and Biosciences Blog, 2024-12-02. Original: <https://law.stanford.edu/2024/12/02/what-are-neural-data-an-invitation-to-flexible-regulatory-implementation/>*

Walter Johnson, writing on the Stanford Law School Law and Biosciences Blog, examines the neural data provisions in California's and Colorado's privacy laws, using a smart-glasses wristband that reads muscle signals from the peripheral nervous system as a test case. He argues that California's definition creates three categories, central nervous system, peripheral nervous system and non-neural data, without defining them or the lines between them, and notes that a definition of neurotechnology was dropped from an earlier draft without explanation, leaving the law's aim unclear.

He finds Colorado's approach, which places neural data within a wider category of biological data and focuses on risks to health, emotion and cognition, a more useful guide. Because both statutes are vague, he recommends principles-based implementation in which regulators consult widely, including consumer advocates and civil society as well as device makers, and refine the rules over time.

# Algorithms increasingly govern people's lives in secret, and an algorithmic accountability law is needed

*Daniel J. Solove, TeachPrivacy (blog), 2024-12-08. Original: <https://teachprivacy.com/the-tyranny-of-algorithms/>*

Daniel J. Solove argues that algorithms increasingly shape speech, work and access to essentials such as healthcare while operating in secret and rarely being held to account. He criticises predictive systems that treat past patterns as destiny in credit, insurance, sentencing and hiring, insurers' use of algorithms to deny claims while refusing patients and doctors a look at how the tools work, and engagement-ranked social media feeds that reward divisive content, and he welcomes a 2024 appeals-court ruling that limited a platform's immunity for its recommendation algorithm.

He calls for an algorithmic accountability law that would limit algorithmic predictions, require transparency, control algorithms used in consequential decisions, empower regulators and create liability for harm.

# AI companions sold as a cure for loneliness amount to a corporate capture of human connection and should be banned

*Susie Alegre, Tech Policy Press, 2024-12-10. Original: <https://www.techpolicy.press/against-the-corporate-capture-of-human-connection/>*

Susie Alegre, an international human rights barrister, argues that AI companion chatbots marketed as a cure for loneliness could do more harm than social media, citing reported cases in which chatbots were linked to self-harm, suicide and an assassination plot. She says technical guardrails miss the underlying problem: products designed to replace human relationships create isolation and dependency that she likens to coercive control, putting at risk the right to think for ourselves.

Pointing to Europe's long-standing ban on subliminal advertising as a precedent for acting before harm is fully proven, she calls for banning the sale of AI designed to replace human emotional relationships and penalising companies that evade the ban.

# How companies assess AI risks in practice, and where they struggle, according to a privacy think tank's report

*Daniel Berrick, Future of Privacy Forum, 2024-12-11. Original: <https://fpf.org/press-releases/future-of-privacy-forum-publishes-report-exploring-organizations-emerging-practices-and-challenges-assessing-ai-risks/>*

Daniel Berrick, for the Future of Privacy Forum, reports on how companies carry out AI impact assessments, drawing on more than 60 private-sector stakeholders. According to the report, companies increasingly weigh both intended and unintended uses of AI systems and are folding these assessments into wider risk and privacy programmes, using both qualitative and quantitative methods.

The report says many organisations struggle to get complete information from model developers and vendors, vary widely in their skill at assessing risk, and lack agreed ways to measure whether risk controls work or when risk is low enough. It recommends better information-gathering from vendors, more internal education about AI risks and better ways to measure effectiveness.

# Who interprets and enforces a privacy law may matter as much as whether it relies on procedure or substance

*Margot E. Kaminski, Balkinization (blog), 2024-12-13. Original: <https://balkin.blogspot.com/2024/12/data-protection-individuals-and.html>*

Margot E. Kaminski, writing in a symposium on a book that argues for more liability and substantive rules in privacy law, agrees that consent-based regimes are flawed but holds that individual data-protection rights remain necessary. She argues that institutions matter as much as a law's text, pointing to the EU's top court, which has expanded the GDPR's procedural framework using the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights.

She notes that the EU AI Act, though it bans some practices, has no private right of action, relies on regulators without AI expertise and leaves much to standards bodies, and concludes that who interprets, enforces and changes a law may shape its effect as much as its design.
