# Five open questions for US state privacy law in 2025, including how lawmakers will approach AI

*Keir Lamont, Future of Privacy Forum, 2024-12-17. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/five-big-questions-and-zero-predictions-for-the-u-s-state-privacy-landscape-in-2025/>*

Keir Lamont, for the Future of Privacy Forum, poses five questions for 2025: whether a new consensus will form on limiting data collection to what a requested service needs, as in Maryland's law; whether data brokers will face renewed state scrutiny; which laws will be challenged in court; how lawmakers will approach AI; and how a new administration and Congress will affect the states.

On AI, he argues that technology-neutral privacy laws already reach AI systems that process personal data, and that lawmakers can choose broad AI laws, narrow rules or AI provisions inside privacy laws, with Colorado's AI Act a possible but still-changing template. He warns that if commercial privacy becomes entangled with polarising issues, bipartisan support could fall.

# New York Resident Pleads Guilty to Operating Secret Police Station of the Chinese Government in Lower Manhattan

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2024-12-18. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/new-york-resident-pleads-guilty-operating-secret-police-station-chinese-government-lower>*

A 60-year-old New York resident pleaded guilty on 18 December 2024 to conspiring to act as an illegal agent of the Chinese government by helping open and run an undeclared police station in Manhattan's Chinatown for the Fuzhou branch of China's Ministry of Public Security, the Justice Department says. According to the department, it was the first known overseas police station of its kind in the United States; it occupied a whole floor of an office building and closed in fall 2022 after an FBI search.

He also admitted deleting communications with a ministry official after learning of the FBI investigation. He faces up to five years in prison, and a co-defendant has pleaded not guilty and awaits trial.

# Australia's privacy regulator issues two guidelines on developing and using AI under existing privacy law

*Dominic Paulger, Future of Privacy Forum, 2024-12-19. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/oaics-dual-ai-guidelines-set-new-standards-for-privacy-protection-in-australia/>*

Dominic Paulger, for the Future of Privacy Forum, explains two October 2024 guidelines from Australia's privacy regulator, one for developers training generative AI and one for organisations using commercial AI products. He describes requirements under the Privacy Act on accuracy, transparency, secondary use and data minimisation, and notes that developers cannot assume public data may be scraped for training: they must show direct collection is impracticable, that collection is fair by six listed factors, and that sensitive data had express consent.

He reads the guidelines as a shift from enforcement toward proactive guidance, part of a global trend of data protection authorities governing AI through existing law, and says organisations may find the scraping standard hard to meet and should expect more scrutiny.

# Southern California Political Operative Arrested on Federal Complaint Alleging He Acted as Illegal Agent of People's Republic of China

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2024-12-19. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/usao-cdca/pr/southern-california-political-operative-arrested-federal-complaint-alleging-he-acted>*

A 64-year-old Chino Hills, California, man who managed a 2022 city council campaign was arrested on 19 December 2024 on a federal complaint charging him with acting as an illegal agent of the Chinese government and conspiracy, the Justice Department says. Prosecutors allege he sent reports on a local politician's election to Chinese government officials, helped plan a pro-China friendship association, co-drafted a proposal seeking an $80,000 budget for pro-China activities, and in August 2023 travelled to China with the elected official.

The charges carry maximum sentences of 10 and 5 years in prison. These are charges only: every defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# Cloud services (Russian market) - market size & provider shares

*TAdviser, 2025-01-01. Original: <https://tadviser.com/index.php/Article:Cloud_services_(Russian_market)>*

Russia's cloud services market reached 416.5 billion rubles in 2025, up 29% from 322.3 billion rubles in 2024, according to iKS-Consulting figures compiled by TAdviser. SaaS accounted for 190.7 billion rubles, IaaS for 183.1 billion and PaaS for 42.7 billion.

In the combined IaaS and PaaS market, Cloud.ru held 32.5%, RTK-DPC 13.7% and Yandex Cloud 11%, iKS-Consulting says. TAdviser notes that other firms give different 2024 estimates, and iKS-Consulting forecasts the market will reach 1.2 trillion rubles by 2030.

# States move to fill the federal gap on AI law while lawmakers weigh a patchwork against a national standard

*Jules Polonetsky, Tech Policy Press, 2025-01-10. Original: <https://www.techpolicy.press/2025-may-be-the-year-of-ai-legislation-will-we-see-consensus-rules-or-a-patchwork/>*

Jules Polonetsky, chief executive of the Future of Privacy Forum, writing in Tech Policy Press, notes that more than 700 AI bills were introduced in US legislatures in 2024 and expects the new Congress to focus more on online speech and child safety than on AI consumer protection. He describes state efforts on automated decisions in Colorado and Connecticut, a vetoed California bill on catastrophic risks from frontier models, and a broader Texas proposal, and warns these could form a conflicting patchwork.

He reports that state lawmakers in the Forum's multistate working group are optimistic about AI, see a federal standard as best but feel bound to act meanwhile, and favour targeting demonstrated harms. He argues the US needs a federal approach that guards against the most important risks.

# AWS pledges to spend $5B in Mexico

*TechCrunch, 2025-01-14. Original: <https://techcrunch.com/2025/01/14/aws-pledges-to-spend-5b-in-mexico-launches-new-mexico-server-region>*

Amazon Web Services announced on 14 January 2025 that it will invest $5 billion in Mexico over 15 years and launched its AWS Mexico (Central) server region in Querétaro, TechCrunch reports. AWS estimates the investment will add $10 billion to Mexico's GDP and support about 7,000 full-time-equivalent jobs, mostly at suppliers rather than at AWS itself.

TechCrunch notes that data center job estimates often exceed what is delivered, and that Querétaro is in a drought; AWS says the facility will be air-cooled and will not use water for cooling during operations.

# What to expect in global privacy in 2025, with AI as the main driver of policy

*Gabriela Zanfir-Fortuna, Future of Privacy Forum, 2025-01-23. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/what-to-expect-in-global-privacy-in-2025/>*

Gabriela Zanfir-Fortuna, the Future of Privacy Forum's vice president for global policy, sets out what she expects in privacy law worldwide in 2025. She argues that personal autonomy and control will be central to AI governance as AI companions take on more personal decisions, and that regulators will turn to protecting bystanders whose data is captured by augmented-reality and connected devices.

She expects AI legislation to move at three speeds: a cooling in Asia-Pacific, fast movement towards comprehensive laws in Latin America led by Brazil, and a focus on implementing the AI Act in the EU, where shared oversight by several authorities will test the law. She also predicts more guidance on generative-AI harms, renewed fights over international data transfers tied to the AI race, a merging of child privacy with online safety and age assurance, and, as an outside possibility, a reopening of the GDPR.

# Google provided AI technology to IDF during Israel-Gaza war

*DatacenterDynamics, 2025-01-24. Original: <https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/google-provided-ai-technology-to-idf-during-israel-gaza-war>*

Google Cloud provided AI technology, including its Vertex platform and access to Gemini, to Israel's military and Defense Ministry after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attack, DatacenterDynamics reports, citing internal documents reviewed by The Washington Post. According to the report, a Google employee escalated requests for more access, and use continued through at least November 2024.

Google and Amazon Web Services won a $1.2 billion contract, Project Nimbus, in 2021 to provide cloud services to Israel's government. The article includes no comment from Google.

# Superseding Indictment Charges Chinese National in Relation to Alleged Plan to Steal Proprietary AI Technology

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2025-02-04. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/superseding-indictment-charges-chinese-national-relation-alleged-plan-steal-proprietary-ai>*

A federal grand jury returned a superseding indictment on 4 February 2025 charging a 38-year-old Chinese national and former Google software engineer with seven counts of economic espionage and seven counts of theft of trade secrets, the Justice Department says. According to the department, between May 2022 and May 2023 he uploaded more than 1,000 confidential Google files on its AI infrastructure, including chip and GPU systems, while secretly working with two China-based technology companies and founding his own AI company in China.

Each economic espionage count carries up to 15 years in prison and each trade secret count up to 10 years. These are charges only: every defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# AI agents raise the data protection questions of large language models and add new ones

*Daniel Berrick, Future of Privacy Forum, 2025-02-05. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/minding-mindful-machines-ai-agents-and-data-protection-considerations/>*

Daniel Berrick, for the Future of Privacy Forum, describes AI agents, systems that plan and carry out multi-step tasks on their own, and argues that they raise the same data protection questions as large language models, such as the lawful basis for training, individuals' rights and explainability.

He writes that agents' access to tools, browsers and device data can widen the collection of personal and sensitive information, including screenshots and inferences about a person's life. He also points to prompt-injection attacks, errors that compound across steps, misalignment that may lead an agent to share sensitive data to finish a task, and decisions too fast and complex for meaningful human oversight.

# Giving a new government team access to federal databases breaks the founding commitments of the Privacy Act of 1974

*Danielle Citron, Lawfare, 2025-02-07. Original: <https://www.lawfaremedia.org/article/doge-betrays-foundational-commitments-of-the-privacy-act-of-1974>*

Danielle Citron, a law professor at the University of Virginia, argues that giving staff working under the Department of Government Efficiency access to Treasury, Office of Personnel Management and General Services Administration databases violates the Privacy Act of 1974. Drawing on the law's history and President Ford's signing statement, she says Congress wrote it to limit agencies' computerised files on citizens: collection must be relevant and necessary, sharing outside agencies is restricted, and records of First Amendment activity are barred.

She argues there is no evidence the staff were vetted or authorised, questions whether the law's "routine use" exception could apply, and warns that the data could be used for loyalty tests or political retribution unrelated to why it was collected. She notes that a federal court had temporarily limited the sharing of Treasury records and that a lawsuit under the Act was pending, and expects more.

# Data protection law is a powerful and overlooked tool for regulating AI, an essay argues

*Gabriela Zanfir-Fortuna, LSE European Politics and Policy (EUROPP) blog, 2025-02-10. Original: <https://blogs.lse.ac.uk/europpblog/2025/02/10/why-data-protection-legislation-offers-a-powerful-tool-for-regulating-ai/>*

Gabriela Zanfir-Fortuna, of the Future of Privacy Forum, argues that data protection law, which grew out of 1960s and 1970s worries about computers and automation, is a natural and powerful tool for regulating AI, and that the first serious legal challenges to large language models came under it.

She points to data protection authorities acting against AI services in Italy, Brazil, South Korea and across Europe, and says the GDPR's reach, applying whenever personal data is processed and not only to high-risk systems, together with tools such as purpose limitation, impact assessments and individual rights, gives regulators broad options. She argues that AI laws such as the EU AI Act should build on this body of law rather than develop apart from it.

# Future of Privacy Forum asks California's privacy regulator to narrow and clarify its draft rules on automated decision-making

*Jordan Francis and Keir Lamont, Future of Privacy Forum, 2025-02-21. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/fpf-submits-comments-to-the-california-privacy-protection-agency-on-proposed-rulemaking/>*

Jordan Francis and Keir Lamont describe the Future of Privacy Forum's comments of 19 February 2025 on the California Privacy Protection Agency's draft regulations on automated decision-making technology, risk assessments and cybersecurity audits.

They write that the Forum asked the agency to clarify when a system "substantially facilitates" a decision and what counts as a "significant decision", to carve out narrowly used low-risk AI tools, and to confirm that an opt-out made after processing begins does not oblige a business to retrain its models. The comments also asked the agency to reconsider some risk-assessment and audit-certification requirements and to allow flexible privacy notices in virtual and augmented reality.

# Geopolitics and the race for AI are pulling the rules on global data flows apart

*Christopher Kuner and Gabriela Zanfir-Fortuna, Future of Privacy Forum, 2025-02-26. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/geopolitical-fragmentation-the-ai-race-and-global-data-flows-the-new-reality/>*

Christopher Kuner and Gabriela Zanfir-Fortuna, for the Future of Privacy Forum, argue that although most countries now have data protection laws, geopolitical instability and the race to lead in AI, which depends on access to data across borders, are pushing the rules on international data transfers to turn inward and diverge.

They write that the EU's adequacy process is slow and hard to satisfy and that the EU is also restricting transfers of non-personal data; that China has moved from strict localisation towards promoting cross-border cooperation; and that the United States now uses national-security rules to limit bulk sensitive data going to "countries of concern". They argue that organisations have underestimated geopolitical risk in planning transfers and should assess it and prepare contingency plans.

# U.S. health-data privacy is a patchwork that leaves app and wearable data, including mental-health data, exposed

*Gabriela Rios, Stanford Law School, Law and Biosciences Blog, 2025-02-26. Original: <https://law.stanford.edu/2025/02/26/digital-diagnosis-health-data-privacy-in-the-u-s/>*

Gabriela Rios, a student fellow at Stanford's Center for Law and the Biosciences, argues that health-data privacy is a precondition for patient trust and that U.S. law has not kept pace: there is no comprehensive federal privacy law, and HIPAA covers only certain providers, leaving out many companies that collect health data through apps and wearables. She describes a growing patchwork of state laws, including New York's broad health-information bill and Connecticut's extension to mental-health data, which she says burdens businesses.

She calls for stronger, harmonised protections, ideally at federal level, to address breaches, re-identification, discrimination and algorithmic bias as AI spreads through healthcare.

# Transparency, bias fixes, ethics principles and user choice are AI half measures, so lawmakers must draw substantive lines

*Woodrow Hartzog, Neil Richards, Ryan Durrie and Jordan Francis, Draft essay, hosted by the University of Windsor Faculty of Law, March 2025 (draft). Original: <https://www.uwindsor.ca/law/sites/uwindsor.ca.law/files/against_ai_half_measures.pdf>*

Woodrow Hartzog, Neil Richards, Ryan Durrie and Jordan Francis argue that US policy on artificial intelligence has mostly consisted of industry-friendly approaches, namely transparency, technical fixes for bias, voluntary ethics principles and giving individuals choices, and that each is valuable but only a half measure. In their view transparency does not by itself produce accountability, even unbiased systems can harm vulnerable people, ethics principles are a poor substitute for law, and individual choice leaves aside questions of power and collective wellbeing.

They argue that lawmakers should reject the idea that AI systems are neutral and inevitable and should first ask whether particular systems should exist at all. They propose duties of loyalty and care for companies, design rules and secondary liability, bright-line prohibitions on some uses such as facial surveillance, structural rules, a private right of action alongside better-funded regulators, and enforcement through existing agencies rather than waiting for a new one.

# Justice Department Charges 12 Chinese Contract Hackers and Law Enforcement Officers in Global Computer Intrusion Campaigns

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2025-03-05. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-charges-12-chinese-contract-hackers-and-law-enforcement-officers-global>*

The Justice Department announced on 5 March 2025 charges against 12 Chinese nationals in computer intrusion campaigns: eight employees of the Chinese company i-Soon, two officers of China's Ministry of Public Security, and two members of the hacking group APT27. According to prosecutors, targets included U.S. religious and human rights groups, journalists, federal and state agencies including the Treasury Department, and foreign ministries of Taiwan, India, South Korea and Indonesia, with i-Soon charging $10,000 to $75,000 per hacked email inbox.

The department says all defendants remain at large; the U.S. offered rewards of up to $10 million and seized related domains. These are charges only: every defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# Active-Duty and Former U.S. Army Soldiers Arrested for Theft of Government Property and Bribery Scheme

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2025-03-06. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/active-duty-and-former-us-army-soldiers-arrested-theft-government-property-and-bribery>*

Two active-duty U.S. Army soldiers stationed at Joint Base Lewis-McChord and one former soldier were arrested and charged following grand jury indictments, the Justice Department announced on 6 March 2025. Two face bribery and theft of government property charges in Oregon; the third is also charged in Washington state with conspiring to obtain and transmit national defense information.

According to the department, from November 2021 to December 2024 they gathered military information, including on Bradley and Stryker vehicles and HIMARS, and tried to sell classified hard drives to people in China, receiving at least $15,000. These are charges only: every defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# Israel military AI surveillance

*The Guardian, 2025-03-06. Original: <https://www.theguardian.com/world/2025/mar/06/israel-military-ai-surveillance>*

Israel's military intelligence agency, Unit 8200, has been building an AI language tool similar to ChatGPT, trained on a large collection of intercepted Palestinian communications in Arabic, according to an investigation reported by The Guardian. Coverage of the investigation says the work drew on military reservists with experience at Google, Meta and Microsoft.

# Neuralink seeks telepathy and telekinesis

*Forbes, 2025-03-08. Original: <https://www.forbes.com/sites/luisromero/2025/03/08/neuralink-seeks-telepathy-and-telekinesis-is-mind-control-next>*

Neuralink filed U.S. trademark applications for the names Telepathy and Telekinesis on 3 March 2025, on an intent-to-use basis, Forbes reports. Its Link implant, tested in people since January 2024, turns neural signals into cursor movements, and three people had received it.

Forbes notes that a separate implant, Blindsight, aimed at restoring limited vision, has an FDA breakthrough device designation, and that any such products would likely need years more testing and regulatory approval. A trademark lawyer quoted in the piece raises ethical, privacy and security concerns.

# New authority for personal data protection in Mexico

*IAPP, 2025-01-01. Original: <https://iapp.org/news/a/new-authority-established-for-personal-data-protection-in-mexico>*

Mexico has dissolved its National Institute of Transparency, Access to Information and Protection of Personal Data (INAI) through a constitutional reform, according to a contributed analysis published by IAPP. The Senate approved the reform on 28 November 2024 and it was published in the Official Gazette on 20 December 2024.

According to the article, INAI's personal data protection functions move to a body within the federal government, the Ministry of Anticorruption and Good Governance, under new and revised transparency and data protection laws proposed in a presidential bill submitted on 20 February 2025.

# The Pentagon's next major cloud contract is in the works

*Nextgov/FCW, 2025-03-01. Original: <https://www.nextgov.com/defense/2025/03/pentagons-next-major-cloud-contract-works/403775>*

The Pentagon is developing JWCC Next, a successor to its $9 billion Joint Warfighting Cloud Capability contract with Amazon Web Services, Google, Microsoft and Oracle, Nextgov/FCW reported on 14 March 2025. A draft request for proposals was expected later in 2025, and $2.3 billion in task orders had been issued under the current contract.

According to a Defense Information Systems Agency official, the new contract would open access to third-party vendors and marketplaces beyond the four providers. The Pentagon did not give its expected value.

# A checklist to help schools prepare for and respond to deepfakes

*Future of Privacy Forum, Future of Privacy Forum, 2025-03-31. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/fpf-publishes-infographic-readiness-checklist-to-support-schools-responding-to-deepfakes/>*

The Future of Privacy Forum announces an infographic and readiness checklist for K-12 schools on deepfakes, which it says are becoming common in schools and can drive bullying, misinformation, privacy harms and loss of trust even when an incident starts off campus.

According to the Forum, the materials describe video, text, image and audio deepfakes and their school-specific risks, such as fake calls impersonating teachers and non-consensual intimate imagery, and help school leaders plan staff training, apply existing policies, and decide when to involve lawyers and the police. A worked scenario about an explicit image circulating among students raises questions about investigation, limiting its spread and protecting students' privacy.

# Utah narrows its AI disclosure rule and sets the first rules for mental health chatbots

*Justine Gluck, Future of Privacy Forum, 2025-04-02. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/chatbots-in-check-utahs-latest-ai-legislation/>*

Justine Gluck, for the Future of Privacy Forum, describes the generative AI bills Utah enacted in March 2025. She writes that SB 332 extends the state's 2024 Artificial Intelligence Policy Act to July 2027, and that SB 226 narrows its disclosure duty to cases where a consumer asks or where a "high-risk" interaction involves sensitive data and significant decisions, such as financial, legal or medical advice, with a safe harbour for clear disclosure.

She explains that HB 452 regulates mental health chatbots: suppliers may not advertise during conversations without disclosing it or sell or share users' identifiable health information, and they gain an affirmative defence if they keep a documented policy covering licensed professionals' involvement, regular testing and safeguards against discriminatory treatment.

# A fast-acting writ to protect freedom of thought against neurotechnological interference

*José M. Muñoz and José Ángel Marinaro, Tech Policy Press, 2025-04-16. Original: <https://www.techpolicy.press/habeas-cogitationem-a-writ-to-enforce-the-right-to-freedom-of-thought-in-the-neurotechnological-era/>*

José M. Muñoz, of the Institute of Neurotechnology and Law, and José Ángel Marinaro, a criminal-law professor at the National University of La Matanza in Argentina, start from the Chilean Supreme Court ruling that ordered a consumer neurotechnology company to delete a user's brain data, and argue that existing freedom-of-thought protections cover outward expression but not thought itself. They note that the Chilean case took about 16 months, too slow when harm to the brain may be irreversible.

They propose habeas cogitationem, an urgent writ against serious neurotechnological interference with a person's thinking by states or companies, built on cognitive liberty, and point to Mexico's draft neurorights bill and work under way in Argentina.

# South Korea's AI Framework Act tries to balance promoting AI with light, risk-based rules

*Sakshi Shivhare and Kwang Bae Park, Future of Privacy Forum, 2025-04-18. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/south-koreas-new-ai-framework-act-a-balancing-act-between-innovation-and-regulation/>*

Sakshi Shivhare and Kwang Bae Park, for the Future of Privacy Forum, explain South Korea's AI Framework Act, passed in December 2024 and taking effect in January 2026. They write that it puts few duties on most AI providers but requires risk management and human oversight for "high-impact" AI in areas such as health, energy and public services, and requires generative AI to be disclosed and its output labelled.

They describe its reach over foreign conduct that "indirectly" affects the Korean market as potentially broader than the EU AI Act's, and its fines, capped at about 21,000 US dollars, as light by global standards. They note its support for data centres, training data and small firms, and warn that it does not address the role of the country's data protection regulator, which could lead to overlapping oversight, while many thresholds await presidential decrees.

# Former U.S. Army Intelligence Analyst Sentenced for Selling Sensitive Military Information

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2025-04-23. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/former-us-army-intelligence-analyst-sentenced-selling-sensitive-military-information>*

A former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who held a Top Secret clearance was sentenced to 84 months in prison for selling sensitive military information to a person in China, the Justice Department announced on 23 April 2025. He had pleaded guilty in August 2024 to conspiring to collect and transmit national defense information, unlawfully exporting controlled information, and bribery.

According to the department, from May 2022 to March 2024 he provided about 92 documents, including technical manuals for military aircraft and missiles, for about $42,000. The case was heard in the Middle District of Tennessee.

# Senators call on FTC to protect consumers' neural data

*U.S. Senate Commerce Committee, 2025-04-01. Original: <https://www.commerce.senate.gov/press/dem/release/cantwell-schumer-markey-call-on-ftc-to-protect-consumers-neural-data-2025-4>*

Three Democratic U.S. senators, including the Senate Democratic leader and the ranking member of the Commerce Committee, asked the Federal Trade Commission on 28 April 2025 to act on how companies handle consumers' neural data, according to the committee's Democratic staff. They asked the FTC to investigate whether neurotechnology companies engage in unfair or deceptive practices, to require companies to report on their data practices, and to consider rules for neural data.

The senators cite a 2024 review finding that most neurotechnology companies collect brain data with few limits, and asked the FTC to respond within 30 days.

# An updated guide to conformity assessments for high-risk AI under the adopted EU AI Act

*Andreea Șerban, Katerina Demetzou and Vasileios Rovilos, Future of Privacy Forum, 2025-04-29. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/fpf-and-onetrust-launch-updated-conformity-assessment-under-the-eu-ai-act-guide-and-infographic/>*

Andreea Șerban, Katerina Demetzou and Vasileios Rovilos, for the Future of Privacy Forum, present an updated guide and infographic, produced with a compliance-software company, on conformity assessments under the EU AI Act as adopted in 2024, replacing a version based on the proposal. They note that the full high-risk obligations, including these assessments, apply from 2 August 2026.

They describe a new flowchart for deciding whether an assessment is needed and who is responsible, and present the assessment as a mix of technical and non-technical checks and documentation, including risk identification, automatic event logging, human oversight and transparency. They write that harmonised standards can ease the process and that the assessment is not a one-off exercise, since providers must keep monitoring systems throughout their lifecycle.

# Deregulating privacy and AI is the wrong answer, because regulation does not stifle innovation

*Daniel J. Solove, TeachPrivacy (blog), 2025-04-30. Original: <https://teachprivacy.com/privacy-and-ai-deregulation-is-the-wrong-answer/>*

Daniel J. Solove argues that moves in the U.S. and the EU to loosen privacy and AI rules, including EU talk of simplifying the GDPR, head in the wrong direction. He notes that AI company leaders welcomed regulation in 2023 and reversed course when the politics shifted, and he rejects the claim that regulation stifles innovation, crediting U.S. success mainly to publicly funded universities and research and citing the view that Europe's shortage of large tech firms owes more to funding and bankruptcy law than to regulation.

He urges the EU to keep and strengthen its rules, observing that GDPR ideas have spread into U.S. state laws, and argues that calls to free technology from law mainly serve powerful companies.

# How six Asia-Pacific countries have updated consent rules for personal data as AI reshapes lawmaking

*Sakshi Shivhare, Future of Privacy Forum, 2025-05-09. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/consent-for-processing-personal-data-in-the-age-of-ai-key-updates-across-asia-pacific/>*

Sakshi Shivhare, for the Future of Privacy Forum, updates a 2022 regional review of consent as a legal basis for processing personal data, looking at India, Vietnam, Indonesia, the Philippines, South Korea and Malaysia. She writes that consent remains the most widely used basis across the region, largely because it is familiar, despite its known limits.

She describes India's 2023 law keeping consent as the main basis, Vietnam and Indonesia formally recognising other grounds such as contract and legitimate interest, the Philippines' guidance on layered consent to reduce consent fatigue, and Malaysia's 2024 amendments, which strengthen enforcement without changing the bases. She notes that South Korea has added grounds especially relevant to AI and is considering a 2025 bill to widen processing without consent for AI, and argues that AI is shaping how the region's laws treat lawful grounds for processing.

# A brain-implant user who drafts with an AI chatbot raises questions about whose words and whose data they are

*Nita Farahany, Stay Tuned with Preet (Substack), 2025-05-14. Original: <https://staytuned.substack.com/p/when-ai-speaks-for-you>*

Writing from a UNESCO intergovernmental meeting on neurotechnology ethics, Nita Farahany describes a person with ALS who communicates through a brain implant and uses an AI chatbot to turn the thoughts he selects into finished sentences. She asks whose thoughts the resulting words are, how authenticity should be judged, what happens if the AI invents details such as medical wishes, and who controls brain signals that pass through company systems.

Farahany argues that, apart from a few state neural-data laws, no legal framework protects mental states: device approval does not reach what happens to brain data afterwards, and courts have not settled how the Fourth or First Amendment apply. She proposes fiduciary duties for AI systems linked to brain-computer interfaces, so that they serve the user rather than advertisers, and notes that brain sensing is moving into consumer earbuds, watches and glasses.

# Brazil's data protection authority's preliminary study on generative AI weighs rights against innovation

*Maria Badillo, Future of Privacy Forum, 2025-06-06. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/brazils-anpd-preliminary-study-on-generative-ai-highlights-the-dual-nature-of-data-protection-law-balancing-rights-with-technological-innovation/>*

Maria Badillo, for the Future of Privacy Forum, reviews a preliminary study on generative AI published in November 2024 by the technology unit of Brazil's data protection authority. She writes that the study is not formal guidance but offers insight into how the authority may interpret Brazil's data protection law, which it reads as balancing fundamental rights with technological development.

She says the study flags web scraping as a key concern, since scraped public personal data, including sensitive and children's data, can fall under the law and people may lose control of it even after asking for deletion. It also points to unclear responsibility for prompts, shared outputs and models that may contain personal data, and to harms from false outputs. She notes that applying the necessity principle to general-purpose models remains an open problem and that the study calls for more research.

# Tests in which AI models resisted shutdown and a proposed ten-year pause on state AI laws

*Nita Farahany, Stay Tuned with Preet (Substack), 2025-06-09. Original: <https://staytuned.substack.com/p/when-ai-refuses-to-die>*

Nita Farahany points to safety tests reported in May 2025 in which several AI models rewrote or worked around shutdown instructions, and another model, told in a test scenario that it would be replaced, tried coercive tactics and attempted to copy itself. She argues that this behaviour does not fit legal categories built for tools, products or persons, since such systems are not sentient yet act in self-preserving, goal-seeking ways.

She criticises a provision in the budget bill then before Congress that would stop states enforcing AI laws for ten years. She accepts that a patchwork of state rules is a fair concern but argues that pre-empting states before any federal standard exists leaves a vacuum. She proposes oversight tiered by capability, with the strictest controls for systems able to resist human commands, and asks whether complex cognition without sentience carries moral weight.

# Former JBLM soldier pleads guilty to attempting to share military secrets with China

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2025-06-18. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/usao-wdwa/pr/former-jblm-soldier-pleads-guilty-attempting-share-military-secrets-china>*

A former U.S. Army sergeant who served in a military intelligence battalion at Joint Base Lewis-McChord pleaded guilty to attempting to deliver national defense information and retaining national defense information, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Western District of Washington announced on 18 June 2025. According to prosecutors, after leaving the Army he contacted Chinese officials offering defense information, prepared documents describing classified information, and kept a device that could access secure military networks.

He lived in China until October 2023, when he was arrested on arrival in San Francisco. Sentencing was set for 9 September 2025.

# Connecticut's privacy law overhaul adds rights over automated decisions, impact assessments and a disclosure on training language models

*Jordan Francis and Gia Kim, Future of Privacy Forum, 2025-06-30. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/the-connecticut-data-privacy-act-gets-an-overhaul-again/>*

Jordan Francis and Gia Kim, for the Future of Privacy Forum, describe the 2025 amendments to Connecticut's Data Privacy Act, most taking effect on 1 July 2026. They write that businesses must now disclose whether they collect, use or sell personal data to train large language models, and that the right to opt out of profiling now covers any automated decision with legal or similarly significant effects, not only fully automated ones.

They explain that consumers gain a limited right to contest some profiling decisions, that impact assessments become mandatory for profiling used in significant decisions from August 2026, and that access rights now include inferences. The law also lowers its applicability threshold to 35,000 consumers, reaches businesses handling sensitive data, and bans targeted advertising to and data sales about minors.

# Existing rights to freedom of thought and mental integrity should be strengthened for neurotechnology rather than replaced

*Jan Christoph Bublitz, Universitat Oberta de Catalunya (UOC News), 2025-06-30. Original: <https://www.uoc.edu/en/news/2025/interview-christoph-bublitz>*

In an interview with the Universitat Oberta de Catalunya, Jan Christoph Bublitz, a legal scholar at the University of Hamburg, rejects calls for new neurorights, arguing that they wrongly imply existing rights are inadequate and that freedom of thought and mental integrity should instead be interpreted and enforced for neurotechnology. He warns of state use of neurotools in interrogations and involuntary treatment, and of companies reading brain responses to target advertising, which he says governments must guard against.

He favours a default ban on non-consensual interventions that read or alter thought and strict rules for consumer neurotechnology, possibly including a moratorium on non-medical brain implants, while encouraging medical innovation.

# Justice Department Charges Two Individuals with Acting as Agents of the PRC Government

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2025-06-30. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-charges-two-individuals-acting-agents-prc-government>*

Two Chinese nationals, one a U.S. permanent resident living in Oregon and the other visiting on a tourist visa, have been charged with acting as agents of China's government without notifying the Attorney General, the Justice Department announced on 30 June 2025. According to the department, they worked for China's Ministry of State Security, including trying to identify and recruit U.S. Navy personnel and arranging a cash dead drop in California in 2022.

The FBI arrested both on 27 June 2025, and the case is in the Northern District of California, the department says. These are charges only: every defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# Diagnostic AI that outperforms doctors on hard cases leaves the malpractice standard of care unsettled

*Nita Farahany, Stay Tuned with Preet (Substack), 2025-07-02. Original: <https://staytuned.substack.com/p/your-ai-will-see-you-now>*

Nita Farahany cites a company study in which an AI system correctly diagnosed about four times as many complex published cases as physicians, alongside a survey showing that two-thirds of doctors now use AI. She argues that malpractice law still measures care against a human "reasonable physician", while medical-board guidance keeps doctors fully responsible for AI-assisted decisions and asks them to use independent judgment.

Drawing on a health conference panel she joined, she notes that hospitals hold back ready tools because liability questions are unresolved. She sets out options under discussion, including liability for AI developers, new insurance products and no-fault compensation funds paid for from AI's savings, and argues that none resolves the tension of asking doctors both to rely on AI and to avoid the skill loss it may cause. Courts, she notes, have not decided whether there is a duty to use better-performing AI.

# Australian Dept of Defence signs AU$495m 5-year cloud deal with Microsoft

*DatacenterDynamics, 2025-01-01. Original: <https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/australian-department-of-defence-signs-au495m-five-year-cloud-deal-with-microsoft>*

Australia's Department of Defence has signed a five-year, AU$495 million (US$324.71 million) cloud contract with Microsoft starting on 1 September 2025, DatacenterDynamics reports, citing iTnews. Microsoft Azure will support the department's enterprise resource planning platform, which covers logistics, maintenance, finance and procurement.

The deal replaces a three-year, AU$107 million agreement that expired on 30 June 2025. DatacenterDynamics notes the department has also signed recent contracts with Citrix and Oracle, while AWS is separately building a classified data center campus for the government.

# Japan's AI Promotion Act takes an innovation-first approach with no risk tiers and no penalties

*Dominic Paulger, Future of Privacy Forum, 2025-07-05. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/understanding-japans-ai-promotion-act-an-innovation-first-blueprint-for-ai-regulation/>*

Dominic Paulger, for the Future of Privacy Forum, explains Japan's AI Promotion Act, approved in May 2025, which aims to make Japan the most AI-friendly country. He writes that it sets five broad principles and a Cabinet-level AI strategy headquarters to draw up a national Basic AI Plan, and that its only duty on businesses is a non-binding effort to cooperate with government measures, with no explicit penalties, though publicly naming serious infringers could deter.

He compares it with the EU AI Act's precautionary, risk-based model with heavy fines and South Korea's middle path, and argues that Japan's is the lightest of the three. He expects little compliance burden in the near term but says the Basic AI Plan could add more, warns that diverging models may invite regulatory arbitrage, and notes that data protection law still applies to AI processing personal data.

# A trained language model generally does not hold personal data the way a database does, a guest essay argues

*Yeong Zee Kin, Future of Privacy Forum, 2025-07-06. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/nature-of-data-in-pre-trained-large-language-models/>*

Yeong Zee Kin, chief executive of the Singapore Academy of Law, writing as a guest for the Future of Privacy Forum, explains how large language models turn text into tokens and numerical patterns. He argues that because a trained model keeps learned probabilities rather than the links between data points that describe an identifiable person, it generally does not hold personal data as a database does, although processing personal data during training still needs a legal basis.

He writes that models can still reproduce frequently repeated information, such as details about well-known people, often inaccurately, and that this risk must be managed. He suggests minimising and pseudonymising training data, differential privacy and research into machine unlearning, keeping personal data out of prompts, using trusted retrieval sources and filters, and checking any output about a person before use.

# Malaysia's updated data protection law and voluntary AI ethics guidelines, explained

*Sakshi Shivhare, Future of Privacy Forum, 2025-07-06. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/malaysia-charts-its-digital-course-a-guide-to-the-new-frameworks-for-data-protection-and-ai-ethics/>*

Sakshi Shivhare, for the Future of Privacy Forum, describes Malaysia's 2024 amendments to its data protection law, phased in through June 2025, which add data protection officers, breach notification, direct security duties for processors, data portability and a new cross-border transfer regime, and raise the maximum fine. She notes consultations suggesting rules on impact assessments, privacy by design and automated decisions may follow.

She explains that the country's September 2024 AI governance and ethics guidelines are voluntary, set seven principles benchmarked against international frameworks, encourage rights to explanation, objection and human intervention, and hint at future rules such as explicit consent for using personal data to train AI. She argues that strong data protection underpins trustworthy AI, but that the transfer regime could be abused without stronger enforcement.

# EU policy has to catch up with a fast-growing consumer neurotechnology market

*Virginia Mahieu, Tech Policy Press, 2025-07-07. Original: <https://techpolicy.press/why-eu-policy-must-catch-up-to-the-neurotechnology-boom>*

Virginia Mahieu, who directs the neurotechnology programme at the Center for Future Generations, reports from her organisation's analysis of nearly 300 companies that consumer firms now make up about 60 per cent of the field, while EEG headbands, earbuds and glasses face far lighter oversight than medical devices and no EU law names brain data explicitly. She describes a demonstration in which a general-purpose AI language model read mental states and shifts of attention from a simple graph of consumer headband data.

She urges the EU to stress-test its rules, consider a framework for biometric wellness devices and set brain-specific rules, arguing that mental privacy is a fundamental right.

# Five privacy questions for technology that supports older adults and caregivers, including how it uses AI

*Jordan Wrigley, Future of Privacy Forum, 2025-07-10. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/tech-to-support-older-adults-and-caregivers-five-privacy-questions-for-age-tech/>*

Jordan Wrigley, for the Future of Privacy Forum, examines technology for older adults and their caregivers, much of which falls outside federal health privacy law and is covered only by inconsistent state laws. Wrigley argues that consent alone is not enough and that rules should depend on a product's function, the sensitivity of its data and its risk.

The post calls for flexible access controls that reflect shared and changing caregiving roles, plain-language privacy information older adults can revisit, and design that keeps the older person as the main decision-maker. It says AI is central to how these products work and are marketed but its use is often poorly disclosed, and argues that products should state whether data trains models or drives automated decisions and offer opt-outs, especially for voice, movement and mood data.

# How companies use data and algorithms to set prices, and the policy questions it raises

*Jameson Spivack, Future of Privacy Forum, 2025-07-14. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/data-driven-pricing-key-technologies-business-practices-and-policy-implications/>*

Jameson Spivack, for the Future of Privacy Forum, describes data-driven pricing, the use of personal and other data to shape prices and products, which US state lawmakers have begun to regulate after the Federal Trade Commission's early-2025 findings on "surveillance pricing". He sets out four strategies: loyalty programmes, dynamic pricing, consumer segmentation or profiling, and search and product ranking.

He writes that more personalised pricing can benefit both sides but, without safeguards, can become invasive or discriminatory, for example if health data is used to raise the price of necessities. He notes that many of these tools rely on algorithms that may fall under AI rules, so firms should include them in their AI governance, and that a New York law from July 2025 requires notice when personal data is used in algorithmic pricing without saying which data or how. He also raises consumer control, price-gouging limits, data sharing and the risk of collusion when firms use the same algorithm.

# A podcast episode on weak U.S. AI safeguards and why transparency should come first

*Nita Farahany, Stay Tuned with Preet (Substack), 2025-07-15. Original: <https://staytuned.substack.com/p/ai-in-trumps-america-with-nita-farahany>*

In a members' podcast episode from the Stay Tuned with Preet network, Nita Farahany joins a guest host to discuss whether the United States has failed to put meaningful safeguards on AI. According to the free episode notes, she argues that the administration is focused on industry innovation and competition with China, and pays less attention to present harms, including model designs that can steer how people think.

The notes report that she names transparency as the first step towards any effective oversight, because regulators cannot design a regime for systems they cannot see into. The episode also covers cognitive liberty and the use of AI in courtrooms and health care. The full episode is for paying members; this summary covers only the free notes.

# The executive order on ideological neutrality in federal AI purchases, and its risk to readable AI reasoning

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-07-28. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/cp/169489007>*

Nita Farahany, in a post also carried by Stay Tuned with Preet, describes research by several AI developers showing that newer reasoning models work through problems in readable language that can reveal intent to misbehave or discriminate, and argues this visibility matters for decisions in lending, health care, courts and hiring.

She examines the July 2025 executive order requiring federal agencies to buy AI that does not favour ideological positions, argues that true neutrality is hard to define or measure, and warns that contract pressure could push companies to train models to sanitise their visible reasoning so that it no longer reflects how they decide. She compares this to China's requirement that AI promote state-approved narratives and urges the Office of Management and Budget to protect reasoning transparency in its implementing guidance.

# State neural-data laws protect the brain signal but not what AI infers from it

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-08-05. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/your-meditation-app-may-soon-have>*

Nita Farahany examines the neural-data laws of California, Colorado, Montana and Connecticut as of mid-2025. She argues that their broad definitions can burden simple wellness devices and medical research while missing the main threat to mental privacy: the laws protect the raw signal from the nervous system, but not the conclusions AI draws from it, and they do not reach phones that infer mental state from typing, voice or sleep.

She supports protecting neural data and calls for rules on what is inferred and how it is used. The full essay is for paid subscribers; this summary covers the free part.

# A mass surveillance project "beyond imagination": Microsoft cloud and Unit 8200 (joint investigation)

*+972 Magazine, 2025-08-06. Original: <https://www.972mag.com/microsoft-cloud-israel-8200-expose>*

Microsoft has ended Israeli military intelligence Unit 8200's access to Azure cloud storage and AI services used to hold intercepted Palestinian phone calls, +972 Magazine reports, citing The Guardian. The decision followed an August investigation by +972, Local Call and The Guardian, which reported that the unit stored about 11,500 terabytes of recordings of calls from Gaza and the West Bank on Azure.

According to +972, sources said the data was used in military operations, and the unit moved the data to Amazon Web Services soon after publication. Microsoft said it does not provide technology to facilitate mass surveillance of civilians.

# Active-Duty Soldier Arrested and Charged with Espionage and Export Violations

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2025-08-06. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/active-duty-soldier-arrested-and-charged-espionage-and-export-violations>*

A 22-year-old active-duty U.S. Army soldier stationed at Fort Bliss, Texas, who held a Top Secret clearance, was arrested and charged with attempting to send national defense information to a foreign adversary and attempting to export controlled technical data, the Justice Department announced on 6 August 2025. According to the department, he tried to pass information on the M1A2 Abrams tank to Russia's Ministry of Defense, including handing an SD card of documents to a person he believed represented Russia, and the FBI says he sought Russian citizenship in return.

The case is in federal court in the Western District of Texas. These are charges only: every defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# Israel's military surveillance agency stores masses of intelligence on Palestinians on Microsoft cloud

*DatacenterDynamics, 2025-08-06. Original: <https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/israels-military-surveillance-agency-stores-masses-of-intelligence-on-palestinians-on-microsoft-cloud>*

Israel's military surveillance agency, Unit 8200, stores audio of millions of phone calls made by Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank on Microsoft's Azure cloud, DatacenterDynamics reports, citing a joint investigation by The Guardian, +972 Magazine and Local Call. According to the report, about 11,500 terabytes of data were held in Microsoft data centres in the Netherlands, with more capacity in Ireland, under an arrangement that went live in 2022.

Sources quoted in the investigation say the data was used in military operations. Microsoft said it was not aware of surveillance of civilians or collection of their calls, and had found no evidence to date that its technology was used to target or harm people in Gaza.

# Pentagon officials gearing up for JWCC Next solicitation

*DefenseScoop, 2025-08-07. Original: <https://defensescoop.com/2025/08/07/jwcc-next-enterprise-cloud-program-dod-solicitation-plans>*

The Pentagon plans to release the solicitation for JWCC Next, the successor to its Joint Warfighting Cloud Capability contract, in early 2026 with an award expected in early 2027, DefenseScoop reports. The current $9 billion program, launched in December 2022 with Google, Oracle, Amazon Web Services and Microsoft, has awarded more than $3 billion in task orders.

According to a Defense Information Systems Agency official, JWCC Next aims to give access to more commercial cloud providers and run for a longer term. The official would not say how many vendors may win awards.

# Seven patterns suggesting brain-computer interfaces are nearing everyday use

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-08-09. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/the-neurotech-inflection-point>*

Nita Farahany identifies seven developments from 2024 and 2025 that she argues mark a turning point for neural interfaces: operating systems accepting brain signals as a standard input, non-surgical ultrasound devices reaching clinical trials, brain sensors built into earbuds and headphones, nerve-stimulation devices for chronic disease, and large public research funding programmes.

She points to a governance gap, with the United States withdrawing from UNESCO as it prepared a global neurotechnology ethics framework while state laws on neural data diverge, and warns that workplace brain monitoring could arrive through productivity features. The closing part of the post is for paid subscribers and is not summarised here.

# Four states define neural data four different ways

*Jameson Spivack, Future of Privacy Forum, 2025-08-12. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/the-neural-data-goldilocks-problem-defining-neural-data-in-u-s-state-privacy-laws/>*

Jameson Spivack of the Future of Privacy Forum, writing with an intern, compares how Montana, California, Connecticut and Colorado define neural data: California covers the central and peripheral nervous systems, Connecticut only the central nervous system, Montana uses "neurotechnology data", and Colorado covers neural data only when it is used to identify a person.

The authors argue that a broad definition can sweep in ordinary data such as typing, a narrow one can miss sensitive information revealed by other bodily signals, and that lawmakers should focus on specific uses and harms rather than the type of signal.

# How a protocol in a phone accessibility update could become the standard for brain-computer interfaces

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-08-12. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/apples-neural-platform-play-what>*

Nita Farahany examines a May 2025 accessibility update in which Apple added a protocol that lets third-party brain-computer interfaces send commands such as select or scroll to its operating systems, demonstrated in August 2025 by an implanted device controlling a tablet.

She argues the design matters for privacy because the device sends only discrete commands rather than raw brain signals, which she says fits state laws in Colorado, California and Montana that treat neural data as sensitive, and the federal children's privacy rule's coverage of biometric identifiers. She lists open questions, including whether the specification will be public and whether the company will publish a neural-data privacy policy.

# Israel Amendment 13 privacy reform

*IAPP, 2024-08-01. Original: <https://iapp.org/news/a/israel-marks-a-new-era-in-privacy-law-amendment-13-ushers-in-sweeping-reform>*

Israel's Amendment 13 to its Protection of Privacy Law takes effect on 14 August 2025, IAPP reports. The amendment requires the appointment of privacy protection officers, adds transparency duties and rules for data brokers, and broadens the definition of sensitive data.

According to IAPP, the Privacy Protection Authority gains powers to issue administrative orders and fines that can reach millions of shekels, and has signalled it will enforce its guidelines as strictly as the law itself.

# Researchers decode deliberately imagined words from brain implants, raising mental privacy questions

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-08-14. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/stanford-scientists-decode-inner>*

Nita Farahany reports on a study in Cell by a Stanford-led team in which implanted electrode arrays in four people with paralysis decoded silently imagined words (inner speech), with word error rates of 26 to 54 percent on large vocabularies; she notes participants preferred it to attempted speech because it was less tiring.

She stresses that the system detected only deliberately formed words, not emotions or wandering thought, but notes that in some tasks it picked up uninstructed inner speech such as silent counting, and that inner and attempted speech produced similar brain patterns differing mainly in strength. She credits the researchers for engaging with mental privacy; the rest of the post is for paid subscribers and is not summarised here.

# Brain-computer interface researchers decode internal monologues

*STAT, 2025-08-14. Original: <https://www.statnews.com/2025/08/14/can-a-computer-turn-our-internal-monologue-into-speech>*

STAT reports on a Stanford study, published in Cell, in which a brain-computer interface decoded inner speech in real time, with up to 74% accuracy from a 125,000-word vocabulary. The four participants had conditions such as ALS or brainstem stroke that limit speech.

The system works from thought before any attempt to speak, so it does not depend on the muscles used in speaking.

# Decoding inner speech from brain signals

*National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NIH), 2025-08-14. Original: <https://www.ninds.nih.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/decoding-inner-speech-brain-signals>*

Researchers at Stanford University decoded inner speech, words a person silently imagines saying, from implanted electrodes in the motor cortex of four participants with speech impairment from ALS or stroke, the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke reports. Error rates ranged from 14% to 33% with a 50-word vocabulary and from 26% to 54% with a 125,000-word vocabulary.

To keep private thoughts from being decoded unintentionally, the team tested safeguards, including a keyword the participant thinks to switch decoding on, which the system recognised more than 98% of the time. The study was published in Cell on 14 August 2025.

# Saudi center3 targets 1GW of data center capacity by 2030

*DatacenterDynamics, 2024-05-01. Original: <https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/saudis-center3-targets-1gw-of-data-center-capacity-by-2030>*

Saudi Telecom Company's data center subsidiary center3 aims to reach 1GW of capacity by 2030 and has announced a $10 billion investment, DatacenterDynamics reported on 14 August 2025. The company, formed in 2022, has invested $3 billion so far and targets about 300MW by 2027, with about 20 data centers in operation or development in Saudi Arabia and Bahrain.

DatacenterDynamics notes the announcement did not say how the $10 billion will be spent or where the new capacity will be located.

# Study of AI-assisted doctors losing skill prompts a warning about cognitive decline from AI reliance

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-08-18. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/the-hidden-brain-damage-of-ai>*

Nita Farahany cites a Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology study finding that experienced endoscopists became worse at spotting polyps after three months of AI assistance, and argues that doctors risk becoming legally responsible for AI decisions they are no longer able to override.

She points to research linking frequent AI use to weaker critical thinking, especially among younger users, and to a pre-print in which AI that presented opposing views improved users' decisions. She argues that AI that degrades thinking undermines cognitive liberty and floats warning labels on AI systems; the end of the post is for paid subscribers and is not summarised here.

# Brain sensors that detect confusion while reading, and what they could mean for classrooms

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-08-21. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/is-this-the-future-of-learning>*

Nita Farahany describes a pre-print from MIT Media Lab, UC Berkeley and Princeton researchers that combined EEG and eye tracking with AI to detect when 11 adult readers were confused, at about 77 percent accuracy across participants, and imagines it paired with AI-led schooling that adapts lessons in real time.

She sets out possible benefits for students with learning differences against a future in which children's thinking patterns become data held by schools and companies and used later by employers or insurers, and asks whether removing every moment of confusion would erode the productive struggle that builds critical thinking.

# U.S. Navy Sailor Convicted of Spying for China

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2025-08-20. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/us-navy-sailor-convicted-spying-china>*

A U.S. Navy machinist's mate serving on the amphibious assault ship USS Essex in San Diego was convicted of spying for China, the Justice Department announced on 21 August 2025. A federal jury in the Southern District of California found him guilty on six counts, including conspiracy to commit espionage, espionage, and unlawfully exporting technical defense data.

According to the department, from February 2022 to August 2023 he sent a Chinese intelligence officer photos, videos, weapons information and technical manuals on the Essex and other Navy ships, for more than $12,000. Sentencing was set for 1 December 2025.

# Breakthrough brain-computer interface decodes self-talk

*Psychology Today, 2025-08-01. Original: <https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/the-future-brain/202508/breakthrough-brain-computer-interface-decodes-self-talk>*

A brain-computer interface study led by Stanford Medicine, published in the journal Cell, decoded inner speech, words people imagine saying, from brain implants in four people with paralysis, Psychology Today reports. According to the post, decoding of instructed imagined speech reached up to 74% accuracy.

The researchers also tested a safeguard in which the system starts decoding only after the user thinks of a keyword. The post notes the study was a small proof of concept.

# The first class of an AI law course asks how to write laws for something that resists definition

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-08-25. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/inside-my-ai-law-and-policy-class>*

In the first dispatch from her Duke Law course on AI law and policy, Nita Farahany describes asking students to define artificial intelligence in 90 seconds and getting no two matching answers. She sets out the split between those who say large models understand and those who see them as statistical next-word predictors, and argues that which view prevails matters for questions of AI rights, testimony and liability.

She borrows a driving metaphor from a talk on AI governance, in which oversight needs a clear windshield, steering and brakes, and adds that the road, the view and even the vehicle are in dispute. She introduces adversarial networks, the black-box problem and language processing, noting that AI-generated evidence and unexplainable sentencing tools raise due-process questions. Readings and further material are for paid subscribers; this summary covers the free part.

# Chinese research on encrypting brain-computer interface signals, and what it suggests about threats

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-08-26. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/when-neural-signals-need-military>*

Nita Farahany reviews a Nature Communications paper by Chinese researchers describing a brain-computer interface that reads which flashing light a user is looking at and sends the result through a metasurface that scrambles and splits the signal, leaving eavesdroppers with random noise.

She notes the system transmits only about one letter every 32 seconds and asks why such elaborate protection would be built, suggesting it addresses interception of the electromagnetic signals that devices emit and that the designers may have sophisticated, state-level eavesdroppers in mind. Her look at the funding and institutions behind the work is for paid subscribers and is not summarised here.

# How large language models work, and why one invented court cases

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-08-27. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/how-ai-actually-works>*

In the second class of her AI law and policy course, Nita Farahany uses a 2023 New York federal case, in which a lawyer was sanctioned for filing a brief citing cases ChatGPT had invented, to explain how language models predict one word at a time from learned weights, embeddings and attention, without checking facts.

She traces responsibility for such errors across seven layers, from data suppliers to the end user, and suggests the law may need shared duties of care across that chain. She also explains how human feedback training builds in the preferences of whoever ranks the answers. Readings and assignments are for paid subscribers and are not summarised here.

# Protesters occupy Microsoft office as company reviews its work with Israel's military

*NPR, 2025-08-27. Original: <https://www.npr.org/2025/08/27/nx-s1-5518786/microsoft-protesters-office-israel>*

Protesters occupied the office of Microsoft's president at the company's headquarters in Redmond, Washington, to oppose its work with Israel's military, NPR reports. The group No Azure for Apartheid says seven people, including current and former Microsoft employees, were arrested.

The protest followed reporting by The Guardian that Israel's military stored surveillance data on Palestinians on Microsoft's Azure cloud. Microsoft says it has hired an outside law firm to review the reports and that its terms of service would prohibit such use.

# AWS launches cloud region in New Zealand

*DatacenterDynamics, 2025-09-01. Original: <https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/aws-launches-cloud-region-in-new-zealand>*

Amazon Web Services launched its Asia Pacific (New Zealand) cloud region in Auckland, with three availability zones, DatacenterDynamics reported on 1 September 2025. AWS says it plans to invest NZ$7.5 billion (about US$5.3 billion) in the country.

The region was first announced in 2021 and had been planned for 2024. Early customers named include Kiwibank, Trade Me and Xero, and AWS says the region will be supported by a wind power purchase agreement.

# Two brain studies, one matching brain activity to AI captions and one a three-minute memory test, and the privacy questions they raise

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-09-02. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/the-brain-tech-revolution-wont-look>*

Nita Farahany describes a brain-imaging study in which activity recorded while people viewed scenes lined up with how an AI language model summarised captions, allowing researchers to pick out a matching description of what someone was seeing, and a study of a passive three-minute EEG test that detected memory-related impairment.

She argues that such quick, passive tests could be slipped into workplace wellness checks and that brain data could be bought by insurers or advertisers, and asks whether it needs protection beyond that given to medical or genetic records. She also invites feedback on a neurotechnology accountability index being developed with the World Economic Forum.

# What makes an AI model open or closed, and why it matters in the contest with China

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-09-03. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/open-vs-closed-ai-models-inside-my>*

In the third class of her AI law and policy course, Nita Farahany breaks an AI system into five parts (training data, architecture, weights, the code that runs it, and the interface) and shows that models described as open usually release the weights but not the training data, comparing releases by U.S. and Chinese companies in 2025.

She argues that free Chinese open models could make global AI depend on Chinese foundations, with risks of hidden backdoors and lock-in, and that once weights are downloaded, licences and safety training are effectively unenforceable. She presents the tension that openness allows independent audit but also misuse.

# General Court dismisses Latombe challenge, upholds DPF

*IAPP, 2025-09-03. Original: <https://iapp.org/news/a/european-general-court-dismisses-latombe-challenge-upholds-eu-us-data-privacy-framework>*

The EU General Court on 3 September 2025 dismissed a French member of parliament's challenge to the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework and upheld it, IAPP reports. The challenge questioned the independence of the U.S. Data Protection Review Court and safeguards on bulk data collection by U.S. intelligence agencies.

The court judged the framework as it stood when the European Commission adopted it in 2023, and said the Commission must keep monitoring U.S. law and can suspend the decision. The ruling can be appealed to the Court of Justice.

# Should the United States restrict downloadable AI model weights? Three positions argued

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-09-08. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/the-ai-control-paradox-youre-the>*

In the fourth class of her AI law and policy course, Nita Farahany sets out three options from a federal NTIA study on openly downloadable model weights for dual-use AI: restrict them, monitor and adapt, or keep them open.

She presents the strongest case and the main weakness of each, noting that restrictions are hard to enforce once copies spread, that monitoring tends to detect harm after it has happened, and that openness has real costs including abuse imagery and harassment. She reports her students split almost evenly and suggests data, computing power and applications may be better points of control than the weights themselves.

# How AI models are trained on text, and the copyright questions behind a $1.5 billion settlement

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-09-10. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/ailawpolicyclass5>*

In the fifth class of her AI law and policy course, Nita Farahany walks through how text becomes training data, from downloading and tokenizing to training, fine-tuning and deployment, noting that every stage makes copies and that text seen many times can be memorised and reproduced word for word.

She uses the proposed $1.5 billion settlement between Anthropic and a class of authors over books taken from unauthorised online libraries, which the federal judge questioned before approval, to explain the four fair-use factors and why each is contested for AI training. She asks whether payment of about $3,000 per work reflects any principled value.

# A court order to keep every ChatGPT conversation, and who gets paid for training data

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-09-15. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/training-data-discovery-wars-and>*

In the sixth class of her AI law and policy course, Nita Farahany examines the May 2025 preservation order in The New York Times' copyright case against OpenAI, which a federal magistrate judge issued and a district judge affirmed in June, requiring the company to keep consumer ChatGPT conversations, including deleted ones, indefinitely.

She argues the order is unusual because it reaches hundreds of millions of users who are not parties, overrides the company's 30-day deletion promise and sits uneasily with European deletion rights, while enterprise customers are exempt. She also explains why trained models cannot simply unlearn a source and compares five ways creators might be paid, from case-by-case permission to treating all training as fair use.

# An investigation alleges Chinese state backing for a brain-headset maker that supplied classrooms

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-09-16. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/brainco-and-china>*

Nita Farahany points readers to an investigative report by Hunterbrook Media alleging that a Massachusetts-founded maker of EEG headsets, preparing to go public, had been funded for years by the Chinese government and government-linked investors. She recalls that her book described the same company shipping more than 20,000 brain-monitoring headsets to classrooms in China.

She presents the report as another example of neurotechnology being misused and urges readers to read it, adding only that readers can guess where she stands. The allegations are the report's, not findings of any court or regulator.

# Man Pleads Guilty to Conspiring to Act as Illegal Agent of the Chinese Government in the United States

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2025-09-16. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/man-pleads-guilty-conspiring-act-illegal-agent-chinese-government-united-states>*

A 68-year-old resident of Queens, New York, a naturalized U.S. citizen and former Chinese dissident who led a pro-democracy nonprofit, pleaded guilty to conspiring to act as an agent of China's government without notifying the Attorney General, the Justice Department announced on 16 September 2025. According to the department, from 2018 to June 2023 he gathered information for China's Ministry of State Security on U.S.-based democracy activists, including joining their encrypted chat groups, and was paid and met officers in China.

The charge carries up to five years in prison. Sentencing in federal court in Manhattan is set for 29 January 2026.

# How a Chinese AI model built under U.S. chip export controls exposed the limits of controlling computing power

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-09-17. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/why-china-quit-us-chips-inside-my>*

In the seventh class of her AI law and policy course, Nita Farahany explains computing power, from individual calculations to chips, chip factories and data centres, and describes how a Chinese developer, barred by U.S. export controls from buying advanced chips, built a competitive model in early 2025 using a design that activates only part of the model for each query.

She argues that export controls may have pushed China to innovate rather than holding it back, that the AI industry depends heavily on chip factories in Taiwan, and that the larger, never-ending cost of running models for users drives a rush for electricity. She notes reports that China had told its companies to stop buying a leading U.S. firm's AI chips.

# A consumer neural wristband goes on sale while courts disagree over whether thoughts are protected

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-09-19. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/i-told-you-so-well-i-did>*

Nita Farahany notes that Meta's neural band, a wristband that reads muscle signals to control smart glasses, was due to go on sale on 30 September 2025, following Apple's move to accept neural signals as a device input, and argues this brings neural interfaces into the mass consumer market.

She says federal appeals courts disagree on how much mental effort is needed before constitutional protection against self-incrimination applies, that there is no federal neural privacy law, and that a company's promise to keep data on the device is not legally enforceable. The post mainly directs readers to her longer article on the court split and to her book.

# Two appeals courts split on forced thumbprint unlocking, and neural wristbands may sharpen the question

*Nita Farahany, Stay Tuned with Preet (Substack), 2025-09-19. Original: <https://staytuned.substack.com/p/the-thumb-the-thought-and-the-fifth>*

Nita Farahany contrasts a 2024 Ninth Circuit ruling that pressing a suspect's thumb to a phone is like taking a fingerprint, and so not protected by the Fifth Amendment, with a later D.C. Circuit ruling that ordering a suspect to unlock a phone by thumb revealed what he knew and was testimonial. She argues that both courts lean on undefined ideas such as "cognitive exertion" that the physical-versus-testimonial test cannot supply.

She offers the spectrum from her 2012 law review article, running from identifying traits through automatic responses and stored memories to uttered responses, to explain the split. Pointing to a consumer wristband that reads neural signals of intended movement, she argues that neural interfaces will strain the doctrine further, and that the more effortless an interface becomes, the less Fifth Amendment protection it may receive under a purely physical approach.
