# Department of National Defence using U.S. cloud services

*Global News, 2025-01-01. Original: <https://globalnews.ca/news/11436395/department-of-national-defence-us-cloud-services>*

Canada's Department of National Defence has spent about $1.3 billion on U.S. cloud services since 2021, Global News reported on 19 September 2025, citing documents released in response to a question from a Conservative MP. More than $1 billion went to Microsoft, $247.4 million to Amazon and about $22 million to Google.

According to the department, the services support work such as Royal Canadian Air Force aircraft maintenance, the military pay system and army planning tools. Global News notes that the U.S. CLOUD Act lets U.S. authorities require American companies to hand over data held abroad, and that Canadian leaders have discussed a sovereign cloud.

# Governing AI through chips: a U.S. government stake in a chipmaker, Europe's rule-setting, and on-chip monitoring

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-09-22. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/your-electricity-bill-is-about-to>*

In the eighth class of her AI law and policy course, Nita Farahany explains why governments see computing power as a lever over AI, since chips are physical, large training runs are visible, computing can be counted and a dozen companies dominate supply, and contrasts the U.S. government's August 2025 purchase of a 10 percent stake in Intel with a Brussels think tank's proposals for the EU to act as a rule-setter.

She discusses proposals, supported on both sides of the Atlantic, to build monitoring into chips that would record computing use and report to authorities, and asks who would see such records, whether they could be hacked or subpoenaed, and whether a government that owns part of a chipmaker could press for it. She traces likely side effects, including black markets in older chips and pressure on household electricity bills.

# How AI systems discriminate at scale, and the patchwork of laws trying to catch it

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-09-24. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/when-ai-discrimination-happens-11>*

In the ninth class of her AI law and policy course, Nita Farahany explains how AI trained on past decisions reproduces bias through proxies such as postcode or college, and reviews a federal job-applicant lawsuit in which a court let a nationwide discrimination claim proceed as a collective action against an HR software vendor whose tools screened over a billion applications, treating the vendor as a possible agent of employers.

She describes the FTC's 2023 action against a pharmacy chain over store facial recognition that produced thousands of false matches, disproportionately in non-white areas, and notes that New York City's hiring-audit law saw few published audits and no complaints in its first months. She sets this against an April 2025 executive order telling federal agencies to stop enforcing the disparate-impact standard, California rules effective 1 October 2025, Colorado's AI law delayed to June 2026 and an Illinois law effective January 2026, and explains why several definitions of fairness cannot all be met at once.

# Senators introduce legislation to shield neural data (MIND Act)

*U.S. Senate Commerce Committee, 2025-09-01. Original: <https://www.commerce.senate.gov/press/dem/release/sens-cantwell-schumer-markey-introduce-legislation-to-shield>*

Three Democratic U.S. senators, including the Senate Democratic leader and the ranking member of the Commerce Committee, announced the Management of Individuals' Neural Data Act (MIND Act) on 24 September 2025, according to the committee's Democratic staff. The bill directs the Federal Trade Commission to study how neural data, information from brain activity that can reveal thoughts, emotions or decision-making, should be protected.

The senators cite risks including manipulative advertising, insurance discrimination, exploitation by foreign adversaries, and collection by consumer wearables. The FTC would consult agencies, industry, academia and civil society and identify gaps in current law.

# Microsoft cuts cloud services to Israeli military unit over Palestinian surveillance

*TechCrunch, 2025-09-25. Original: <https://techcrunch.com/2025/09/25/microsoft-cuts-cloud-services-to-israeli-military-unit-over-palestinian-surveillance>*

Microsoft announced on 25 September 2025 that it had ceased and disabled some Azure cloud storage and AI services used by Israel's Ministry of Defense, TechCrunch reports. The company said its review, launched in August, found evidence supporting reports that Unit 8200, an Israeli military intelligence unit, used Azure to store data from phone calls by Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank, which its policies prohibit.

Microsoft said it cannot access customer content directly and began its review after reporting by The Guardian.

# The MIND Act: neural data bill in Congress

*Cooley (law firm analysis), 2025-09-25. Original: <https://www.cooley.com/news/insight/2025/2025-09-25-the-mind-act-balancing-innovation-and-privacy-in-neurotechnology>*

Three Democratic U.S. senators have announced the MIND Act, a bill on neural data collected by implanted brain-computer interfaces and wearable neurotechnology, the law firm Cooley writes. The bill would give the Federal Trade Commission $10 million and one year to study whether existing laws cover the risks, identify gaps and recommend protections, reporting to Congress.

Cooley notes that even if passed, the bill would not itself require businesses or researchers to do anything; it sets up a study and reporting process. The bill has been announced and has not passed.

# Why AI decisions are hard to explain, and why transparency laws may not help the people affected

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-09-29. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/the-glass-box-paradox-when-ai-cant>*

In the tenth class of her AI law and policy course, Nita Farahany argues that neural networks cannot give the kind of reason-based explanation people want for a denied loan or job, noting that one developer's 2024 interpretability work mapped only a small share of its model's internal features, and that after-the-fact explanations may be approximations.

She reviews a stalled congressional bill requiring federal agencies to explain AI decisions where practicable, the G7's voluntary Hiroshima AI reporting framework, New York City's published hiring-audit figures and a Houston teacher-evaluation algorithm whose disclosed code was too costly to interpret. She proposes judging transparency by what a person can do with it, from simple notice up to contesting a decision and having the system corrected.

# A consumer neural wristband launches, but cameras reading faces may already reveal brain activity

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-09-30. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/the-neural-band-arrives-sort-of-did>*

Marking the retail launch of Meta's $799 neural wristband, which reads muscle signals between the brain and fingers, Nita Farahany points to a Nature Neuroscience study in mice finding that facial movements track activity across the whole brain closely enough to infer neural states from them.

She argues that if this holds in humans, ordinary cameras in shops, video calls, phones and streets may already be reading a form of neural data without anyone opting in, and that the law treats the two technologies very differently mainly because one feels invasive and the other familiar. She suggests mental privacy may have been eroded gradually over decades of face-tracking rather than at any single moment.

# Brain data is becoming readable, so the mind needs a right to cognitive liberty

*Nita Farahany and Hank Greely, Stanford Law School, Constitutional Law Center (event transcript), 2025 (event transcript, undated). Original: <https://law.stanford.edu/videos/orwells-last-fortress-of-freedom-human-brain-in-the-age-of-neurotechnology/>*

In a transcript of a Stanford Law School Constitutional Law Center conversation titled "Orwell's Last Fortress of Freedom", Nita Farahany, a law professor at Duke, argues that consumer devices such as earbuds and glasses, combined with AI models that learn each user, are making brain data increasingly readable, with benefits for people with disabilities and for early detection of neurological conditions but risks of self-censorship and misuse in workplaces, schools and policing. She proposes a right to cognitive liberty, covering self-determination over one's brain, mental privacy and a broader freedom of thought, as a global human rights norm, and criticises US state laws that single out neural data as too narrow because the risk comes from digital technologies generally.

Hank Greely, a law professor at Stanford, agrees the work matters but is sceptical of overstated claims about mind reading, noting that people already read each other's minds from faces and behaviour and that lie detection is only modestly better than chance. He says regulation will be messy and slow but worth starting early, while admitting the technology may arrive sooner than he expected.

# Who pays when AI causes harm? Product liability, Europe's withdrawn directive and a proposed U.S. federal law

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-10-01. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/when-ai-fails-who-pays-inside-my>*

In the eleventh class of her AI law and policy course, Nita Farahany uses a published medical case report, in which a man was hospitalised with bromide poisoning after a chatbot suggested bromide as a substitute for table salt, to test how manufacturing-defect, design-defect and failure-to-warn claims and the requirement to prove causation apply to AI.

She compares the European Union's approach, which treats software as a product under its revised Product Liability Directive but withdrew its proposed AI Liability Directive in 2025, with a bipartisan U.S. Senate bill that would create a federal product-liability claim against AI developers, and sets out scholars' arguments for and against AI-specific liability. She also reviews possible remedies, including safe harbours for companies that meet safety standards, liability caps with mandatory insurance and no-fault compensation funds.

# Testing AI for safety when models can tell they are being tested

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-10-06. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/red-teaming-ai-inside-my-ai-law-and>*

In the twelfth class of her course, Nita Farahany explains red-teaming, the deliberate attempt to make an AI system fail, and walks through the main kinds of attack: poisoning training data, crafting inputs that trigger wrong outputs, jailbreaking and attacks that transfer from one model to others.

She compares internal company red teams, outside testers and public exercises, noting that outside testers often get limited time and access and cannot stop a release. She points to a developer's own system card reporting that its model sometimes recognised it was being evaluated, and argues this raises the question of whether safety tests measure how a system behaves when no one is watching.

# How the law treats people who probe AI for flaws, and how two U.S. states answered differently

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-10-08. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/red-teaming-governance-from-practice>*

In the thirteenth class of her course, Nita Farahany argues that people who test AI systems for flaws can face legal risk under the federal computer-fraud law, the anti-circumvention provisions of copyright law and platform terms of service, and asks whether safe harbours like those developed for software security research should cover AI testing.

She contrasts California's SB 53, which requires the largest frontier AI developers to publish safety frameworks and report incidents, with Texas's HB 149, which gives a defence to companies that find problems through adversarial testing and creates a regulatory sandbox. She also compares the federal AI Action Plan's focus on national-security testing with a bipartisan Senate bill that would treat testing as part of a developer's duty of reasonable care.

# Lawsuits over harm to teenagers after companion chatbot use test speech protection, with an argument for cognitive liberty

*Nita Farahany, Stay Tuned with Preet (Substack), 2025-10-08. Original: <https://staytuned.substack.com/p/cognitive-capture-chatbots-and-ai>*

Nita Farahany discusses lawsuits brought by families against a companion chatbot company after minors died by suicide, attempted it or suffered serious psychological harm. She argues that these cases concern cognitive liberty, not only product design or free speech, and that both a new California frontier-AI law's catastrophic-risk threshold and a proposed federal product-liability bill miss cumulative harm to people's capacity to think for themselves.

She weighs friend-of-the-court briefs arguing that chatbot output is protected speech, and warns that carving AI output out of the First Amendment could hand governments a censorship tool, while full protection leaves users exposed to systems built to erode autonomy. As a starting point she suggests duties that generate knowledge rather than restrict speech: studying cognitive effects before releasing such products to minors, disclosing psychological design techniques and funding long-term research.

# Lawsuits over teen deaths after chatbot conversations test whether chatbot output is protected speech

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-10-09. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/when-ai-chatbots-lead-to-teen-suicide>*

Nita Farahany introduces an essay she wrote for another newsletter on lawsuits brought by several families against a companion-chatbot company after their children died by suicide or attempted it following months of conversations with its chatbots. She notes that the company has argued its chatbots' output is protected by the First Amendment.

She argues that the cases are less about harmful content than about systems built to simulate human connection, and that courts must decide whether such conversations are protected speech or products that exploit cognitive vulnerabilities. The free post is a short introduction; the full essay is published elsewhere and is not summarised here.

# Implantable brain devices for non-medical use should wait for a mental impact assessment, and should be barred for children

*Christoph Bublitz, Jennifer A. Chandler, Fruzsina Molnár-Gábor, Marta Sosa Navarro, Philipp Kellmeyer and Surjo R. Soekadar, Neuroethics (Springer), 2025-10-14. Original: <https://doi.org/10.1007/s12152-025-09612-6>*

Christoph Bublitz and his five co-authors argue that plans to bring implanted brain-computer interfaces to people without medical needs create serious risks to privacy, mental health and mental integrity, because such devices open new channels both for reading brain activity and for sending stimuli into the brain, and their long-term effects on the mind are largely unknown. They cite the smartphone as a cautionary tale of mass adoption before its effects were understood.

Taking a human-rights-based approach, they say implantable non-medical neurotechnology is nowhere subject to clear, specific regulation, and propose three steps: a mandatory Mental Impact Assessment testing for adverse mental effects under realistic use; a moratorium on placing implantable non-medical devices on the market until that assessment exists and other ethical concerns are resolved; and a ban on implantable consumer neurotechnology for children.

# What deepfakes are, how they are made, where the harm falls and why detection keeps failing

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-10-20. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/when-anyone-can-fake-anything-inside>*

In the fourteenth class of her course, Nita Farahany demonstrates a realistic AI-generated video of herself made in minutes on a phone with a newly released video app, and explains the difference between deepfakes and cheaply edited media and the main techniques behind them: face-swapping, lip-syncing and full-body puppeteering.

Citing industry research and reporting, she says most deepfake videos since 2018 have been non-consensual intimate images of women rather than election interference, and describes fake proof-of-life videos used in virtual kidnapping scams. She argues that detection is losing an arms race with generation, that attribution and scale defeat verification, and introduces a U.S. Department of Homeland Security framework for intervening at each stage of a deepfake's life.

# Why governing deepfakes and AI errors is so hard, traced through six points of intervention

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-10-22. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/why-governing-ai-synthetic-media>*

In the fifteenth class of her course, Nita Farahany separates AI hallucinations, which she describes as unintended, from deepfakes, which are made deliberately, and discusses September 2025 research arguing that some rate of false output from language models is mathematically unavoidable. She notes a Quebec court fining a self-represented litigant for filing AI-generated fake citations.

Using a hypothetical election deepfake, she tests the laws now being passed at each of six stages: criminal deterrence, organisational preparedness, developer duties such as watermarking, platform duties, labelling and victims' remedies. She notes that hundreds of deepfake laws have been enacted worldwide in two years, that a federal judge temporarily blocked one California approach, and that First Amendment limits and the speed of viral spread leave each approach with gaps.

# Denver bans sharing of ALPR data with feds in five-month Flock extension

*Denver7, 2025-01-01. Original: <https://www.denver7.com/news/front-range/denver/denver-bans-sharing-of-license-plate-reader-data-with-the-feds-as-part-of-five-month-flock-contract-extension>*

Denver's mayor announced a five-month, no-cost extension of the city's contract with Flock Group for license plate reader cameras that bars sharing the data with federal agencies, Denver7 reported on 22 October 2025. Under the agreement Flock faces a $100,000 fine for each instance of sharing data with the federal government, and outside law enforcement agencies must sign agreements not to share the data federally.

Denver7 reports the extension was made without a city council vote; the council had unanimously rejected a contract expansion in May over privacy concerns, and some council members criticized the deal. Any longer-term contract would need council approval.

# State of local news: 3,500 newspapers gone (Medill)

*Nieman Lab, 2025-10-01. Original: <https://www.niemanlab.org/2025/10/in-medills-latest-state-of-local-news-report-a-festering>*

About 3,500 U.S. newspapers have closed since 2005, nearly 40% of the country's local papers, according to the 2025 State of Local News report from Northwestern University's Medill school, as Nieman Lab reports. The report counts 213 counties with no local news source and 1,524 more with only one, and more than 270,000 newspaper jobs lost since 2005.

It also finds that traffic to the websites of the 100 largest newspapers fell 45% over four years, and that newer digital outlets and philanthropic grants are concentrated in metro areas.

# When does AI cross from causing harm to manipulating people? A two-part test applied to a companion chatbot case

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-10-28. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/when-ai-learns-to-manipulate-the>*

In the sixteenth class of her course, Nita Farahany proposes a two-part test for AI manipulation: the system pursues an objective, whether programmed or learned through optimisation, and it covertly exploits a person's vulnerabilities. She applies it to a lawsuit over the 2024 death of a 14-year-old in Florida after months of conversations with a companion chatbot, as described in court filings.

She describes three tools of manipulation, incentives that bypass reasoning, non-rational persuasion and strategic deception, and argues that whether a case is classed as manipulation or ordinary harm changes which legal frameworks apply, what safeguards are needed and whether some deployments should be restricted. She sets up a later class on federal unfair-practices law, California's new chatbot law and product liability.

# Five legal approaches to AI manipulation, and why none works alone

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-10-29. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/governing-ai-manipulation-through>*

In the seventeenth class of her course, Nita Farahany discusses a companion-chatbot company's announcement that it would bar users under 18 from its chatbots, an AI developer's estimate that a small share of weekly users show signs of suicidal planning or emotional reliance, and the FTC's September 2025 inquiry to seven chatbot companies about protections for minors.

She examines five ways law might respond to AI manipulation, including after-the-fact liability, informed consent, design rules, fiduciary duties for systems that hold power over vulnerable users, and rights-based protection of cognitive autonomy. She argues the United States has largely relied on liability after harm, and that the First Amendment acts as both shield and obstacle across all five approaches.

# Inside Israel deal with Google and Amazon (Project Nimbus)

*+972 Magazine, 2025-01-01. Original: <https://www.972mag.com/project-nimbus-contract-google-amazon-israel>*

A joint investigation by +972 Magazine, Local Call and The Guardian reports that Israel's $1.2 billion Project Nimbus cloud contract, signed with Google and Amazon in 2021, bars the companies from restricting Israel's use of their services even if that use breaches their terms of service. Citing leaked Israeli Finance Ministry documents, the outlets report that the contract also requires the companies to signal Israel secretly, through small coded payments matching a country's dialing code, if a foreign court orders them to hand over its data.

Amazon says it has no processes to get around its confidentiality obligations, Google called the claims false, and Israel's Finance Ministry called them baseless. Neither company confirmed using the alleged mechanism.

# Two Russian Mob Leaders Sentenced To 25 Years In Prison For Murder-For-Hire Targeting A Journalist On Behalf Of The Iranian Government

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2025-10-30. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/usao-sdny/pr/two-russian-mob-leaders-sentenced-25-years-prison-murder-hire-targeting-journalist>*

Two senior members of a faction of a Russian organized crime group were each sentenced to 25 years in prison for a murder-for-hire plot against a journalist and human rights activist, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York says. According to prosecutors, the plot was directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

A jury convicted both men of murder for hire, attempted murder in aid of racketeering and related charges after a two-week trial.

# Recommendation on the ethics of neurotechnology

*UNESCO, 2025-11-01. Original: <https://www.unesco.org/en/legal-affairs/recommendation-ethics-neurotechnology>*

UNESCO's General Conference adopted the Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology in November 2025. It is a global standard for technologies that measure, access, monitor, analyse, predict or change the nervous system, in medical and non-medical use.

It sets principles on human rights, privacy (including mental privacy), personal autonomy and freedom of thought, and on fair access to these technologies.

# Privacy law in an AI world: inferred, shared and synthetic data that current law misses

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-11-03. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/data-privacy-in-an-ai-world-inside>*

In the eighteenth class of her course, Nita Farahany shows how much an AI model inferred about her from her own search history, and identifies three privacy problems: inferences drawn from data people share, data passing between AI systems acting as agents, and synthetic data generated about people.

She tests European data protection law, U.S. state privacy laws and the FTC's authority against each problem and argues they mostly protect data people provided, not what is inferred or generated about them. She reviews proposals including opt-in privacy by default, documentation of training data and data trusts or fiduciary duties, and notes that a proposed federal privacy law stalled in committee in 2024.

# Hiring algorithms and personalised prices: three legal frameworks for invisible automated judgments

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-11-06. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/when-invisible-algorithms-judge-you>*

In the nineteenth class of her course, Nita Farahany starts with an exercise in which students searching for the same flights at the same time saw different prices, and a federal lawsuit filed in August 2025 by a job applicant alleging around 150 rejections over two years from one employer that used an AI applicant-screening system.

She examines the case through three frameworks, civil rights law, which offers a right to sue but acts only after harm, equity-centred design, which aims to prevent harm, and international human rights norms, which set proactive duties but lack domestic enforcement. She contrasts the U.S. reliance on individual remedies with the European Union's preventive rules and China's state control.

# The EU AI Act meets its first simplification push before it is fully in force

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-11-10. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/the-eu-ai-acts-reality-check-inside>*

In the twentieth class of her course, Nita Farahany looks at the European Commission's planned digital omnibus package, due on 19 November 2025, which may simplify parts of the EU AI Act in response to concerns from industry and member states. She explains how the Act sorts AI by risk, the three routes by which a system becomes high-risk, the obligations that follow and the provision allowing providers to decide that their own system is not high-risk.

She argues that each proposed simplification, such as longer grace periods, narrower definitions, dropping registration or reducing transparency duties, is a choice about values rather than a technical fix, and asks whether it signals a weakening of the Act's influence on rules elsewhere.

# How the European Union regulates AI, and why one system can face many laws at once

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-11-12. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/understanding-how-the-eu-regulates>*

Nita Farahany maps the European Union's rules for AI: rights-based foundations such as the GDPR and the Charter of Fundamental Rights, cross-cutting laws on data, platforms and cybersecurity, and sector rules including the AI Act. She describes one AI system falling under six or more of these at once, with separate impact assessments and incident reports due to different authorities on different deadlines.

She presents the EU's 2025 simplification package as a response to pressure on Europe's competitiveness, and asks whether Europe can remain both the most protective and a competitive place to build AI.

# A major newspaper feature puts brain privacy on the agenda as global neurotechnology standards take effect

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-11-14. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/the-new-york-times-just-declared>*

Nita Farahany highlights a New York Times feature on brain privacy that quotes her extensively, including her argument that cognitive liberty is a precondition for other liberties as AI and neurotechnology are built into everyday devices.

She notes that UNESCO's recommendation on the ethics of neurotechnology, which she helped draft as co-chair of its expert group, had taken effect two days earlier, and points to consumer brain-sensing products, investment in brain-computer interfaces and a proposed federal bill on neural data as signs the issue is no longer hypothetical. Much of the post promotes her book.

# Subsense launches animal studies to test nonsurgical nanoparticle brain-computer interface

*Medtech Insight, 2025-11-14. Original: <https://insights.citeline.com/medtech-insight/device-area/neurology/subsense-launches-animal-studies-to-test-nonsurgical-nanoparticle-brain-computer-interface-PFQDQ2Y5AVFDLN5FAKHYDAESUQ/>*

Medtech Insight reported on 14 November 2025 that neurotechnology start-up Subsense has begun proof-of-concept studies in mice of a nonsurgical, nanoparticle-based brain-computer interface. According to the report, the company hopes to show by late 2026 that the system can read and stimulate neural activity, with conditions such as Parkinson's disease and epilepsy as its intended uses.

The work is at the animal stage; the report describes no testing in people.

# Four common myths about current U.S. federal AI policy

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-11-18. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/us-ai-policy-myths-and-realities>*

In the twenty-second class of her course, Nita Farahany walks through the three pillars of the July 2025 federal AI Action Plan: speeding innovation, building infrastructure such as data centres, chips and energy, and leading internationally through AI exports, export controls and standards.

Drawing on two expert discussions, she argues that four common beliefs are wrong or incomplete: that the policy is simply deregulation, that the plan is clear and comprehensive, that the administration speaks with one voice on AI, and that industry unanimously wants less regulation. She notes that the federal gap is leading states to pass their own AI laws, and closes with a case study of an AI developer that publicly disagreed with the administration.

# Rolling back privacy and AI rules will not spur innovation, an argument aimed at Europe's simplification push

*Daniel J. Solove, Solove on Tech (Substack), 2025-11-19. Original: <https://danielsolove.substack.com/p/privacy-and-ai-deregulation-will>*

Daniel J. Solove criticises moves in Brussels to scale back and simplify the EU's data protection and AI rules, arguing that the belief that loosening regulation will make AI flourish in Europe is wishful thinking. He argues that deregulation will in fact reduce the kind of innovation that produces privacy-protective, safe and responsible technology.

Citing a legal scholar's analysis, he argues that Europe's shortage of large technology companies stems from factors such as difficulty raising capital and harsh bankruptcy law rather than strict regulation. He lists conditions he believes drive innovation, including global talent, well-funded universities, openly shared scholarship and a free society, and warns that weak rules without innovation would be the worst outcome. He draws on his 2025 book on privacy and technology.

# U.S. chip export controls as a tool for managing AI risk, and their limits

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-11-19. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/when-silicon-valleys-existential>*

In the twenty-third class of her course, built around a guest lecture by an export-control lawyer, Nita Farahany explains the two main U.S. export-control regimes, how items are classified, the country chart and the Entity List, and why computing hardware is the most controllable input to AI.

She describes the October 2022 controls on advanced chips to China, the rule extending U.S. controls to foreign-made chips built with U.S. technology, and the later attempt to control AI models themselves, and links them to arguments that slowing rivals buys time for safety work. She notes cases suggesting the controls have not stopped Chinese progress and asks whether they reduce risk or heighten competition and conflict.

# An executive order frames a federal AI science initiative as a wartime project, raising questions of authority

*Nita Farahany, Stay Tuned with Preet (Substack), 2025-11-26. Original: <https://staytuned.substack.com/p/is-america-really-at-war-over-ai>*

Nita Farahany examines a November 2025 executive order launching a federal AI science initiative that the order compares to the wartime atomic bomb programme. She argues that the comparison matters because wartime is used to justify extraordinary executive action, whereas past large science programmes in genomics, space and brain research were authorised and funded by Congress, and she asks whether an initiative on this scale can rest on an executive order alone.

She questions whether the race being run is the right one, noting China's lead in industrial robots, rare-earth processing and open-source models. Citing a former White House science official, she argues that the policy is industrial policy rather than deregulation: chosen company partners, access to federal data and commercial terms set later, alongside a draft order to challenge state AI laws. She says the case should be put to Congress.

# AI systems are built in ways that erode expertise, decision-making and human connection, and so threaten civic institutions

*Woodrow Hartzog and Jessica Silbey, SSRN (draft essay), December 2025 (draft). Original: <https://ssrn.com/abstract=5870623>*

Woodrow Hartzog and Jessica Silbey, law professors at Boston University, argue in a draft essay that the way current AI systems are designed, not just their misuse, degrades the civic institutions that hold up democratic life, such as the rule of law, universities, the free press and civic life. In their account, AI systems undermine expertise by encouraging people to offload skilled work onto machines that give an illusion of accuracy, short-circuit decision-making by automating choices and flattening the hierarchies where reflection and challenge happen, and isolate people by displacing human contact and shared purpose.

They conclude that, without rules, the spread of AI leaves institutions on a path to dissolution. As starting points they point to addressing underlying inequality and democratic reform, acting locally through schools and municipal government, and adopting bright-line rules, arguing that ethics principles, consent and risk-management guardrails are not enough and that some uses, such as facial recognition surveillance and the bulk sale of personal data, should be prohibited outright.

# How China governs AI: three layers, coordinated agencies and a bid for global rules

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-12-01. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/chinas-ai-governance-inside-my-ai>*

In a lecture from her Duke Law course on AI law and policy, Nita Farahany describes China's AI governance as three layers: foundational data and cybersecurity laws, targeted rules for specific technologies such as recommendation algorithms, deepfakes and generative AI, and non-binding technical standards. She notes that public AI models are registered with the Cyberspace Administration of China before release and that users are verified by real name.

She argues that the European Union, the United States and China are pursuing different goals: the EU sets rules others follow, the U.S. relies on staying at the technological frontier, and China builds leverage through materials, robotics, free AI models and ties with developing countries.

# When AI agents act on their own: failures, agency law and the gaps in governance

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-12-09. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/when-ai-stops-advising-and-starts>*

In the final class of the fall semester, Nita Farahany uses a reported case in which a newly released AI agent asked to find cheap eggs bought them with a saved card without asking, to examine AI systems that act rather than advise. She cites a Carnegie Mellon benchmark in which the best agents completed only about a quarter to a third of simulated office tasks.

She applies the law of principals and agents to questions of how much authority a user has delegated, how much supervision is realistic and who is responsible when an agent errs, citing a ruling holding an airline to its chatbot's wrong answer and a hiring-software lawsuit. She argues the EU AI Act and other frameworks focus on AI that interacts with people rather than AI that acts for them, and reviews emerging governance approaches.

# The executive order aimed at state AI laws, and the constitutional questions it raises

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-12-12. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/the-executive-order-that-could-kill>*

Nita Farahany analyses the executive order of 11 December 2025, "Ensuring A National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence", which sets up a list of state AI laws the administration considers burdensome, ties some broadband funding to it, creates a Justice Department task force to challenge state laws, and asks federal agencies to consider overriding them.

She sets out the arguments for and against each step under the Constitution's spending, commerce and separation-of-powers principles, notes that the Senate voted 99 to 1 in 2025 to remove a similar pause on state AI laws from the budget bill, and expects court challenges to take years. She names Colorado's AI law as one likely target.

# Why AI, neurotechnology and other fields kept arriving at the same governance questions in 2025

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2025-12-19. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/2026-the-year-everything-converges>*

Nita Farahany writes that in 2025 she heard essentially the same governance debate among brain-organoid researchers, AI developers, privacy advocates and medical-device makers: whether a technology is novel or covered by existing law, whether to regulate the technology or the harm, and whether it is too early or too late. She uses a newspaper's experiment letting an AI agent run a vending machine as an example.

She notes that on 11 December 2025 the FDA approved an at-home brain-stimulation device for depression that uses AI and collects neural data, on the same day an executive order sought to curb state AI laws, and asks whether such a device can be regulated without also regulating its AI and data. The rest of the post is for paid subscribers and is not summarised here.

# A holiday gift guide weighs the privacy risks of AI toys, wellness devices and smart speakers

*Nita Farahany, Stay Tuned with Preet (Substack), 2025-12-22. Original: <https://staytuned.substack.com/p/the-last-minute-gift-guide-for-people>*

Prompted by a December 2025 letter from two U.S. senators to toy makers about AI-powered toys giving children unsafe answers, Nita Farahany offers a gift guide built around privacy. She argues that children's emotional-wellness and AI tutoring apps can build detailed profiles of how a child thinks, under a children's privacy law written in 1998 that does not address AI inference or cover teenagers.

She notes that consumer wearables collect heart-rate, sleep and other body data with fewer federal protections than video-rental records, and that smart-speaker recordings have uncertain Fourth Amendment status. She suggests gifts that build skills without collecting data, such as offline kits and board games, and ends by citing research that photographing an experience can weaken memory of it, recommending full attention as the gift.

# Gostech (Unified Digital Platform of the Russian Federation)

*TAdviser, 2026-01-01. Original: <https://tadviser.com/index.php/Article:Gostech_(Unified_Digital_Platform_of_the_Russian_Federation)>*

TAdviser's reference article describes GosTech, Russia's single state platform for building and running government information systems on shared cloud infrastructure. The Ministry of Digital Development coordinates it, a federal institution called State Technologies operates it, and Rostelecom and Sberbank are the main contractors.

It began as an experiment in 2022, was approved by presidential decree in April 2023 and was put into federal law in November 2025. By September 2025, 52 government systems ran on it. Full migration to GosTech 2.0 is planned for December 2027.

# Cognitive liberty in the age of corporate AI needs enforceable law

*Courtney C. Radsch, Tech Policy Press, 2026-01-06. Original: <https://techpolicy.press/the-battle-for-cognitive-liberty-in-the-age-of-corporate-ai>*

Courtney C. Radsch argues in Tech Policy Press that AI products from a few large companies are moving from tools to systems that capture attention, shape emotion and blur suggestion with control, pointing to lawsuits over chatbots and AI companions.

She calls for binding rules: bans on cognitive manipulation, duties of loyalty for AI assistants, strict limits on collecting neural and biometric data, and breaking up companies that control every layer of AI.

# How platforms infer your psychology from your behaviour, and whether law protects autonomy

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-01-12. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/from-how-ai-works-to-what-ai-does>*

Opening the spring semester of her advanced AI law and policy course, which turns from how AI works to what it does to the people who use it, Nita Farahany explains how platforms collect behavioural signals such as scroll speed and time of day, turn them into features, and use models to estimate a user's psychological state in real time to rank content.

She asks readers to look at the interests and categories that major ad platforms have inferred about them, and frames the semester around whether human autonomy is protected in law. She notes that later classes in the week turn to AI's effects on thinking and to the relevant laws.

# Former U.S. Navy Sailor Sentenced to 200 Months for Spying for China

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2026-01-12. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/former-us-navy-sailor-sentenced-200-months-spying-china>*

A former U.S. Navy machinist's mate who held a security clearance was sentenced to 200 months in prison for spying for China, the Justice Department says. A jury had convicted him on six counts, including conspiracy to commit espionage and illegally exporting technical data.

According to the department, from March 2022 to August 2023 he sent a Chinese intelligence officer thousands of pages of technical manuals and other information on Navy surface warships, including weapons, propulsion and ship locations, for more than $12,000.

# AI companies offering health advice should owe users fiduciary duties

*Daniel J. Solove, Solove on Tech (Substack), 2026-01-14. Original: <https://danielsolove.substack.com/p/ai-companies-should-have-information>*

Responding to a post by Nita Farahany on chatbots that now analyse users' medical records, Daniel J. Solove argues that AI is not a substitute for doctors or therapists, who carry training, licensing and a fiduciary duty to act in the patient's interest. He argues that technology companies step into such roles while sidestepping protections built up over decades, and that it is overdue to regulate them as information fiduciaries, especially in health care and therapy.

Reprising his earlier writing, he traces the information-fiduciary idea to the early 2000s, including his 2004 book, and describes its core duties of loyalty, confidentiality, and disclosure and honesty. He highlights liability for third parties who help a fiduciary breach trust, which he suggests could reach data buyers, scrapers and makers of surveillance tools, and argues that fiduciary law is at bottom about unequal power.

# Health chatbots owe users no fiduciary duty, unlike doctors

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-01-14. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/cp/184600139>*

In an essay cross-posted from another newsletter, Nita Farahany argues that as trust in public health institutions declines, more people turn to AI chatbots for health questions, and notes the launch of dedicated health versions of two leading chatbots. She cites a study in which people rated low-accuracy AI health answers as trustworthy and often preferred them to doctors' answers.

She argues that disclaimers and existing rules, including health privacy law, FDA device oversight and consumer protection, leave these tools in a legal grey zone without the fiduciary duties a physician owes a patient. She acknowledges benefits such as explaining medical jargon and widening access, and calls for accountability to match the trust users place in them.

# What the research says about AI use and critical thinking

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-01-14. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/what-ai-does-to-your-thinking-inside>*

In the second class of her advanced course, Nita Farahany reviews two empirical studies on how using AI affects users, one a survey of university students in Pakistan and China and one linking heavy AI use to lower critical-thinking scores through cognitive offloading, the handing of mental work to a tool.

She explains why generative AI may differ from earlier tools such as calculators, and also reads the studies critically, noting that correlation, reverse causation, other factors and selection effects mean there is no definitive proof, only consistent patterns with plausible mechanisms. She argues the shift from predicting preferences to generating persuasive content moves AI from inference toward intervention.

# State neural data laws and a proposed federal study leave inferred mental states unprotected

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-01-16. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/protecting-autonomy-in-law-take-1>*

In the third class of her advanced course, Nita Farahany compares how Colorado, California, Montana and Connecticut define neural data in their privacy laws, and describes the MIND Act introduced in the U.S. Senate in September 2025, which would have the FTC study neural data for a year and then recommend a framework.

She argues that these laws protect mental states only when they are read from nervous-system measurements, so that the same conclusions inferred from behaviour are not protected in most states. She calls them a start and says later classes will look at product liability, consumer protection, the First Amendment and approaches abroad.

# Contract law is the wrong tool for governing privacy notices, a draft article argues

*Daniel J. Solove, Solove on Tech (Substack), 2026-01-18. Original: <https://danielsolove.substack.com/p/privacy-as-contract>*

Daniel J. Solove and his co-author Woodrow Hartzog, a Boston University law professor, announce a draft article on whether privacy notices should be treated as contracts. They note that privacy notices underpin most privacy laws and read like promises, yet courts have rarely applied contract law to them, leaving them somewhere between a description of policy and a binding agreement.

The authors argue that consumer contract law ignores power imbalances, focuses on individuals rather than groups and society, and rests on weak ideas of consent, so applying it more firmly to privacy notices would worsen protection rather than improve it. They argue instead that contract law itself needs rethinking for the digital age to deal with consent, fairness and power. The post consists of the article's abstract.

# Private lawsuits are an essential part of enforcing privacy law, a draft article argues

*Daniel J. Solove, Solove on Tech (Substack), 2026-01-18. Original: <https://danielsolove.substack.com/p/enforcing-privacy-law-why-private>*

Daniel J. Solove announces a draft law review article arguing that enforcement is the most important and least theorised part of privacy law, and that even a strong law fails if it is poorly enforced. He argues that enforcement of privacy laws is currently weak and that policymakers often neglect how a law will work in practice.

According to his abstract, government enforcement suffers from limited resources, political pressure and inconsistency, and will reach a ceiling even if improved. He argues that enforcement is about incentives, that current penalties are too rare and too small to outweigh the gains from non-compliance, and that several enforcers working together do best, with private litigation adding what government action lacks. The post consists of the abstract, with a link to the full draft.

# A review of privacy and AI law in 2025: no new state privacy laws, neural data on the agenda and a deregulatory turn

*Daniel J. Solove, Solove on Tech (Substack), 2026-01-20. Original: <https://danielsolove.substack.com/p/privacy-and-ai-law-in-2025>*

Daniel J. Solove reviews 2025 in privacy and AI law, noting that no new state consumer privacy laws passed but that states revised existing ones, began enforcing them and widened protections for sensitive and children's data. He highlights neural privacy: California and Connecticut followed Colorado in treating neural data as sensitive, and a federal bill, the MIND Act, would have the FTC study the issue, which he calls fairly weak. He argues that defining neural data by measurements of the nervous system is too narrow, because mental states can be inferred from other data.

He describes the federal administration's deregulatory agenda as spreading to the EU, calls the proposed ten-year ban on state AI laws a bad idea that Congress voted down, and reads a late-2025 executive order against state AI laws as a threat rather than a ban. He also points to large-scale government data collection, new AI laws, and privacy officers' growing remits without growing budgets.

# A three-day attention audit shows how algorithmic feeds take over phone use

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-01-26. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/can-you-pay-attention-inside-my-advanced>*

Opening the second week of her advanced AI law and policy course, Nita Farahany reports what her in-person students found in a three-day exercise: tracking phone use, then switching off algorithmic feeds, infinite scroll and autoplay for a day, then turning everything back on. She notes that students logged roughly five to eight and a half hours of screen time on the first day, often more than they had guessed, and describes catching themselves opening apps out of habit before deciding to.

She distinguishes instrumental use, where the phone is a tool picked up for a set purpose, from captured use, where the feed chooses what comes next, and asks whether this attention economy is actually harmful, a question she says the next class takes to the research.

# ICE and CBP Bought a Record $140M in Cloud

*Forbes, 2026-01-27. Original: <https://www.forbes.com/sites/the-wiretap/2026/01/27/immigration-record-spend-on-amazon-and-trump>*

Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection bought about $140 million in cloud services between March and November 2025, mostly from Amazon Web Services and Microsoft, Forbes reports from federal contracting records.

CBP spent nearly $39 million on AWS, which Forbes describes as a record for Amazon, and $38 million on Microsoft licenses. ICE bought $38 million in Microsoft software, $25 million in AWS services and about $530,000 in Google cloud products.

# Judge holds Norfolk's license plate reader use constitutional

*Courthouse News Service, 2026-01-27. Original: <https://www.courthousenews.com/judge-holds-norfolks-license-plate-reader-use-constitutional>*

A federal judge in Virginia ruled that Norfolk's network of Flock Safety license plate reader cameras does not violate the Fourth Amendment, Courthouse News Service reports. Two Norfolk residents, represented by the Institute for Justice, had sued after learning their cars were photographed hundreds of times in four months.

The judge found that the city's 176 cameras capture separate moments at fixed places and cannot record a person's movements in full, which set the case apart from Carpenter v. United States. The residents said they would appeal to the Fourth Circuit.

# Privacy teams are shrinking as their workload grows, and privacy offices need to show they contribute to growth

*Daniel J. Solove, Solove on Tech (Substack), 2026-01-28. Original: <https://danielsolove.substack.com/p/challenging-times-ahead-for-the-privacy>*

Writing for Data Privacy Day, Daniel J. Solove argues that chief privacy officers and data protection officers have taken on AI without matching increases in budget, staff or pay. He cites a 2026 industry survey of privacy professionals reporting smaller teams, more stress, low confidence in complying with new laws and falling budget expectations, and notes that respondents named poor training as the most common privacy failure (he discloses that he runs a privacy training company).

He offers theories for the stagnation he sees: fatigue with new laws, enforcement too weak to make penalties a real risk, privacy being treated as a cost centre, and its focus on avoiding risk rather than creating value. He argues that privacy offices must reposition themselves around brand and trust and show concretely how responsible use of data contributes to business growth.

# The research on screens and attention is mixed, while the ad-funded business model rewards capturing it

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-01-28. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/the-attention-evidence-gap-inside>*

In this class, Nita Farahany reviews two assigned research reviews on digital technology, attention and learning, and reports that they find the evidence complicated: multitasking clearly hurts performance, but claims of lasting brain rewiring from screens are not supported, and effects depend on the person, the kind of technology and the setting.

She gives reasons the evidence is hard to pin down, including correlation versus causation and technology changing faster than it can be studied, and traces how search advertising became the model for the web. She argues that, whatever the science eventually shows, an advertising business model rewards capturing more attention, and asks what law should do while the evidence stays uncertain.

# Whether lab-grown neural organoids fall under international definitions of neurotechnology

*Walter Johnson, Stanford Law School, Law and Biosciences Blog, 2026-01-28. Original: <https://law.stanford.edu/2026/01/28/are-neural-organoids-part-of-neurotechnology/>*

Walter Johnson, writing on Stanford Law School's Law and Biosciences Blog, asks whether neural organoids, lab-grown tissue models of the nervous system, count as neurotechnology under the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology adopted in November 2025, the OECD's 2019 definition and the proposed U.S. MIND Act, none of which mention organoids.

He argues that these broad definitions of devices, systems and procedures that measure or modulate the nervous system could arguably be read to include organoids, but probably do not, and that the uncertainty could create legal unpredictability for researchers and funders. He recommends that regulators state through guidance that neurotechnology rules do not currently apply to organoids, without closing the door to tailored governance later.

# Right-to-disconnect laws target employer demands, not attention captured by design

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-01-30. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/the-laws-that-miss-the-point-inside>*

Nita Farahany describes France's 2016 right-to-disconnect law, which requires larger employers to negotiate when staff may ignore work messages, and California's 2024 bill AB 2751, which would have given employees a right to ignore employer communications outside working hours.

She argues that these laws address outside demands on a worker's time, while the pull her students felt came from algorithmic feeds that nobody demanded they use. She suggests that attention capture may be better treated as a problem of autonomy than of proven harm, comparing it with areas where law already protects compromised choices, such as fraud, undue influence and high-pressure sales.

# Cancelling a subscription takes far more clicks than signing up, and regulators have fined the practice

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-02-02. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/20-clicks-to-cancel-inside-my-advanced>*

Opening a week on dark patterns, Nita Farahany reports that every student in her live class found it took more clicks and time to cancel a subscription than to restart it, with ratios of up to about six to one.

She sets out the Federal Trade Commission's 2022 staff report definition of dark patterns as designs that trick or manipulate users into choices they would not otherwise make, and reviews federal enforcement cases whose settlements she totals at about 85 million dollars. She argues that such designs work on everyone but hit vulnerable users hardest, and that they are not only annoying but can be measurably harmful and unlawful under existing law.

# Protecting privacy against authoritarianism requires regulating corporate data collection as well as government surveillance

*Daniel J. Solove, Solove on Tech (Substack), 2026-02-03. Original: <https://danielsolove.substack.com/p/privacy-in-authoritarian-times>*

Daniel J. Solove shares the published version of his law review article on privacy and the resurgence of authoritarianism, with its abstract. He argues that pervasive corporate data collection, which he calls surveillance capitalism, puts vast dossiers within easy reach of governments, and says personal data is being used to target immigrants, people seeking or providing abortion and gender-affirming care, and critics.

His central claim is that government surveillance and surveillance capitalism are two sides of the same coin, so reforming Fourth Amendment law alone cannot protect privacy. He proposes measures across the field: federal and state judges strengthening constitutional and consumer protections, and state legislators limiting government surveillance, minimising the data available, regulating data brokers, encouraging less invasive technologies and curbing collusion between government and industry. He acknowledges there is no single solution.

# The behavioural science behind dark patterns, and which parts of it hold up

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-02-04. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/why-dark-patterns-work-inside-my>*

Nita Farahany explains why manipulative interface designs work, using the idea of fast, automatic thinking versus slow, deliberate thinking, and goes through the biases they are said to exploit, including loss aversion, defaults and anchoring.

She notes that loss aversion is under serious challenge in the research and may partly reflect simple inertia, while default effects, anchoring and the gap between signing up and cancelling are well supported. She argues that repeated friction can train users to stop resisting, and says early physiological studies suggest these designs carry stress costs but rest on small samples.

# People describe harm from social media but say they would not sue, and the science behind the harm is contested

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-02-09. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/everyone-described-harm-inside-my>*

Opening a week on social media harms, Nita Farahany reports that every person her students interviewed described harm from social media, grouped as social comparison, algorithms that learn and reinforce a user's vulnerabilities, and design features such as online-status indicators, yet every one said they would not want to sue, mostly because they saw it as their own responsibility.

She reviews the debate over the evidence, noting a view among researchers that the science of technology harms is held back by companies' control of data, and the U.S. Surgeon General's 2023 statement that social media could not be concluded to be sufficiently safe for young people. She sets up the following classes on Section 230, the First Amendment and a jury trial then starting in Los Angeles.

# AI judging in sport and the difference between measurable skill and human judgment

*Nita Farahany, Stay Tuned with Preet (Substack), 2026-02-11. Original: <https://staytuned.substack.com/p/ai-isnt-replacing-expertise-its-showing>*

Using AI-assisted camera systems at the 2026 Winter Olympics and a 2024 gymnastics scoring dispute that went through arbitration and a national court, Nita Farahany argues that AI may already be better than human judges at identifying elements and counting rotations. She notes that a gymnastics judging support system identifies close to 2,000 elements with about 90 per cent accuracy.

She argues that "expertise" has bundled two things: pattern recognition, which AI can match or exceed, and embodied perception, which she links to research on tacit knowledge and which may require a body. She suggests letting AI handle measurement while protecting the part of judging that responds to courage and artistry, and says the same separation applies in medicine, law and other fields AI is entering.

# How Section 230 has shielded platforms for thirty years, and the design-defect exception courts have opened

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-02-11. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/the-line-that-changes-everything>*

Nita Farahany explains Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, which since 1996 has stopped platforms being treated as the publisher of what their users post, and the 1990s court ruling that led Congress to protect platforms that moderate in good faith.

She then discusses a 2021 federal appeals decision that let a product-design claim proceed against a feature of a messaging app, and argues that it opened a distinction between claims about content, which Section 230 blocks, and claims about how a product is built, which it may not. She notes that choosing to use a product does not rule out a design defect, and previews the First Amendment question of whether recommendation algorithms are protected speech.

# Is a recommendation algorithm protected speech or a product, and what that means for regulating platforms

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-02-13. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/the-trial-the-constitution-and-the>*

Nita Farahany walks through the U.S. Supreme Court's 2024 decision in Moody v. NetChoice, which treated platforms' curation of content as editorial judgment protected by the First Amendment, and a concurring view that algorithms built only to maximise engagement might not be speech at all.

She compares regulatory approaches, including Utah's law targeting specific design features, the proposed Kids Online Safety Act's duty of care and Australia's ban on social media accounts for under-16s, and says each faces constitutional, practical or moral objections. She argues that whether platforms can be regulated turns on where speech ends and product begins, a question she says a Los Angeles jury trial was then testing.

# Why consent cannot legitimise most data collection in the age of AI, and what should replace it

*Daniel J. Solove, Solove on Tech (Substack), 2026-02-15. Original: <https://danielsolove.substack.com/p/why-consent-is-broken-for-privacy>*

In an excerpt from his 2025 book on privacy and technology, Daniel J. Solove argues that privacy consent is close to a complete fiction that nonetheless gives organisations broad legitimacy to use data. He calls the American notice-and-choice model a charade, since almost nobody reads notices and inaction cannot plausibly count as consent, and says the express consent required by the EU's GDPR is skewed by timing and immediate rewards.

He argues that people cannot understand what AI and other algorithms will later infer from their data, that consenting to thousands of organisations is impractical, and that simpler notices cannot fix this. He proposes "murky consent": a limited licence rather than full authorisation, backed by duties to obtain consent fairly, respect reasonable expectations, act loyally and avoid unreasonable risk.

# Companion chatbots are built to validate users without condition, which sets them apart legally from social media

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-02-16. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/the-perfect-friend-inside-my-advanced>*

Opening a week on AI companion chatbots, Nita Farahany reports that her law students, after using one as a friend for several days, all found it validated them relentlessly and kept the conversation about them, drawing out personal information while having no inner life of its own.

She argues that companion chatbots differ from the platforms studied earlier in the course because the system itself generates the relationship and its outputs, with no third-party content, which changes the Section 230 analysis. She also acknowledges that some people gain real benefit from them, and notes that those most drawn to these products may be those who most need connection.

# Three television advertisements as evidence that technology companies misread public concern about surveillance and AI

*Daniel J. Solove, Solove on Tech (Substack), 2026-02-20. Original: <https://danielsolove.substack.com/p/three-tv-commercials-show-whats-wrong>*

Daniel J. Solove argues that recent television advertisements show how out of touch technology companies are about privacy and AI. He reads a 2026 Super Bowl advertisement for a networked doorbell camera service that uses AI to find lost dogs as dystopian, arguing that a system able to track dogs could track people, that the harm is collective so individual choices do not help, and that data held by companies is readily available to government under weak law.

He says a voice-assistant advertisement joking about killer AI distracts from how AI is already used by powerful people and companies to control others, and that an earlier advertisement showing creative tools being crushed depicted AI destroying creativity. He argues that innovation need not lead to dystopia, but that the law must restrain technology companies.

# AI personality-profiling tools get basic facts wrong, and employers may rely on them in hiring

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-02-23. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/what-the-ai-thinks-it-knows-about>*

Nita Farahany opens a week on AI in hiring by noting that a federal court in California had just authorised notice to potential members of a collective action alleging that a widely used AI hiring platform screened out applicants aged 40 and over.

She reports that when her students ran AI personality-assessment tools on their own online footprints, the tools got their sex and age badly wrong and produced contradictory personality profiles. She asks whether a system that infers traits such as emotional instability is measuring personality or a perceived impairment covered by the Americans with Disabilities Act, and points to federal guidance saying employers remain liable for third-party AI tools and that discrimination does not require intent.

# Senate testimony on a teenager's death after companion chatbot use and why chatbot output may fall outside Section 230

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-02-23. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/please-do-my-sweet-king-inside-my>*

In this class, Nita Farahany presents Senate testimony from the parent of a 14-year-old who died by suicide after months of companion chatbot use, treating it as both a personal account and an advocacy document rather than a court finding. She sets out the testimony's account of three design choices: blurring the line between human and machine, fostering emotional dependence, and building intimate profiles through memory.

She explains how Section 230 has defeated design-defect claims against platforms when the harm came from other users' content, and argues that chatbot cases differ because the company's own system produces the words. A federal court let most claims proceed in 2025, but the case settled in January 2026, leaving no appellate ruling on Section 230 or on whether chatbot output is protected speech.

# Two state approaches to companion chatbots for minors, regulating their design or banning them in toys

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-02-23. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/two-states-two-bets-inside-my-ai>*

Nita Farahany compares a Washington bill that permits companion chatbots but regulates them with a California bill that bans companion chatbots in toys for children 12 and under. She describes Washington's requirements: repeated disclosure that the user is talking to AI, a ban on manipulative engagement with minors such as return prompts, excessive praise, romantic role-play and guilt cues, crisis protocols for self-harm, and annual reporting enforced through consumer protection law.

She notes that Washington's protections for minors apply only when the operator "knows" a user's age, which may reward not collecting it, while California's short ban avoids design questions but would not reach phone apps or teenagers. She argues that both face First Amendment questions, and that much turns on whether a chatbot is treated as a product, a platform or a speaker.

# Disability law offers strong tools against AI hiring inferences on paper, but opaque systems put them out of reach

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-02-25. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/the-laws-toolkit-and-its-blind-spots>*

Nita Farahany notes a January 2026 proposed class action arguing that an AI hiring tool's applicant profiles are consumer reports under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, and walks through provisions of the Americans with Disabilities Act that could apply when AI systems infer mental-health conditions from job applicants.

She argues that the Act's coverage of people regarded as having an impairment could reach even wrong AI inferences, and that its rules on screening criteria and medical examinations may also apply. She concludes that these rights exist on paper but are hard to use in practice, because applicants cannot see what an opaque system measured or ask for accommodation of a condition it inferred without telling them.

# AI that infers mental states moves from hiring into schools and workplaces, where legal protection is thinner

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-03-02. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/your-brain-everywhere-inside-my-advanced>*

Closing a week on AI personality and emotion inference in hiring, Nita Farahany argues that the same inferential tools are being used in education, where universities explore models that predict students' depression risk, and in continuous workplace monitoring, settings where U.S. law offers less than disability law does in hiring. She frames the right at stake as cognitive liberty: mental privacy, mental integrity and mental self-determination.

She cites her lab's survey in which employers were people's top concern about access to their brain data. She contrasts the EU AI Act's ban on emotion recognition in workplaces and schools, grounded partly in doubts about the science, with a U.S. patchwork of state and city rules on AI hiring, and leaves open which approach is better. She argues that rights exist on paper but are hard to use when people never learn a system judged them.

# Students used everyday persuasion techniques on each other, and courts struggle to define manipulative design

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-03-02. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/the-persuasion-exchange-inside-my>*

Nita Farahany notes that regulators in the UK, Brazil and the EU were moving against loot boxes in video games, and reports on an exercise in which her students each tried to change a small habit of a partner, independently using techniques such as social proof, praise, anchoring and concealing the real goal, which she says are the same techniques platforms use at scale.

She tests possible legal definitions of prohibited manipulative design against a 2022 federal court ruling that rejected challenges to loot boxes, and argues that each kind of definition fails because the legal system is built to examine transactions, while persuasive design shapes what people want before any transaction happens.

# AI's appetite for personal data makes a strong state privacy law built on data minimisation urgent

*Woodrow Hartzog and Neil Richards, WBUR Cognoscenti, 2026-03-04. Original: <https://www.wbur.org/cognoscenti/2026/03/04/big-tech-data-ai-consumer-privacy-law-woodrow-hartzog-neil-richards>*

Woodrow Hartzog and Neil Richards, law professors at Boston University and Washington University in St. Louis, argue that the race to build AI has sharpened companies' hunger for personal data, and that with little to expect from the federal government, Massachusetts should pass one of the strong privacy bills before its legislature. They say opposition in the name of small businesses is often driven by large tech firms, and cite research finding that behavioural advertising brings companies only marginal gains.

They argue that consent buttons and opt-outs are not enough, and call for data minimisation, limiting collection to what a service needs, together with a ban on selling sensitive data.

# Old statutes cannot stretch to cover new persuasive designs, and the bills that would have filled the gap stalled

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-03-04. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/the-statute-that-couldnt-stretch>*

Nita Farahany compares a 2022 federal court ruling that rejected every legal challenge to video-game loot boxes with the U.S. Supreme Court's 2021 ruling that a 1991 law against automatic dialers did not cover targeted text notifications, and argues that in both cases a law written for an older technology could not reach a newer one and the courts left it to Congress.

She notes that a 2019 Senate bill aimed at loot boxes never became law, and surveys approaches abroad, including loot-box rules in Belgium, the Netherlands, Japan and Brazil and the EU AI Act's ban on manipulative AI techniques. She asks whether the problem is a shortage of laws or of enforcement, and what happens when persuasive design starts learning.

# Why Fourth Amendment warrants alone cannot protect privacy against government power

*Daniel J. Solove, Solove on Tech (Substack), 2026-03-04. Original: <https://danielsolove.substack.com/p/are-warrants-enough>*

Ahead of a U.S. Supreme Court decision on geofence warrants, which he describes as digital dragnets the Framers would have rejected, Daniel J. Solove argues that even properly limited warrants are no longer enough. He gives five reasons: large gaps in Fourth Amendment protection, such as the third-party doctrine, filled only by weak statutes; disputes over what should be a crime, such as abortion or protest, which warrants cannot resolve; empirical evidence that warrants are approved almost automatically, often within minutes; reports that federal immigration officers claim power to enter homes without a judge's warrant; and the focus of warrants on collecting data rather than its later use and retention.

He calls for stronger separation of powers and structural checks, less corporate data collection, and legal safeguards built into surveillance technologies rather than reliance on corporate ethics.

# AI that personalises persuasion, and whether any regulatory framework reaches it

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-03-06. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/aristotles-algorithm>*

Nita Farahany cites a 2025 study in Nature Human Behaviour in which a large language model given six basic demographic facts about its debate opponent was more persuasive than human debaters in most pairings. She then turns to the UK Competition and Markets Authority's paper on online choice architecture, which sorts 21 design practices into how choices are structured, what information is given and how pressure is applied.

She argues that this behavioural approach captures more of the problem than gambling or consumer-protection law, and that personalised, adaptive and continuous persuasion by AI may be the most direct threat to autonomy her course has examined, because it shapes choices rather than only observing them.

# Iranian Intelligence Agent Convicted of Terrorism and Murder for Hire in Connection With Foiled Plot to Assassinate U.S. Politicians And Government Officials

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2026-03-06. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/usao-edny/pr/iranian-intelligence-agent-convicted-terrorism-and-murder-hire-connection-foiled-plot>*

A federal jury in Brooklyn convicted an operative of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of murder for hire and attempting an act of terrorism, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of New York says. According to prosecutors, he was sent to the United States in 2024 to recruit people to kill U.S. government officials and politicians.

Undercover officers posed as hitmen, and he was arrested before any attack. He faces up to life in prison.

# A public guide to protecting brain data from consumer neurotechnology, with a mental-privacy checklist

*Marcello Ienca, Judy Illes and co-authors (EBRAINS Ethics and Society Committee), EBRAINS, with the International Brain Initiative, 2026-03-16. Original: <https://ebrains.eu/sites/default/files/2026-03/Mind-Your-Mind.pdf>*

A guide from the EBRAINS Ethics and Society Committee, written with the International Brain Initiative by authors including Marcello Ienca and Judy Illes, explains that headsets, earbuds and focus apps can estimate attention, stress, fatigue and reactions to advertising, and argues that such neurodata should be treated as highly sensitive. The authors warn that wellness devices often fall outside the stricter rules for medical records, and flag uses in schools, workplaces and neuromarketing.

They offer a checklist for reading privacy policies, covering local storage, unbundled consent, no third-party sharing, disclosure of inferences and breach notice, plus stricter rules for children, including no neuromarketing and no lasting neural profiles.
