# Clicking agree to terms of service is rarely meaningful consent, and three theories of what goes wrong

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-03-16. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/the-biggest-lie-on-the-internet-inside>*

Opening a week on consent, Nita Farahany cites research showing that few adults read privacy policies and that reading all of them would take weeks a year, and notes that the law nonetheless treats a click as consent. She points to the Federal Trade Commission's 245 million dollar settlement with a video-game maker over interfaces it said led to unintended purchases.

She sets out three explanations for failed digital consent, each with its own remedy: an information failure fixed by better disclosure, a design failure fixed by regulating how products are built, and a capacity failure fixed by protecting vulnerable users such as children. She links them to the GDPR, the U.S. children's privacy law and California's Age-Appropriate Design Code Act respectively.

# The design of the choice environment, not only missing information, undermines online consent

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-03-18. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/the-environment-is-the-argument-inside>*

Nita Farahany argues that even a fully informed user operates in an environment engineered to produce outcomes unrelated to their preferences, using the example of an in-game currency sold in bundles that always leave an unspendable remainder and weaken the link between money and purchases. She notes that the UK Competition and Markets Authority classed virtual currencies in games as usually or always harmful.

She contrasts an information theory of consent, which calls for better notices, with an architecture theory, which looks at what the environment does to the ability to choose, and argues that cognitive liberty requires preserving the conditions for genuine choice. She previews three laws that try to close the gap, including California's design code for children.

# Non-medical neurotechnology should be presumptively restricted and regulated by what is inferred from brain data

*Marcello Ienca, Deutscher Ethikrat (German Ethics Council), public hearing, 2026-03-19. Original: <https://www.ethikrat.org/fileadmin/PDF-Dateien/Veranstaltungen/anhoerung-2026-03-19-ienca.pdf>*

Marcello Ienca, an ethicist at the Technical University of Munich, told a public hearing of the German Ethics Council that non-medical neurotechnology, in uses ranging from the military and the workplace to education and entertainment, calls for five ethical priorities aimed at protecting human rights. He argues that applications which record or infer mental states outside medicine should be restricted by default and allowed only where there is a demonstrable, legitimate need, no less intrusive alternative and an independent human rights and data protection impact assessment, backed by binding oversight.

He argues that current rules such as the GDPR and Chile's focus on raw data rather than its use, which over-regulates research and medicine while under-regulating consumer devices, and proposes risk-based regulation of the models that draw inferences from neural data. He also calls for stronger security of neurotechnology infrastructure, explainable AI in neurotechnology, user-centred research, and protection of patients from unrealistic expectations, and notes that the EU AI Act regulates emotion recognition in some settings but does not expressly cover decoding thoughts, intentions or other cognitive states.

# The Senate passed an updated children's online privacy bill unanimously, but it does not require age verification

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-03-23. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/the-senate-just-agreed-on-something>*

Opening a week on children's online safety, Nita Farahany notes that the U.S. Senate passed the Children and Teens' Online Privacy Protection Act, known as COPPA 2.0, by unanimous consent on 5 March 2026, the first major update to children's online privacy law in 27 years, and that it still needed to pass the House and expressly does not require platforms to verify age.

She sets out competing views of whether platforms exploit young users' vulnerable moments, and compares methods of age verification, including identity documents, credit cards, facial age estimation and device-level signals, noting the privacy, accuracy and concentration-of-power risks of each. She also notes the Supreme Court's 2025 decision upholding a Texas age-verification law for pornographic sites.

# Three theories of broken online consent tested against a data-broker deletion law, children's privacy rules and a design code

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-03-23. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/what-the-law-is-trying-to-do-about>*

Nita Farahany sets out three accounts of why online consent fails, each with its own remedy: missing information, met with disclosure; limited capacity, met with protections for vulnerable users; and manipulative design, met with rules on how products are built. She applies them to California's law creating a single deletion request to all registered data brokers, which she says makes leaving cheaper but does not change how data is collected.

She argues that the federal children's privacy rule's "actual knowledge" standard rewards platforms that avoid learning users' ages, and notes a regulator's promise not to penalise data collected only for age checks. She then reviews a March 2026 Ninth Circuit ruling that let parts of California's children's design code proceed, and argues the open question is whether product design is protected speech. The closing section is for paid subscribers; this summary covers the free part.

# New lipid nanoparticle design improves precision of mRNA vaccine delivery

*Penn Engineering, University of Pennsylvania, 2026-03-24. Original: <https://www.engineering.upenn.edu/stories/new-lipid-nanoparticle-design-improves-precision-of-mrna-vaccine-delivery/>*

University of Pennsylvania engineers report a redesigned lipid nanoparticle, the fatty carrier that delivers mRNA in vaccines, published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society. According to the university, in animal studies the new particles sent at least ten times less mRNA to the liver than the formulation used in the Moderna COVID-19 vaccine, while delivery to the lymph nodes, where immune responses are trained, stayed similar.

The university says the particles produced antibody responses comparable to those of clinically approved formulations. The results are from animal models; no human testing is reported.

# Design codes, access limits and data minimisation as strategies to protect children online, and the costs of each

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-03-25. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/the-law-that-kept-getting-blocked>*

Nita Farahany notes that a New Mexico jury had just found that a major social media company violated parts of the state's Unfair Practices Act, and then compares regulatory strategies for children's online safety, beginning with the UK Information Commissioner's Children's Code, which sets 15 design standards such as high-privacy defaults without requiring age verification.

She says the UK code's enforcement record is mixed, and weighs access restrictions, design mandates, data minimisation, fraud enforcement, product liability and transparency rules, concluding that each carries real costs and benefits and none solves the problem alone. She argues that whether harm is seen as coming from content or from platform design decides which less restrictive alternatives courts will accept.

# HMRC hands GBP473M migration deal to AWS after rivals walk

*The Register, 2026-03-25. Original: <https://www.theregister.com/2026/03/25/hmrc_fujitsu_contract_aws>*

Amazon Web Services won a £472.8 million contract, as the only bidder, to move HM Revenue & Customs systems out of three data centres run by Fujitsu, The Register reports. The systems run older operating systems, including HP-UX, IBM AIX and Solaris. The contract runs at least seven years, to 2033.

Google and IBM withdrew. Sources told The Register the tender ruled out hybrid cloud and left the government no leverage to negotiate.

# A negligent-design verdict against social media platforms and the case for private lawsuits over technology harms

*Daniel J. Solove, Solove on Tech (Substack), 2026-03-27. Original: <https://danielsolove.substack.com/p/accountability-for-technology-and>*

Daniel J. Solove treats a March 2026 Los Angeles jury verdict against two large platforms on a negligent-design theory, together with a larger New Mexico verdict on child safety, as a milestone for technology accountability. Without taking a view on the addiction claims, he notes that the design theory avoids Section 230 immunity by treating technology as a product rather than speech.

He argues that regulating design is essential for privacy and for AI, and that the law can set meaningful standards as it does for cars. He says public frustration with technology harms is justified and that the industry's race for speed needs legal limits. Drawing on his forthcoming article, he argues that private lawsuits are a vital supplement to under-resourced government enforcers and give people harmed a way to seek accountability.

# An appeals court ruling on California's children's design code shows where the constitutional line sits

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-03-27. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/the-ninth-circuit-told-california>*

Nita Farahany analyses the Ninth Circuit's 12 March 2026 opinion on California's Age-Appropriate Design Code Act, the second time the same panel reviewed the law. She explains that its earlier ruling struck the law's risk-assessment requirement under strict scrutiny as compelled speech, while the new ruling upheld the law's coverage definition against the facial challenge and sent the age-estimation requirement back to the trial court, noting that platforms could instead apply child-level privacy settings to everyone.

She argues that the court has drawn a line between rules that make platforms judge which content harms children and rules that set privacy and design defaults, and that a law closer to the UK model might have survived. She leaves open whether the line is drawn in the right place.

# The Fifth Amendment protects thought, not the body; neural devices blur the line

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-03-30. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/the-government-can-take-your-blood>*

In a class on cognitive evidence, Nita Farahany explains that the Fifth Amendment protects a person from being forced to testify against themselves, which courts have read to cover what comes from the mind but not physical evidence such as blood or fingerprints. She traces how Fisher v. United States (1976) and United States v. Hubbell (2000) extended protection to producing evidence when it requires a suspect's own thinking.

She argues that wristbands that read the intention to move before movement happens, and AI conversation logs that record thinking in progress, strain the line between body and mind, and that courts have not settled where it now falls.

# Who owns digital thoughts? The limits of property law and UNESCO's neurotechnology recommendation

*Bo Hyoung Lee, Stanford Law School, Law and Biosciences Blog, 2026-03-30. Original: <https://law.stanford.edu/2026/03/30/who-owns-digital-thoughts-the-limits-of-property-law-and-the-2025-unesco-recommendation-on-the-ethics-of-neurotechnology/>*

Writing on Stanford Law School's Law and Biosciences Blog, Bo Hyoung Lee argues that treating neural data as property that can be sold risks making it a routine condition of jobs, insurance and services, and that U.S. notice-and-consent privacy law does not fit information about a person's mental life.

The post describes UNESCO's 2025 Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology as a human-rights framework built on dignity, freedom of thought and mental privacy, but notes it is not binding and relies on consent. It recommends stronger safeguards for neural data, limits on requiring it for work or services, and a right to see and contest AI inferences.

# Two appeals courts split on whether forcing a thumbprint unlock is self-incrimination

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-04-02. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/two-courts-one-test-one-thumb-inside>*

In the second of three classes on the Fifth Amendment and cognitive evidence, Nita Farahany reviews how courts have handled orders to unlock encrypted devices, including a 2019 Massachusetts high court ruling that a passcode cannot be compelled because it exists only in the suspect's mind, and two 2024 federal appeals rulings, from the Ninth Circuit and the D.C. Circuit, that reached opposite results on forced thumbprint unlocking.

She argues that both courts applied the same test but measured different things, and offers the spectrum from her 2012 law review article (identifying, automatic, memorialized and uttered evidence) in place of the testimonial/physical divide. She warns that a test based on the absence of "cognitive exertion" would give the least protection to interfaces that read intention directly, such as neural wristbands.

# Fraud claims may survive appeal where design-defect claims against social media companies may not

*Nita Farahany, Stay Tuned with Preet (Substack), 2026-04-03. Original: <https://staytuned.substack.com/p/the-strongest-case-against-meta-is>*

In a guest post for the Stay Tuned with Preet newsletter, cross-posted to Thinking Freely, Nita Farahany compares two jury verdicts from late March 2026 against social media companies: a Los Angeles verdict resting on the theory that platform features were defectively designed to be addictive, and a New Mexico verdict, in a case brought by the state attorney general, finding that a company made false or misleading statements about platform safety.

She argues that the design theory is exposed on appeal to Section 230 and to the First Amendment reasoning of the Supreme Court's 2024 ruling in Moody v. NetChoice, while a fraud and misrepresentation theory is not, because knowing deception is not protected speech. She likens this to the turn in tobacco litigation toward what companies knew, and suggests the fraud route can protect cognitive liberty without new doctrine.

# US states build patchwork of neural data privacy laws

*Inside BCI, 2026-04-03. Original: <https://insidebci.com/policy/2026-04-03-us-states-build-patchwork-of-neural-data-privacy-laws-as-bci-market-accelerates>*

Inside BCI reports that four U.S. states, Colorado, California, Montana and Connecticut, have passed laws protecting neural data, each written differently. Colorado's law applies when the data is used to identify someone. California's covers information from nervous-system activity. Montana amended its genetic privacy law and added a warrant requirement. Connecticut's covers central nervous system activity.

A federal bill, the MIND Act, would have the FTC study neural data and recommend national standards. As of April 2026 it had not left committee.

# Neural evidence strains the Fifth Amendment, and state neural data laws do not stop a subpoena

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-04-04. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/when-the-interface-is-neural>*

In the last of three classes on the Fifth Amendment and cognitive evidence, Nita Farahany separates two kinds of neural evidence: deliberate neural commands used to unlock a device, and involuntary brain responses such as the P300 recognition signal used in "brain fingerprinting", which she argues reveal stored memory rather than a bodily fact. She explains why the foregone-conclusion doctrine cannot apply to neural data that only comes into being as it is recorded.

She notes that neural data laws in Colorado, California and Montana, and Chile's constitution, govern what companies may do but do not stop a grand jury from subpoenaing data once collected. She weighs the Fourth Amendment as a procedural alternative, calls neural monitoring as a bail condition an open question, and sets out three paths courts could take, arguing that a mechanical reading of current doctrine would protect nothing.

# The First Amendment wall shields users and platforms alike, and whether an algorithm speaks is unsettled

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-04-07. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/the-wall-that-cuts-both-ways-and>*

Opening three classes on the First Amendment and cognitive liberty, Nita Farahany explains that the state action doctrine both protects users from government pressure on platforms and protects platforms from users' free-speech claims. She traces a 2019 appeals ruling on a public official blocking critics on social media, the Supreme Court's 2021 order vacating it as moot alongside a concurrence suggesting platforms could be treated as common carriers, and the Court's 2024 test for when an official's posts count as state action.

She then asks whether algorithmic curation is speech, contrasting a 2013 ruling that treated search results as protected editorial judgment with recommendation feeds that no person reviews, and describes a proposal that speech requires the speaker to know what was said. She argues the result is a double bind: users have no constitutional claim against platforms, while platforms are increasingly shielded from regulation of their editorial choices.

# A children's book read as a parable of relentless targeted marketing that ignores people's refusals

*Daniel J. Solove, Solove on Tech (Substack), 2026-04-08. Original: <https://danielsolove.substack.com/p/green-eggs-and-ham-how-not-to-market>*

Daniel J. Solove reads Dr. Seuss's Green Eggs and Ham as a story of persistent privacy invasion by a marketer who will not accept a clear and repeated no. He imagines that a modern version of the character would rely on a detailed digital dossier and an AI prediction that the consumer will like the product before he knows it himself.

He argues that the book's apparent lesson about persistence is a bad one, because it suggests it is acceptable to pester people however often they refuse, which he calls the opposite of good marketing. He compares it to online advertising that follows people around the web after a single search, and offers a comic rewritten ending. He notes that the post adapts one he wrote more than a decade earlier.

# INBRAIN completes enrolment of first-in-human study of graphene neural interfaces

*Business Wire, 2026-04-20. Original: <https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260420000990/en/INBRAIN-Neuroelectronics-Completes-Enrolment-of-Worlds-First-in-Human-Study-of-Graphene-Neural-Interfaces-for-Brain-Decoding-Mapping>*

Barcelona-based INBRAIN Neuroelectronics says it has completed enrolment in the first study in people of its graphene brain interface, a thin, flexible sheet of electrodes that uses graphene in place of metal contacts. According to the company, the study (NCT06368310) is sponsored by the University of Manchester and run with an NHS trust; the device was placed on the brain's surface during brain tumour surgery in eight patients, and in some awake operations it recorded activity while patients named objects.

The company reports no device-related adverse events in the eight patients up to discharge from hospital. These are preliminary, company-reported results: the study's safety endpoint includes 90 days of follow-up, and the full results had not been published at the time of the release.

# AI that finds software flaws faster than they can be fixed, and an Illinois bill to shield AI companies from catastrophe liability

*Nita Farahany, Stay Tuned with Preet (Substack), 2026-04-22. Original: <https://staytuned.substack.com/p/nothing-stays-safe-ai-anthropic-security>*

In a guest post for the Stay Tuned with Preet newsletter, cross-posted to Thinking Freely, Nita Farahany treats repeated leaks from the U.S. Supreme Court as the floor of institutional privacy and an AI developer's decision to withhold a model it said was highly effective at finding exploitable software flaws as the ceiling, arguing that such a capability, if it spread, could expose hospitals, power grids, banks and election systems at once.

She criticises Illinois SB 3444, which she describes as backed by OpenAI, for offering AI companies immunity from civil liability for mass-casualty events if they publish a safety plan and avoid intentional or reckless conduct, and notes that a rival developer opposes it and backs a narrower bill. She argues that lawsuits are how powerful actors have been held to account and that the bill would remove that route before any case is brought.

# A proposed federal privacy bill would leave people less protected and could wipe out stronger state laws

*Daniel J. Solove, Solove on Tech (Substack), 2026-04-25. Original: <https://danielsolove.substack.com/p/a-disastrous-federal-privacy-bill>*

Daniel J. Solove argues that the SECURE Data Act, a federal privacy bill drafted by Republicans, would do more harm than good and is closer to an anti-privacy law. He says it copies the weakest state consumer privacy laws and their notice-and-choice model, whose individual rights he regards as an illusion of control, particularly when people cannot foresee what AI will infer. He calls its data minimisation language empty, its data broker rules little more than registration, its duties and governance requirements minimal, and its enforcement weak, with no fines and no private right of action.

His sharpest objection is preemption: he argues the bill's broad "relates to" wording could displace thousands of state laws, including torts, wiretap laws and specific statutes such as Illinois's biometric privacy law, and invite endless litigation. A good federal law, he argues, would make preemption unnecessary.

# Chile's neurorights leave data inferred from brain activity in a legal gray zone

*Bo Hyoung Lee, Stanford Law and Biosciences Blog, 2026-04-27. Original: <https://law.stanford.edu/2026/04/27/even-chiles-neurorights-leave-inferred-mental-data-in-a-gray-zone/>*

Bo Hyoung Lee writes that Chile has gone further than most countries in protecting brain data, through its 2021 constitutional amendment and a 2023 Supreme Court order to delete brain-activity data stored by a consumer EEG headset maker. The author argues that both focus on collected and stored data and leave unclear how the law treats scores, profiles and other information that software infers from brain signals.

The author also points to a 2024 finding by Chile's health regulator that the same headset is not a medical device, which in the author's view shows how consumer products can sit outside medical oversight. Noting that a bill to implement the constitutional provision has passed the Senate and is before the Chamber of Deputies, the author presents Chile as still turning constitutional recognition into working regulation.

# Arcadia, California, Mayor Federally Charged with Acting as Illegal Agent of the People's Republic of China

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2026-05-11. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/arcadia-california-mayor-federally-charged-acting-illegal-agent-peoples-republic-china>*

The mayor of Arcadia, California, was charged with acting as an illegal agent of the People's Republic of China, the Justice Department announced. According to the plea agreement, from late 2020 through 2022 the mayor promoted PRC propaganda in the United States at the direction of PRC government officials, including through a website that published content they supplied.

The mayor agreed to plead guilty to the charge, which carries up to 10 years in prison. Until convicted, the mayor is presumed innocent.

# Pacemaker data used as evidence shows how personal devices let police turn intimate data against their users

*Daniel J. Solove, Solove on Tech (Substack), 2026-05-15. Original: <https://danielsolove.substack.com/p/your-pacemaker-can-now-testify-against>*

Daniel J. Solove presents an online conversation with law professor Andrew Guthrie Ferguson about Ferguson's 2026 book on policing in an age of self-surveillance. Solove's framing is that the devices people use gather large amounts of data that is readily available to the government.

He highlights an example Ferguson gives, quoted in the post: a man whose pacemaker data, held by his doctor, was obtained by detectives with a warrant in an arson investigation and contradicted his account. Ferguson argues that the technology is beneficial and the police acted lawfully, yet that intimate data from hearts, wrists, cycle-tracking apps or smart beds should perhaps be beyond police reach even with a warrant, since nearly everything digital passes through a third party. The full discussion is in a video in the post.

# Bronx Man Convicted of Operating Police Station for the Chinese Government in New York City and Obstruction of Justice

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2026-05-20. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/bronx-man-convicted-operating-police-station-chinese-government-new-york-city-and>*

A federal jury in Brooklyn convicted a Bronx resident of acting as an illegal agent of China's Ministry of Public Security and of obstruction of justice, the Justice Department says. According to the department, from January 2022 he ran an undeclared police station for the Chinese government in Manhattan's Chinatown, tasked in part with gathering information on political dissidents.

A co-defendant pleaded guilty in December 2024. The convicted man faces up to 30 years in prison at sentencing.

# Minority Report and the case against using AI to predict human behaviour

*Daniel J. Solove, Solove on Tech (Substack), 2026-05-22. Original: <https://danielsolove.substack.com/p/dangerous-oracles-minority-report>*

In an essay in his technology and humanities series, Daniel J. Solove uses Philip K. Dick's 1956 story and the 2002 film Minority Report to argue that AI predictions of human behaviour are deeply problematic. Drawing on an article written with Hideyuki Matsumi, he argues that such predictions are "power dressed up with math", used to shape and control the future rather than to understand it.

He criticises a 2016 Wisconsin Supreme Court decision upholding a sentence informed by an algorithmic recidivism score, arguing that such tools punish people for crimes other people committed. He sets out four problems the co-authored article identifies: predictions fossilise the past, cannot be disproved, remove the feedback needed to check accuracy when acted on in advance, and can fulfil themselves. He cites other scholars who argue that predicting social behaviour is not a solvable technical problem.

# A 1909 story about a machine-run society as a warning about AI replacing first-hand experience

*Daniel J. Solove, Solove on Tech (Substack), 2026-05-30. Original: <https://danielsolove.substack.com/p/a-century-ago-em-forsters-the-machine>*

In his technology and humanities series, Daniel J. Solove argues that E.M. Forster's 1909 story "The Machine Stops", in which isolated people live underground and communicate through screens, anticipated how AI and digital technology are hollowing out human experience. He links the story's acceptance of something "good enough" to AI output that reads smoothly but is often hollow or wrong.

He argues that AI summaries in search are turning the internet from a place of first-hand discovery into reconstituted second-hand material, cutting traffic to the creators whose work it draws on, and cites a columnist's account of falling traffic. Citing the scholars Woodrow Hartzog and Jessica Silbey, he argues that AI is shifting from a tool that helps people to one that replaces them and weakens institutions.

# ICE to spend $25M on iris recognition

*FedScoop, 2026-06-01. Original: <https://fedscoop.com/dhs-ice-agents-biometrics-contract-iris-recognition>*

Immigration and Customs Enforcement awarded BI2 Technologies a $25 million contract for 1,570 iris-scanning devices for field agents, running June 2026 to May 2027, FedScoop reports. The devices combine iris, fingerprint and face recognition and connect to the vendor's system of about 5 million booking records from 47 states. FedScoop notes the vendor does not hold FedRAMP authorization.

House Democrats have criticized mobile biometric collection, and the DHS Inspector General is auditing how the agency collects and shares this data.

# State consumer privacy laws are being weakened by industry lobbying, with Vermont as the latest example

*Daniel J. Solove, Solove on Tech (Substack), 2026-06-02. Original: <https://danielsolove.substack.com/p/state-consumer-privacy-laws-are-being>*

Daniel J. Solove argues that the U.S. state consumer privacy laws passed since 2018, now in roughly half the states, are mostly poor, grading most a D or F, and blames industry lobbying that followed California's law. He describes a weak Virginia law becoming the template other states copied, and this year's laws in Alabama, Oklahoma and Louisiana as very weak.

He calls Vermont's case a tragedy: a strong earlier bill with a private right of action was vetoed, and a later version was weakened so much that its lead sponsor voted against it, describing a lobbying playbook that he quotes. He argues the laws are toothless, lack private rights of action, rely on rarely used individual rights, contain hollow duties outside Maryland and repackage notice and choice, and that policymakers too readily accept industry's appeals to innovation.

# American Citizen Pleads Guilty to Working as an Agent for the People's Republic of China

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2026-06-04. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/american-citizen-pleads-guilty-working-agent-peoples-republic-china>*

An American citizen pleaded guilty to acting as an agent of China's Ministry of State Security without notifying the U.S. government, the Justice Department says. According to the department, from 2019 to February 2026 he worked his way into U.S. political circles, recruited intelligence sources and passed sensitive information to his handlers, for more than $100,000.

The charge carries up to 10 years in prison. Sentencing was set for 1 September 2026.

# Orwell or Huxley: both dystopias describe today's world, but neither foresaw the role of corporations

*Daniel J. Solove, Solove on Tech (Substack), 2026-06-06. Original: <https://danielsolove.substack.com/p/orwell-vs-huxley-which-dystopia-was>*

In his technology and humanities series, Daniel J. Solove revisits the debate over whether George Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four, with its surveillance and terror, or Aldous Huxley's Brave New World, with its control through pleasure and manipulation, was more prophetic. He sets out each author's comments on the other, including Huxley's 1949 letter predicting that rulers would prefer conditioning to force, and Neil Postman's argument that Huxley was right.

Solove concludes that both were right: people live in a surveillance society they embrace because it pleases them, under governments and companies that manipulate them. He argues that the core element the two share is the suppression of independent thought, and that both missed the private sector, which he says amplifies government power and exercises its own, echoing his argument that surveillance capitalism and government surveillance must be regulated together.

# A bipartisan US House draft would federalise frontier AI safety rules and pause some state AI laws for three years

*Justine Gluck, Future of Privacy Forum, 2026-06-09. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/frontier-ai-goes-federal-how-the-great-american-ai-act-compares-to-state-laws/>*

Justine Gluck, for the Future of Privacy Forum, analyses a bipartisan discussion draft of the Great American AI Act of 2026 released in the US House. Gluck says it is one of the first bipartisan attempts in Congress to address both frontier model safety and federal preemption of state AI laws, though its prospects are uncertain.

Gluck finds that the draft's frontier provisions closely track recent state laws in California, New York and Illinois, with frameworks, transparency reports and incident reporting, but differ in places, adding a revenue threshold and dropping the requirement that a critical safety incident cause actual harm. It would also create federally licensed independent auditors for the largest developers. Its three-year preemption clause covers state laws that specifically regulate AI model development, which Gluck calls far narrower than the ten-year moratorium the Senate rejected in 2025 but open to difficult questions where state laws mix development and deployment. The draft also proposes a content-moderation study, a voluntary testing programme and notice of AI-driven mass layoffs.

# A television drama read as a study of authoritarian rule, surveillance and the people who serve it

*Daniel J. Solove, Solove on Tech (Substack), 2026-06-10. Original: <https://danielsolove.substack.com/p/andor-and-authoritarianism>*

Daniel J. Solove argues that the Star Wars series Andor is one of the finest portrayals of authoritarian rule and of resistance to it, and that it explores surveillance, disinformation and the dehumanising effect of bureaucracy. He values its refusal to draw simple moral lines and reads its exhausting, costly picture of rebellion as a warning about what defending freedom takes.

Drawing on Hannah Arendt, he argues that much harm is done by careerists who never decide whether to be good or evil, and he compares them to technology leaders who chase growth whatever the harm, while saying he does not consider those leaders evil. He treats technology as a tool of power rather than its source, and argues that such regimes grow through lies, manipulation and the capitulation of ordinary people, while their rigid bureaucracy leaves cracks for resistance.

# Privacy law should protect obscurity as a right grounded in dignity, with bans for some threats and targeted remedies for others

*Woodrow Hartzog and Evan Selinger, California Law Review Online, 2026-06-15. Original: <https://www.californialawreview.org/online/right-obscurity>*

Woodrow Hartzog of Boston University and Evan Selinger of the Rochester Institute of Technology argue that US privacy law has neglected obscurity, the state in which information about a person is hard to find or understand, which they say gives people the breathing room needed for free expression, protest, intimate relationships and self-development. Responding to an article proposing a central system for removing people's data from data brokers, they welcome such targeted remedies but argue that obscurity should be treated as a legally protected right tied to human dignity and the capabilities people need to flourish.

Doubting that a single constitutional right is workable in the US, they draw on the international human rights framework of duties to respect, protect and fulfil, and argue that responsibility should shift from individuals to those who create visibility, such as brokers, platforms and governments, with forward-looking standards, impact assessments and sunset clauses. They conclude that threats such as mass facial recognition call for bright-line bans, while brokered abuse calls for targeted remedies.

# AWS secures $2.6B DHS-wide Cumulus cloud project

*FedScoop, 2026-06-15. Original: <https://fedscoop.com/dhs-cumulus-cloud-project-aws-contract>*

FedScoop reports that the Department of Homeland Security awarded Amazon Web Services a $2.6 billion contract for cloud infrastructure, training and marketplace services across the department. It is the first award in Cumulus, the department's first department-wide cloud buying program, with a one-year base period and four option years.

DHS expects at least $142 million in savings in the first year. Oracle, Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure are expected to join later.

# DHS finalizes first Cumulus cloud contract with AWS

*Nextgov/FCW, 2026-06-16. Original: <https://www.nextgov.com/acquisition/2026/06/dhs-finalizes-first-cumulus-cloud-contract-aws/414197>*

The Department of Homeland Security has finalized the first of four cloud awards under its Cumulus program, with Amazon Web Services, Nextgov/FCW reports. The award has a ceiling of $2.5 billion over up to five years: a one-year base period and four option years.

DHS planned similar awards with Oracle, Google Cloud and Microsoft by the end of June 2026. The aim is to bring the department's cloud buying together and see its cloud spending in one place.

# Six reasons why treating personal data as property would not protect privacy

*Daniel J. Solove, Solove on Tech (Substack), 2026-06-17. Original: <https://danielsolove.substack.com/p/privacy-as-property>*

Daniel J. Solove sets out the case for giving people ownership of their personal data and then argues against it on six grounds. He says that property can be sold, so companies would acquire people's data and could press them to give up protections that current law makes non-waivable; that labelling data as property would legitimise the existing trade of data for free services; and that people cannot price their data, because its risks depend on aggregation and unknown future uses.

He adds that privacy's value is not only financial, that much data is shared between people and has no single owner, and that ownership is too individualistic when AI trained on other people's data affects everyone. He concludes that ownership and individual control are the wrong tools and argues for consumer-protection rules aimed at risk and harm.

# Data embassies misread how real embassies work, a guest post argues, proposing data corridors between states instead

*Yeong Zee Kin, Future of Privacy Forum, 2026-06-18. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/understanding-data-embassies-and-corridors/>*

Yeong Zee Kin, in a guest post for the Future of Privacy Forum that he says reflects only his own opinion, examines 'data embassies', offered by governments and businesses as an answer to the spread of data localisation rules driven by data sovereignty and security concerns. He argues the concept misreads how real embassies work: under the 1961 Vienna Convention the receiving state's laws still apply to embassy premises, so data stored in a data embassy is not simply governed by the sending state's law.

He distinguishes a security model, pioneered by Estonia as an offsite backup of state data, from a developmental model used to attract cloud investment, citing Bahrain and a draft Saudi law, and warns that the latter could leave breaches uninvestigated by either state. He proposes instead a two-way 'data corridor' set up between states, for example in a special economic zone, that supports choice of law, benchmarks against a shared standard such as ASEAN's data protection framework, and provides for access by regulators and law enforcement.

# AWS pledges further $13bn investment in India

*DatacenterDynamics, 2025-01-01. Original: <https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/aws-pledges-further-13bn-investment-in-ai-and-cloud-infrastructure-in-india>*

Amazon Web Services has pledged a further $13 billion for AI and cloud infrastructure in India, expanding data center capacity in Mumbai and Hyderabad, DatacenterDynamics reported on 25 June 2026. Amazon says this brings its total planned investment in India across all its businesses to $48 billion between 2026 and 2030.

# A satirical television series about a tech billionaire as a portrait of an industry that mines personal data

*Daniel J. Solove, Solove on Tech (Substack), 2026-06-28. Original: <https://danielsolove.substack.com/p/the-audacity-big-tech-and-the-battle>*

Daniel J. Solove reviews the 2026 television series The Audacity, which he describes as a satire combining the bleakness of Succession with the workplace comedy of Silicon Valley. He argues that privacy is at its centre: the fictional company treats personal data as a resource to mine and sell, and he likens one of its business models, charging people for protection while selling the data of those who decline, to extortion.

He argues that the series shows the technology industry itself as pathological, with constant pressure to attract investors pushing founders to abandon ethics, so that even powerful figures do not control the game. He recommends it to viewers who enjoy dark satire about privacy and technology.

# Harms from technologies like facial recognition are foreseeable enough to justify early bans, before people grow dependent on them

*Evan Selinger and Woodrow Hartzog, Boston University Law Review Online, July 2026. Original: <https://www.bu.edu/bulawreview/files/2026/07/SELINGER-HARTZOG.pdf>*

Evan Selinger and Woodrow Hartzog, responding to a 2025 book on method in law and technology, argue that although the future cannot be predicted with certainty, some things can be relied on, such as commercial incentives and predictable human reactions, so the foreseeability of harm should be the main factor when lawmakers decide whether and how to intervene. They say those deploying new technologies avoid accountability by demanding rigorous proof of harm and waiting until people are too accustomed and dependent to demand rules.

They argue that probabilistic "slippery slope" predictions grounded in real causal drivers justify early, robust measures such as bans and bright-line rules, as they have long proposed for facial recognition, and that small privacy losses, which they call "nicks", add up as surveillance is normalised until society can no longer find the political will to regulate.

# Is the third-party doctrine dead? A geofence ruling narrows it, a concurrence offers a property theory, and warrants stay weak

*Daniel J. Solove, Solove on Tech (Substack), 2026-07-02. Original: <https://danielsolove.substack.com/p/is-the-fourth-amendment-third-party>*

Daniel J. Solove reads the U.S. Supreme Court's 2026 geofence-warrant decision as holding that people have a reasonable expectation of privacy in location data held by a company, so the Fourth Amendment applies. He argues that the Court narrowed the third-party doctrine rather than abolishing it, and identifies three limits it drew: data that forms an exhaustive chronicle of a life, tools that are indispensable to daily life, and data people regard as their own.

He discusses Justice Gorsuch's concurrence, which treats such data as a person's effects under a property theory; he says he is generally sceptical of property theories but thinks this one fits the Fourth Amendment better. He argues that geofence warrants resemble the general warrants the amendment was meant to stop, cites research showing warrants are almost always approved, and asks whether some data should be off-limits to the government even with a warrant.

# Italo Calvino's stories as a warning against treating data as an idol, and what that means for AI

*Daniel J. Solove, Solove on Tech (Substack), 2026-07-08. Original: <https://danielsolove.substack.com/p/the-false-idolatry-of-data-calvinos>*

Daniel J. Solove reads Italo Calvino's collection Numbers in the Dark as a prescient critique of excessive faith in data. He argues that the story "World Memory", about an archive meant to record everything before humanity ends, anticipates AI, with the collection becoming an end in itself and records starting to replace the people they describe.

He finds a story Calvino wrote for a computer company playful but slight, while drawing from it the point that a machine can generate endless combinations yet cannot match open-ended human imagination. From the title story, in which a century-old accounting error grows into a distortion machines cannot correct, he draws what he calls the core lesson: AI is only as reliable as its underlying data, and flaws at the foundation keep compounding.

# US chatbot laws demand 'evidence-based' suicide detection that, an FPF analysis argues, current AI cannot reliably deliver

*Jordan Wrigley, Future of Privacy Forum, 2026-07-15. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/mandating-evidence-based-suicide-detection-in-chatbots/>*

Jordan Wrigley, for the Future of Privacy Forum, examines state chatbot laws enacted in 2025 and 2026 that require operators to detect users' suicidal ideation using 'evidence-based methods'. Wrigley argues that the term and 'suicidal ideation' are undefined, leaving developers unsure what regulators will accept, and that Wrigley knows of no scalable, highly accurate or validated method for predicting intent to self-harm outside strict clinical settings.

Wrigley cites pilot studies showing that large language models handle explicit statements well but are inconsistent with ambiguous or passive ideation, a gap that also affects mandatory reporting of referral data. Wrigley identifies a tension with privacy law: detection means inferring mental health from conversations and keeping sensitive data, which collides with consumer health privacy laws, de-identification limits and revocable consent. The author urges lawmakers to align these rules, consider human-in-the-loop review and clarify safe harbours.

# AI already acts as a tax on society by pushing its costs onto the public, an essay argues

*Daniel J. Solove, Solove on Tech (Substack), 2026-07-22. Original: <https://danielsolove.substack.com/p/ais-tax-on-society>*

Daniel J. Solove argues that AI already works as a large tax on society, because it depends on constant venture investment and on shifting its costs to the public, and might not survive ordinary market pressure. He lists the costs he sees as externalised: water and electricity use that raises utility bills and harms the environment; training on personal data scraped from the internet, which he says is not free to take merely because it is online; and creative work used without payment.

He adds the displacement of workers and creators, extra labour for schools and publishers dealing with misuse, and direct harms such as deepfakes and chatbots encouraging self-harm. He says he is not against AI, and argues that making companies bear their own costs, follow the same rules as everyone else and stop lobbying against controls would reveal its genuinely useful applications.

# Young people do care about privacy, and why what they share online does not show otherwise

*Daniel J. Solove, Solove on Tech (Substack), 2026-07-23. Original: <https://danielsolove.substack.com/p/do-young-people-care-about-privacy>*

Daniel J. Solove rejects the common claim that young people do not care about privacy because they share so much online, arguing that older generations built a technological environment that pushes the young to disclose, and that blaming them shifts responsibility onto those with the least control. Reprinting an earlier essay, he cites research finding that young people's privacy attitudes differ little from older adults', and a poll in which college students ranked privacy and security as their top online concern.

He offers four reasons for the gap between attitude and behaviour: teenagers may not weigh consequences carefully yet; digital tools are woven into daily life and hard to avoid; posting online lacks the social cues of speaking to a room; and young people understand privacy as managing who sees what, not as hiding everything.

# A first commercially approved brain implant shows why rules on payment and neural data should come before the next approval

*Ebani Dhawan, Tech Policy Press, 2026-07-24. Original: <https://techpolicy.press/chinas-first-commercial-brain-implant-shows-why-neurotechnology-needs-governance>*

Ebani Dhawan, a technology-policy analyst, argues that China's approval of a commercial brain implant in March 2026, which received a reimbursement code within 48 hours, reflects payment categories China defined in advance, while the U.S. lacks a coherent coverage pathway for breakthrough devices. She adds that approval addresses only safety and effectiveness, leaving open who controls neural data, which may reveal more about a person over time, whether it can be used to train AI and how long it is kept.

She proposes defining coverage categories ahead of approvals, widening agency coordination to include consumer-protection and health regulators, and separate, revocable consent for clinical, research and commercial or AI-training uses.

# Future of Privacy Forum comments on Colorado's rules for its automated decision-making and chatbot safety laws

*Tatiana Rice, Daniel Hales and Justine Gluck, Future of Privacy Forum, 2026-07-24. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/fpf-submits-comments-to-inform-colorado-automated-decision-making-technology-and-chatbot-rulemaking-processes/>*

Tatiana Rice, Daniel Hales and Justine Gluck of the Future of Privacy Forum summarise the Forum's comments to Colorado's Department of Justice ahead of rules for two 2026 laws: the Automated Decision-making Act, which replaced the state's earlier AI Act, and the Chatbot Safety Act. They say the aim was to resolve compliance ambiguities while keeping the rules compatible with existing state and federal privacy law.

For the automated decision law, which requires developer documentation, notices and explanations after adverse decisions, and rights to access and correct data and to ask for human review, the authors report that the Forum asked for an aligned definition of the covered technology, transparency duties that fit the state privacy act, and streamlined consumer rights. For the chatbot law, which covers age estimation, minors' settings, engagement rewards, AI disclosure and content limits, it asked for clearer exemptions, age-estimation rules compatible with the state's age-assurance law, and rules for suicide and self-harm crisis protocols.

# eBay harassment civil suit settles

*The Boston Globe, 2026-07-27. Original: <https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/07/27/business/ebay-harassed-ina-david-steiner-settlement>*

A Natick, Massachusetts, couple who ran a website covering eBay settled their civil suit against eBay, its former chief executive and two other former executives for $55.7 million, the Boston Globe reports. eBay pays $46.15 million of it.

In 2019, eBay employees carried out a harassment campaign against the couple that included threatening messages, disturbing deliveries and physical surveillance. Seven employees later pleaded guilty to criminal charges, and four served prison time.

# The EU's AI Omnibus delays the AI Act's high-risk rules to 2027 and 2028 and adds a new ban

*Andreea Șerban and Bianca-Ioana Marcu, Future of Privacy Forum, 2026-07-28. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/the-ai-act-implementation-timeline-what-changes-under-the-ai-omnibus/>*

Andreea Șerban and Bianca-Ioana Marcu, writing for the Future of Privacy Forum, explain how the AI Omnibus, published in the EU's Official Journal on 24 July 2026, changes the AI Act's timetable. The biggest change, they say, is postponing the high-risk requirements: to 2 December 2027 for the uses listed in Annex III and to 2 August 2028 for AI built into regulated products.

The authors list other changes: a new prohibition from December 2026 on AI that generates child sexual abuse material or non-consensual intimate images; a softer AI literacy duty that asks organisations to support literacy rather than ensure it; permission to use sensitive data for bias detection in any AI system; more central supervision by the AI Office, including over AI in very large platforms; and simpler compliance for small mid-sized companies. They note that many member states had not yet named their market surveillance authorities.

In their reading, the Omnibus is a targeted change that leaves the Act's core intact, gives high-risk providers more time while bans and general-purpose AI duties already apply, and shifts supervision toward Brussels; what the revised literacy duty means will depend on guidance still to come.

# DHS release: DHS Highlights Successful Arrests and Rescues in Crackdown on Human Trafficking During FIFA World Cup

*U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 2026-07-29. Original: <https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/07/29/dhs-highlights-successful-arrests-and-rescues-crackdown-human-trafficking-during>*

The Department of Homeland Security reported on 29 July 2026 that operations against human trafficking during the 2026 FIFA World Cup, led by Homeland Security Investigations and the DHS Center for Countering Human Trafficking with federal, state and local partners, led to the arrest of 905 suspects and the rescue of 180 victims: 150 adults and 30 children.

The figures are the department's own count across the tournament's host cities. An arrest is not a conviction: every person arrested is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# An Asimov story about a computer that picks an election winner, read as a warning about faith in AI prediction

*Daniel J. Solove, Solove on Tech (Substack), 2026-08-02. Original: <https://danielsolove.substack.com/p/blind-faith-in-tech-asimovs-franchise>*

Daniel J. Solove uses Isaac Asimov's 1955 story "Franchise", in which a computer decides a national election by questioning one chosen citizen, to argue that blind faith in prediction has become literal. He says algorithmic forecasts now shape hiring, credit, education, pretrial detention and sentencing, although human behaviour remains hard to predict reliably.

Drawing on other scholars, he argues that predictions about people tend to steer outcomes rather than simply foresee them, taking choices away from individuals, and that people defer too readily to machines and to AI companies' promotional claims. He points to a Wisconsin court decision that refused a defendant access to a proprietary risk algorithm used at sentencing, arguing that it let a trade-secret claim outweigh due process and shows how law can entrench unjustified trust in technology.

# The EU's proposed Cloud and AI Development Act treats AI as industrial policy, a turn from the AI Act's risk approach

*Gabriela Zanfir-Fortuna, Future of Privacy Forum, 2026-08-06. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/cada-an-eu-turn-on-ai-regulation/>*

Gabriela Zanfir-Fortuna, writing for the Future of Privacy Forum, examines the Cloud and AI Development Act the European Commission proposed in June 2026, focusing on its aim of boosting competitiveness rather than its cloud procurement rules. She calls it arguably the first major EU tech law built to enable AI adoption rather than restrain it, with duties falling mostly on the Commission and member states rather than companies, and compares it with the US AI Action Plan and Japan's AI Promotion Act.

She describes its tools: leadership initiatives tied to 'grand challenges', national AI centres and strategies, fast-track zones for data centres, priority compute for frontier projects, and the EU's first legal definitions of frontier AI and AI agents. She notes that an 'AI first' principle would enter law without a clear definition, that making data available for AI training becomes a strategic goal building on proposals to loosen GDPR rules for AI, and that several measures favour European AI.

Zanfir-Fortuna sees a real turn from the AI Act's treatment of AI as a risk, reinforced by the AI Omnibus delaying high-risk duties, but argues that the Act adds an enabling layer on top of the safety law rather than replacing it, which may make its promotion measures easier to accept.

# Zamyatin's We as the founding modern dystopia and a warning about trading freedom for efficiency

*Daniel J. Solove, Solove on Tech (Substack), 2026-08-12. Original: <https://danielsolove.substack.com/p/the-novel-that-influenced-a-century>*

Daniel J. Solove argues that Yevgeny Zamyatin's novel We deserves recognition as a founding dystopian work, because it shaped later books including Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four. He recounts how the manuscript was smuggled out of the Soviet Union and how Zamyatin died in poverty in Paris, and reads the novel chiefly as a commentary on the Soviet state and the loss of individuality, in a world of numbered citizens and glass buildings.

Disagreeing with a reading that faults the book's focus on rational order, he argues that an excess of almost anything, efficiency included, produces dystopia, and sees in it a critique of scientific management that persists in corporations. He links its warning to present-day fulfilment centres, gig-work apps, data brokers, licence-plate and facial-recognition cameras, and government efficiency drives.

# New Jersey becomes the third US state in 2026 to restrict algorithmic pricing based on personal data

*Jordan Francis, Justine Gluck and Jameson Spivack, Future of Privacy Forum, 2026-08-18. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/clean-up-on-aisle-three-new-jersey-becomes-third-state-to-regulate-data-driven-pricing-this-year/>*

Jordan Francis, Justine Gluck and Jameson Spivack of the Future of Privacy Forum compare three state laws enacted in 2026 on data-driven or 'surveillance' pricing, in Maryland, Connecticut and New Jersey, noting that the Forum tracked more than 100 such bills that year. Maryland's applies to large grocers and delivery services and bars using personal data to raise food prices; Connecticut's covers retail broadly and requires a disclosure when personal data has raised a price.

The authors describe New Jersey's law as covering groceries and household goods, reaching price cuts as well as rises, defining surveillance pricing as prices set by an algorithm or automated system using personal or inferred data, pausing new electronic shelf labels for a year, and being the first such law with a private right to sue, though how a consumer's loss would be measured is unclear. They note New Jersey also made coordinated algorithmic rent-setting an antitrust violation.

In their view, the three laws share no common framework in scope, definitions or enforcement, and the topic will stay high on legislative agendas into 2027.

# FBI: violent crime drop in 2025

*Axios, 2026-08-18. Original: <https://www.axios.com/2026/08/18/fbi-violent-crime-drop-2025>*

Axios reports FBI figures showing violent crime in the United States fell 9.7% in 2025, which the FBI calls the largest one-year drop since its national estimates began in 1936. Murder and non-negligent manslaughter fell 18.1%, to a rate of 4.1 per 100,000 people.

The figures are estimates built from about 17,000 law enforcement agencies covering more than 96% of the population. Axios notes the drop was broad enough that no single policy explains it.

# U.S. state consumer privacy laws share more than they differ: a primer on scope, rights and enforcement

*Daniel J. Solove, Solove on Tech (Substack), 2026-08-23. Original: <https://danielsolove.substack.com/p/understanding-the-patchwork-of-us>*

Daniel J. Solove argues that the U.S. state consumer privacy laws that began with California's in 2018, and by 2026 covered nearly half the states, look like a daunting patchwork but share a common framework. He explains that they reach out-of-state businesses serving residents, mostly exempt small businesses, and all exempt data covered by federal laws such as HIPAA and FERPA.

He describes their basic approach as notice and choice, with opt-in consent and impact assessments for sensitive data in most states, though the sensitive categories vary. He says the individual rights are broadly consistent: to know, access, delete, port and usually correct data, and to opt out of targeted advertising, profiling and sales. Enforcement, he notes, rests mostly with state attorneys general, with modest fines, cure periods and rarely a private right of action, while a few states, such as Maryland with strict data minimisation, go further.

# A new run of an AI law course opens with why the law struggles to define artificial intelligence

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-08-24. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/what-is-ai-inside-my-ai-law-and-policy>*

In the first class of the fall 2026 run of her Duke Law AI law and policy course, which she publishes free for online readers, Nita Farahany asks how laws can be written for something experts call an umbrella term whose target keeps moving, noting that tasks once seen as AI, such as search, come to be treated as ordinary software.

She sets out competing views on whether large language models understand anything, from claims that they are already conscious to the view that they only predict text, and argues the answer bears on legal responsibility and on whether AI could have rights. She introduces basic terms, including machine learning, generative adversarial networks, the black box problem and natural language processing.

# Why AI-invented case citations keep reaching courts, explained through how language models predict text

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-08-26. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/how-ai-actually-works-inside-my-ai>*

In the second class of her fall 2026 AI law and policy course, Nita Farahany recounts the 2023 New York sanction of a lawyer who filed cases invented by a chatbot, and later examples including a sanction of more than $110,000 in Oregon and an attorney's suspension in Nebraska. She explains tokens, parameters and weights, embeddings and the attention mechanism.

She argues that invented citations follow from the design: a model predicts the next plausible word, can place distinct legal concepts so close together that it cannot tell them apart, and, in newer reasoning models, can produce convincing explanations for answers that are still made up. She concludes that every AI-assisted citation needs to be checked.

# Watermarks on AI-generated text are imperfect provenance data and should not be treated as proof of authorship

*Lilian Edwards, CREATe blog (University of Glasgow), 2026-08-27. Original: <https://www.create.ac.uk/blog/2026/08/27/watermarks-watermarks-everywhere-and-not-a-stop-to-think-eu-ai-act-art-50-comes-to-town/>*

Lilian Edwards, an honorary professor at CREATe, University of Glasgow, discusses Anthropic's plan to watermark text generated by its Claude models to meet the EU AI Act's Article 50 marking duty, and a tool a developer released to strip the mark. She explains that text, unlike images, loses file metadata when copied, so marks are built into word choices, and argues that at scale it is impractical to tell wholly AI-written text from AI-assisted text, though the Act does not forbid marking both; she has reservations about labelling mandates, which ordinary users follow and bad actors evade, but regards the company's approach as a good-faith effort to comply.

In her analysis the developer is not in breach of the Act, whose duties fall on providers, and probably not of UK computer misuse law, though the company's consumer terms could ground a contract claim she doubts it would bring. She warns that watermarks are provenance data rather than proof of authorship or intent, that removal tools will let lawyers cast doubt on them in court, and that platforms may come to treat their presence or absence as evidence of deception, and she also notes California's coming rules on detection tools.

# What 'open' means for an AI model, and why open-weight releases gained the upper hand in 2026

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-08-31. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/open-vs-closed-ai-models-inside-my-1a0>*

In the third class of her fall 2026 AI law and policy course, Nita Farahany breaks an AI system into training data, architecture, weights, inference code and interface, and compares what leading U.S. and Chinese models disclose, finding that "open" models usually publish their weights but not their training data.

She traces six weeks in which a Chinese lab released a high-performing open-weight model, more than 150 companies signed a letter urging U.S. support for open weights, and a developer that had raised concerns said it never sought a ban, concluding that as of August 2026 open release has won the argument. She argues that released weights cannot be recalled, that open-weight models ship without U.S. government testing, and that the companies backing them are following their own business models.

An American citizen was sentenced to two years in prison for acting as an agent of China's Ministry of State Security from 2019 to February 2026, the Justice Department says. # Four questions for judging any open-weight AI release, and three ways to govern such models

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-09-02. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/four-key-questions-about-open-ai>*

In the fourth class of her fall 2026 AI law and policy course, Nita Farahany uses a Chinese lab's newly posted open-weight model as a case study, noting that it includes weights but not training data or training code, and a licence requiring very large commercial users to pass a security review whose scope the developer itself decides.

She proposes four questions to ask of any release: what was actually released, who can use it and whether it can be recalled, whether it adds risk beyond what already exists, and how it should be governed. Reviewing risks one by one, she finds the clearest added risk in abuse imagery from models stripped of safeguards, and sets out three options: gating models by capability before release, regulating specific harms, or regulating by country of origin.

# Study demonstrates the potential of magnetoelectric nanoparticles for wireless neuromodulation

*META-BRAIN (EU-funded research project), 2026-09-02. Original: <https://meta-brain.eu/news/magnetoelectric-nanoparticles-neuromodulation/>*

META-BRAIN, a research project funded by the European Union, reported on 2 September 2026 on a study published in the journal Advanced Science by researchers from institutes in Spain, Switzerland and Italy. According to the release, low-intensity static magnetic fields on their own did not change the activity of cultured cortical neurons, but in the presence of magnetoelectric nanoparticles the same fields made the neuronal networks more active and excitable.

The project describes the work as a step towards wireless, less invasive ways of modulating brain activity. The study was done in vitro, on neurons grown in the laboratory, with no animal or human testing reported, and the project says clinical use remains a future goal.

# Ten films that help explain the current AI moment, and what each got right and wrong

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-09-08. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/ten-movies-that-help-us-understand>*

Nita Farahany lists ten films she recommends for understanding AI today, from The Matrix and Minority Report to Gattaca, Blade Runner and WALL-E, and says each gets the present at least half right. She argues, for example, that memory and belief are now shaped by everyday devices rather than clinics or dream teams, that life-shaping predictions come from consumer genetic kits and data brokers rather than blood tests at birth, and that handing every task to machines risks what she calls cognitive extinction.

She ties the list to the argument of her books that cognitive liberty depends on a self-determined mind.

# How AI training data is gathered and processed, and why the U.S. government now frames it as national security

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-09-09. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/how-training-data-became-a-national>*

In the fifth class of her fall 2026 AI law and policy course, Nita Farahany opens with the Justice Department's filing arguing that a ruling for OpenAI in The New York Times' copyright case would serve U.S. national security, then walks through how training data is acquired (scraped, torrented from shadow libraries, bought and scanned, or licensed), processed, including the stripping of attribution, and used in training and fine-tuning.

She reviews the 2025 ruling in the authors' case against Anthropic that training on lawfully bought books was fair use while pirated copies were not, followed by a $1.5 billion settlement, applies the four fair-use factors, and notes that California's training-data disclosure law has so far revealed little. She argues that memorisation, which researchers doubt can be eliminated, weakens the analogy that models learn the way people do.

# Drug-delivering particles aim to breach the blood–brain barrier

*Nature, 2026-09-09. Original: <https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-02655-6>*

An article in Nature's Outlook supplement on drug delivery, published on 9 September 2026, reviews efforts to carry medicines across the blood–brain barrier, the lining of the brain's blood vessels that keeps most substances out. According to the article, small molecules can cross it but larger drugs such as proteins and messenger RNA cannot, which has held back treatment of brain cancers and neurodegenerative diseases for decades.

The article describes techniques based on nanoparticles and exosomes, tiny natural carriers released by cells, as competing to solve the problem. Nature notes that the supplement was produced with financial support from a pharmaceutical company and that it retains editorial independence.

# A satirical sketch of contradictions in how AI companies and policymakers talk about AI

*Daniel J. Solove, Solove on Tech (Substack), 2026-09-11. Original: <https://danielsolove.substack.com/p/the-absurd-discourse-of-ai>*

In a short satirical piece, Daniel J. Solove presents imagined exchanges between technology companies, investors, politicians and the public to highlight what he sees as contradictions in public talk about AI. He depicts companies calling their systems dangerous enough to need regulation and later opposing it, and predictions repeated over five decades that a technological singularity was only a few years away.

He also depicts politicians answering public worries about jobs and manipulation by asking how to help the industry, and companies building chatbots to give legal, medical or therapy help without the licences those professions require, then blaming the bot when things go wrong. He presents the piece as satire while suggesting that the line between satire and reality has blurred.

# Who owns what AI models produce, and whether AI-detection tools and labels earn the trust placed in them

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-09-14. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/what-comes-out-of-ai-models-inside>*

In the sixth class of her fall 2026 AI law and policy course, Nita Farahany sorts AI output into memorised text (citing a November 2025 Munich court ruling that a model's reproduction of song lyrics breached copyright), newly generated text and hybrid human-machine writing, and summarises U.S. Copyright Office guidance on each.

She questions commercial AI-detection tools, which she says perform well on wholly generated text but cannot meaningfully score hybrid writing, compares relying on their scores to spectral evidence, and asks who gains from labelling: detector companies, model makers wanting to avoid training on their own output, and governments, pointing to the EU AI Act's Article 50 labelling duties in force since 2 August 2026. She argues that what matters is answerability, whether an author stands behind every claim, rather than whether a tool was used.

# DHS signs Cumulus cloud contract with Google

*Washington Technology, 2026-09-15. Original: <https://www.washingtontechnology.com/contracts/2026/09/dhs-signs-cumulus-cloud-contract-google/415994/>*

Washington Technology reported on 15 September 2026 that the Department of Homeland Security has signed a Cumulus cloud contract with Google's public sector unit, worth up to $875.6 million over five years (a one-year base period and four option years). The contract covers infrastructure, platform and software services for use across the department.

The publication says this is the third of four planned Cumulus awards, after Amazon Web Services in June 2026 and Oracle in August 2026, with Microsoft's still being completed. DHS then plans a separate competition for Cumulus operations support.

# Human neural cells grown into the cortex of mice raise ethical questions about part-human brains

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-09-16. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/breakthrough-in-science-human-brain>*

Nita Farahany shares a new paper in Nature in which a Stanford team transplanted organoids made from human neural cells into mice bred without a cortex, and reports that three months later the cortex of the animals measured was about 92% human-derived cells by volume. She calls it a major advance for studying neurological disease and for drug discovery, and notes that nothing the researchers measured suggests human-like experience.

She says she was one of the outside ethicists the researchers consulted, and that a forthcoming commentary she co-wrote will set out an ethical roadmap, including how to judge whether such animals have human-like capacities and who decides the next steps.

# Liability for Unregistered Foreign Agents

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2026-09-16. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/liability-unregistered-foreign-agents>*

The Justice Department issued a public reminder on 16 September 2026 that people acting in the United States at the direction of a foreign government or foreign principal must register under the Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA) or give notice under 18 U.S.C. § 951. The department says the duty applies to citizens and non-citizens alike, and can cover public activity, including demonstrations that advance a foreign government's goals or messaging.

According to the release, violations can bring civil or criminal liability, with prison terms of up to five years. The department says it continues to protect First Amendment rights, and points people who are unsure of their obligations to the FARA Unit's advisory opinions or to their own lawyers.

# The ladder beneath AI models: how rules on chips, memory, networks and power trail the technology

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-09-17. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/compute-the-chip-war-that-has-run>*

In the seventh class of her fall 2026 AI law and policy course, Nita Farahany describes a seven-rung ladder beneath AI models (computation, chips, memory, networking, power, software and the models) and who dominates each rung, stressing the industry's dependence on one Taiwanese chipmaker and one Dutch equipment maker.

She traces how regulation has aimed at each rung: the computing-power reporting threshold in a 2023 executive order, U.S. chip export controls since 2022 and their reversals, a reported diversion of advanced servers through Southeast Asia and a pending remote-access bill, a new FCC equipment rule reaching optical components, South Korea's expanded espionage law, and China's consideration of limits on exporting its own models. She argues the law has repeatedly reached a rung after the contest moved past it, and has served more to slow competitors than to align models, and reads a reported $12.9 billion bid by the leading chipmaker for the largest open-model platform as an attempt to own the ladder from the top down.

# A bonus class on calls to slow frontier AI and the physical levers that could actually do it

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-09-18. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/a-bonus-class-on-the-amodei-letter>*

Nita Farahany notes that an AI company chief executive's essay urging a slower pace of capability gains drew quick agreement from rivals, while the President, in a call put on speaker at a conference, dismissed the concern as a hoax. She argues that the debate has focused on the models and ignored the physical layers beneath them, such as chips and chipmaking equipment, that could actually slow AI development and may already be doing so, and points to computing power as a lever for governing AI.

The video and readings are for paid subscribers; this summary covers only the free introduction.

# Governor issues executive order to accelerate independent oversight and advance the creation of an AI kill switch

*Office of the Governor of California, 2026-09-18. Original: <https://www.gov.ca.gov/2026/09/18/governor-newsom-issues-executive-order-to-accelerate-independent-oversight-and-advance-the-creation-of-an-ai-kill-switch/>*

The Governor of California's office announced on 18 September 2026 an executive order directing the state's Government Operations Agency to speed up two recently signed laws, SB 813 (an independent verification framework for AI) and AB 1405 (a registry of AI auditors), and to bring in outside experts to make recommendations within two months.

According to the release, the order seeks an emergency shut-off capability for the most advanced ("frontier") AI models, onsite independent verification at frontier AI companies, and a wider definition of critical safety incidents that includes loss-of-control incidents. The office says the order responds to recent AI security incidents.

# Lawsuit says Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXAI and Google made illegal deal on AI slowdown

*CBS News (Associated Press), 2026-09-19. Original: <https://www.cbsnews.com/news/ai-slowdown-lawsuit-openai-anthropic-google/>*

The Associated Press reported on 19 September 2026 that paying subscribers to four AI chatbot services filed a lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, on behalf of a proposed nationwide class. According to the report, the suit claims that four AI developers broke antitrust law by agreeing, around 12 September, to coordinate a slowdown in AI development after one company's chief executive called publicly for industry-wide cooperation on safety.

The plaintiffs argue that a coordinated slowdown would reduce what consumers get from paid subscriptions. The report says the companies did not immediately respond, and that the original call for cooperation had itself acknowledged possible antitrust problems. The case has only been filed; no court has ruled on the claims.
