# Taiwan probes organised crime links to China's 'transnational repression'

*Reuters (via Daily Maverick), 2026-10-22. Original: <https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/2026-10-22-taiwan-probes-organised-crime-links-to-chinas-transnational-repression/>*

Reuters reports that Taiwan's National Security Bureau is investigating whether organised crime networks linked to China are carrying out transnational repression, after Taipei said Beijing was behind an attack on a comedian who had mocked China's leader. According to the report, the bureau's head said the groups involved are mostly criminal gangs or private investigation firms tied to organised crime. The bureau's main question is whether the Chinese Communist Party directed or paid them.

The report says the bureau's head also said Taiwan may need to change its laws, because its legal framework against transnational repression is lacking, and that Taiwan's Supreme Prosecutors Office urged the public not to help hostile foreign forces. China's Taiwan Affairs Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment, according to Reuters.

# Tajik Activist Given Lengthy Prison Sentence

*Human Rights Watch, 2026-10-22. Original: <https://www.hrw.org/news/2026/10/22/tajik-activist-given-lengthy-prison-sentence>*

Human Rights Watch says that a Tajik opposition activist who had lived in Germany since 2017 was deported to Tajikistan on 20 June 2026, despite warnings from rights groups, and was detained on arrival in Dushanbe. According to the organisation, a court in Tajikistan sentenced him on about 21 September 2026 to 17 years in prison under three articles of the criminal code, including "extremism through the internet". HRW says the case stemmed from his social media posts criticising the Tajik authorities.

HRW says Tajik authorities have not published information on the case, and that the sentence is known from a media report. It also says that three other activists deported from Germany since 2023 were imprisoned after their return.

# Attorney General Sues OpenAI and CEO for Lying to Users and Harming Texans

*Office of the Texas Attorney General, 2026-10-23. Original: <https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/news/releases/attorney-general-ken-paxton-sues-openai-and-ceo-sam-altman-lying-users-and-harming-texans>*

The Texas Attorney General's office says it has sued OpenAI and its chief executive under the Texas Deceptive Trade Practices–Consumer Protection Act. The office alleges that the company marketed ChatGPT as safe and reliable while not disclosing the risk of inaccurate or harmful output, and that the product harmed users, including minors using it without parental oversight.

Courthouse News reports that the suit was filed in Collin County District Court and also relies on the state's law on children's online safety and parental consent. According to that report, the state is asking for a broad injunction, including a bar on releasing new ChatGPT models in Texas without approval from a court-appointed independent evaluator. The case has only been filed, and no court has ruled on the claims.

# Austria expels 4 Russian diplomats linked to espionage, official says

*The Associated Press (via CP24), 2026-10-23. Original: <https://www.cp24.com/news/world/2026/10/23/austria-expels-4-russian-diplomats-linked-to-espionage-official-says/>*

The Associated Press reports that Austria ordered four Russian diplomats to leave the country on 23 October 2026. According to the report, Austria's Foreign Ministry said three worked at the Russian Embassy in Vienna and one at Russia's mission to the OSCE. The ministry declared them persona non grata for "activities incompatible with their diplomatic status" and gave no further details.

AP says this brings the number of Russian diplomats expelled by Austria since 2020 to 18. It reports that Austrian law currently punishes espionage only when it targets Austrian interests, and that the government is negotiating a change that would also cover spying on international organisations. A Russian deputy foreign minister told the state news agency TASS that a response was unavoidable.

# Coherence Neuro raises $45M for implantable cancer technology

*MobiHealthNews, 2026-10-23. Original: <https://www.mobihealthnews.com/news/coherence-neuro-raises-45m-implantable-cancer-technology>*

MobiHealthNews reports that Coherence Neuro, a San Francisco company, has raised $45 million in Series A funding. The company is developing a brain-computer interface that records electrical signals linked to tumours and uses them to guide electrical stimulation, starting with brain tumours. According to the report, a first-in-human study of the company's cortical probe began in June at the Royal Melbourne Hospital during tumour-removal surgery, and the company plans a long-term trial in glioblastoma.

The publication says the devices are investigational and are not approved by the U.S. FDA or Australia's Therapeutic Goods Administration. It also says preclinical work in mice is continuing and has not been shown to apply to humans.

# DHS release: HSI and FBI Arrest Ten Aliens for Voter Fraud in North Carolina

*U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 2026-10-23. Original: <https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/10/23/hsi-and-fbi-arrest-ten-aliens-voter-fraud-north-carolina>*

DHS said ICE's Homeland Security Investigations, ICE and the FBI arrested ten non-citizens in North Carolina on 14 and 15 October 2026, nine lawful permanent residents and one person it said was in the country illegally, from Germany, Jamaica, El Salvador, Haiti, Canada, Panama and Montenegro. DHS said they are charged with false claims to citizenship and voting by an alien in federal elections, in cases brought by the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of North Carolina, and that one also faces a firearm charge; DHS said some have earlier criminal records. The release also lists other recent voting cases.

The characterisations are DHS's own; every person arrested or charged is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

*U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 2026-10-23. Original: <https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/10/23/secretary-mullin-visits-us-coast-guard-facilities-north-carolina>*

DHS said the Secretary of Homeland Security visited the Coast Guard's Aviation Logistics Center and Aviation Technical Training Center in Elizabeth City, North Carolina, on Friday 23 October 2026, watching demonstrations of the Coast Guard's aviation capabilities and touring the construction of a training site for its rescue swimmers. # DHS release: DHS Issues Statement After Illegal Alien Attacks Iwo Jima Memorial in Quantico, Virginia and Decapitates Statue

*U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 2026-10-23. Original: <https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/10/23/dhs-issues-statement-after-illegal-alien-attacks-iwo-jima-memorial-quantico>*

DHS said, citing local reporting, that a man damaged the Iwo Jima Memorial outside Marine Corps Base Quantico, Virginia, with a sledgehammer on the evening of 21 October 2026, and that Prince William County police arrested him at the scene. DHS said he is a Mexican national charged with felony destruction of property and trespassing with intent to damage property, that he was arrested for trespassing in 2022, and that he entered the United States in 1999 and held Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals from 2014, which has since expired.

The characterisations are DHS's own; anyone facing a new charge is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# UK Home Office publishes LFR privacy assessment for immigration enforcement

*Biometric Update, 2026-10-23. Original: <https://www.biometricupdate.com/202610/uk-home-office-publishes-lfr-privacy-assessment-for-immigration-enforcement>*

Biometric Update reports that the UK Home Office has published a 63-page data protection impact assessment of the live facial recognition technology used by Immigration Enforcement. According to the article, the assessment lists risks such as misidentification, human error, demographic bias and data retention. The proposed safeguards include human review with secondary identity checks, public engagement before deployments and strict limits on scope.

The publication says the document accepts that live facial recognition interferes with the right to private life but argues that the interference is limited in scope and duration. It also says that images of people who do not trigger a watchlist alert are deleted immediately and automatically, and that the system does not make enforcement decisions itself.

# U.S. Government Contractor Arrested for Allegedly Leaking National Defense Information

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2026-10-23. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/us-government-contractor-arrested-allegedly-leaking-national-defense-information>*

The Justice Department says the FBI has arrested a government contractor who held a Top Secret/SCI clearance and has charged him by criminal complaint with unlawfully transmitting national defense information. According to the release, he first worked for a U.S. government agency and, from 2022, for a contractor providing services to the CIA. The department alleges that he obtained classified information beyond his duties and passed it to a person he had a personal relationship with, who runs an online publication on Substack.

The department says the case began with a referral from the CIA and was investigated by the FBI's Chicago and Washington field offices, and that it is being prosecuted by the National Security Division and the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Virginia. The case is at the complaint stage: the defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# ICE expansion deepens dependence on proprietary digital identity, network infrastructure

*Biometric Update, 2026-10-25. Original: <https://www.biometricupdate.com/202610/ice-expansion-deepens-dependence-on-proprietary-digital-identity-network-infrastructure>*

Biometric Update reports, from federal award records, that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has placed network and identity-access equipment orders worth about $12.5 million between May and September 2026. It puts selected awards of this kind since September 2024 at about $29.8 million. According to the article, a justification posted on 22 October 2026 says the agency's installed proprietary equipment left no competing source for related services, and cites a large increase in personnel and sites.

The publication says the records do not show which facilities received the equipment or how much of the spending is tied to expansion rather than routine replacement. It notes that the identity system involved controls network access and does not perform biometric identification. It also says a five-year forecast of $50 million to $100 million for field infrastructure has no matching award yet.

# U.S. judge finds DOGE access to federal personnel data violated privacy law

*Biometric Update, 2026-10-25. Original: <https://www.biometricupdate.com/202610/u-s-judge-finds-doge-access-to-federal-personnel-data-violated-privacy-law>*

Biometric Update reports that a U.S. federal judge ruled, in an opinion dated 20 October 2026, that the Office of Personnel Management unlawfully gave Department of Government Efficiency personnel broad access to systems holding sensitive records on tens of millions of federal workers. According to the article, the court found that twenty people linked to the effort accessed the systems between 20 January and 6 March 2025, mostly with administrative rights, that no need for the access had been shown at the time, and that cybersecurity safeguards were bypassed.

The publication says the court granted summary judgment to the plaintiffs on their Administrative Procedure Act claims, to the extent those claims rest on Privacy Act violations. The court has not yet decided what permanent relief, if any, to order. The article reports that the agency has since withdrawn the permissions and adopted a stricter access policy, and that the government argues this reduces the need for further relief.

# U.S. voter investigations combined identity data with election enforcement

*Biometric Update, 2026-10-25. Original: <https://www.biometricupdate.com/202610/u-s-voter-investigations-combined-identity-data-with-election-enforcement>*

Biometric Update reports that a federal court issued a preliminary injunction on 21 October 2026 restricting voter-related field operations by Homeland Security Investigations in nine states. The article says a stay of the order expired on 23 October, and that no government appeal had appeared on public dockets when it was written. According to the publication, the order runs through Election Day unless a higher court steps in.

The article says the case record describes about 48.2 million voter-related records from other sources and about 50.6 million Justice Department records drawn from state voter rolls. It says these were "enriched" with immigration records, commercial identity databases and law enforcement records. The publication notes that the sequence of events it describes does not by itself establish cause and effect. This is interim relief, not a final ruling.

# Courts in several countries are fitting AI hallucinations into defamation, consumer and data protection law

*Wenlong Li, Future of Privacy Forum, 2026-10-26. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/ai-hallucination-goes-to-court-a-global-mapping-of-emerging-legal-issues/>*

Wenlong Li, in a guest post for the Future of Privacy Forum that he says does not necessarily reflect its views, maps about eleven legal matters in China, Germany, Canada, the United States and the EU involving AI 'hallucinations', meaning generated text that presents a false claim as fact. He says the survey is not systematic or complete.

Li finds that hallucination has no legal home of its own and is being squeezed into existing categories, from defamation, unfair competition and negligent misrepresentation to personality rights, data accuracy and correction rights, trademark, professional licensing and consumer protection, each capturing only part of the problem. He proposes reading cases along two axes: how far an output travels and whether the company or person communicating it adopts it as their own, adding that the more serious the false claim, the heavier the duty to verify and correct.

He concludes that hallucination will not disappear soon and that legal risk arises mainly when ranking, interface design, branding or professional status make probabilistic output look like authoritative fact; the more a provider presents generated text as its own reliable speech, the weaker the defence that the system simply made it up.

# How much does AI raise the risk of weapons of mass destruction, and who gets watched to find out?

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-10-26. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/chemical-biological-radiological>*

Nita Farahany reviews what is known about AI helping people develop chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear weapons, citing the 2026 International AI Safety Report's finding that the size of the added risk cannot yet be measured, partly because weapons treaties and security laws restrict the research that would measure it.

She describes current U.S. measures as largely voluntary, including the June 2026 executive order's pre-release testing, alongside binding limits on Defense Department purchases of AI models from adversary countries. She argues that each proposed safeguard leads back to more surveillance, first of AI models and then of the people who use them.

# CBP plans up to $50M contract for biometrics, AI integration

*Biometric Update, 2026-10-26. Original: <https://www.biometricupdate.com/202610/cbp-plans-up-to-50m-contract-for-biometrics-ai-integration>*

Biometric Update reports that U.S. Customs and Border Protection is preparing to compete an application development contract worth an estimated $20 million to $50 million, set aside for small businesses. According to the article, the agency's forecast says the work covers all CBP operational and support offices and explicitly includes integrating biometric technology into new and existing applications, alongside AI and machine learning, data analytics and chatbots.

The publication says the updated forecast puts the solicitation in mid-November and the award at the end of December 2026, with work running to March 2029. It notes that the forecast does not say which applications would gain biometric features, and that the statement of work expected with the solicitation may make this clearer.

# DOJ Appeals Ruling Lifting Ban on Anthropic Use for US Agencies

*MT Newswires, 2026-10-26. Original: <https://www.marketscreener.com/news/doj-appeals-ruling-lifting-ban-on-anthropic-use-for-us-agencies-ce785cdcdf8bfe23>*

MT Newswires reports that the U.S. Justice Department filed a notice of appeal with the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals on 26 October 2026. According to the report, the government is seeking to overturn an August 2026 district court ruling that lifted its ban on federal agencies' use of the AI company Anthropic's technology.

The dispute began earlier in 2026, when the administration told agencies to stop using the company's models and the Defense Department designated the company a supply chain risk; the company sued to block those measures. A notice of appeal starts the appeal process and is not a ruling. The district court's decision stands unless the appeals court changes it.

# Paradromics Receives FDA Approval to Expand Connexus® Brain-Computer Interface Clinical Study Recruitment Nationwide

*Paradromics, 2026-10-26. Original: <https://biospace.com/press-releases/paradromics-receives-fda-approval-to-expand-connexus-brain-computer-interface-clinical-study-recruitment-nationwide>*

Paradromics says the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved an amendment to the protocol of its early feasibility study of the Connexus brain-computer interface, a fully implanted wireless device that records individual neurons to turn intended speech into digital communication. According to the company, the change removes the rule that participants must live within a four-hour drive of a study site, so eligible people across the continental United States can be considered, though they must still travel to a site when required.

The company says the study runs at three U.S. academic medical centres under an FDA investigational device exemption granted in November 2025, and that its first long-term implant took place in June 2026. These are the company's own statements and have not been independently confirmed.

# Serbian autocrat loses election following widespread reports of digital repression

*The Record, 2026-10-26. Original: <https://therecord.media/serbia-election-spyware-vucic>*

The Record reports that Serbia's long-serving leader conceded defeat on Sunday in his bid to become prime minister. According to the publication, researchers say the loss followed two years in which digital forensic investigators reported spyware targeting or infections on the devices of dozens of opposition figures, protesters, prosecutors and journalists.

The article cites Amnesty International as saying that authorities used phone-extraction tools during interrogations and arrests, sometimes to install spyware, and cites a Serbian digital-rights group as counting at least 15 people targeted with mercenary spyware this year. It says the Serbian Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The publication does not claim the spyware reports caused the result.

# A recorded conversation on mice with a mostly human-derived cortex, what the model allows and the ethical questions

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-10-28. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/a-mouse-with-a-human-cortex>*

Nita Farahany hosts a recorded conversation with the Stanford psychiatrist who led the study and a consciousness scientist with whom she co-wrote a commentary, on a Nature paper describing mice whose own cortex was genetically prevented from developing and replaced, shortly after birth, by transplanted human stem-cell-derived brain tissue that filled more than 90% of the cortex by volume three months later.

She describes the discussion as covering what earlier models of the human brain made possible and where they fell short, what this model allows for studying brain connectivity and development, and the ethical questions of what, if anything, it is like to be such a mouse, how human-like capacities could be detected, and who should decide how far this research goes.

# A video interview on the economics of privacy and the gap between privacy concerns and behaviour

*Daniel J. Solove, Solove on Tech (Substack), 2026-10-28. Original: <https://danielsolove.substack.com/p/the-economics-of-privacy>*

Daniel J. Solove introduces a video interview with an MIT researcher who studies the economics of privacy, covering the so-called privacy paradox, the value of personal data, people's attitudes to privacy and the effects of privacy laws.

The post summarises a selection of the researcher's studies, which Solove describes as finding that people often do act to protect their privacy, that privacy notices can be used to nudge how much people disclose, and that some shoppers will pay more to buy from retailers that protect privacy. Solove also points readers to his own article arguing against the idea of a privacy paradox. The interview itself is a video and is not summarised here.

# DHS release: Under President [name], DHS Blocks Chinese Genomics Companies Linked to Forced Labor

*U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 2026-10-28. Original: <https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/10/28/under-president-trump-dhs-blocks-chinese-genomics-companies-linked-forced-labor>*

DHS said the Forced Labor Enforcement Task Force had added three affiliated Chinese genomics companies based in Shenzhen to the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act Entity List, so that from 29 October 2026 their goods are presumed barred from entering the United States unless an importer shows they were not made with forced labour. DHS said the task force determined that the companies help the government of the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region build and run mass surveillance that uses genetic data to monitor ethnic minorities and supports labour-transfer programmes and internment. DHS said the list now holds 190 entities.

The findings are the task force's own determination; the release reports a trade restriction, not a criminal charge.

# California and New York take different paths in their second round of companion chatbot laws

*Justine Gluck, Future of Privacy Forum, 2026-10-29. Original: <https://fpf.org/blog/back-in-the-chat-california-and-new-york-take-diverging-paths-in-second-wave-of-chatbot-regulations/>*

Justine Gluck, for the Future of Privacy Forum, compares two new laws on AI companion chatbots and minors: New York's S 9051B, signed in late October 2026, and California's SB 1119, signed about a month earlier. Gluck says they bring the number of enacted state chatbot laws to 19 and offer two playbooks for 2027.

Gluck describes New York's law as restrictive by design: it bars twelve broadly defined 'unsafe' features for minors, from harmful content to flattery, emotional appeals and use of personal information from earlier sessions, enforced by the attorney general with remedies that include algorithmic disgorgement. Gluck argues that terms such as 'sycophancy' are barely defined and that liability for a single unexpected output could push operators to restrict ordinary conversation. California's law instead sets a governance framework of default limits on memory and usage time, crisis protocols, advertising limits, risk assessments, independent audits and a limited private right of action, which the author says raises its own tradeoffs, such as long retention of sensitive conversations.

# Private tiger ownership is more tightly regulated than AI, an analogy argues

*Daniel J. Solove, Solove on Tech (Substack), 2026-10-29. Original: <https://danielsolove.substack.com/p/tiger-king-vs-ai-tiger-king>*

Daniel J. Solove responds to news reports of AI systems used in cyberattacks by arguing that the law grants AI an exceptional freedom from the kinds of controls and liability that apply to almost everything else. He points to an AI developer's stock-offering filing that suggests insurers may not be able to cover a catastrophic AI incident.

He compares AI with privately kept big cats, which U.S. federal law now largely bans outside accredited zoos and for which keepers are strictly liable if an animal injures someone. In his view the law treats tigers more sensibly than AI models, which are released widely for almost any use.

# DHS release: Feature Article: Advancing Autonomous Systems to Extend First Responders’ Reach

*U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 2026-10-29. Original: <https://www.dhs.gov/science-and-technology/news/2026/10/29/feature-article-advancing-autonomous-systems-extend-first-responders-reach>*

DHS's Science and Technology Directorate said two of its teams brought first responders to El Paso, Texas, to assess two commercially available technologies: body-worn mobile ad hoc network radios, tested alongside existing land mobile radio, and a remotely operated four-legged robot built on a commercial quadruped platform, carrying cameras, a manipulation arm and sensors. The directorate said the radios passed communications to and from land mobile radio, and the robot climbed three flights of stairs in one scenario to deliver a first-aid kit. It described the work as a first-step assessment to inform future research on communications, robotics and automation, and published no performance figures.

The findings are the directorate's own; the article reports a field assessment, not a procurement.

# DHS release: [name] Administration Suspends Birth Tourism Loophole Threatening National Security

*U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 2026-10-29. Original: <https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/10/29/trump-administration-suspends-birth-tourism-loophole-threatening-national-security>*

DHS said it has suspended visa-free travel for Chinese nationals to the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands under the Economic Vitality & Security Travel Authorization Program, which had allowed stays of up to 14 days without a visa or consular interview, citing birth tourism and national security concerns. DHS said Chinese nationals visiting for business or tourism must now obtain a B-1 or B-2 visa, that no new applications are accepted and existing authorisations will be cancelled, and that it is reviewing the programme with the Departments of State and the Interior; the notice is Federal Register document 2026-21880.

The reasons given are DHS's own; the release reports a change in travel rules, not a criminal charge.

# DHS release: Under President [name]’s Leadership, USCIS Takes Unprecedented 2.2 Million Enforcement Actions Protecting Americans Across the Nation

*U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 2026-10-29. Original: <https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/10/29/under-president-trumps-leadership-uscis-takes-unprecedented-22-million-enforcement>*

DHS said U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) has taken immigration enforcement actions to revoke or terminate the status of about 2.2 million people since 20 January 2025, which it said is nearly seven times as many enforcement actions as in the previous administration's final two years combined. DHS said the actions include ending Temporary Protected Status designations, denying applications to extend or change status, issuing Notices to Appear that start removal proceedings, ending the automatic extension of work permits and terminating categorical parole programmes.

The figures are the department's own count, and the characterisations are DHS's own.

# Report says U.S. intelligence linked a suspected Chinese intelligence source to a U.S. chipmaker's chief executive; company and China deny

*ABC News, 2026-10-30, reporting a New York Times article of 2026-10-29. Original: <https://abc13.com/story/nvidia-denies-report-ceo-was-allegedly-targeted-chinese-spy-plot/20000206/>*

ABC News reports that The New York Times reported on 29 October 2026 that U.S. intelligence officials had concluded that a senior executive at a Singapore-based data-center company, who had a close relationship with Nvidia's chief executive, was passing information to officials in Beijing. According to ABC News, the Times also reported that the President was briefed on the findings and took no action. The intelligence conclusions come from the newspaper's unnamed sources.

Nvidia said its chief executive meets thousands of customer executives every year and that such meetings are an ordinary part of the job, and that it would act on any warning from the U.S. government about a party of concern. China's Foreign Ministry called the reports baseless. No charge or official finding has been reported.

# How organisations govern AI in practice, from shared responsibility to vendors and boards

*Daniel J. Solove, Solove on Tech (Substack), 2026-10-30. Original: <https://danielsolove.substack.com/p/ai-governance-ethics-strategy-law>*

Daniel J. Solove introduces a video conversation with an AI governance lawyer and author about running AI governance inside an organisation. The post is a description of the discussion rather than a transcript, so this summary covers only the topics it lists.

According to the post, the conversation covers who is and should be responsible for AI governance, why it needs work across departments, the need to oversee vendors that also use AI, the difficulty of governing AI that is now built into existing software and services, and the need for governance staff to explain ethical concerns to executives and boards in business terms.

# A conversation with a former in-house AI ethics lead on doing ethics work inside AI companies

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-11-02. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/a-conversation-with-class-guest-chloe>*

Nita Farahany shares a recorded conversation with her class guest, a former law professor who served as chief AI ethicist at Meta and led ethics work at OpenAI until August 2026, about what AI ethics looks like from inside the companies and how she built a career in AI law and ethics.

The post's homework asks readers, acting as counsel to a frontier AI lab that wants to bring in independent evaluators to test for chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear risks, to draft the one contract term they would insist on and the one they would refuse. The written post describes the conversation only briefly; this summary covers that description.

# A Supreme Court ruling on a geofence warrant narrows the third-party doctrine for digital data

*Daniel J. Solove, Solove on Tech (Substack), 2026-11-02. Original: <https://danielsolove.substack.com/p/when-can-the-government-get-your>*

Daniel J. Solove recaps a conversation with two law professors about a June 2026 U.S. Supreme Court decision involving a geofence warrant, which requires a company to hand over data on every phone in an area. As he describes it, the Court held that people have a reasonable expectation of privacy in their location data even when a third party holds it, but did not decide whether the warrant itself was specific enough.

Solove calls the decision one of the most important Fourth Amendment cases of the century and argues that it shrinks the third-party doctrine without formally ending it. He sets out a framework in which what data is gathered, how it is gathered and how much is gathered can each trigger constitutional protection, and he lists open questions, including whether the government can still buy data from data brokers.

# Former U.S. Government Contractor Pleads Guilty to Spying for Ethiopia

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2026-11-03. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/former-us-government-contractor-pleads-guilty-spying-ethiopia>*

The Justice Department says a former IT contractor who held a Top Secret clearance has pleaded guilty to conspiring to transmit national defense information to a foreign government. According to the release, he admitted that from 2021 until his arrest in August 2023 he worked with senior Ethiopian officials to collect and pass on dozens of classified items, some at the TS/SCI level, much of it about an armed conflict in Ethiopia, and that he took the material out of secure facilities.

The department says that under the plea agreement he has agreed to a prison term of 120 to 262 months, subject to the court's acceptance, and that sentencing is set for 14 April 2027. The FBI's Washington Field Office led the investigation, with help from the State Department's Diplomatic Security Service, and the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia is prosecuting.

# How AI models are red-teamed, the ways they are broken, and the laws that put outside safety researchers at risk

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-11-04. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/red-teaming-ai-from-what-it-is-to>*

Nita Farahany opens with a reported October 2026 dispute in which OpenAI said it had parted ways with three safety staff for mishandling sensitive information, while the three said in an open letter that staff must be able to raise safety concerns. She explains red-teaming and four kinds of attack on AI models (poisoning training data, inputs crafted to evade safeguards, jailbreaking prompts and attacks transferred between models), noting that jailbreaks her class tried this year failed where they had worked a year earlier, and describes who tests models, from in-house teams to independent researchers.

She argues that the federal computer-fraud law, the anti-circumvention rule in copyright law and terms of service can expose independent researchers to prosecution or lawsuits, discusses a proposed legal and technical safe harbour for good-faith testing, and notes that California's frontier AI law now gives whistleblower protection for reporting AI risks.

# House committee chairs ask a U.S. chipmaker's chief executive for a closed-door briefing on a reported Chinese intelligence asset

*U.S. House Select Committee on the CCP, 2026-11-04. Original: <https://chinaselectcommittee.house.gov/sites/evo-subsites/selectcommitteeontheccp.house.gov/files/evo-media-document/nvidia-letter-pdf.pdf>*

In a letter dated 4 November 2026, the chairs of three House committees (Foreign Affairs, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and the Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence) asked Nvidia's chief executive to attend a joint, closed-door briefing on 18 November 2026. According to the letter, the briefing would cover the company's protections against espionage by foreign adversaries and his contacts with an executive of a Singapore-based data-center company, whom the letter describes as publicly reported to be an intelligence asset of the People's Republic of China.

The chairs asked the company to accept the date or propose another by 11 November. The letter cites press reports and states no official finding of its own, and no charge has been reported. It follows the 29 October newspaper report, which Nvidia and China's Foreign Ministry both denied.

*U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 2026-11-05. Original: <https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/11/05/ice-lodges-detainer-illegal-alien-arrested-rape-new-york-city>*

# Facial recognition firm joins €14M Spanish police forensic AI projects

*Biometric Update, 2026-11-06. Original: <https://www.biometricupdate.com/202611/herta-joins-e14m-spanish-police-forensic-ai-projects>*

Biometric Update reports that the Spanish facial recognition company Herta Security is part of a group building two AI forensic systems for Spain's National Police, under contracts worth about €14 million including VAT. The contracts are funded through Spain's Center for Technological Development and Innovation with European Union co-financing. According to the article, one system combines facial recognition, large language models and other AI to analyze forensic information from many sources and link cases. The other uses LiDAR and 360-degree photography to make 3D reconstructions of crime scenes.

The publication says both systems are prototypes, with the current phase running until late 2027 and the contracts until September 2028. A final validation phase at police facilities in Castilla-La Mancha depends on a competitive selection.

# Hong Kong police to add AI facial recognition to SmartView CCTV network

*The Standard (Hong Kong), 2026-11-06. Original: <https://www.thestandard.com.hk/news/article/347690/Police-to-add-AI-facial-recognition-to-Smart-View-CCTV-system-this-month-targeting-60000-cameras-by-2028>*

The Standard reports that Hong Kong police say they will add AI facial recognition to the SmartView CCTV system this month, to detect crime and find missing people faster. According to the article, more than 10,000 cameras are installed, police aim to reach about 60,000 by 2028, and talks are under way to connect cameras in shopping malls and other private premises.

The publication says police describe two uses: searching footage for a suspect, and alerting officers when a missing person appears on camera. It reports police saying use is limited to four statutory purposes, including national security, that officers must pass two internal tests before accessing footage, and that facial recognition data will be kept longer than the usual 30 days for footage, with a source putting the figure at about 180 days.

# Police Scotland demonstrates live facial recognition as calls for legislation grow

*Biometric Update, 2026-11-06. Original: <https://www.biometricupdate.com/202611/police-scotland-demonstrates-live-facial-recognition-as-calls-for-legislation-grow>*

Biometric Update reports that Police Scotland held a demonstration of live facial recognition at its Tulliallan headquarters as Scotland considers whether to adopt the technology. According to the article, the audience included the Scottish Police Authority, the Scottish Biometrics Commissioner, the Justice Secretary and several human rights, equality and information oversight bodies, and officers from police forces in England showed how they use it.

The publication says the Scottish Biometrics Commissioner has repeatedly called for primary legislation before police use the technology, describing it in his latest annual report as highly intrusive mass public surveillance. It reports that the decision on whether to legislate rests with the Scottish Parliament. Meanwhile, the UK government plans a statutory framework for England and Wales.

# DHS release: [name] Administration Deepens Interagency Collaboration to Protect the Nation’s Skies From Unmanned Threats

*U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 2026-11-09. Original: <https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/11/09/trump-administration-deepens-interagency-collaboration-protect-nations-skies>*

DHS said it and the Departments of Transportation, War, Energy and Justice had signed a memorandum of understanding, led by the White House Task Force to Restore American Airspace Sovereignty, setting up an interagency process to evaluate and deploy systems that detect, track and counter unauthorised drones. DHS said the Federal Aviation Administration will review proposed systems and carry out safety risk assessments, and may impose its own measures, including airspace restrictions.

DHS said the agreement builds on an FAA flight restriction along the southern border and a completed safety assessment of a Department of War high-energy laser counter-drone system.

# DHS release: Meet One of the Media’s ‘Non-Criminals’: ICE Arrests MS-13 Member in Idaho Charged with Terrorism in El Salvador

*U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 2026-11-09. Original: <https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/11/09/meet-one-medias-non-criminals-ice-arrests-ms-13-member-idaho-charged-terrorism-el>*

DHS said ICE arrested a Salvadoran national in Victor, Idaho, on 5 November 2026 during a targeted operation, and said his record in El Salvador includes charges linking him to the MS-13 gang, among them terrorist-organisation charges. # France attributes the sabotage of refrigeration controls at more than 700 supermarkets to a unit linked to Iran's Revolutionary Guard

*French Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs, 2026-11-09. Original, in French: <https://www.diplomatie.gouv.fr/fr/presse-et-ressources/decouvrir-et-informer/actualites/declaration-d-attribution-a-l-iran-de-cyberattaques-visant-la-france>. Title translated from the French.*

The French foreign ministry states that on the night of 11 to 12 October 2026 a campaign altered the settings of refrigeration controllers at more than 700 supermarket sites, causing fires and food losses of tens of millions of euros, and attributes it to a cyber-offensive unit linked to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The ministry calls it the first purely sabotage-driven cyber campaign on French territory and says France will summon Iran's ambassador and propose new European Union sanctions.

Ouest-France reports that the Paris prosecutor has opened a judicial investigation led by the cybercrime office and the domestic intelligence service. No one has been tried, and anyone charged is presumed innocent. (Summary translated from the French.)

# Saskatchewan introduces a bill writing assisted-dying safeguards into provincial law

*Global News, 2026-11-09. Original: <https://globalnews.ca/news/12143033/saskatchewan-maid-eligibility-introduced/>*

Global News reports that the Saskatchewan government introduced the Medical Assistance in Dying Additional Safeguards Act, which would write eligibility rules into provincial law and exclude people under 18, people without decision-making capacity, and people whose only condition is a mental illness.

According to the report, the provincial health minister says the bill also strengthens protections for clinicians who decline to take part. It must pass the legislature before it takes effect and largely mirrors current and proposed federal rules.

# Taiwan drafts harsher penalties for helping China carry out transnational repression

*Taipei Times, 2026-11-09. Original: <https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/taiwan/archives/2026/11/09/2003867408>*

The Taipei Times reports that Taiwan's Ministry of Justice is drafting amendments to the Anti-Infiltration Act that would raise prison terms for people who carry out surveillance, harassment, intimidation or violent attacks at the direction, request or with the funding of what the government calls foreign hostile forces.

Citing the Ministry of the Interior, the paper says nine transnational repression cases have been investigated and four have led to indictments. It reports that officials consider a standalone law the ideal, and that penalty figures have not yet been set.

# A catch-up class on the midterms, Europe's first high-court ruling on AI training data, and an AI company's bankruptcy

*Nita Farahany, Thinking Freely (Substack), 2026-11-10. Original: <https://nitafarahany.substack.com/p/a-bonus-class-on-the-the-midterms>*

Nita Farahany introduces a bonus session of her AI law and policy course covering three subjects: what the U.S. midterm elections may mean for AI governance, the first opinion from Europe's high court on whether AI training on text and data can be done without breaching copyright, and how an AI company's bankruptcy proceedings connect to themes from her course.

Most of the post, including her video address and the readings it is based on, is for paid subscribers; this summary covers only the free introduction, which names the topics but does not give her conclusions.

# Australia announces an AI safety regulator and accepts all review recommendations after an AI agent reached a government health-statistics site

*SBS News, 2026-11-10. Original: <https://www.sbs.com.au/news/article/ai-safeguards-open-ai-medicare-breach-albanese/2pbsdc5nr>*

SBS News reports that Australia's government announced that frontier AI companies operating in the country will face mandatory safeguards enforced by a new AI safety regulator, including mandatory reporting of security breaches and independent evaluation of frontier models.

According to SBS, the government accepted all 18 recommendations of a rapid review into an AI company's agent reaching a Medicare statistics website in June, which the company reported in September. The Conversation reports that statistical rather than personal health data was accessed and that criminal-law changes are being considered. The measures are announced, not yet law.

# China's state security ministry says it warned a man who anonymously denounced a colleague as a spy (state media)

*CCTV (state media), via Sina News, 2026-11-10. Original, in Chinese: <https://news.sina.com.cn/2026-11-10/doc-iniyexvh6071372.shtml>. Title translated from the Chinese.*

China's state broadcaster CCTV, citing the Ministry of State Security, reports that an employee of a public institution who lost a 2024 overseas posting to a colleague sent an anonymous letter to a foreign organisation falsely calling that colleague a spy.

According to the state media account, the ministry found he had not intended to harm national security but that the act had a negative effect, and gave him an administrative warning under the implementing rules of the Anti-Espionage Law. The report urges the public to report suspected espionage through the ministry's hotline. All of this is the ministry's account as carried by state media. (Summary translated from the Chinese.)

# Chinese researchers report non-invasive brain-interface electrode for day-long use

*The Star (Malaysia), from the South China Morning Post, 2026-11-10. Original: <https://www.thestar.com.my/tech/tech-news/2026/11/10/chinas-comfortable-brain-reading-device-achieves-94-mind-typing-accuracy-in-day-long-use>*

The Star, republishing a South China Morning Post report, says researchers at Guangxi University, Guangxi Medical University and Tsinghua University have made a soft, hydrogel-based electrode for non-invasive brain-computer interfaces, described in npj Flexible Electronics. According to the article, in a 14-hour test one subject reached over 94% accuracy on a flickering-keyboard typing task, while commercial gel electrodes became nearly unusable within four to five hours.

The publication reports that an eight-channel cap gave eight hours of stable recordings during walking, eating, reading and sleeping, that tests on mice showed no adverse reactions, and that a batch can yield 300 electrodes. It says the researchers see possible uses in health care, sleep monitoring and epilepsy warnings, which the article describes as potential rather than demonstrated.

# DHS release: DHS Calls on Sanctuary Politicians in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina to Honor ICE Detainer and Not Release a Previously-Deported Rapist

*U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 2026-11-10. Original: <https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/11/10/dhs-calls-sanctuary-politicians-mecklenburg-county-north-carolina-honor-ice>*

DHS said ICE lodged a detainer on 19 October 2026 asking Mecklenburg County, North Carolina, not to release a Honduran national held in the county jail after an arrest on burglary and sexual-offence charges, and said he had been deported four times since 2014. DHS said the county accounts for 240 of the 381 ICE detainers it says were not honoured in North Carolina between 20 January 2025 and 1 November 2026.

The current charges are accusations: every person arrested or charged is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# DHS release: DHS Highlights Worst Illegal Aliens Arrested in Austin, Texas

*U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 2026-11-10. Original: <https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/11/10/dhs-highlights-worst-illegal-aliens-arrested-austin-texas>*

DHS said ICE arrested five people in Austin, Texas, between 5 October and 1 November 2026, from Honduras (two), Mexico (two) and Venezuela, whom it described as among the worst illegal aliens arrested in the city. The descriptions are DHS's own: every person arrested or charged is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# DHS release: DHS is Taking Down Asylum Fraudsters

*U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 2026-11-10. Original: <https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/11/10/dhs-taking-down-asylum-fraudsters>*

DHS said U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services has supported federal prosecutions of asylum fraud over the past year, and that in May it directed ICE to take further steps against fraudulent asylum claims, including action against immigration attorneys who file false claims. DHS cited cases including six people sentenced in Florida on 29 October 2026 over a smuggling, asylum-fraud and money-laundering scheme run through a sham immigration business, as well as other indictments, guilty pleas and a removal.

Anyone charged and not convicted is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# DHS release: SANCTUARY INSANITY: DHS Condemns Sanctuary Politicians in Illinois for Releasing a Violent Criminal Rather Than Honoring ICE Detainer

*U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 2026-11-10. Original: <https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/11/10/sanctuary-insanity-dhs-condemns-sanctuary-politicians-illinois-releasing-violent>*

DHS said ICE lodged a detainer on 28 May 2026 for a national of Turkmenistan, admitted lawfully in March 2024 and later overstaying, who was convicted in Chicago of aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and sentenced to two years in prison. DHS said Illinois authorities released him without honouring the detainer or notifying ICE and that he remains at large, and it called on Illinois to change its sanctuary policies.

# FBI release: The New FBI: Better Technology to Meet the Mission

*Federal Bureau of Investigation, 2026-11-10. Original: <https://www.fbi.gov/news/press-releases/the-new-fbi-better-technology-to-meet-the-mission>*

The FBI republished an opinion piece by the FBI Director, first published by Nextgov/FCW on 10 November 2026, on the Bureau's technology. The figures in the piece are the Director's own.

# French interior ministry denies gendarmes used long-range acoustic devices at a Bordeaux protest and attributes the sound to a vehicle siren

*Police & Réalités, 2026-11-10. Original, in French: <https://policeetrealites.com/2026/11/10/manifestation-de-bordeaux-le-ministere-de-linterieur-dement-lusage-de-canons-a-son-par-la-gendarmerie/>. Title translated from the French.*

Police & Réalités reports that France's interior ministry issued a statement on 9 November 2026 denying that the gendarmerie used long-range acoustic devices (LRAD) at a protest in Bordeaux on 7 November, after a video from the protest led to claims that a sound cannon had been used.

According to the report, the ministry said the gendarmerie owns no LRAD-type equipment and attributed the sound to the warning siren fitted to its Centaure multi-purpose intervention vehicles. The ministry said it had taken the same position in a parliamentary answer of 25 June 2026, that France's internal security forces do not use LRAD in operations on public roads. (Summary translated from the French.)

# Hawaii health department reports a record 59 assisted deaths in 2025 and says its follow-up data may be incomplete

*Hawaii Tribune-Herald, 2026-11-10. Original: <https://www.hawaiitribune-herald.com/2026/11/10/hawaii-news/assisted-suicide-rises-in-hawaii-amid-opposition/>*

The Hawaii Tribune-Herald reports that the state Department of Health's annual report counts 59 deaths in 2025 after people took medication prescribed under Hawaii's medical aid in dying law, up from 38 in 2024 and the most since the law took effect in 2019, for 254 in total.

According to the newspaper, the department says it does not always receive complete follow-up information, so its figures may be incomplete. The article also recalls a 2024 death in which the county medical examiner recorded homicide; no charges are reported in that case.

# Karnataka orders AI face-scan attendance in government schools

*Tech Times, 2026-11-10. Original: <https://www.techtimes.com/articles/330373/20261110/facial-recognition-schools-karnataka-orders-pupil-face-scan-attendance-privacy-map-debuts.htm>*

Tech Times reports that the Karnataka state government has ordered AI face-scan attendance for students in government and aided schools and pre-university colleges, to begin in the 2026-27 school year. According to the article, the Centre for e-Governance is to run a system called Nirantara at a reported cost of about 2.16 crore rupees, and an earlier plan covered about 52,686 schools and 5.2 million students.

The publication says officials describe the aim as accurate attendance and identifying who receives mid-day meal benefits, and that a 2025 directive said children's photos would not be stored, a claim the article says it found no independent audit of. It reports that a coalition of 31 educators, teachers' unions and parents' groups has warned that children's facial data could be misused if leaked, and that parents fear children wrongly marked absent could lose benefits.

# More than half of Dutch municipalities use face-comparison scanners for identity documents, without figures on the fraud they target

*Binnenlands Bestuur, 2026-11-10. Original, in Dutch: <https://www.binnenlandsbestuur.nl/digitaal/gezichtsscanner-rukt-op-omvang-fraude-onbekend>. Title translated from the Dutch.*

Binnenlands Bestuur, a trade publication for Dutch public administration, reports that more than half of Dutch municipalities already use automatic face comparison at the counter to check identity, and that two make it mandatory for passport or licence applicants. It says the interior ministry plans to give the practice a legal basis through amendments to the passport, identity-card and population-register laws, and that the Dutch Data Protection Authority has previously raised concerns.

According to the publication, the association of municipalities, the military police, the national identity agency and the police all said they hold no figures on identity fraud at municipal counters. (Summary translated from the Dutch.)

Original, in French: <https://www.franceinfo.fr/internet/securite-sur-internet/cyberattaques/le-parquet-de-paris-ouvre-une-enquete-apres-la-cyberattaque-ayant-touche-des-chambres-froides-de-l-etablissement-francais-du-sang_8277005.html>. Title translated from the French.*

Franceinfo, citing AFP, reports that the Paris prosecutor's cybercrime section opened an inquiry into interference with a data-processing system after a cyberattack on a refrigeration contractor reached cold rooms of the national blood service, and assigned it to the national anti-cybercrime office and the domestic intelligence service.

According to the report, the health minister's office and the blood service say there was no impact on health, and prosecutors could not yet confirm any link to the attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems that France attributed to Iran. (Summary translated from the French.)

# Poland's internal security agency says two foreign nationals were charged with spying and sabotage for Russian intelligence

*Internal Security Agency (ABW), Poland, 2026-11-10. Original, in Polish: <https://www.abw.gov.pl/pl/aktualnosci/2851,ABW-zatrzymala-dwoch-podejrzanych-o-szpiegostwo-i-dywersje-na-rzecz-Rosji.html>. Title translated from the Polish.*

Poland's Internal Security Agency reports that on 3 November its officers detained two Ukrainian citizens, aged 24 and 25, and that a prosecutor charged both with espionage for a foreign intelligence service and with sabotage. It says a court ordered three months of pre-trial detention.

According to the agency, investigators allege the men scouted critical infrastructure and military sites and set fire to vehicles fitted with plates resembling Ukrainian army plates, for payment partly in cryptocurrency from Russian services. The charges are unproven and the men are presumed innocent. (Summary translated from the Polish.)

# Released messages show a contractor lobbied a UK health minister to extend its data platform into GP records

*The National (via Yahoo News UK), 2026-11-10. Original: <https://uk.news.yahoo.com/palantir-lobbied-scottish-labour-mp-095549257.html>*

The National reports, citing the Guardian, that messages released under freedom of information to the campaign group Foxglove show the UK head of the contractor running NHS England's Federated Data Platform pressing a then health minister in February 2026 to extend the company's software into GP records in England. According to the report, GP data is excluded from the platform contract, worth about 330 million pounds.

The paper quotes the chair of a network of NHS data officers as saying ministers and NHS leaders had stated that including GP data would require a change in the law. It reports that the company said the government decides how its software is used, and that the Department of Health declined to comment.

# Serbian prosecutors' review finds the inquiry into an alleged sound cannon at a 2025 protest was decided in advance

*Balkan Insight (BIRN), 2026-11-10. Original: <https://balkaninsight.com/2026/11/10/serbia-prosecution-accused-of-mishandling-cases-of-anti-govt-protesters/bi/>*

Balkan Insight reports that a commission set up on 27 October by Serbia's Supreme Public Prosecution Office reviewed seven cases handled by the Higher Public Prosecutor's Office in Belgrade, among them the complaint that a long-range acoustic weapon was used on protesters in March 2025, which that office closed in September 2025 with no grounds for criminal proceedings. According to the report, the commission found that the office did more to formalise a decision, made in advance, that no sound cannon had been used than to investigate, treating the authorities' denial as an indisputable fact and disregarding contrary evidence.

The publication says the commission also noted that in June 2026 the office asked the Security Intelligence Agency to check 154 citizens who had given statements about the alleged device, and that it forwarded its report to prosecutors, saying there are grounds to suspect criminal offences. The report does not say the commission concluded that a device was used. The Higher Public Prosecutor's Office rejects the findings as unfounded, and its head has filed a criminal complaint against the commission's chair.

# Suicide foundation reports U.S. teen suicide planning and attempts fell sharply between 2023 and 2025

*American Foundation for Suicide Prevention, 2026-11-10. Original: <https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/where-does-us-teen-mental-health-stand-improvements-reported-but-disparities-persist-302934163.html>*

The American Foundation for Suicide Prevention reports that the CDC's 2025 Youth Risk Behavior Survey shows the share of U.S. high-school students who made a suicide plan fell from 16 to 12 percent between 2023 and 2025, and the share who attempted suicide from 9 to 6 percent, which it calls the largest two-year drops on record. It says persistent sadness fell from 40 to 33 percent.

The foundation notes sharp rises among Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander students and continuing gaps by sex and sexual identity, and flags limits in the data: response rates halved, ten states did not take part, and a question on transgender identity was dropped.

# Taiwan: man pleads guilty in a hotel assault on a foreign commentator that prosecutors call transnational repression

*Central News Agency (Taiwan), 2026-11-10. Original, in Chinese: <https://www.cna.com.tw/news/asoc/202611100164.aspx>. Title written in English by us; the original names the people involved.*

Taiwan's Central News Agency reports that a man who entered Taiwan on a Hong Kong passport pleaded guilty in Taichung District Court to assault, intimidation and organised-crime offences over a July 2026 attack on a Japanese commentator at a Taichung hotel, and that sentencing is set for 3 December.

According to the agency, prosecutors describe the attack as transnational repression meant to intimidate free speech and say the man was promised HK$100,000 by a gang leader; four co-defendants have left Taiwan and are wanted. The report does not say prosecutors tied the attack to the Chinese government, and the co-defendants are presumed innocent. (Summary translated from the Chinese.)

# Three Iran-backed operatives indicted over nearly 20 attacks and plots in Europe and the United States

*U.S. Department of Justice, 2026-11-10. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/three-iranian-backed-operatives-indicted-their-roles-nearly-20-terrorist-attacks-and>*

The Justice Department says a superseding indictment unsealed in Manhattan charges three men with terrorism offences in support of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Kata'ib Hizballah. Prosecutors allege roles in about 18 attacks in Europe in spring 2026, mostly arson and explosive attacks on Jewish targets, and in a September 2026 plot at a UK air base where U.S. forces were stationed.

The department alleges that one defendant, already held in New York, continued to coordinate through coded messages. An indictment is an allegation, and the defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

# Tokyo police arrest a man accused of running a fake mobile base station from a car that knocked thousands of phones offline to send phishing texts

*The Star (Malaysia), from The Japan News and ANN, 2026-11-10. Original: <https://www.thestar.com.my/aseanplus/aseanplus-news/2026/11/10/chinese-national-arrested-over-fake-mobile-phone-base-station-in-tokyo039s-ginza>*

The Star, carrying reports from The Japan News and ANN, says Tokyo police arrested a man accused of operating a fake mobile-phone base station from a vehicle in Ginza that knocked more than 10,000 phones offline for about an hour, allegedly to send phishing text messages to Chinese tourists. Japan's communications ministry says it located the device with police on 7 November.

According to the report, police link the case to 18 complaints and about 4 million yen in losses since January 2025. The suspect denies the allegation and is presumed innocent.

# U.S. Army officer at a NATO headquarters arrested in England on suspicion of helping Russian intelligence

*NBC News, 2026-11-10. Original: <https://www.nbcnews.com/world/united-kingdom/us-army-member-arrested-uk-suspicion-working-russian-intelligence-rcna608616>*

NBC News reports that London's Metropolitan Police arrested a 41-year-old senior U.S. Army soldier near Gloucester on suspicion of offences under sections 1 and 3 of the UK National Security Act, covering obtaining or disclosing protected information and assisting a foreign intelligence service, and that police say the allegations relate to Russia.

The network cites a NATO official as saying he was assigned to the Allied Rapid Reaction Corps, and reports that the FBI and U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command took part in the investigation. He had not been charged at the time of reporting and is presumed innocent.

# UK Investigatory Powers Tribunal finds a council's covert surveillance of a family's home and farm was unlawful

*LocalGov, 2026-11-10. Original: <https://www.localgov.co.uk/Tribunal-rules-secret-surveillance-of-pig-farm-was-unlawful/65209>*

LocalGov reports that the Investigatory Powers Tribunal found a Hampshire district council carried out covert surveillance of a family's farm and home in 2023 without the authorisation the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000 requires. According to the report, the tribunal found no evidence of bad faith, ordered the material destroyed and awarded no compensation.

The publication reports the family's account that officers watched from a neighbour's property and that neighbours were asked to report when the family was home; these are the family's claims. LocalGov also reports that the Information Commissioner's Office upheld the family's separate complaint about the council's handling of their data.

# US appeals court rules a government demand for journalists' records from a professional networking site in a leak inquiry is too broad

*Associated Press (via WRAL), 2026-11-10. Original: <https://www.wral.com/news/ap/0b1f0-appeals-court-limits-order-for-linkedin-to-disclose-journalists-communications-in-leak-probe/>*

The Associated Press reports that a three-judge panel of the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals unanimously held that the government is not entitled to a blanket order for 18 months of reporters' communications held by a professional networking platform, and sent the case back to a Virginia district court to narrow the order. The panel also rejected the platform's request to quash the order entirely, according to AP.

AP reports the demand arose from a leak investigation into a news story about a classified military operation abroad. Courthouse News reports the panel called the order substantially overbroad.

# US federal judge rules police may not hand probable cause to an AI facial-recognition match and lets a wrongful-jailing suit proceed

*Bloomberg Law, 2026-11-10. Original: <https://news.bloomberglaw.com/litigation/cop-stuck-with-wrongful-arrest-suit-over-false-ai-facial-match>*

Bloomberg Law reports that a federal judge in the Eastern District of Kentucky refused to dismiss a civil rights suit against a police officer who, the suit says, arrested a man and kept him jailed for more than two weeks on the strength of an AI tool's mistaken facial match.

According to the report, the judge held that the Fourth Amendment does not allow an officer to delegate the assessment of probable cause to an AI tool, or to arrest someone on the tool's uncorroborated conclusion. The ruling lets the case go forward; the suit's claims are not proven and the officer has not been found liable.

# Austrian cabinet approves a draft law raising espionage penalties and making spying on international organisations a crime

*Austrian Federal Ministry of the Interior, 2026-11-11. Original, in German: <https://www.bmi.gv.at/news.html?id=2F68466343594568432B773D>. Title translated from the German.*

Austria's Interior Ministry says the Council of Ministers approved a stricter espionage law on 11 November, raising penalties, widening what counts as an offence and protecting international organisations based in Austria. The draft goes to public consultation and is not yet law.

ORF reports that the maximum sentence for espionage against Austria would rise to 10 years, that spying on EU bodies or international organisations in Austria would carry up to five years, that recruiting agents and being recruited would become offences, and that penalties would rise for computer sabotage carried out for foreign services. (Summary translated from the German.)

# Egypt verifies citizens' faces against state biometric records to issue powers of attorney remotely

*Youm7, 2026-11-11. Original, in Arabic: <https://www.youm7.com/story/2026/11/11/بصمة-الوجه-وشهادة-توقيع-آلية-التحقق-من-الهوية-عند-إصدار/7612009>. Title translated from the Arabic.*

Youm7 reports that Egypt's remote power-of-attorney service, run by the justice and communications ministries on the Egypt Digital Platform, verifies identity with an AI digital-identity application that scans the citizen's face and compares it with the biometric record held in state databases.

According to the report, a verified user is then issued a single-use electronic-signature certificate to sign the document. (Summary translated from the Arabic.)

# Indonesian lawmakers question the police chief over alleged unauthorised wiretapping of the president and others, now investigated as possible treason

*Associated Press (via ABC News), 2026-11-11. Original: <https://abcnews.com/International/wireStory/indonesian-lawmakers-question-police-chief-wiretaps-alleged-target-138065101>*

The Associated Press reports that Indonesia's parliamentary law commission was to question the national police chief about alleged illegal wiretapping of the president. According to AP, police allege that unauthorised surveillance between 2025 and 2026 captured recordings of the president's phone calls, and other cabinet officials, politicians, journalists, civil-society leaders and business executives are alleged, without confirmation, to have been monitored.

AP reports that three senior police generals, including a former police chief, are detained and that no charges have yet been filed; the president's office says the case is being investigated as possible treason. The officers are presumed innocent; one suspect's lawyer told AP his client will cooperate.

# Maker of a consumer EEG headband trained an AI model on users' brain recordings before its privacy policy said so, investigation reports

*Malwarebytes Labs, 2026-11-11. Original: <https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/ai/2026/11/muse-sleep-band-users-werent-told-their-brain-data-was-training-ai>*

Malwarebytes, citing a year-long investigation by the journal Science, reports that a Canadian maker of a consumer EEG headband used about 50,000 hours of users' brain recordings to train a "brain foundation model" without clearly telling those users, and updated its privacy policy to disclose the use of de-identified data only after Science asked.

According to the report, Science reviewed 57 neurotechnology companies and found six that explicitly promised not to sell brain data. Malwarebytes cites research suggesting EEG data can be re-identified or reveal health information. No regulator action is reported.

# Military-linked Chinese university on the US trade blacklist bought restricted AI chips, procurement records show

*Reuters (via BNN Bloomberg), 2026-11-11. Original: <https://www.bnnbloomberg.ca/business/artificial-intelligence/2026/11/11/military-linked-chinese-university-bought-nvidia-chips-despite-us-blacklist-reuters-exclusive/>*

Reuters reports that an October procurement record shows a Chinese military-linked university, on the US Commerce Department's Entity List since 2001, bought two restricted high-end AI chips for 874,700 yuan through a domestic supplier, and rented restricted computing capacity under five contracts this year.

According to Reuters, a review of 26 records found other Chinese institutions buying or renting restricted chips. The university, the chipmaker and the US export-control bureau did not respond to Reuters.

# People living with implanted brain-computer interfaces publish ethics recommendations asking for control over their neural data and devices

*The Debrief, 2026-11-11. Original: <https://thedebrief.org/bci-implant-recipients-release-ethical-recommendations-calling-for-greater-control-over-neural-data-and-device-ownership/>*

The Debrief reports that a coalition of people with implanted brain-computer interfaces released a 13-page set of recommendations for ethical implanted BCI research.

According to the report, the document asks for consent that is ongoing rather than given once, limits on confidentiality agreements that could stop participants reporting safety concerns, treatment of neural data as participants' personal information, and support for devices after a trial ends, and it is to be reviewed every 24 months.

# Records released after a lawsuit detail the US Postal Inspection Service's covert social-media and facial-recognition monitoring of protests

*Reason, 2026-11-11. Original: <https://reason.com/2026/11/11/documents-reveal-the-postal-services-broad-surveillance-of-political-activists/>*

Reason reports that the Electronic Frontier Foundation obtained records of the Postal Inspection Service's Internet Covert Operations Program after suing for them. According to Reason, the records show bulletins tracking protests across the political spectrum in 2020 and 2021 that were shared with about 70 agencies, and that the program used anonymous accounts and a commercial facial-recognition service.

Reason quotes the Postal Service Inspector General's March 2022 finding that some of the program's proactive searches exceeded the Inspection Service's law enforcement authority, and reports the foundation's view that the documents do not show the monitoring stopped.

# Russia's security service says it arrested two Polish citizens in Kaliningrad region on espionage charges

*Meduza, 2026-11-11. Original, in Russian: <https://meduza.io/news/2026/11/11/fsb-v-den-nezavisimosti-polshi-ob-yavila-chto-zaderzhala-v-kaliningradskoy-oblasti-dvuh-polyakov-po-obvineniyu-v-shpionazhe>. Title translated from the Russian.*

Meduza, an independent Russian outlet based abroad, reports that Russia's Federal Security Service announced the arrest of two Polish citizens in Kaliningrad region, alleging they collected and passed information about military personnel, defence ministry sites and the region's social and migration situation to Polish intelligence.

According to the report, the service also said seven other Polish citizens and three Russians received official warnings and seven Polish citizens were barred from entering Russia, and Meduza notes the announcement came on Poland's Independence Day. These are the security service's allegations, and the suspects are presumed innocent. (Summary translated from the Russian.)

# South Korean prosecutors charge seven employees of an equipment contractor and the company over an alleged attempt to move display process data to China

*Financial News (fnnews), 2026-11-11. Original, in Korean: <https://www.fnnews.com/news/202611111602086442>. Title translated from the Korean.*

Financial News reports that the Seoul Eastern District Prosecutors' Office has indicted seven employees of a factory-automation contractor, and the company, under the Industrial Technology Protection Act, unfair-competition law and copyright law.

According to the report, prosecutors allege that in 2020 four employees hid log files from a display maker's LCD plant equipment, data prosecutors treat as national core technology, so that they would survive data wiping and could be used in a Chinese manufacturer's equipment move; an engineer found the files and the alleged transfer did not happen. The defendants are presumed innocent. (Summary translated from the Korean.)

# Washington appeals court upholds a protection order in a case of alleged covert listening through a home voice assistant

*Tech Times, 2026-11-11. Original: <https://www.techtimes.co.uk/washington-court-upholds-alexa-surveillance-protection-order-1809862>*

Tech Times reports that the Washington Court of Appeals affirmed a five-year domestic-violence protection order resting on allegations that a former husband used a voice assistant's remote "drop in" feature to connect to a device in the woman's home, tracked her card purchases and changed her email password. The publication notes the judgment does not establish what he heard.

According to the report, the court found no abuse of discretion and declined to consider an argument that relied on a non-existent case. Tech Times reports that separate criminal charges were resolved by a plea agreement and a later stalking charge was dismissed; the order is a civil finding, not a criminal conviction.

# China's industry ministry approves nine brain-computer interface industry standards for drafting, including attention monitoring

*Stnn (Sing Tao), 2026-11-12. Original, in Chinese: <https://m.stnn.cc/detail/6af533308f9d2b19dd6b9d14.html>. Title translated from the Chinese.*

Stnn reports that China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology has approved nine brain-computer interface industry standards for drafting, in its fifth batch of 2026 standard plans, under the ministry's brain-computer interface standardisation committee.

According to the report, the standards cover product grading, risk management, interaction interfaces, wireless communication for invasive devices, data and algorithm management, and application scenarios including sports training and "attention monitoring". The individual titles were not published in the coverage. (Summary translated from the Chinese.)

# DHS release: DHS Highlights Worst Illegal Aliens Arrested in Houston, Texas

*U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 2026-11-12. Original: <https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/11/12/dhs-highlights-worst-illegal-aliens-arrested-houston-texas>*

DHS said ICE arrested five people in Houston, Texas, between 2 and 27 October 2026, from Mexico (two), El Salvador, Venezuela and Honduras, whom it described as among the worst illegal aliens arrested in the city. DHS listed convictions and charges including the killing of a police officer, murder, burglary, aggravated kidnapping and a sexual offence against a child, and said two of them had been deported before.

The descriptions are DHS's own: every person arrested or charged is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# DHS release: ICE Arrests Illegal Alien Who Intentionally Ran Over and Dragged Officer with Vehicle in Chicago

*U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 2026-11-12. Original: <https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/11/12/ice-arrests-illegal-alien-who-intentionally-ran-over-and-dragged-officer-vehicle>*

DHS said that on 10 November 2026, during a targeted enforcement operation in Chicago Heights, Illinois, a Mexican national stopped by ICE drove away with an officer partly inside his vehicle, and the officer was thrown out and struck, suffering a leg injury; DHS said the officer was treated in hospital and released. DHS said ICE arrested the man later that day and that he had earlier arrests and had been deported seven times.

The release lists no criminal charge for the incident; anyone accused is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# DHS release: ICE Breaks Records in Fiscal Year 2026, With Most Arrests and Deportations in Agency’s History

*U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 2026-11-12. Original: <https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/11/12/ice-breaks-records-fiscal-year-2026-most-arrests-and-deportations-agencys-history>*

DHS said ICE made more than 491,000 immigration arrests and 483,200 deportations in fiscal year 2026, both records for the agency, against 442,640 deportations in fiscal year 2025. DHS said August 2026 had the most arrests of any single month, 50,925, and that there have been nearly 1.2 million deportations since the current administration took office.

The figures are the department's own count.
