# Polish transparency group takes Poland to the European Court of Human Rights after prosecutors refused to say who was surveilled with Pegasus spyware

*Sieć Obywatelska Watchdog Polska, 2026-11-17. Original, in Polish: <https://siecobywatelska.pl/pegasus-skarzymy-polske-do-strasburga/>. Title translated from the Polish.*

Watchdog Polska, a civic transparency group, says that since April 2025 it has asked the National Prosecutor's Office, the Justice Ministry and the Central Anti-Corruption Bureau who was surveilled with Pegasus spyware, how often and at what cost, and that all three refused, citing lack of competence, classification or the secrecy of criminal investigations.

The group reports five administrative-court rulings with differing outcomes: in July 2026 the Supreme Administrative Court sided with the prosecutors, holding that criminal-procedure rules govern access, and on 5 November 2026 it ordered the ministry to consider the request. The group says it has now complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the refusal breaches the right to information under Article 10 of the Convention; the court has not yet acted on the complaint. (Summary translated from the Polish.)

# Serbia's organised-crime prosecutors open a case on the review that found the sound-cannon complaint from the March 2025 protest was not properly investigated

*Danas (FoNet), 2026-11-17. Original, in Serbian: <https://www.danas.rs/vesti/drustvo/jtok-formirao-predmet-vjt-stefanovic/>. Title translated from the Serbian.*

Danas, carrying the FoNet agency, reports that Serbia's Prosecutor's Office for Organised Crime told the broadcaster N1 it received the first report of the Supreme Public Prosecutor's Office commission on 10 November and opened a case the same day. The commission's report concerns the work of the Higher Public Prosecutor's Office in Belgrade and its chief, and lists among the irregularly handled matters the complaints about a "sound cannon" at the 15 March 2025 protest in Belgrade.

According to the report, the office said only that it is acting within its legal powers. No charges have been reported. (Summary translated from the Serbian.)

# Taiwan prosecutors charge three private investigators accused of tracking two anti-China online commentators and their relatives for Chinese police

*Public Television Service (PTS), 2026-11-17. Original, in Chinese: <https://news.pts.org.tw/article/836077>. Title translated from the Chinese.*

Taiwan's Public Television Service reports that the New Taipei District Prosecutors Office has charged the business manager of a private investigation firm and two of its field staff under the Personal Data Protection Act. Prosecutors allege that the manager met a Shanghai public security official in China in March 2025, then took paid work from a contact described as sent by the Chinese Communist Party, used household-registration data bought in 2020 to look up seven people, including two online commentators critical of China and their relatives, and sent staff to photograph the two at rallies in 2025.

According to the report, China's Taiwan Affairs Office and police in Quanzhou later issued a bounty notice publishing the pair's personal details. Prosecutors asked for a sentence of three years and six months for the manager. These are charges; no verdict has been given and the three are presumed innocent. (Summary translated from the Chinese.)

# Turkish court remands 14 of 79 people detained in a 42-province operation against the theft and sale of personal data

*Sivas Ekspres, carrying Anadolu Agency (state media), 2026-11-17. Original, in Turkish: <https://www.sivasekspres.com/haber/42-ilde-kisisel-veri-operasyonu-14-tutuklama-100618.html>. Title translated from the Turkish.*

Anadolu Agency, Turkey's state news agency, as carried by Sivas Ekspres, reports that police cyber-crime units working under the Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor's Office detained 79 people in 42 provinces on suspicion of obtaining personal and financial data without authorisation and selling it, with the data allegedly used for threats, blackmail and card fraud. The agency reports that an AI-assisted application was used in the investigation.

According to the report, of 50 suspects brought before a court, 14 were remanded in custody and 36 released under judicial control. The claims are the authorities' as relayed by state media, and the suspects are presumed innocent. (Summary translated from the Turkish.)

# UK health minister says the NHS national data-platform contract will run to 2029 rather than ending at the 2027 break clause

*Dataconomy, 2026-11-17. Original: <https://dataconomy.com/2026/11/17/uk-to-end-palantirs-nhs-data-contract-in-2029/>*

Dataconomy reports that a UK health minister told MPs that the NHS Federated Data Platform contract with Palantir would be extended to March 2029 instead of being ended at the spring 2027 break clause, with a procurement for a replacement to start in late 2027. According to the report, the minister described the extension as a bridge, not the destination.

Dataconomy reports that the chair of the Commons science committee called the decision deeply disappointing and that campaign groups had urged the government to end the contract. It also reports that NHS England removed a claim that 137 trusts were benefiting from the platform after data showed 29 rarely or never used it.

# UN crime agency and INTERPOL report warns that coercive neural lie detection and neurotechnology in interrogation raise serious human rights concerns

*The Conversation, 2026-11-17. Original: <https://theconversation.com/can-the-police-monitor-a-suspects-brain-during-interrogation-a-new-report-issues-a-stark-warning-295555>*

Writing in The Conversation, two University of Sydney law academics report that a new assessment by the UN Office on Drugs and Crime and INTERPOL examines neurotechnology in criminal justice, including EEG headsets said to detect recognition of crime-scene images and neural lie detectors. According to the authors, the report says neither approach has been scientifically proven, and that compulsory or coercive neural lie detection, memory retrieval and guilty-knowledge testing, and neurotechnology used for interrogation, behavioural compliance or involuntary treatment, raise significant human rights concerns, including for privacy, the right against self-incrimination and freedom of thought.

The authors say the report calls for binding legal frameworks and independently verifiable scientific standards. They write that police in the United Arab Emirates and India already use such tests on suspects, that India's Supreme Court ruled in 2010 that evidence from involuntary use is inadmissible, and that Australian law has not been tested on the question.

# US Commerce and Justice departments say a Singapore company has been under investigation since 2024 for possible diversion of advanced AI chips

*U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs, 2026-11-17. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/joint-statement-department-commerce-and-department-justice-megaspeed-investigation>*

The Departments of Commerce and Justice said in a joint statement that Commerce began investigating a Singapore-based company in 2024 after its monitoring flagged possible diversion of advanced semiconductors, that in 2025 it requested sales records from the chipmaker, which then placed the company on a no-sell list, and that Commerce carried out an on-site check with Singaporean law enforcement.

The departments said the Justice Department now leads a criminal investigation. The statement announces no charges or findings, and the company is not accused of any offence in it.

# US court sentences a man recruited by Iran's Revolutionary Guards to more than 27 years over a plot to hire killers to assassinate US officials

*U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs, 2026-11-17. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/iranian-intelligence-agent-sentenced-over-27-years-prison-foiled-plot-assassinate-us>*

The Justice Department reports that a Pakistani national was sentenced in federal court in Brooklyn to 330 months in prison after a jury convicted him of attempting an act of terrorism transcending national boundaries and of murder for hire. According to the department, he was recruited by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, met a handler in Tehran and was trained in counterintelligence techniques.

The department says he paid $5,000 to undercover FBI employees he believed were hitmen, toward a plan to kill US politicians or government officials. The account is the department's, based on the evidence at trial.

# US House Intelligence Committee votes to release an unclassified interim report on how intelligence agencies handled anomalous health incidents

*U.S. House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, 2026-11-17. Original: <https://intelligence.house.gov/2026/11/17/house-intelligence-committee-approves-release-of-committees-unclassified-investigative-report-into-anomalous-health-incidents/>*

The House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence said it voted at a business meeting to approve the release of an unclassified interim report on part of its investigation into the Intelligence Community's handling of anomalous health incidents. The committee said the report addresses a limited topic within a complex issue and will be released once a security review is complete.

The committee's chairman said the issue is far more complex than public reporting can depict and that he looks forward to the report's imminent release. No findings have been published.

# US requires export licences for advanced AI chips going to five countries, to stop remote access by Chinese developers through overseas data centres

*Al Jazeera, 2026-11-17. Original: <https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/11/17/us-moves-to-block-chinas-remote-access-to-ai-chips-amid-nvidia-scandal>*

Al Jazeera reports that the US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security announced on 16 November that advanced AI chips shipped to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand now need an export licence, saying those countries pose an unacceptable risk of diversion. According to the report, the bureau calls the rule a logical extension of the existing licence requirement for firms based in China.

Al Jazeera reports that the aim is to stop Chinese developers from using data centres in third countries to get around export controls, and places the rule in the context of a controversy at a leading US chip maker. Other outlets quote the bureau as saying chip restrictions cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements in third countries.

# Burkina Faso opens terrorism cases against at least 45 exiled critics and seeks their arrest abroad, a rights group reports

*Human Rights Watch, 2026-11-18. Original: <https://www.hrw.org/news/2026/11/18/burkina-faso-targets-critics-in-exile>*

Human Rights Watch reports that Burkina Faso's prosecutor general announced on 13 November 2026 that a special terrorism court had opened six cases against at least 45 people and entities, including exiled journalists, activists and a former minister, on charges including complicity in terrorist associations and financing terrorism.

According to the group, international arrest warrants and extradition requests went to Côte d'Ivoire, France and the United States, and the authorities asked the United States to have a social-media company help identify and prosecute the administrators of Facebook pages. Human Rights Watch describes this as transnational repression; the charges have not been tested in court and the people named are presumed innocent.

# DHS release: CCHT Chronicle: November 2026

*U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 2026-11-18. Original: <https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/USDHS/bulletins/432ed4e>*

The November 2026 issue of the monthly newsletter of the DHS Center for Countering Human Trafficking focuses on familial trafficking, in which a relative exploits a family member for labour or commercial sex, and warns jobseekers about seasonal hiring scams that DHS said can lead to forced labour. It also describes the Center's 2026 webinar series on coercion in trafficking and an HSI Dallas investigation that DHS said led to eight federal indictments for alleged sex trafficking and money laundering.

Those indicted are presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# DHS release: DHS Denounces Texas Officials for Allegedly Planning to End Cooperation with ICE

*U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 2026-11-18. Original: <https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/11/18/dhs-denounces-texas-officials-allegedly-planning-end-cooperation-ice>*

The Department of Homeland Security said on 18 November 2026 that Texas officials plan to end the state's cooperation with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) once the incoming governor takes office, and the Secretary of Homeland Security urged state leaders to keep cooperating. DHS said ending cooperation would increase crime, and it listed 19 recent Texas cases of people it described as illegal aliens who were arrested, convicted or removed, with offences it listed including murder, sexual offences against children, drug trafficking and gang membership.

The cases are DHS's own account: every person arrested or charged is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# DHS release: ICE Lodges Detainer for Alien Arrested in Oklahoma for Kidnapping and Raping a Minor

*U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 2026-11-18. Original: <https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/11/18/ice-lodges-detainer-alien-arrested-oklahoma-kidnapping-and-raping-minor>*

DHS said ICE lodged a detainer on 26 October 2026 asking Tulsa County, Oklahoma, to hold a Guatemalan national arrested by Tulsa police over an attack on a teenager on 17 October, on charges including kidnapping and sexual offences against a minor. DHS said he entered the United States in 2014, was released after a Border Patrol arrest and later received legal status, and that it will work with Oklahoma to prevent his release and to remove him.

He is charged, not convicted: every person arrested or charged is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# Germany's parliament passes an intelligence reform obliging carmakers and transport firms to hand vehicle data to the intelligence services

*netzpolitik.org, 2026-11-18. Original, in German: <https://netzpolitik.org/2026/heimlicher-zugriff-auf-fahrzeugdaten-die-auto-branche-als-verlaengerter-arm-der-geheimdienste/>. Title translated from the German.*

Netzpolitik.org, a digital-rights news outlet, reports that the Bundestag passed by majority a broad reform of the intelligence laws under which carmakers and workshops, rental, carsharing and freight companies and operators of reservation systems must hand vehicle data to the domestic intelligence agency and the foreign intelligence service on request, covertly. According to the report, the data can include vehicle identification numbers, telemetry such as speed and mileage, driving profiles and seat occupancy, GPS routes and parking positions, and possibly identifiers of phones connected to the car.

The outlet reports objections and requests for clearer definitions from industry associations. The article does not say when the law takes effect. (Summary translated from the German.)

# Police in south-west England postpone their first live facial-recognition deployment, in Bath, after objections from elected representatives

*Bath Echo (Local Democracy Reporting Service), 2026-11-18. Original: <https://www.bathecho.co.uk/news/crime/police-pause-plans-facial-recognition-bath-120725/>*

Bath Echo reports that Avon and Somerset Police had planned to start using live facial recognition in Bath city centre on 25 November, the day before its Christmas market opens, checking faces against a pre-authorised watchlist and deleting non-matches.

According to the report, the local MP and a member of the House of Lords urged the chief constable to wait until Parliament legislates, and the force said it would postpone the deployment after feedback from elected representatives and local stakeholders. The Police and Crime Commissioner's office welcomed the pause, saying local leaders had raised concerns about disproportionality and a lack of consultation.

# Russia's security service tells a court that a restricted government decree is the basis for regional mobile internet shutdowns

*Novaya Gazeta Europe, 2026-11-18. Original, in Russian: <https://novayagazeta.eu/articles/2026/11/18/fsb-otkliuchaet-internet-v-regionakh-na-osnovanii-sekretnogo-postanovleniia-pravitelstva-news>. Title translated from the Russian.*

Novaya Gazeta Europe reports that the Volgograd regional directorate of Russia's FSB told a district court that it instructs mobile operators when to cut mobile internet, citing a government decree of September 2025 on mobile services during drone-attack threats that is marked for official use only and has not been published.

According to the report, the statement came in a lawsuit by 24 Volgograd residents against the FSB, the communications regulator and mobile operators, seeking compensation for shutdowns between September and December 2025; the first hearing was held on 17 November after the court had three times declined to hear the case. The Moscow Times reports that the FSB asks the court to reject the claims in full. The court has not ruled. (Summary translated from the Russian.)

# Spain's health ministry reports 574 assisted deaths in 2025 and 382 applicants who died while their request was being processed

*Ministerio de Sanidad (Spain), 2026-11-18. Original, in Spanish: <https://www.sanidad.gob.es/gabinete/notasPrensa.do?id=7006>. Title translated from the Spanish.*

Spain's Ministry of Health reports that its annual report on the assisted-dying law counts 1,284 new requests in 2025, up from 983 in 2024, and 574 assisted deaths, up from 423.

According to the ministry, of 1,219 procedures closed in 2025, 574 ended in an assisted death, 382 in the applicant's death during processing, 165 in a denial and 98 in a withdrawal; 72 people appealed to the oversight commissions and 20 appeals were upheld. The average time to the commission's decision was 46.5 days, and the release reports no irregularities. (Summary translated from the Spanish.)

# UK Home Office publishes its live facial-recognition policy for immigration enforcement and lists city-centre deployments in Manchester

*Home Office (GOV.UK), 2026-11-18. Original: <https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/live-facial-recognition>*

The Home Office published a policy paper on 18 November setting out how Immigration Enforcement uses overt live facial recognition in public places. The policy says only people in strict predefined categories, such as those under a current deportation order, are placed on watchlists, under-18s are excluded, images that raise no alert are deleted automatically and alert data within 24 hours, and no action is taken on a system alert alone.

The department says the policy creates no new powers. On 19 November it listed its next deployments, in Manchester city centre on 25 and 26 November 2026.

# US audit office covertly tests four widely used AI chatbots and obtains workable attack plans from all of them

*U.S. Government Accountability Office, 2026-11-18. Original: <https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-27-108814>*

The Government Accountability Office said its testers prompted four widely used generative AI platforms in spring 2026 and that all four produced information that could help plan an attack: two on an explosive device intended to cause mass casualties and two on attacking the electrical grid. GAO said the platforms' safeguards were triggered but were bypassed using common techniques, and that experts judged the resulting plans viable.

GAO said the information itself was not new, but that the systems assembled it into workable plans in under 12 hours.

# US health statistics agency moves provisional death rates to a new dashboard, showing the 12-month suicide rate at 13.2 per 100,000 to July 2026

*CDC National Center for Health Statistics, 2026-11-18. Original: <https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nvss/vsrr/viser.html>*

The CDC's National Center for Health Statistics said its quarterly provisional mortality dashboard was archived on 18 November 2026 and that provisional figures now appear on its Vital Statistics Early Release dashboard. According to the dataset, for the 12 months ending July 2026 the suicide rate was 13.2 deaths per 100,000, against 13.7 a year earlier, and the rates for all causes, cancer, Alzheimer disease, stroke, chronic liver disease and kidney disease were also lower than a year before.

The agency notes that provisional figures lag by about three months, and by six months for drug overdose, whose latest 12-month rate is 18.8 per 100,000 to April 2026. The figures are provisional and may be revised.

# US indicts a Russian national accused of acting as Russia's agent by surveilling and stalking employees of a Silicon Valley defence-technology company

*U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs, 2026-11-18. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/russian-national-indicted-acting-foreign-agent-russia-target-silicon-valley-technology-and>*

The Justice Department reports that a federal grand jury in the Northern District of California has indicted a Russian national on charges of conspiring to act as an agent of a foreign government, acting as such an agent without notifying the Attorney General, interstate stalking and identification-document fraud.

The department alleges he was recruited through Telegram, entered the United States unlawfully in 2026, photographed employees' laptop screens near the company's office, searched for employees' home addresses and, around 3 September, followed one employee for nearly 30 miles until she called 911. It says FBI agents later recovered cash, false identity documents and a notebook of employees' addresses and profiles. These are charges; he is presumed innocent, and his next court date is 24 November.

# US intelligence, FBI and homeland security officials tell Congress the recent run of outages showed no sign of a cyberattack

*CBS News, 2026-11-18. Original: <https://www.cbsnews.com/news/network-outages-cyber-malicious-activity-homeland-security-hearing/>*

CBS News reports that at a House Homeland Security Committee hearing on 18 November, the Director of National Intelligence described the recent outages, including the 13 November FAA ground stop and disruptions to Microsoft, Apple and bank services and an internal NSA network, as separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes, not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.

According to CBS, the FBI's deputy director said there was no indication of malicious cyber activity, and the Homeland Security secretary said he was 98% confident the outages were not foreign malicious activity. CBS reports that the FAA's telecommunications contractor was replacing copper with fibre when a newly switched router flooded other routers. No final official cause report has been published.

# US woman sues a technology company alleging its tracking tags let a former partner secretly follow her for years

*AboutLawsuits.com, 2026-11-18. Original: <https://www.aboutlawsuits.com/apple-airtag-lawsuit/lawsuit-hidden-airtags-stalk-abuse-mother/>*

AboutLawsuits.com reports that a Washington woman filed a complaint on 10 November 2026 in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Washington alleging that the maker of a widely sold Bluetooth tracking tag failed to build adequate safeguards into it, allowing her former partner to track her location covertly for years.

According to the report, the complaint brings claims of design defect, failure to warn, negligence, strict product liability and violation of the state consumer-protection law, and follows a federal panel's decision to centralise similar tracking-tag lawsuits in the Northern District of California. These are allegations in a newly filed complaint; no court has ruled, and the report gives no response from the company.

# White House release: Fact Sheet: President [name] Secures Historic Economic Deals for American Workers and Strengthens America’s Leadership in Asia

*The White House, 2026-11-18. Original: <https://www.whitehouse.gov/fact-sheets/2026/11/fact-sheet-president-donald-j-trump-secures-historic-economic-deals-for-american-workers-and-strengthens-americas-leadership-in-asia/>*

The White House said the President ended a two-day visit to the Philippines, including a state visit and the ASEAN Summit, having announced more than $17 billion in commercial deals and investments, the largest a $12 billion sale of passenger aircraft to Philippine Airlines. It listed defence financing for the Philippines, a $63 million Philippine defence cloud modernisation using U.S. technology it calls super intelligence, a substantially concluded reciprocal trade agreement with Thailand, a planned sovereign government cloud in Malaysia and a data-centre build in Brunei.

The amounts are the White House's own figures.

# White House release: “No Indication of a Cyberattack”: DNI [name] and Secretary [name] on Recent Tech Outages

*The White House, 2026-11-18. Original: <https://www.whitehouse.gov/releases/2026/11/no-indication-of-a-cyberattack-dni-clayton-and-secretary-rubio-on-recent-tech-outages/>*

The White House published remarks by the Director of National Intelligence and the Secretary of State, speaking as National Security Adviser, about a run of recent technology outages, including a Microsoft incident, an FAA disruption and a problem affecting banks. Both said they had seen no sign of a cyberattack or of a link between the incidents, and the release attributed the disruptions to companies patching vulnerabilities and upgrading systems.

These are the officials' own assessments, not a published investigation.

# CDC report finds US stroke death rates fell by about a third from 2000 to 2024, rose again in 2018–2021, and have been rising among adults aged 35–44 since 2013

*CDC, Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report, 2026-11-19. Original: <https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/75/wr/mm7545a1.htm>*

CDC researchers report in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report that the age-adjusted stroke death rate among US adults fell from 81.4 per 100,000 in 2000 to 51.9 in 2024, a drop of 36.3%. They say the rate fell until 2009, levelled off until 2018, rose by about 4% a year from 2018 to 2021, and fell again from 2021 to 2024, leaving 2024 above the 2018 and 2019 levels.

The authors report rising rates since 2013 among adults aged 35–44, and recent rises among women, people aged 85 and over, and in the Midwest and South. They suggest disruption to care during the pandemic and rising hypertension, obesity and smoking among younger adults as possible factors, and say the study cannot identify what drove the changes.

# DHS release: White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud Initiative Results in DHS and GSA Identifying Potentially $53 Billion in Federal Contracts that are Noncompliant with E-Verify

*U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 2026-11-19. Original: <https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/11/19/white-house-task-force-eliminate-fraud-initiative-results-dhs-and-gsa-identifying>*

DHS and the General Services Administration said that, working with the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, they had identified 1,579 federal contractors holding more than $53 billion in contracts as potentially not complying with the federal requirement to use E-Verify, the online system that checks whether new hires may legally work in the United States. The agencies said the firms have been sent notices and given 30 days to show proof of compliance, and that contractors found not to comply could lose their contracts or be suspended or debarred.

The agencies said they also wrote to senior procurement executives across government asking for closer compliance screening. "Potentially noncompliant" is the agencies' own assessment; no finding against any firm is reported.

# DHS release: SANCTUARY INSANITY: ICE Arrests Previously-Deported Pedophile After He was RELEASED by California Sanctuary Politicians

*U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 2026-11-19. Original: <https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/11/19/sanctuary-insanity-ice-arrests-previously-deported-pedophile-after-he-was-released>*

DHS said ICE lodged a detainer on 10 November 2026 asking Riverside County, California, not to release a Mexican national whose record, it said, includes convictions for annoying or molesting a child under 18, sexual battery and driving under the influence causing bodily injury. DHS said county officials released him instead, that ICE then arrested him and that he remains in ICE custody; it said he had a final removal order from 2009 and had been deported four times. The release also lists earlier California cases that DHS cites against the state's policies.

The characterisations are DHS's own; anyone facing a new charge is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# DHS release: WORST OF THE WORST: ICE Arrests Sexual Deviants, Violent Assailants, Drug Dealers, and Other Public Safety Threats

*U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 2026-11-19. Original: <https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/11/19/worst-worst-ice-arrests-sexual-deviants-violent-assailants-drug-dealers-and-other>*

# France's health authority publishes 60 practice recommendations on the substances and procedures for assisted dying

*VIDAL (APMnews), 2026-11-19. Original, in French: <https://www.vidal.fr/actualites/38615-substances-letales-preparation-gestion-des-complications-ce-que-recommande-la-has-pour-l-aide-a-mourir.html>. Title translated from the French.*

VIDAL, republishing APMnews, reports that France's Haute Autorité de santé published a good-practice recommendation on 19 November setting out the lethal substances and conditions of administration for assisted dying under the law of 18 August 2026, in 60 recommendations covering the choice of oral and intravenous products, preparation by hospital pharmacies and the handling of complications.

According to the report, the authority calls for every professional involved to be trained both technically and in supporting patients and families, and for psychological support for staff. The recommendations are not binding, and the authority's president said an implementing decree is still being prepared. (Summary translated from the French.)

# Russia's interior ministry is to charge banks and telecom operators for each lookup in its databases on individuals

*Meduza, 2026-11-19. Original, in Russian: <https://meduza.io/news/2026/11/19/mvd-budet-brat-s-bankov-i-operatorov-svyazi-po-50-rubley-za-kazhdyy-zapros-k-bazam-dannyh-za-god-eto-dast-byudzhetu-esche-okolo-120-milliardov-rubley>. Title translated from the Russian.*

Meduza, citing Forbes Russia, reports that Russia's first deputy prime minister told a meeting with ministries, the central bank and banks that the interior ministry will charge 50 roubles for each information-exchange session with its databases on individuals, which banks and telecom operators use for identity checks.

According to the report, a law of November 2025 allows the fee, a draft government decree published in March estimates about 119.6 billion roubles a year in revenue, and the central bank and the financial-monitoring agency objected in April; bankers warned it could lead to less thorough client checks. (Summary translated from the Russian.)

# Serbian security agency wiretapped a news magazine's newsroom for four months under court orders citing espionage, then told the court it had found no espionage

*The Insider, 2026-11-19. Original, in Russian: <https://theins.ru/news/299792>. Title translated from the Russian.*

The Insider reports that documents obtained by the Serbian weekly Radar show that the director of the country's security agency asked for secret surveillance of the magazine's editor-in-chief and two journalists on suspicion of espionage, and that the Belgrade Higher Court approved it on 12 June 2026, including the recording of conversations inside the newsroom.

According to the report, the measures were extended in July and September, and on 22 October the agency asked the court to end them, writing that the material gathered did not indicate the journalists were involved in espionage. The agency has called the magazine's allegations false, and no court has ruled on whether the surveillance was lawful. (Summary translated from the Russian.)

# Taiwan's justice ministry adds a transnational-repression offence to its draft Anti-Infiltration Act amendment and sends it to the cabinet

*Liberty Times, 2026-11-19. Original, in Chinese: <https://news.ltn.com.tw/news/politics/paper/1778989>. Title translated from the Chinese.*

Liberty Times reports that Taiwan's justice minister told the Legislative Yuan on 18 November that a new offence of transnational repression has been added to the draft amendment of the Anti-Infiltration Act, which also raises penalties for people in Taiwan who help foreign hostile forces.

According to the report, the draft defines the offence as a foreign hostile force attacking people, groups or public servants across borders in order to interfere with Taiwan's democratic order and make people censor themselves, punishable by three to ten years in prison. The minister said the draft has been sent to the Executive Yuan for review; it has not yet reached the legislature. (Summary translated from the Chinese.)

# Texas county pulls a proposed no-bid contract for a facial-recognition tool built on scraped online images from its commissioners' agenda

*Houston Public Media, 2026-11-19. Original: <https://www.houstonpublicmedia.org/articles/news/harris-county/2026/11/19/567529/harris-county-officials-pull-no-bid-contract-for-controversial-facial-recognition-technology/>*

Houston Public Media reports that Harris County, Texas, removed from its commissioners court agenda a proposed no-bid contract worth more than $280,000, running to November 2027, that would have let county law enforcement search a vendor's database of more than 70 billion images collected from the internet to identify victims or persons of interest.

According to the report, a sheriff's office spokesperson said the item was postponed because it was not ready and did not say whether it would return. The outlet adds that the county is separately reviewing who can access data from its licence-plate-reader cameras.

# UK surveillance tribunal rules the government must confirm it served a secret encryption-access notice on a technology company

*The Record (Recorded Future News), 2026-11-19. Original: <https://therecord.media/apple-uk-encryption-notice>*

The Record reports that a three-judge panel of the Investigatory Powers Tribunal rejected the UK government's "neither confirm nor deny" stance and found that confirming the existence of a technical capability notice served on a technology company would not harm national security. According to the report, the notice requires the company to keep the ability to access users' cloud-stored content, and the company withdrew its end-to-end encrypted cloud option for UK users in February.

The Record says the ruling does not decide whether the notice is lawful, and that a full hearing is expected in the first half of 2027.

# US immigration agency pays a major telecom carrier for access to its raw call data and analysts, an internal document shows

*404 Media, 2026-11-19. Original: <https://www.404media.co/ice-is-paying-at-t-to-dig-through-a-mountain-of-call-records-hemisphere-data-analytical-services/>*

404 Media reports that an internal Immigration and Customs Enforcement document describes paying a major U.S. telecom carrier millions of dollars for a "Data Analytical Services" product that, in the document's words, gives the agency access to the carrier's raw data and experienced analysts. The outlet says the product appears related to Hemisphere, an earlier call-records programme that was shut down.

According to the report, the carrier says it provides data only under valid legal process; experts quoted by the outlet note that the process is an administrative subpoena, which needs no judge's approval, and civil-liberties advocates describe the arrangement as mass surveillance. No court or regulator has ruled on it.

# White House release: U.S.-Russia-China Heads of State Declaration toward Peace

*The White House, 2026-11-19. Original: <https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefings-statements/2026/11/u-s-russia-china-heads-of-state-declaration-toward-peace/>*

The White House published a joint declaration by the leaders of the United States, Russia and China after a trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China. According to the text, the three committed to maintaining strategic stability, to reforming the United Nations, to increasing the production and supply of refined petroleum products, and to limiting the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court and similar bodies over state officials.

The declaration restates that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought, and says the three countries will hold a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the spread of nuclear weapons.

# Brain-implant trial participants call for ownership of their neural data, post-trial care and fairer consent

*STAT, 2026-11-20. Original: <https://www.statnews.com/2026/11/20/ian-burkhart-how-brain-implant-trials-can-serve-patients-better/>*

STAT reports that a coalition of early brain-computer-interface trial participants has published 13 recommendations for companies, researchers and regulators on post-trial care, informed consent and the privacy of neural data. A co-founder of the coalition told STAT his own implant was removed when funding for an earlier study ran out, called current consent forms one-sided in favour of research teams, and proposed that participants own their neural data, with the research team getting first access.

A university ethicist quoted by STAT said there is no good solution yet for protecting participants, and mentioned ideas such as mandatory insurance and escrow funds.

# Denmark expels Russia's defence attaché after a failed assassination attempt its security service links to a banned gang

*DR, 2026-11-20. Original, in Danish: <https://www.dr.dk/nyheder/indland/russisk-diplomat-bliver-udvist-af-danmark-efter-sag-om-attentatforsoeg>. Title translated from the Danish.*

DR, the Danish public broadcaster, reports that Denmark's foreign minister announced on 20 November that Russia's defence attaché is being expelled and must leave within seven days, and that the Russian ambassador was called to the foreign ministry, after what the government called a failed Russian assassination attempt in September against a Ukrainian-American rapper. According to the report, the Danish security service PET said there are indications that leading members of a banned gang helped plan the attempt.

DR reports that the government will also stop issuing non-essential visas to Russian citizens and plans bills raising penalties for crimes committed on behalf of a foreign state. The report does not give a Russian response; the people suspected in the case have not been convicted and are presumed innocent. (Summary translated from the Danish.)

# DHS release: ICE HSI, Nebraska State Patrol Secure 50-Year Sentence for Child Exploitation Offender

*U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 2026-11-20. Original: <https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/11/20/ice-hsi-nebraska-state-patrol-secure-50-year-sentence-child-exploitation-offender>*

DHS said a 42-year-old Omaha man was sentenced in federal court in Omaha on 4 November 2026 to 50 years in prison, followed by 15 years of supervised release, after his conviction for producing and possessing child sexual abuse material, in an investigation led by the Nebraska State Patrol with help from ICE's Homeland Security Investigations (HSI). DHS said the case was brought under the Justice Department's Project Safe Childhood, and it listed recent HSI child-exploitation sentences in Florida, Texas, New Jersey, Kentucky and Pennsylvania. DHS said HSI opened more than 7,200 child sexual exploitation and abuse investigations in fiscal year 2026, made 4,989 arrests and identified or rescued more than 1,900 victims.

The figures are the department's own count. The release reports sentences after conviction, not a new charge.

DHS said ICE placed a detainer on 11 November 2026 on an Ecuadorian national held at the Hennepin County Jail in Minneapolis, Minnesota, after his arrest for criminal sexual conduct, and that the jail released him without notifying ICE; DHS said he remains at large. # Iran's Revolutionary Guards spokesman names a London-based Persian-language broadcaster among the Guards' military targets, the broadcaster reports

*Iran International, 2026-11-20. Original: <https://www.iranintl.com/en/202611201108>*

Iran International, a London-based Persian-language broadcaster, reports that the spokesman of Iran's Revolutionary Guards said at the University of Tehran on 19 November that the broadcaster is among the Guards' military targets, and links the remark to an August warning by the armed forces against it and other Persian-language media abroad.

The broadcaster also cites a UK case in which two men were convicted on 12 November of assisting a foreign intelligence service by surveilling its journalists, with sentencing set for 17 December, and three people awaiting trial over an April arson attack near its studios, who are presumed innocent. The account of the 19 November remark is the broadcaster's own and has not been independently confirmed.

# Japan's government panel is shown a proposal to penalise posing under a false identity to interfere for a foreign government, with a foreign-agent registration system

*Daily Sports, 2026-11-20. Original, in Japanese: <https://www.daily.co.jp/society/politics/2026/11/20/0021056004.shtml>. Title translated from the Japanese.*

Daily Sports reports that at its third meeting on 20 November, the government's expert panel on strengthening intelligence capabilities was shown a proposal to penalise people who, for a foreign government, falsely claim a status or use threats to interfere in Japan's politics or administration. According to the report, foreign-agent registration would be required when an activity is directed by a foreign government, seeks to influence elections or policy, and involves contact with officials, publicity or financial benefit.

The paper says panel members supported regular reporting to the Diet, and that a draft outline is due in December, with a bill possible in the next ordinary Diet session. (Summary translated from the Japanese.)

# London police begin a six-month pilot letting 100 officers photograph people on phones and match them against about a million custody images

*Evening Standard (Press Association), 2026-11-20. Original: <https://www.standard.co.uk/news/crime/phone-facial-recognition-technology-metropolitan-police-b1305602.html>*

The Evening Standard, carrying Press Association reporting, says the Metropolitan Police began a six-month pilot on 17 November in which 100 officers can use a phone app to compare a person's face against about one million custody images. According to the report, the force said officers must tell people before taking a photograph but do not need their permission, will not use force if someone covers their face, and will not photograph under-18s.

A police commander told the Press Association that 15 photographs were uploaded in the first 24 hours and that officers would not photograph people who are not suspected of an offence. The report says a civil-liberties group and a stop-and-search monitoring group raised concerns about intrusion and racial bias.

# New York City's police inspector general finds facial-recognition policy breaches and disclosure gaps across about 26,000 searches

*Biometric Update, 2026-11-20. Original: <https://www.biometricupdate.com/202611/nypd-facial-recognition-oversight-gaps-exposed-after-26000-searches>*

Biometric Update reports that the Inspector General for the New York Police Department, in the city's Department of Investigation, found the department ran about 26,000 facial-recognition analyses in 2025 and largely complies with the city's surveillance-technology disclosure law, but breached some of its own policies. According to the report, these included 98 searches outside police image repositories that did not follow the policy then in force, seven searches of juvenile arrest photos, no supervisory review for about a third of one division's searches, and image editing beyond policy limits; the inspector general also found that naming vendors but not products was contrary to the disclosure law.

The report makes 17 recommendations. Biometric Update says the department told the inspector general it has centralised searches and does not use real-time facial recognition.

# Russia's justice ministry adds 13 people who left the country to a register that cuts them off from property registration, online state services and Russian banking apps

*Mediazona, 2026-11-20. Original, in Russian: <https://zona.media/news/2026/11/20/ogranicheniya>. Title translated from the Russian.*

Mediazona, an independent Russian outlet, reports that the justice ministry added 13 people, including journalists, actors, politicians and a political scientist, to its register of "temporary restrictive measures", which it says began on 23 October and now lists 35 people. According to the outlet, the register covers people who have left Russia and have criminal convictions or unpaid administrative penalties.

Mediazona says those listed lose the right to register real estate, some consular services, electronic signatures, access to online government services and the use of Russian banks' apps and websites. (Summary translated from the Russian.)

# Two US House committees report on US companies' use of China-developed open-weight AI models and recommend barring them from federal contracts

*The Record (Recorded Future News), 2026-11-20. Original: <https://therecord.media/chinese-open-weight-AI-use-by-US-companies-house-investigation>*

The Record reports that the House Homeland Security Committee and the House Select Committee on China released a joint investigative report warning that US companies adopting China-developed open-weight AI models could face costly removal later. According to the outlet, the report says federal investigators found Chinese developers used proxy networks and fraudulent accounts to collect outputs from US frontier models.

The report recommends 12 steps, including an AI bill of materials and a ban on such models in federal contracts and sensitive critical infrastructure, The Record says. These are the committees' findings; no court or agency has ruled on them.

# US court sentences a man to more than 19 years for a murder-for-hire plot against a US activist that prosecutors say an Indian government employee directed

*U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs, 2026-11-20. Original: <https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/indian-national-sentenced-over-19-years-prison-plotting-assassinate-us-citizen-new-york-city>*

The Justice Department said an Indian national was sentenced in federal court in Manhattan to 235 months in prison after pleading guilty in February 2026 to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire and money-laundering conspiracy, over a plot to kill a U.S.-citizen attorney and activist in New York City. The department said the plot was directed by an employee of India's Cabinet Secretariat, which houses the country's foreign intelligence service, who agreed to pay $100,000, about $15,000 of it in advance in June 2023.

According to the department, the man hired for the killing was in fact an undercover officer working with a Drug Enforcement Administration source. The official alleged to have directed the plot has been charged but not arrested, and is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# White House release: PROTECTING THE EXECUTIVE’S PRIVILEGES AND ENHANCING EFFICIENCIES IN FEDERAL CONTRACTING

*The White House, 2026-11-20. Original: <https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2026/11/protecting-the-executives-privileges-and-enhancing-efficiencies-in-federal-contracting/>*

The White House published an executive order requiring federal contractors and subcontractors to notify the White House and the contracting agency promptly of any congressional request about their work for the executive branch, and to follow instructions to withhold communications the executive deems privileged. According to the text, agencies must consider termination, suspension or debarment for contractors that do not comply.

The order states that it creates no rights enforceable by anyone against the United States.

# White House release: NATIONAL ADOPTION MONTH, 2026

*The White House, 2026-11-20. Original: <https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2026/11/national-adoption-month-2026/>*

The White House published a presidential proclamation marking November 2026 as National Adoption Month. The proclamation honours adoptive families and cites expanded adoption and child tax credits and the administration's "Fostering the Future" initiatives.

# An exiled Belarusian woman says she was lured, under a real exile outlet's name, into a filmed interview in Vilnius that then aired on Belarusian state television

*Novaya Gazeta Europe, 2026-11-21. Original, in Russian: <https://novayagazeta.eu/articles/2026/11/21/sofiu-sapegu-obmanom-priglasili-na-interviu-ot-imeni-novoi-evropy-news>. Title translated from the Russian.*

Novaya Gazeta Europe, an exile outlet, reports that someone posing as one of its former correspondents commissioned a video series with a Belarusian woman living in exile, which a freelance crew unaware of the client filmed in Vilnius on 15 November. The outlet says recordings from the shoot appeared in a programme on a Belarusian state television channel on 19 November, whose presenter called the operation a "small spy game".

According to the report, the woman says her words were distorted and denies the presenter's claim that she was paid for information about the opposition. Novaya Gazeta Europe says it had no part in the project. (Summary translated from the Russian.)

# Brazilian law researchers call for neurorights to be a separate constitutional right, as a Senate amendment on mental integrity has waited for a rapporteur since 2023

*O POVO, 2026-11-21. Original, in Portuguese: <https://www.opovo.com.br/noticias/brasil/2026/11/21/protecao-da-mente-diante-da-ia-e-tema-de-proposta-no-senado.html>. Title translated from the Portuguese.*

O POVO reports that two law researchers at the Pontifical Catholic University of Paraná argue in the journal Direito e Práxis that neurorights should be an autonomous category of fundamental rights, because existing rights protect ideas only once they are expressed, and warn that neural data could become a commodity that threatens privacy, identity and autonomy.

The paper says the constitutional amendment PEC 29/2023, on mental integrity and algorithmic transparency, has been waiting for a rapporteur in the Senate's Constitution and Justice Committee since June 2023. (Summary translated from the Portuguese.)

# China's state telecoms research academy hosts a national brain-computer interface conference, announces 15 "landmark achievements" and begins building a BCI data platform

*Science and Technology Daily (state media), 2026-11-21. Original, in Chinese: <https://www.stdaily.com/web/gdxw/2026-11/21/content_617106.html>. Title translated from the Chinese.*

Science and Technology Daily, a Chinese state newspaper, reports that the 2026 Brain-Computer Interface Conference, hosted by the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology, ran from 19 to 22 November in Beijing's Changping district. According to the paper, 15 "landmark" BCI achievements were announced at the main forum on 21 November, including an implanted system developed in Beijing.

The paper says construction began on two public-service platforms, one for evaluating BCI professionals and one for "high-quality" BCI data. These are the state newspaper's own descriptions. (Summary translated from the Chinese.)

# Cyprus expels two Russian diplomats its intelligence service suspected of seeking classified security data and technology barred by EU sanctions

*ProtoThema (English edition), 2026-11-21. Original: <https://en.protothema.gr/2026/11/21/cyprus-expels-two-russian-diplomats-over-espionage-targeting-state-secrets-and-european-technology/>*

ProtoThema, citing the Cypriot broadcaster ANT1, reports that two Russian diplomats were made to leave Cyprus at the start of the week after the Cyprus Intelligence Service exposed them. According to the report, they were believed to be intelligence officers under diplomatic cover who sought classified information on the security of Cyprus and the EU, and access to technology whose transfer to Russia is banned under EU sanctions, through contacts with Cypriot citizens who had access to confidential information.

The report says an unnamed Cypriot security official did not deny it. There has been no official government statement, no names and no criminal proceedings, and no Russian response is reported.

# Dutch data protection authority tests six AI camera glasses, finds weak recording warnings and security flaws, and advises consumers not to buy them

*Biometric Update, 2026-11-21. Original: <https://www.biometricupdate.com/202611/dutch-tests-find-smart-glasses-privacy-safeguards-fail-in-practice>*

Biometric Update reports that the Dutch Data Protection Authority tested six pairs of AI camera glasses and found that on almost all of them the recording light was hard to see or easy to cover, and that most kept recording when it was covered. According to the report, the authority also found security weaknesses that could let someone nearby connect without permission, reach recordings or operate the camera, and that users were not clearly told where their images and audio were processed, often on servers outside the EU.

The authority advised consumers against buying the devices and did not name the manufacturers, the report says.

# European human rights court asks Serbia to answer by 15 January on the alleged use of a sound cannon at the March 2025 Belgrade protest

*Vreme, 2026-11-21. Original, in Serbian: <https://vreme.com/vesti/srbija-evropski-sud-za-ljudska-prava-zvucni-top-vladica-ilic/>. Title translated from the Serbian.*

Vreme reports that the European Court of Human Rights has asked Serbia to set out its position by 15 January in the case over the alleged use of a "sound cannon" at the 15 March 2025 protest in Belgrade. The weekly says the request was announced by a lawyer at the Belgrade Centre for Human Rights in an interview with the public broadcaster RTS, and N1 reports a second lawyer as saying the court has treated the application as a priority.

According to the lawyer, more than 150 people gave statements to prosecutors that they were injured by a device used during the protest, and prosecutors closed the domestic case with an official note without telling the complainants. Serbian authorities have denied that any such device was used; the court has not ruled on the application. (Summary translated from the Serbian.)

# European security sources link a phishing campaign against investigative journalists and a French legislator to a hacking group tied to Russia's security service

*Meduza, 2026-11-21. Original, in Russian: <https://meduza.io/feature/2026/11/21/hakery-fsb-nachali-novye-fishingovye-ataki-na-zhurnalistov-sredi-tseley-okazalis-hristo-grozev-i-odin-iz-avtorov-panamskogo-arhiva>. Title translated from the Russian.*

Meduza, an independent Russian outlet based abroad, reports that since at least mid-October investigative journalists in several European countries, a co-author of a major offshore-leaks investigation and a member of France's National Assembly have received Signal messages, sometimes sent from hacked contacts' accounts, with links to fake Telegram login pages. Citing a 20 November Le Monde report that draws on European security sources, Meduza says the campaign is attributed to a hacking group that US authorities link to a unit of the FSB's border service.

According to the report, a threat analyst at a large technology company said the targets are people who work on Russia in journalism, politics and defence. The attribution is the sources' own; the FSB is not quoted. (Summary translated from the Russian.)

# Exiled Belarusian analyst says security officers called him from his detained wife's phone to try to recruit him, and pressed him over her future

*Zerkalo, 2026-11-21. Original, in Russian: <https://news.zerkalo.io/economics/140972.html>. Title translated from the Russian.*

Zerkalo, an independent Belarusian outlet in exile, reports that a Belarusian political analyst living abroad has said that about two hours after his wife was detained in June 2025, officers of Belarus's KGB called him from her phone. According to his account, the call lasted almost three hours and combined an attempt to recruit him, seeking information on Belarusians fighting for Ukraine and his contacts in Ukrainian state bodies, with pressure over his wife's future and her seriously ill mother.

He says he recorded the conversation and gave it to Ukraine's security service, the outlet reports. Zerkalo reports that his wife was sentenced on 20 November 2026 to 10 years, mainly for treason. This is his account; no response from the KGB is reported. (Summary translated from the Russian.)

# FBI release: Senior Leader of the Sinaloa Cartel and One of FBI’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives Arrested in Mexico Following a Homeland Security Task Force Investigation

*Federal Bureau of Investigation, 2026-11-21. Original: <https://www.fbi.gov/news/press-releases/senior-leader-of-the-sinaloa-cartel-and-one-of-fbis-ten-most-wanted-fugitives-arrested-in-mexico-following-a-homeland-security-task-force-investigation>*

The FBI said a man it describes as an alleged leader of the Sinaloa Cartel, and one of the fugitives on its Ten Most Wanted list, has been captured by the Mexican military following a Homeland Security Task Force investigation.

# Former Massachusetts police officer indicted over alleged unauthorised searches of police records and a shared licence-plate camera network

*NBC Boston, 2026-11-21. Original: <https://www.nbcboston.com/news/local/swampscott-police-officer-camera-charges/4052840/>*

NBC Boston reports that a grand jury indicted a former Swampscott, Massachusetts, police officer on five counts of requesting or obtaining criminal offender record information under false pretences and six counts of unauthorised access to a computer system, in a case announced by the Essex County District Attorney's Office. According to the report, the neighbouring city's police flagged unusual access to a licence-plate camera network they had shared with Swampscott detectives, and the officer was placed on leave on 18 August and later resigned.

The report says the town's internal investigation found harassment, unauthorised personal use of the licence-plate reader system and untruthfulness, and that the district attorney said using such platforms for anything other than legitimate law enforcement purposes will not be tolerated. These are charges, not findings of guilt; the officer is presumed innocent, and no arraignment date or response from him is reported.

# Iran's judiciary warns citizens abroad that critical posts online could lead to frozen assets and arrest on return, an exile broadcaster reports

*Iran International, 2026-11-21. Original: <https://www.iranintl.com/en/liveblog/202611214578#202611210347>*

Iran International, a London-based Persian-language broadcaster, reports that the spokesman for Iran's judiciary said people abroad who post criticism under their real names are identified from law-enforcement reports and could have their assets in Iran frozen and be arrested if they return. According to the broadcaster, citing an Iranian outlet, the spokesman said the authorities could also seek arrests through Interpol, impose travel restrictions and suspend some government services case by case.

The account of the remarks is the broadcaster's own, relayed from Iranian media, and has not been independently confirmed.

# Pro-Kremlin hackers publish the names of about 105 post-Soviet activists who attended an international rights association's conference, and the association confirms the leak

*Novaya Gazeta Europe, 2026-11-21. Original, in Russian: <https://novayagazeta.eu/articles/2026/11/21/prokremlevskie-khakery-opublikovali-dannye-rossiian-sotrudnichaiushchikh-s-mezhdunarodnoi-lgbt-assotsiatsiei-ilga-news>. Title translated from the Russian.*

Novaya Gazeta Europe, citing the outlet SOTA, reports that a pro-Kremlin hacking group published the names of about 105 people from Russia and other post-Soviet states who attended an October 2025 conference of an international LGBT rights association, together with grant documents. The outlet says the association's European branch confirmed that sensitive data had been exposed, apologised and is contacting the people most at risk.

According to the report, people working with organisations Russia has declared "undesirable" can face prosecution there. The report makes no state attribution for the leak. (Summary translated from the Russian.)

# A second seizure of a school photo directory in Brittany draws protest over police and gendarmes collecting thousands of students' photos in protest-related inquiries

*France 3 Régions (France Télévisions), 2026-11-21. Original, in French: <https://france3-regions.franceinfo.fr/bretagne/finistere/brest/liberez-les-trombis-manifestation-apres-la-saisie-d-un-nouveau-trombinoscope-d-un-lycee-breton-3453459.html>. Title translated from the French.*

France 3 reports that in early November police officers obtained, under a judicial requisition, the names and photos of nearly 4,500 students at three schools in Brest, which the Brest prosecutor linked to an inquiry into clashes outside the city's police station during a 17 October demonstration. Gendarmes then asked for the photo directory of a Breton-language high school in Carhaix, which the prosecutor said concerns an attempt to block a main road.

According to the report, the prosecutor described the requests as gathering evidence to establish the truth, while about 200 people rallied outside the Brest courthouse on 20 November and the local Human Rights League and three members of parliament criticised the method. The report does not say how the photos are used, and states no use of facial recognition. (Summary translated from the French.)

# Taiwan prosecutors indict a local-election candidate and four others under the Anti-Infiltration Act over alleged Chinese funding and fake-account support

*Taipei Times, 2026-11-21. Original: <https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/taiwan/archives/2026/11/21/2003868135>*

The Taipei Times reports that the New Taipei District Prosecutors' Office indicted a local-election candidate and four others under the Anti-Infiltration Act, alleging she received NT$300,000 a month, free online campaign support and US$10,000 in cash in Xiamen from two Chinese officials, and that about 20,000 fake accounts were used to boost her posts. According to the report, prosecutors say the officials expected access to political intelligence and stopped the funding after she lost a primary, and they are seeking a six-year sentence.

The charges also include data-protection and breach-of-trust offences. These are accusations; every defendant is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# Taiwan prosecutors search homes and release a local-election candidate and two others on bail under the Anti-Infiltration Act over a hosted trip to China

*Liberty Times, 2026-11-21. Original, in Chinese: <https://news.ltn.com.tw/news/politics/breakingnews/5648772>. Title translated from the Chinese.*

The Liberty Times reports that the Tainan District Prosecutors Office searched four locations on 20 November and questioned 12 defendants and witnesses, acting on information from the Investigation Bureau. According to the report, prosecutors suspect that a small party's chairman and his brother were hosted by local Chinese Taiwan Affairs officials on a trip to China in November 2025, took instructions there, and then campaigned for a city-council candidate from February to September 2026.

The three were released on bail of NT$300,000, NT$200,000 and NT$50,000, and the two brothers were barred from leaving Taiwan, the paper says. No one has been charged; China Times reports that the candidate denies receiving money or instructions, and all are presumed innocent. (Summary translated from the Chinese.)

# UN weapons convention ends without a mandate to negotiate a binding ban on lethal autonomous weapons, agreeing instead to draft an instrument within two years

*blue News (AFP), 2026-11-21. Original: <https://www.bluewin.ch/en/news/international/the-u.s.-and-russia-block-rules-for-autonomous-killer-robots-li.3682236>*

AFP, carried by blue News, reports that the 128 states parties to the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons agreed in Geneva early on Saturday to draft an "international instrument on lethal autonomous weapons systems" within two years, but not a mandate to negotiate a legally binding ban, although nearly 100 states had backed one. According to the report, the United States blocked the agenda from the start and Russia blocked a concrete negotiating mandate, while several other states had reservations.

The Swiss president of the conference said the next phase would clarify which weapons could be banned under international humanitarian law and which could only be regulated, the report says. A coalition of campaign groups called the result a watered-down mandate.

# Artist living in Germany says an Iranian judiciary official phoned to warn that people attending her murdered parents' memorial would be punished if she spoke critically

*Iran International, 2026-11-22. Original: <https://www.iranintl.com/en/202611222534>*

Iran International reports that an artist and rights activist living in Germany said on 21 November that an Iranian judiciary official had called her, accused her of speaking against the system at last year's memorial for her parents, who were killed in the 1998 "chain murders", and warned that attendees would be punished and she could be prosecuted if her remarks were found problematic.

The outlet recalls that Iran's Intelligence Ministry acknowledged in 1999 that its agents carried out those killings, saying they acted on their own. This is her account; the official is not named and no response from the judiciary is reported.

# FAA issues a short ground stop into Atlanta after an airline's aircraft-weight system fails, delaying about two-thirds of its flights

*PBS NewsHour (Associated Press), 2026-11-22. Original: <https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/automation-system-problem-at-delta-causes-flight-delays-as-americans-travel-for-thanksgiving>*

The Associated Press reports that on Sunday, 22 November, a problem with the system Delta Air Lines uses to calculate aircraft weight forced the airline onto manual workarounds, and the FAA issued an hour-long ground stop for some flights into Atlanta. According to AP, the FAA said the delays were not related to its own air traffic systems.

Citing FlightAware, AP reports that about 67% of the airline's flights, roughly 1,000, were delayed by mid-afternoon, and that the airline attributed about 70% of the disruption to the automation problem and the rest to weather. The causes are the airline's and the FAA's own statements.

# Former Colombian intelligence director says his agency asked for the national voter roll over cyber risks and accepted the refusal, as a former agency software contractor is held in a separate hacking case

*Infobae, 2026-11-22. Original, in Spanish: <https://www.infobae.com/colombia/2026/11/22/exjefe-de-la-dni-revela-que-paso-con-el-hacker-oyola-y-explica-por-que-pidio-el-censo-electoral-a-la-registraduria/>. Title translated from the Spanish.*

Infobae reports that the former director of Colombia's National Intelligence Directorate confirmed that the agency asked the National Registry for the national voter roll on 9 April 2026, citing technological threats to election systems, and said the agency accepted the Registry's refusal. He called reports that the agency interfered in the 2026 presidential election false; the Registry has said the electoral system was not altered or breached, according to the report.

Citing El Tiempo, Infobae reports that a man hired by the agency as an intelligence officer and software developer was arrested by the Attorney General's Office under a warrant issued on 7 May 2026 in an investigation into a hack of a public university. No charges or court stage are stated in the report, and he is presumed innocent. The claims of an agency plan against election systems come from leaked documents reported in mid-November and have not been tested in court. (Summary translated from the Spanish.)

# Poland's data protection authority argues in court that people should be able to learn what police and security services collected about them once operations end

*Telepolis.pl, 2026-11-22. Original, in Polish: <https://www.telepolis.pl/wiadomosci/uodo-dane-osobowe-sluzby-informacje>. Title translated from the Polish.*

Telepolis reports that the President of Poland's Personal Data Protection Office filed a formal view under Article 99 of the GDPR in an appeal brought by a journalist who asked the police, the Internal Security Agency and the Central Anticorruption Bureau what data they had gathered on her between 2012 and 2016, and was refused by all three. According to the report, the court of first instance ruled against her.

The authority argues, Telepolis says, that the secrecy rule in the Police Act protects only ongoing proceedings, and that once operations end there is no basis to refuse disclosure automatically. The outlet notes that the filing is an opinion, not a ruling, and recalls a 2024 European Court of Human Rights judgment criticising Poland for having no mechanism to notify people that they were watched. (Summary translated from the Polish.)

# US governors' AI council issues policy principles asking for federal handling of national risks while leaving states room to govern AI use

*National Governors Association, 2026-11-22. Original: <https://www.nga.org/news/press-releases/governors-call-for-ai-action/>*

The National Governors Association says its bipartisan council on artificial intelligence issued policy recommendations calling for AI rules that protect public safety, civil rights and privacy, with national and international risks handled federally while states keep flexibility to govern AI use within their own responsibilities.

The association recommends risk-based safeguards with technically informed definitions and regular review, and fewer duplicative or conflicting federal and state requirements. Its release takes no explicit position on federal pre-emption of state AI laws.

# Active-duty US Army sergeant pleads guilty to conspiring to gather and pass national defence information to buyers in China

*KPTV, on a release of the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Oregon, 2026-11-23. Original: <https://www.kptv.com/2026/11/24/washington-based-us-soldier-pleads-guilty-selling-classified-military-info-china/>*

KPTV reports that, according to federal prosecutors in Oregon, an active-duty sergeant at Joint Base Lewis-McChord pleaded guilty to conspiracy to gather and transmit national defence information, after being recruited by a former soldier who pleaded guilty in September. Prosecutors say the material, sold to buyers in China and people linked to China, included rocket-artillery system manuals, government hard drives and Army operations documents.

He faces up to 10 years in prison and agreed to forfeit $17,500; sentencing is set for March 2027. A third person charged in the case has not pleaded and is presumed innocent.

# Brain-implant developer partners with a chipmaker to run speech decoding on portable AI hardware, targeting delays under 10 milliseconds

*Paradromics (press release, via BioSpace), 2026-11-23. Original: <https://www.biospace.com/press-releases/paradromics-advances-high-performance-ai-computing-for-brain-computer-interfaces-with-nvidia>*

Paradromics says it will add NVIDIA's Holoscan platform and edge computing to its brain-computer interface system, starting with speech and communication, with stated targets of under 10 milliseconds for direct brain-to-speech and under 100 milliseconds for brain-to-text-to-speech. The company says its roadmap includes decoders that recalibrate in the background and systems for academic partners studying stroke, spinal cord injury and movement disorders.

The implant is investigational, in an FDA-approved early feasibility study, and the release reports no clinical results. The release says nothing about who can access users' neural recordings; the targets are the company's own.

# China's state-secrets agency account reports that a ministry official was sentenced to death for spying for a foreign intelligence service

*Sichuan Online, republishing the Baomiguan account (state media), 2026-11-23. Original, in Chinese: <https://focus.scol.com.cn/zgsz/202611/83361431.html>. Title translated from the Chinese.*

A post on the Baomiguan account of China's state-secrets agency, republished by the state-owned outlet Sichuan Online, says a ministry employee was recruited by a foreign intelligence officer while posted abroad, signed a "cooperation" document and was paid monthly, and after returning to China passed more than a hundred items of intelligence, including 35 classified documents, through an espionage website, receiving more than one million yuan.

The account says a court convicted him of espionage and sentenced him to death, with confiscation of all his property. It names no court, case number, date or country, so the case cannot be checked beyond the state account's own text; these are its claims, not established facts. (Summary translated from the Chinese.)

# DHS release: HSTF Investigation Leads to Venezuelan National and Alleged Tren de Aragua Gang Member Pleading Guilty to New England “Jackpotting” Scheme

*U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 2026-11-23. Original: <https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/11/23/hstf-investigation-leads-venezuelan-national-and-alleged-tren-de-aragua-gang-member>*

DHS said a Venezuelan national, whom it describes as an alleged Tren de Aragua member, pleaded guilty to two counts of conspiracy to commit bank theft and to damaging a protected computer, after a Homeland Security Task Force investigation into ATM "jackpotting", in which malware is used to make cash machines pay out. DHS linked him to three completed and three attempted thefts in Connecticut, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island and Maine between December 2025 and February 2026, and said he has a final order of removal and faces removal after any sentence.

The release does not name the court. The gang membership is DHS's allegation, not part of the plea it reports.

# DHS release: ICE Arrests Illegal Alien MS-13 Member in California Whose Criminal History Includes Cruelty Toward Child and DUI

*U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 2026-11-23. Original: <https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/11/23/ice-arrests-illegal-alien-ms-13-member-california-whose-criminal-history-includes>*

DHS said ICE arrested a man from El Salvador on 6 November 2026 during a targeted operation in San Mateo, California, and described him as an MS-13 member. DHS said his record includes a conviction for driving under the influence and an arrest for cruelty toward a child, and that El Salvador has an international warrant for him on charges including homicide, extortion, drug trafficking and robbery; DHS said he resisted and tried to flee on foot before he was taken into custody.

The descriptions are DHS's own; an arrest or a warrant is not a conviction, and anyone charged is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

*U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 2026-11-23. Original: <https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/11/23/ice-arrests-illegal-alien-venezuela-linked-threats-assassinate-president-trump>*

DHS said HSI arrested a Venezuelan national in Provo, Utah, on 16 October 2026, after the FBI passed on information drawn from his online activity. # DHS release: ICE Lodges Detainer Asking Virginia Sanctuary Politicians to Not Release Illegal Alien Arrested for Raping 12-Year-Old Girl

*U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 2026-11-23. Original: <https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/11/23/ice-lodges-detainer-asking-virginia-sanctuary-politicians-not-release-illegal-alien>*

DHS said police in Culpeper, Virginia, arrested a Guatemalan national on 18 November 2026 after a family reported concerns about their 12-year-old daughter, and that he faces nine felony charges, including four counts of rape of a child under 13. DHS said ICE lodged a detainer with the county jail the same day and asked Virginia's governor and state officials to honour it; DHS said he entered through Texas in January 2021 and was released into the country under the previous administration, and the release lists earlier Virginia cases that DHS cites against the state's policies.

The charges are allegations, not a conviction; he is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

# DHS release: WORST OF THE WORST: ICE Arrests Pedophiles, Sexual Predators, and Domestic Abusers Over the Weekend

*U.S. Department of Homeland Security, 2026-11-23. Original: <https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/11/23/worst-worst-ice-arrests-pedophiles-sexual-predators-and-domestic-abusers-over>*

DHS listed 15 people ICE arrested over the weekend of 21 to 22 November 2026: six from Mexico, two each from Cuba and India, and one each from Honduras, Thailand, Nigeria, El Salvador and Guatemala. DHS said their prior convictions include sex offences against children, rape, domestic violence, aggravated assault, drug trafficking, theft and driving under the influence, in twelve states from Florida to Washington.

The descriptions are DHS's own; anyone facing a new charge is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.
